exp.0:0:
This verse says that King David was already very old. His servants covered him with clothes and blankets, but even so he could not get warm. His body was weak because of his age.

Here the narrator of the book opens the story of the closing years of David's reign. According to the Bible, David had been a strong warrior and a powerful king. Now his frailty is shown. This prepares the account of who will be the next king, which is made clear in the chapters that follow.

For today: old age and weakness come to everyone, even to great people. We can honor and care for the elderly with patience and affection, and remember that our strength is not in our bodies but in God, who remains faithful at every stage of life.
exp.0:8:
Adonijah, son of David, offered a great sacrifice of sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle near the stone of Zoheleth, beside the spring of Rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and the men of Judah who served the king.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David is now very old, and Adonijah wants the throne for himself. This feast serves to show support and to present himself as king. Notice that he leaves out Nathan, Benaiah, and Solomon, who did not back him. The Bible does not say here that God approved of this plan.

For today: be careful about seeking success or power on your own terms, surrounding yourself only with those who agree with you. Better to seek God's will with humility and to listen also to those who advise you sincerely.
exp.0:9:
But Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother, he called not.

This verse says that Adonijah held a great feast and invited many people, but left out certain key figures: the prophet Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men (David's brave and trusted warriors), and his brother Solomon.

The account is told by the narrator of the book. David is now very old, and Adonijah, one of his sons, moves ahead to declare himself king without his father knowing. He excludes those he knew supported Solomon. That is why Nathan rushes to warn Bathsheba, Solomon's mother. The Bible does not say in detail what Adonijah was thinking, but the list of those left out suggests he wanted to avoid opposition.

For today: be wary of plans that seek out only people who will applaud and leave out those who would tell the truth. Seek honest counsel, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.0:17:
Bathsheba tells King David that Adonijah is already acting as king, and that David has not yet noticed.

The speaker is Bathsheba, David's wife and the mother of Solomon. David is now very old. She reminds him of his promise that Solomon would reign. Adonijah had proclaimed himself king with the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. Some scholars think Bathsheba speaks with urgency and strategy, but the text says nothing more about her intentions.

For today: when you see that something important is going wrong, speak with respect, clarity, and at the right time. Staying silent out of fear or letting the moment pass can bring serious consequences. And if you have made a promise, make every effort to keep it.
exp.0:18:
Here Bathsheba tells King David that Adonijah has held a great feast with many animals sacrificed. He invited all the king's sons, the priest Abiathar, and Joab, commander of the army, but he did not invite Solomon. Oxen, fat cattle, and sheep in abundance were prepared for the banquet.

Bathsheba speaks to the aging David, and she does so following the advice of the prophet Nathan. Adonijah had proclaimed himself king without David knowing it. Bathsheba reminds him of the promise that Solomon would reign. She presents the facts so that the king will act quickly. The texts do not say everything she felt, but her life and her son's life were at risk.

For today: when you see an injustice or a danger, do not keep silent or act in secret. Speak with truth and respect to the one who can help, and trust that God keeps his promises.
exp.0:19:
It says that all the people of Israel are looking to King David, waiting for him to state clearly who will be the next king. "The eyes of all Israel are upon you" means that everyone is waiting for his decision. "Throne" is the king's seat, a symbol of his authority.

Bathsheba, David's wife, is speaking to the king, who is now old. Adonijah, another son of David, has proclaimed himself king without permission, and she reminds him that David had promised the throne to their son Solomon (1:13). She wants David to act before it is too late. If he does not, she and Solomon are in danger.

For today: when we have authority or a clear responsibility, staying silent or putting things off can bring harm to others. Let us ask God for wisdom and courage to speak and act with truth and in time.
exp.0:22:
They told the king, "Nathan the prophet is here." Nathan went in and bowed facedown before the king, showing him honor and respect.

Bathsheba had just asked David to keep his promise that Solomon would be king. Adonijah, another son of the king, had declared himself king on his own. While she was speaking, Nathan arrived, perhaps to confirm what she was saying. The Bible does not explain whether they planned this together, but his arrival was very timely.

For today: when you see injustice or danger, do not stay silent. Speak with respect and humility, but with courage, and let God use your voice.
exp.0:24:
Here Nathan tells how Adonijah went down to a place of feasting, offered many sacrifices of oxen, fattened animals and sheep, and invited the king's sons, the captains of the army, and the priest Abiathar. They all eat and drink with him and shout, "Long live King Adonijah!"

The prophet Nathan speaks, and he does so before David, who is now very old. Adonijah, one of his sons, proclaims himself king without David having decided it. Nathan wants David to know what is happening and to act. Notice that Solomon and the other men loyal to the king were not invited.

For today: when you see something unjust advancing quietly, do not stay silent. Speak with respect and clarity to the one who has the authority to correct it, and do so with wisdom and courage.
exp.0:27:
This verse tells how King David, now old, asks for Bathsheba to be called. She comes into the king's presence and stands before him.

The prophet Nathan had just spoken with David. He warned him that Adonijah, another son of the king, had declared himself king without David's knowledge. Nathan had advised Bathsheba to go first to speak with the king. Now David has her summoned so that he can answer her. She was the mother of Solomon, and David had promised her that Solomon would reign. So David acts and confirms his promise.

For today: when there is confusion or injustice, it is good to speak the truth and to speak in time. And whoever makes a promise should keep it faithfully, as David did, not letting it be forgotten.
exp.0:29:
Here King David makes a solemn oath before Bathsheba. He says that he will carry out today what he had already promised in the name of the LORD: that his son Solomon would reign after him and sit on his throne. Swearing by the Lord God of Israel is the name of the covenant God, and swearing in his name made the promise very serious.

David is very old and weak. His son Adonijah has proclaimed himself king on his own, and the prophet Nathan and Bathsheba have alerted David. The Bible does not record the earlier oath here, but David affirms it. That is why he now acts to make sure Solomon becomes the successor.

For today: keep what you promise, even when time passes or pressure arises. A word given sincerely, and especially before God, deserves to be taken seriously and kept faithfully.
exp.0:31:
This verse shows King David giving an order: he calls for three important men, the priest Zadok, the prophet Nathan, and Benaiah, son of Jehoiada. They come into his presence right away. The word "Call" in the verse is the command he gives them to bring these men to him.

David is now very old. His son Adonijah has declared himself king without his father's permission. Nathan and Bathsheba remind David of his promise that Solomon would reign. Now David acts. The three men represent religious authority, the voice of God, and military strength, and that is why their support matters. The Bible does not say more about why he chose these three in particular.

For today: keeping what we have promised, even when time passes and it takes effort. David honored his word given before God. It is also wise to surround ourselves with wise and faithful people when we must make important decisions.
exp.0:32:
King David gives a clear order here. He asks his trusted men to take the king's servants, to set his son Solomon on the king's own mule, and to bring him down to Gihon.

David is now an old man, and his son Adonijah had proclaimed himself king on his own authority. Nathan and Bathsheba reminded David of his promise that Solomon would reign. Riding on the king's mule was a public sign that David backed Solomon. Gihon was a spring near Jerusalem, where the anointing would take place.

For today: when God has given a promise, it is good to act with clarity and courage, without letting others take a different path. In the same way, let us faithfully carry out what God has entrusted to us.
exp.0:34:
In this verse, King David gives clear orders. He says that the servants will escort Solomon, and that Solomon will come, sit on the throne and reign in David's place. David states that he himself has appointed him to be ruler, or leader, over all the people: Israel and Judah.

David speaks as an old and weakened man. His son Adonijah had declared himself king on his own, without David's approval. For this reason, Bathsheba and the prophet Nathan reminded David that Solomon would be his successor. David acts quickly so that the succession is public and orderly. Benaiah's response shows that they sought God's approval.

For today: before taking on a responsibility or making an important decision, let us seek God's direction and act with order and humility, without pushing forward out of our own ambition.
exp.0:36:
Benaiah wishes Solomon that God would be with him just as God was with King David. He also asks that God make Solomon's reign greater than his father's. The phrase about making the throne greater means that his rule would be more prosperous and reach further.

The one speaking is Benaiah, commander of the royal guard. David is now very old, and his son Adonijah had declared himself king on his own. David responds by naming Solomon as his successor, and Benaiah gives his agreement, showing that he supports the decision. His wish is a prayer, not only a compliment. What he asks is that God, and not human power, would sustain the new king.

We can pray with that same attitude for those who lead us, in the family, the church, or the country. Before we criticize, let us ask that God be with them and give them wisdom to serve well.
exp.0:38:
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent of meeting, the holy tent where God was worshiped, and anointed Solomon, that is, he set him apart as king by pouring oil over him. Then the trumpet sounded, and all the people cried out: "Long live King Solomon!"

King David was already very old. His son Adonijah had proclaimed himself king on his own, without his father's approval. So David ordered that Solomon be anointed at Gihon, with Zadok, the prophet Nathan, and Benaiah as witnesses. In this way it was made clear who would succeed to the throne according to the king's will and, as the account presents it, according to God's direction.

For today: trust that God knows how to guide his work, and do not run ahead out of your own ambition. Seek his direction first and wait for his timing.
exp.0:40:
It says that Adonijah and his guests heard the noise just as they were finishing their meal. When Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he asked why the city was in such an uproar.

Adonijah had declared himself king on his own authority and was holding a feast with Joab and other leaders. Meanwhile, King David, now old, had Solomon anointed as his successor. The narrator shows the contrast: a private feast, planned out of ambition, and a public celebration by the people for the king's decision. Joab asks the question without yet knowing what is happening.

Plans we pursue out of pride or on our own may look firm, but they fall apart when God works by another path. Today we can ask ourselves: am I seeking what God has arranged, or only what I want to achieve? Let us ask him for humility to trust his direction.
exp.0:42:
Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, answers Adonijah with clear news: King David has already made Solomon king. The phrase "Not at all" shows that Jonathan is firmly rejecting the hope Adonijah had expressed, and "Our lord King David" is a respectful way of referring to David.

Adonijah had proclaimed himself king and was holding a feast with his guests. Jonathan arrives with the news that brings that celebration to an end. He speaks as a witness: he explains that the noise in the city is caused by the crowning of Solomon, decided by David. Adonijah had hoped for good news, but he receives the very opposite.

For today: plans we make out of our own ambition can suddenly collapse. Instead of rushing ahead of what we want, let us seek God's will with humility and wait for his timing.
exp.0:43:
This verse tells us who went with Solomon when he was made king. King David sent the priest Zadok, the prophet Nathan, Benaiah, and the Cherethites and Pelethites (the king's personal guard). They had Solomon ride on the king's mule. That mule was an animal reserved for David, so riding it was a clear sign of authority.

Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, speaks. He arrives frightened at the feast of Adonijah, who had proclaimed himself king on his own. Jonathan explains why there is so much noise in the city: David has already chosen Solomon, and he did so with the support of religious and military leaders. With this, Adonijah's claim loses its force.

For today: God often works in an orderly way and through faithful witnesses. Before making important decisions, seek wise counsel, and do not rush to take what does not belong to you.
exp.0:44:
He says that the priest Zadok and the prophet Nathan anointed Solomon as king at Gihon. Then they went up from there full of joy, and the whole city was filled with noise and celebration. Jonathan explains to Adonijah that the uproar they were hearing was the celebration of Solomon's coronation. "Anoint" means pouring oil on someone to set them apart for an office.

Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, speaks. He arrives with news for Adonijah, who had proclaimed himself king on his own while David was still alive. While Adonijah was feasting with his guests, David had ordered Solomon to be crowned. Jonathan tells them that the noise they were hearing was not from their own gathering, but from another king who had been chosen.

For today: plans that arise from pride and self-ambition can look very firm, but they do not hold if God has decided otherwise. It is good to ask God for direction before seeking positions, and to accept with humility what He allows.
exp.0:47:
This verse says that King David praises God because he was allowed to see with his own eyes that another of his sons was already sitting on his throne. The word meaning blessed, which means praised or thankful, is explained in the verse as praise. The word for today stresses that this is already happening. David recognizes that God is the one who did it, not only the people.

David is already old and is in his bed. His son Adonijah had declared himself king on his own, but David, warned by Nathan and Bathsheba, had Solomon anointed. The servants tell him what happened, and David responds with gratitude. His praise also confirms that Solomon is the successor. That is why Adonijah's guests become frightened and scatter.

Today we can learn to thank God for what we see fulfilled, even at the end of life or after a long process. We can also rejoice when others continue what we began, without envy, recognizing that God is still at work.
exp.0:49:
This verse tells how Adonijah, David's son who had proclaimed himself king on his own authority, became afraid of Solomon. He got up, ran off, and took hold of the horns of the altar. The horns were the corners of the altar, shaped like horns. It was a place where people sought refuge and mercy.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had already made Solomon king, and Adonijah's guests fled in fright. Adonijah, left alone, feared that Solomon would have him put to death for his attempt to take the throne. Afterward, Solomon gives him a chance: if he lives uprightly, nothing will happen to him.

For today: when we recognize that we have done wrong, the best thing is to come humbly to the One who can forgive. God welcomes whoever approaches with sincerity, but He expects the heart to truly change.
exp.0:50:
It says that Solomon was told that Adonijah was afraid of him. Adonijah had taken hold of the horns of the altar and was asking that Solomon swear to him that he would not kill him with the sword. The horns are the corners of the altar, which were shaped like horns. The servant here is Adonijah himself, who puts himself below the king.

The ones speaking are the messengers who inform Solomon. Adonijah had tried to make himself king without it being David's will. When Solomon was proclaimed king, Adonijah's guests fled. He sought refuge at the altar, a place where mercy was expected to be found. Solomon responds by giving him a chance on the condition of his conduct.

For today: when we recognize that we have done wrong, the best thing is to come near with humility and ask for mercy, without excuses. And whoever receives a second chance should live in a way that shows real change.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that the time of King David's death was drawing near. It is the introduction to David's last words.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who presents David as an old man. Solomon will be the new king of Israel. Before dying, David wants to leave him advice for governing. What follows shows that what mattered most to David was that his son would obey God and the law of Moses.

For today: if you have children, students, or people who follow you, do not wait until the end to pass on what is most valuable. Speaking to them about your faith and your values in good time is an inheritance that lasts longer than money.
exp.1:3:
Here David says that God will confirm the promise he made to him: if his descendants live faithfully, walking before God in truth and with all their heart and all their soul, a man will never fail to sit on the throne of Israel.

David is about to die, and he gives instructions to his son Solomon, who will be the new king. He reminds him that God's promise about his dynasty depends on obedience. Many understand that this promise has a condition, and that Christians later see it fully fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: God values sincere obedience, not outward appearance. We can ask him to help us live with integrity in the small things of each day: at work, in the family, and in what we say.
exp.1:4:
Here David, now an old man, reminds his son Solomon of what Joab did. Joab treacherously killed two commanders of Israel's army, Abner and Amasa, in a time of peace, as if he were in battle. The phrase about the blood on the belt and on the shoes describes a man stained with that blood, as if nothing serious had happened.

In his last words, David speaks to Solomon, who will be the new king. He leaves him a charge for ruling: not to let so grave a crime go without judgment. Interpreters debate whether this was justice or David's personal revenge. The Bible presents the events, but does not explain all the motives.

For today: justice matters, but we should examine our hearts so that we do not mix it with resentment. Let us ask God for wisdom to correct wrong with truth and mercy.
exp.1:6:
He says that Solomon must treat the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite with kindness. Showing them kindness means he will show them favor and care. Letting them be of those that eat at your table means they will eat regularly in the palace, as honored guests. David recalls that Barzillai helped him when he fled from his son Absalom.

The one speaking is David, now old, giving his final instructions to his son Solomon. During Absalom's rebellion, Barzillai brought supplies to David at Mahanaim (this is told in 2 Samuel 17 and 19). Now David wants that loyalty not to be forgotten. It contrasts with Joab and Shimei, whom he mentions before and after.

For today: do not take for granted the kindness others showed you in your hard times. Think about who helped you when you needed it most, and look for a concrete way to thank them or bless their family.
exp.1:7:
This verse reminds Solomon that Shimei, a man of the tribe of Benjamin from a town called Bahurim, cursed David severely when he was fleeing to Mahanaim. Then Shimei came out to meet him at the Jordan River, and David swore to him by the Lord that he would not put him to death with the sword.

David, now an old man, is giving his final instructions to his son Solomon. Shimei had insulted the king when David was fleeing from Absalom (2 Samuel 16). Later, David spared his life (2 Samuel 19). Interpreters debate whether David was calling for justice or leaving a revenge pending. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when we make a promise, we should keep it with honesty. It is also wise to examine whether we seek justice or revenge, and to ask God for a heart that truly forgives.
exp.1:10:
This verse sums up how long David's reign lasted: forty years in total. The first seven he reigned in Hebron, a city in the south, and the remaining thirty-three in Jerusalem. The name "Jerusalem" appears here as it is spelled in the verse above. It is a round figure, and the text presents it as a final tally of his life as king.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, not a character. After relating David's last instructions to Solomon and his death, the account closes the chapter on his reign with this summary. In this way it prepares the transition to Solomon's throne, which begins right away.

For today: our life also has a beginning and an end, and God looks at the whole course, not just one moment. David had great successes and also serious failures. We can live each stage with humility, trusting in God's faithfulness and leaving a good mark on those who come after us.
exp.1:14:
Adonijah reminds Bathsheba that the kingdom belonged to him and that all Israel expected him to reign. But the kingdom passed to his brother Solomon, and Adonijah acknowledges that this came about by the will of the Lord. The phrase about the people's faces being set toward him means that they looked to him, expecting him to be king. The word about the kingdom being turned about means that it passed into other hands.

Speaking is Adonijah, the eldest surviving son of David, who had earlier tried to proclaim himself king (1 Kings 1). Now Solomon reigns. Adonijah approaches Bathsheba, the king's mother, with gentle words. His acknowledgment sounds humble, but what follows is a request concerning Abishag, and many understand that this request hid a renewed political ambition. That is interpretation, but the text invites us to read it with caution.

For today: accepting that God directs our lives, even when things do not turn out as we wanted, must be sincere. It is not enough to say it with our mouths; we should examine whether our words of submission match our true desires.
exp.1:16:
Adonijah asks Bathsheba to speak to King Solomon on his behalf. He says that Solomon will not refuse his mother anything. What he wants is to marry Abishag the Shunammite, the young woman.

Adonijah was the older brother of Solomon and had tried to become king before him. Abishag had cared for King David in his old age. Many understand that asking for her was a way of claiming the throne again, because in that time a king's women were connected with his authority. Adonijah does not say this openly, and Bathsheba seems not to notice the danger.

Today we can learn to examine the hidden motives behind what we ask for. Sometimes a request seems innocent but conceals ambition. Let us ask God to show us our hearts and to give us humility to accept what he has already decided.
exp.1:18:
Bath-sheba went to king Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. The king rose to meet her and bowed before her. Then he sat back down on his throne and had a seat brought for his mother, and she sat at his right hand. The "right hand" is the right side, a place of honor.

Adonijah, Solomon's older brother, had tried to make himself king before. Now he uses Bath-sheba, the king's mother, to ask for something. The verses that follow show that Solomon saw in that request a threat to his reign, though Bath-sheba perhaps did not notice it.

Honor those who deserve respect, as Solomon did with his mother. But before asking for or carrying a favor on someone else's behalf, ask wisely what intentions lie behind it.
exp.1:20:
Bathsheba asks her son, King Solomon, to give Abishag the Shunammite to his brother Adonijah as his wife. The word "Let" in this verse is the request itself, and "as his wife" simply means she is to be his wife.

It is Bathsheba, the king's mother, who speaks, acting as an intermediary for Adonijah. Abishag had cared for King David in his old age. Adonijah had already tried to make himself king before. Solomon understood the request as a new attempt at the throne, since in that culture marrying someone so close to the former king could strengthen a claim to the kingdom. That is why he responds so harshly. The Bible does not say whether Bathsheba noticed this.

For today: before we ask or intervene on behalf of others, let us consider hidden intentions and consequences. Let us ask God for wisdom so that we are not used in plans we do not fully know.
exp.1:21:
Solomon answers his mother, Bathsheba, with a sharp question: why are you asking for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? It is as if you were asking for the kingdom for him as well, since Adonijah is his older brother and has the support of the priest Abiathar and the general Joab, son of Zeruiah.

Bathsheba had brought Solomon Adonijah's request. Adonijah had earlier tried to make himself king, and Solomon had spared his life. Abishag had cared for King David in his old age. Many understand that Solomon saw in this request an attempt to claim the throne, although the Bible does not explain all the details of the custom.

For today: not everything that seems small or innocent is so. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern the intentions behind things, and act with humility and justice.
exp.1:23:
Solomon makes a solemn oath. "As the Lord lives" is a way of swearing by the living God. He says that the Lord has established him and set him on the throne of his father David, and has made him a house, that is, given him a royal family that would continue, just as he had promised. For this reason he declares that Adonijah will be put to death that very day.

The king Solomon speaks here, responding to his mother Bathsheba. She had brought Adonijah's request to marry Abishag. Solomon saw it as a new attempt by Adonijah to take the throne. Many regard it as justice to protect the kingdom; others also see a harsh political decision. The text relates the events without approving of every action.

For today: before using God's name to support a decision, examine your heart with humility. Ask for wisdom to act with justice and also with mercy.
exp.1:24:
And King Solomon sent by the hand of Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada; and Benaiah attacked him, and he died. These words are a reminder that Solomon gave an order to Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, the commander of his guard. Benaiah went and struck down Adonijah, and Adonijah died.

Solomon had just sworn before God that Adonijah would die that very day. Adonijah was his older brother and had earlier wanted to become king. Now he had asked to marry Abishag, the young woman who had cared for David, and Solomon understood that this was another attempt to take the throne. Some believe it was a fair decision to protect the kingdom; others see it as very harsh. The Bible only tells what happened.

For today: crooked ambitions and secret plans end badly. Let us seek to serve with humility, accepting the place God gives us, without taking anything from anyone.
exp.1:25:
He tells that King Solomon spoke to the priest Abiathar and ordered him to go to Anathoth, to his own fields. He said Abiathar deserved death, but that he would not put him to death that day. There were two reasons: Abiathar had carried the ark of the Lord before David, and he had shared in all of David's afflictions.

Solomon speaks here, already established as king. Abiathar had supported Adonijah, who wanted to take the throne. Solomon punishes him by removing him from the priesthood, but spares his life because of his past loyalty to David. The passage that follows connects this with what was said about the house of Eli.

For today: God is just, but He also remembers past faithfulness. This invites us to be faithful to the end, because a wrong step has consequences. It also encourages us to show mercy, remembering the good that others have done.
exp.1:27:
It tells that news reached Joab about what had happened with Adonijah and Abiathar. Joab had supported Adonijah, though earlier he had not supported Absalom. Then he fled to the tent of the Lord and took hold of the horns of the altar, which are the corners shaped like horns.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Solomon is establishing his reign after David's death. Joab, the commander of the army, had followed Adonijah in his attempt to become king. When he saw how Solomon was acting, he became afraid. Holding on to the altar was a way of seeking protection, but the Bible does not say that this erased his guilt.

For today: taking refuge in religious things does not replace sincere repentance. God invites us to come to Him in humility, acknowledging our wrongs, and not merely to seek an escape when the consequences arrive.
exp.1:28:
It was reported to King Solomon that Joab had taken refuge in the tabernacle, beside the altar. Then Solomon sent Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, to put him to death.

The narrator shows how Solomon secures his kingdom. Joab had supported Adonijah in his attempt to become king, and earlier he had killed two innocent army commanders, Abner and Amasa. Joab clung to the horns of the altar seeking protection. But the law of Moses did not shelter someone who had committed deliberate murder (Exodus 21:14). Some scholars debate how fair Solomon's decision was; the text presents it as justice for the blood that had been shed.

For today: we cannot hide our wrongdoing behind religious things. God asks for a sincere and repentant heart, not merely a sacred place to hide in.
exp.1:29:
In this verse, Benaiah goes into the tent of worship and passes on the king's order to Joab: to come out. Joab refuses and says he would rather die right there. Benaiah goes back and tells Solomon Joab's answer.

Background: Solomon, the new king, had been given the task by his father David of seeing justice done for the killings Joab had committed. Joab had supported Adonijah against Solomon and had taken refuge by the altar, perhaps expecting protection. The law of Moses did not protect someone who killed with intent (Exodus 21:14). Joab chooses to stay there.

For today: Seeking refuge in religious places does not erase our guilt. God asks for a sincere heart, not merely to be near what is sacred. Let us acknowledge our wrongs and seek his forgiveness with humility.
exp.1:30:
The king tells Benaiah to do what Joab asked: to strike him down right there and bury him. With this, the king wants to remove from himself and from David's family the guilt for the innocent blood that Joab shed.

King Solomon speaks here, newly established on the throne. Joab, David's former general, had killed Abner and Amasa in a time of peace, and he also supported Adonijah against Solomon. Joab had taken refuge by the altar and refused to come out. Some scholars see here justice for unresolved murders; others also notice a political motive. The text presents the death as justice for those crimes.

For today: injustice does not disappear with time, and God takes innocent blood seriously. This invites us to act justly, not to cover up wrongdoing, and to let God be the final judge.
exp.1:31:
God would bring Joab's guilt back down on his own head for his own violence. Joab had killed two men more righteous and better than he was, with the sword, and David had not known about it. Rewriting the phrase about the blood returning to his head: it means Joab would bear the consequences of those deaths.

The speaker is Solomon, now king, and he gives the reason for the order against Joab. Joab had killed Abner and Amasa, military leaders, in a treacherous way. David, before he died, had charged Solomon to bring about justice. Joab took refuge in the tabernacle, but Solomon ordered that he be executed right there. Some see justice here; others see a political act. The Bible presents it as justice.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, even when it is hidden or slow to be brought to light. Let us try to act with honesty and not hide wrong, trusting that God judges with justice.
exp.1:35:
It says that King Solomon sent for Shimei and ordered him to build a house in Jerusalem, to live there and not to go out to any other place.

Solomon was speaking after he had secured his kingdom following the death of David. Shimei was the man who had cursed David when David was fleeing from Absalom (2 Samuel 16). David had spared Shimei's life, but he warned Solomon not to leave him unwatched. Solomon does not put him to death, but places him under a clear restriction, so as to keep him close and avoid trouble.

For today: clear limits can be a sign of mercy. When God or life sets limits for us, it is wise to obey them sincerely, because the freedom we are given has conditions, and respecting them protects us from serious consequences.
exp.1:39:
This verse tells how Shimei got up, saddled his donkey (that is, he got it ready for riding), and went to Gath, where King Achish was, to look for his servants who had run away. He found them and brought them back. But in doing so, he left Jerusalem.

Solomon had ordered Shimei to live in Jerusalem and not leave the city, under penalty of death. Shimei had accepted that condition. Three years passed, and he broke it to get his servants back. The narrator only reports the facts; later Solomon will call him to account for his disobedience.

For today: sometimes we break a commitment because it seems to us that what we gain is worth it. This passage invites us to keep what we have promised and to think about the consequences before we act.
exp.1:44:
This verse says that Solomon will be blessed and that his kingdom, the throne of David, will stand firm forever before God. "Forever" is the word used in the verse itself, and the phrase "before the Lord" means under God's watchful eye and approval.

The speaker is King Solomon, at the end of his conversation with Shimei. Shimei had cursed David when David was fleeing from Absalom, and later Solomon had ordered him under oath not to leave Jerusalem. Shimei disobeyed. Solomon sees his punishment as justice and declares that his kingdom is secured. Some think this shows political firmness; others, that it is an expression of faith. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: our words and promises carry weight. Keeping what we promise is a way of living with integrity before God and before others.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that, at that time, the people of Israel offered sacrifices at the high places, which were raised places where worship took place. This happened because there was still no temple built to honor the name of the Lord, that is, to worship him.

The author of the book tells the story and explains why this was practiced. Solomon was a new king and was building the temple, his palace, and the walls of Jerusalem. High places were common, but later the Bible will see them as a danger, because they could become mixed with the customs of neighboring peoples. Even so, the text says that Solomon loved the Lord.

Today, we can learn that loving God includes seeking his guidance and not settling for what is merely customary. Ask yourself: does my way of worshiping God come from his Word, or only from habit?
exp.2:2:
This verse says that Solomon loved God and lived by the laws and teachings that his father David had left him. But there was a detail: he offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places, which were raised places of worship outside an official temple.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings. He wants to show that Solomon started well, with sincere love for God, although not everything was perfect. It is pointed out that the temple was not yet finished, and for that reason the people used those high places. Some scholars see here a gentle warning, because later the high places became a problem. Others see it as understandable at that time.

For today: loving God truly is what matters most, but it is good to examine with humility whether there are habits in our lives that are not fully in line with what He teaches.
exp.2:3:
It says that King Solomon went to Gibeon, because it was the most important high place for worship there, and that he offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. A high place is an elevated place where sacrifices were made. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned completely as an offering to God.

The narrator of the book explains that the temple did not yet exist, which is why the people offered sacrifices in these places. It says that Solomon loved the LORD and followed the way of his father David. This act of worship prepares the moment when God appears to him in a dream. Scholars regard these high places with some caution, because later they became a source of trouble.

For today: before asking anything of God, Solomon gave him his time and his devotion. We can set apart moments of sincere worship, not only to ask for things, but to love and honor God.
exp.2:5:
Solomon reminds God that he had shown great kindness to his father David. David lived before God with faithfulness, with righteousness, and with a sincere heart. God showed him his steadfast, generous love, and kept that kindness going by giving him a son to sit on his throne, as it is seen today, that is, as it is evident now.

Solomon speaks in prayer, at Gibeon, after offering many sacrifices. God appeared to him in a dream and told him to ask for whatever he wanted. Before asking, Solomon begins by acknowledging God's faithfulness to his family. Afterward he will say that he feels too small to govern.

For today: before asking God for something, take a moment to thank him for what he has already done for you and for those who came before you. Remembering his faithfulness strengthens confidence when you pray.
exp.2:7:
Verse 8 says that Solomon sees himself as God's servant, placed in the middle of a people that God chose. That people is so large that it cannot be counted; there are too many people to number. The word "servant" here means someone who serves his Lord with humility.

Solomon speaks this prayer to God at Gibeon, after he became king in place of his father David. He had already said that he felt like a little child, not knowing how to conduct himself. Here he acknowledges the size of his responsibility: to rule the people who belong to God, not to him. That is why he will soon ask for an obedient heart, that is, one that is attentive and willing to learn.

For today: when you have a responsibility that is larger than you, whether in your family, your work, or your church, imitate Solomon. Humbly acknowledge your limits, and ask God for wisdom before you act.
exp.2:9:
The verse says that the request pleased God, that it gave him delight that Solomon asked for wisdom. The word "pleased" means that something was to his liking. In this Bible the name Lord appears, which refers to God.

Solomon had just become king, after his father David. God appeared to him in a dream and told him to ask for whatever he wanted. Solomon felt small before such a numerous people, so he asked for an understanding heart, that is, a heart ready to listen and learn, so that he could govern with justice and tell good from evil.

For today: before asking God for things for ourselves, we can ask what we need in order to serve others well. Asking for wisdom for our decisions, at home or at work, is a prayer that pleases God.
exp.2:11:
God tells Solomon that he grants him what he asked for. He gives him a wise and understanding heart, that is, a mind and character able to discern what is right. Solomon's request is described as being done according to his words, meaning according to what he asked for. And God promises that no one before him or after him will have wisdom like his.

God speaks to Solomon in a dream at Gibeon, at the beginning of his reign. Solomon was young and felt the weight of governing the people. Instead of asking for long life, riches, or victory over his enemies, he asked for the understanding to judge well. God was pleased with that humble and generous request.

Before we ask for things for ourselves, we can ask God for wisdom to act with justice and love in what is ours to do: in the family, at work, or in the church. He takes pleasure in that kind of prayer.
exp.2:12:
God tells Solomon that, besides the wisdom he asked for, he also gives him what he did not ask for: riches and honour. They will be such that, as long as Solomon lives, no other king will compare with him. The verse's wording is rendered here as the verse itself reads.

God speaks to Solomon, who sees him in a dream at Gibeon at the beginning of his reign. Solomon did not ask for long life, riches, or the defeat of his enemies, but for an understanding heart to govern with justice. God answers with generosity. But the next verse makes clear that a long life depended on Solomon continuing to obey, as David did.

For today: when you seek first what pleases God, such as wisdom, honesty, and service, trust that he knows how to care for the rest. Even so, this is not an automatic promise of wealth, but an invitation to put God first.
exp.2:14:
He says that Solomon woke up and realized that God had spoken to him in a dream. Then he went to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. There he offered burnt offerings (offerings that were burned completely for God) and peace offerings (offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving). Then he made a feast for all his servants.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Earlier, at Gibeon, God promised Solomon wisdom, riches and honor, and encouraged him to walk in obedience as David had. Solomon responded with worship and generosity. After this passage comes the case of the two women, where his wisdom will be seen.

When God blesses us or guides us, we can respond with concrete gratitude: giving thanks to him, worshiping him, and sharing what we have received with others.
exp.2:15:
At that time, two women who lived by prostitution came before King Solomon and stood before him.

The narrator of the book now speaks. Solomon had just asked God for wisdom in a dream and worshiped him in Jerusalem. Now a real test begins: two women with a dispute that no one else could settle. The text does not say why they came to the king, but it was the place where justice was sought.

For today: God gives us wisdom to use in concrete situations, even with people others despise. We can treat with respect and attention those whom society ignores, because before God their cause matters too.
exp.2:17:
She says that one woman gives birth, and three days later the other woman also gives birth. The two of them were living together in the same house, and no one else was with them.

The first woman is the one speaking, and she accuses the other before King Solomon. Both were prostitutes, and they were arguing over a living child. She stresses that there were no witnesses, to explain that only the two of them knew what had happened. This is the case where Solomon showed the wisdom he had asked God for.

For today: when there is no proof and the accounts contradict each other, let us not rush to judgment. Let us ask God for wisdom, listen with patience, and seek the truth with justice and compassion, especially for the most vulnerable.
exp.2:18:
In this verse, a woman tells how the child of her housemate died one night. According to her, the cause was that the other woman lay on the baby, probably without realizing it while she slept.

The speaker is one of the two women who came before King Solomon to ask him for justice. Both claimed to be the mother of the child who was still alive. This woman gives her version of events and accuses the other of having swapped the babies during the night. Later, Solomon uses his wisdom to discover who is telling the truth.

For today: before judging a situation, it is wise to listen calmly to all sides. Let us ask God for wisdom, as Solomon did, to seek the truth with justice and compassion.
exp.2:21:
This verse shows two women arguing before the king. Each one says that the living child is hers and that the dead child belongs to the other. Neither gives way, and they speak in the king's presence, that is, before Solomon, who must judge.

The second woman speaks, and then the first one answers. Earlier, one of them had told how, during the night, her son died and was swapped for the other woman's son. Solomon had just asked God for wisdom to rule, and this case tests that gift. There were no witnesses, so the matter was very hard to settle.

For today: when there are conflicts and opposing accounts, let us not take sides in a hurry. Let us ask God for wisdom, as Solomon did, and listen patiently before we judge.
exp.2:22:
Here the king Solomon repeats what he has heard: one woman claims that the living child is hers and that the dead one belongs to the other woman, and the other woman says exactly the opposite. There are no witnesses to make clear who is telling the truth.

Solomon is the new king of Israel, and shortly before this he had asked God for an understanding heart to judge the people. Two women come before him with a difficult case: they live in the same house, and a baby died during the night. Solomon sums up the conflict out loud, like someone putting the facts in order before deciding. Soon he will call for a sword to uncover the truth.

Before judging or taking sides in a conflict, take the time to listen calmly to both accounts. Ask God for wisdom, as Solomon did, and seek the truth with patience, without letting yourself be swayed by your first impression.
exp.3:2:
These verses name three officials of Solomon's kingdom. Elihoreph and Ahiah, the sons of Shisha, were scribes, that is, secretaries who wrote out and kept the king's documents. Jehoshaphat, the son of Ahilud, was the recorder, the one who kept a record of events and looked after important matters of government, something like a chronicler or secretary of state.

The narrator of 1 Kings gives this list of Solomon's chief officials, which comes right after he says that Solomon ruled over all Israel. The list shows a kingdom already well organized, with priests, military commanders, and administrators. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact scope of the scribe and recorder roles, but both had to do with keeping records and administration.

For today: God uses both those who stand at the front and those who work in simple, orderly tasks. Do faithfully and in an orderly way what has been entrusted to you, even when no one applauds it.
exp.3:5:
This verse names two officials of King Solomon. Ahishar was over the household, meaning he was in charge of managing the house and the affairs of the palace. Adoniram, son of Abda, was over the tribute, that is, he oversaw the forced labor or the payments that the people owed the king. Some scholars think this refers to compulsory labor; the text does not specify the details.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator of the book, who lists the principal officials of Solomon. This list shows that his kingdom was already well organized, with priests, an army, governors, and administrators. The passage prepares the account of the prosperity of his reign, although later the burden of the tribute will bring tensions.

For today: God values order and faithful service, even in tasks that receive little attention. Let us do faithfully what has been entrusted to us, and those who hold authority, let them exercise it with justice and without taking advantage of others.
exp.3:6:
Salomón organized the kingdom into twelve districts, each with its own governor. Together they secured the food and everything else needed for the king and his household. Each governor was responsible for this duty for one month of the year.

The word "provide" means to supply what is needed, and it was their job to cover the costs of the royal household.

This is part of a list of Solomon's officials. The narrator of the book describes how the kingdom was run during its time of greatest prosperity. This arrangement spread the burden across all Israel, and it is not known with certainty whether the districts matched the tribes exactly. The text then gives the names of the governors.

God often sustains ordinary life through shared work. When each person does their part, no one carries everything alone. Think about your family, your church, or your work: what part of it are you called to fulfill faithfully?
exp.3:10:
This verse speaks of one of the twelve governors that Solomon appointed over Israel. It names the son of Abinadab, who was in charge of all the region of Dor, a district on the Mediterranean coast. He was also married to Taphath, a daughter of Solomon.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. He is describing how Solomon organized his kingdom into districts, and each governor was responsible for providing food for the king and his household for one month of the year. That the governor was the king's son-in-law shows that Solomon trusted his own family with certain posts. The text says nothing more about what kind of person he was.

For today: God works through organization and teamwork. Even tasks that seem small or administrative serve others. Let us carry out whatever is entrusted to us with responsibility and honesty.
exp.3:11:
Baana, son of Ahilud, is mentioned in this verse, one of the twelve officers that Solomon appointed over Israel. He was given a territory in the north: the cities of Taanach and Megiddo, and the whole region of Beth-shean, near Zartanah, beneath Jezreel. His territory reached from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, and as far as the place beyond Jokneam.

This is part of an administrative list within the account of Solomon's kingdom. The text does not say who is speaking; it is the narrative of the writer of Kings. Each officer gathered provisions for the king and his household during one month of the year. Some details about the places are uncertain, since the exact location of every one of them is not known.

God often works through ordinary tasks and little-known people. Today, your faithful work, though no one applauds it, also counts. Do it with responsibility and gratitude.
exp.3:12:
This verse speaks of another of Solomon's twelve governors. The son of Geber was in charge of Ramoth-gilead, of the towns of Jair in Gilead, and of the region of Argob, in Bashan. There were sixty large cities there, surrounded by walls and with gates strengthened with bronze bars. The "bars" mentioned here refers to the bolts or bars of the gates.

The narrator is the author of Kings, whose name we do not know. He presents the organization of Solomon's kingdom. These men gathered supplies from their regions to maintain the king's household, each one for a month of the year. The list shows that the kingdom was well ordered and prosperous. Later on, the people would complain about the burden this placed on them.

For today: God uses order and shared responsibility, and each person serves in the place entrusted to them. But whoever holds authority must use it with justice, without placing excessive burdens on others.
exp.3:13:
This verse is part of a list of governors. It says that Ahinadab, son of Iddo, was in charge of the city of Mahanaim. It is a brief detail, with nothing more said about him. Mahanaim was in the region of Gilead, east of the Jordan River.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book, who lists the twelve officials that Solomon placed over Israel. Each one had to gather provisions for the king and his household during one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7). The author shows how well organized the kingdom was. About the son of Iddo we know no more than what is said here.

God uses both well-known people and those who are little mentioned. Even if your service seems small or goes unnoticed, when it is done faithfully it has value. Serve wherever you are, with responsibility and honesty.
exp.3:16:
This verse names Jehoshaphat, son of Paruah, as one of the twelve governors that Solomon set over Israel. His district was Issachar. These men were in charge of gathering food for the king and his household.

The passage is a historical account from the book of Kings. It is not spoken by any particular character, but by the narrator, who lists the organization of Solomon's kingdom. Each governor covered a region and supplied food for one month of the year. Scholars hold different views on whether these regions matched the tribes exactly.

For today: God uses ordinary people in tasks that seem small, such as organizing and serving with order. Even if your name appears only in a list, your faithfulness counts. Serve responsibly wherever you are.
exp.3:17:
This verse is part of a list of twelve governors whom King Solomon appointed over Israel. Here Shimei, the son of Elah, is named as being in charge of the tribe of Benjamin. Each of these men had an assigned region.

The text is part of an account of how Solomon organized his kingdom. According to the nearby verses, each governor had to provide food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Not much more is said about Shimei, so we do not know with certainty any further details about him. Some believe he might be the same Shimei mentioned in other parts of the Bible, but that is not certain.

For today: God uses people with simple, little-known tasks so that everything works well. Even if your work seems small or goes unnoticed, when it is done faithfully it becomes part of the well-being of many.
exp.3:19:
This verse says that the people of Judah and Israel were very numerous, as countless as the sand on the seashore. Furthermore, they lived well: they ate, drank, and were glad.

The Book of Kings is told by a narrator who remembers the reign of Solomon. Here he describes the prosperity and peace of those years, after mentioning the governors who organized the kingdom. The text recalls God's promise to Abraham to give him numerous descendants. Scholars often see in this a fulfillment of that promise, although the book later also shows Solomon's failures.

Today we can thank God for everyday things: bread, companionship, and joy. Let us enjoy his blessings with gratitude, never forgetting that they come from Him and not from our own strength.
exp.3:21:
This verse tells what was needed each day to feed Solomon's household. The daily supply of food is what is described here. Thirty measures of fine flour were used, along with sixty measures of ordinary flour. The measure in view was a large one; by calculation it comes to about 200 liters, though scholars do not agree exactly on the figure.

The author of the book, who is not named with certainty, describes Solomon's kingdom at its best: peace, abundance, and a great many happy people. He wants to show that God had kept his promise to bless Israel. Such a large amount of food was also needed to sustain the court, the officials, and the servants.

For today: when God gives us abundance, the right response is gratitude and generosity. We can ask ourselves how to use what we have to bless others, and not only ourselves.
exp.3:25:
The verse says that Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses in his stables, meaning the places where they were kept, for his chariots of war, and also twelve thousand horsemen, that is, soldiers who rode on horseback. It should be noted that 2 Chronicles 9:25 gives the figure of four thousand stalls, and scholars do not agree on how to explain the difference.

Here the narrator of the book describes the splendor of Solomon's kingdom. The text has just said there was peace and security throughout the land, and right after this it shows how much it cost to sustain that power and who bore the burden of maintaining it.

For today: having resources and strength is not wrong, but trusting in them more than in God is. Examine where your security rests, and remember that God sustains you better than any army (Psalm 20:7).
exp.3:26:
Solomon's twelve governors took turns supplying the king and everyone who ate at his table. Each one was assigned a month of the year, and they made sure that nothing was lacking. The verse of the word "provided" is that they supplied food and everything needed.

The account in the book of Kings, whose author is not named with certainty, describes here the peace and good organization of Solomon's kingdom. It shows that Israel's prosperity had a practical order: the work was shared among many people. This goes hand in hand with the wisdom God gave him, mentioned right after.

For today: God often sustains things through the faithfulness of many people, each in their turn. Carry out with steady commitment the task that falls to you, in your family, your work, or your church, even when it seems small. In this way others are not left without what they need.
exp.4:0:
This verse tells how Hiram, king of the city of Tyre, sent his servants or messengers to Solomon as soon as he learned that they had anointed him king in place of his father. To anoint was to pour oil on someone as a sign that God had set him apart to rule. The text gives the reason: Hiram had always loved David.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Tyre was a Phoenician city on the coast, a neighbor of Israel. Hiram had enjoyed a good relationship with David, and now he extends it to David's son. This friendship prepares the agreement between the two kings to build the temple. The Bible does not detail how that friendship began.

For today: a relationship based on affection and loyalty can open doors for the generations that follow. Take care of your friendships and your good witness; they can bless your children and others after you.
exp.4:5:
Here Solomon asks Hiram, king of Tyre, to have cedar trees cut from Lebanon for the temple. Solomon's servants will work alongside Hiram's servants, and Solomon will pay whatever wages Hiram sets. He acknowledges that the Sidonians, people of the Phoenician coast, were the best at working timber. Cutting and shaping the wood is what the work involves.

Solomon speaks now that he has peace throughout his kingdom and wants to fulfill the promise made to his father David: to build a house for the name of God. Hiram had been a friend of David, and that is why Solomon writes to him. Hiram is glad and agrees willingly.

For today: God can use the gifts of other people to accomplish what He has entrusted to us. Solomon did not want to do everything alone; he asked for help, recognized the skill of others, and offered to pay fairly. We can learn to work as a team, value others, and deal with them honestly.
exp.4:8:
Hiram, king of Tyre, promises that his servants will bring the logs down from Lebanon to the sea. There they will bind them into rafts and carry them by water to the place Solomon indicates. Then they will untie them, and Solomon will collect them. In return, Solomon must provide food for his household.

Hiram is replying to Solomon, who asked him for cedar wood to build the temple. Hiram was glad and praised the LORD for the new king. Here he proposes how he will do the work and what he expects to receive. Afterward, the text shows that both sides kept the agreement year after year.

For today: good agreements are clear and fair to both parties. If we work together with others, it is wise to speak honestly about what each will do and to keep what has been promised.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that the Lord gave Solomon wisdom, just as he had promised. It also says that there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and that the two of them made an agreement or covenant.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings summarizes what happened while Solomon was preparing to build the temple. Hiram, king of Tyre, supplied him with cedar and cypress wood, and Solomon sent him wheat and oil. The text presents that good relationship as a sign that God kept his promise to give Solomon wisdom (1 Kings 3:12).

For today: God's wisdom shows in how we treat other people. Seek to be someone who builds fair agreements, keeps your word, and promotes peace at work, in the family, and in business.
exp.4:14:
Solomon had seventy thousand men who carried loads and eighty thousand who cut stone in the mountains. The phrase about those who carried loads refers to moving heavy materials from place to place. Those who cut stone in the mountains were the men who quarried rock.

This is part of the account of how Solomon prepared for building the temple. The narrator describes the huge amount of labor that was needed. These workers appear to be different from the thirty thousand sent to Lebanon in shifts. Some scholars believe they were non-Israelite workers, but the text does not make this entirely clear, and it is understood in several different ways.

For today: the great works of God are built through the labor of many people, and often no one remembers their names. Serve with willingness in the ordinary tasks, even when no one sees. God does see it, and He values it.
exp.4:15:
This verse says that, in addition to the workers, Solomon placed 3,300 chiefs or supervisors over the work on the temple. They directed the people who did the labor. The leaders in charge of the workers were the senior overseers, and they were responsible for watching over and organizing the people.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings describes how Solomon prepared for the building of the temple. Earlier, Solomon had asked Hiram, king of Tyre, for cedar wood from Lebanon. This verse shows the size and good organization of the project: there were laborers, carriers, cutters, and supervisors. Some texts give a different number of supervisors (for example, 2 Chronicles 2:18 mentions 3,600), and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: serving God requires order and teamwork. If you have a responsibility in your church, family, or work, carry it out with care and humility, looking after those who work alongside you.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that Solomon began to build the temple of the Lord 480 years after Israel came out of Egypt. It was in the fourth year of his reign, in the month Zif, which is the second month of the Hebrew calendar.

It is the narrator of the book of Kings who is speaking. He marks a key date: the temple was a milestone in the history of Israel, linking the people to their deliverance from Egypt. Some scholars take the 480 years literally, and others think it is a symbolic or approximate figure. The ancient texts do not fully agree, and that is why it is debated.

For today: God acts in history and remembers his work. Take a moment to recall how God has guided you, and let that encourage you to give him your time and strength with gratitude.
exp.5:1:
This verse gives the measurements of the temple that Solomon built for God: sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and thirty high. A cubit was an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger; it is estimated at about 45 to 50 centimeters, though the exact length is not known.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He wants to make clear that the work began on a precise date, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, and that it was done with order and care. For Israel, this temple was the place where God was present in the midst of his people.

For today: if Solomon took such care in building a place for God, we too can offer God the best of our time and effort. Doing things with order and dedication can be a way of honoring him.
exp.5:2:
This verse describes the porch, which was a covered entrance at the front of the temple. It was twenty cubits long, matching the width of the house, and ten cubits wide going forward. A cubit was an ancient measure of about 45 centimeters, so the porch measured roughly nine meters by four and a half meters.

The account is told by the author of the book of Kings, who is not identified with certainty. He records in detail the measurements of the temple that Solomon began to build for the LORD. These details remind us that the temple was a work planned and carried out with order, and that it belongs to a key moment in the history of Israel.

For today: before entering the presence of God, it is good to pause, as one who passes through a porch. We can spend a few minutes praying and quieting the heart before reading the Bible, gathering with others, or beginning the day.
exp.5:3:
This verse says that Solomon made windows in the temple that looked wide from the inside and narrow from the outside. The phrase about inside and outside should not be quoted here, and the words meaning inside and outside are simply translated. The Hebrew of this phrase is difficult, and some translations speak of windows with frames or fixed grates. For that reason it is not known with certainty what they were like.

The author of the book of Kings, not Solomon, tells how the temple was built. He gives measurements and details to show the order and care with which this house for worshiping the LORD was raised.

For today: although we do not know what symbolism it had, we can learn to guard what we let in. Let us open our hearts within to the light of God through prayer and the Bible, and be wise about what we allow to shape us.
exp.5:6:
What it says: The temple was built with stones that had already been cut and finished at the quarry. So when it was put up, no sound of hammers, axes, or iron tools was heard at the site.

Context: This is the account in the book of Kings about the building of the temple in the time of Solomon. It is not a speech but a narrative. It describes the care and order of the work. The text does not explain the reason for the silence; many believe it expresses respect for the holy place, though that is an interpretation. It has also been seen as a sign of good planning.

For today: God values order and preparation. Before serving in the church, at work, or in the family, prepare yourself in prayer and with calm, so that what you do is done with respect and without so much disorder.
exp.5:7:
It says the entrance to the middle floor was on the right side of the temple. From there one went up by a winding stair, that is, a spiral staircase, to the middle floor, and from that floor to the third. The side rooms that surrounded the temple are what is meant here, and the second level is what is meant by the middle floor.

This is the account of the writer of Kings about the construction of Solomon's temple. It is not a character speaking; the narrator gives details of the work. He tells how the side rooms were built, each floor a little wider than the one below, and how one reached them. Some scholars think they were used to store objects and offerings, but the text does not say so clearly.

For today: God pays attention to order and to the details of what is done for Him. We can serve Him with care in small and little-seen things, and not only in what is striking.
exp.5:10:
This verse says that God spoke to Solomon while he was building the temple. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to Solomon" means that the Lord gave him a direct message.

Who is speaking is God. The construction of the temple was already well along: the ceilings and the side rooms of cedar were being built. Right there, God interrupts to remind Solomon of something more important than the work: obedience. The verses that follow explain that if Solomon obeyed, God would keep his promise to David and would live among Israel.

For today: we can work very hard on good projects, even for God, but he looks first at an obedient heart. Before you go on with your plans, take a moment to listen to his word in the Bible and ask yourself whether you are living out what he has already told you.
exp.5:11:
God speaks to Solomon while he is building the temple. He tells him that the house is important, but what matters most is his obedience. If Solomon walks in the statutes, keeps the judgments, and observes all the commandments, God will keep firm the promise he made to David, Solomon's father.

The one speaking is the LORD, in the middle of the work on the temple. The promise to David (2 Samuel 7) spoke of a son of his who would build a house for God and of a lasting kingdom. God makes clear that the promise comes with a call to obey: a beautiful building is not enough. The next verse says that God would dwell among his people.

For today: do not confuse religious activity with a life given over to God. Before your projects, service, or achievements, ask yourself whether you are obeying God in everyday life: how you speak, how you treat others, and how you make decisions.
exp.5:13:
This verse says that Solomon built the temple until he had finished it. The word "built" simply means he worked on and constructed the house, and the phrase "finished it" means he completed it. It is a brief sentence that marks the close of the main work of the construction.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells this right after God spoke to Solomon while he was building. God reminded him that the temple alone was not enough: if Solomon obeyed his commandments, God would keep his promise to David and dwell among his people. Then the account goes on with the details of the inside of the temple.

For today: finishing a good project is valuable, but the most important thing is to keep walking in obedience to God. We can ask ourselves: do my life and my achievements go together with a faithful heart toward Him?
exp.5:15:
King Solomon built, at the back of the temple, a room twenty cubits long, lined with cedar boards from the floor up to the ceiling. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so the room measured about ten meters. The verse's word for the room where God was present is the inner sanctuary, the most sacred room of the temple.

This is part of a historical account of how the temple in Jerusalem was built. No one is speaking; the narrator describes the work in detail. This room held the ark of the covenant and symbolized God's presence among his people. Scholars do not fully agree on exactly how the space was arranged.

For today: God deserves the best of our care and dedication. We can set aside a calm, orderly time each day to be with him in prayer, without rush or distraction.
exp.5:16:
This verse says that the main part of the temple, the inner room, measured forty cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of length, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters, so the room would have been about 18 to 20 meters long.

No character speaks here; this is the account from the writer of Kings about how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. The author gives exact measurements to show that the work was done with order and care, as a place for God's presence among his people.

For today: God cares about details and about doing things with diligence. We can offer him our work, our family, and our life of prayer with order and dedication, not halfheartedly, because everything we do can be a way of honoring him.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that Solomon prepared and decorated the inner room, the most sacred place in the temple, the innermost chamber. There the ark of the covenant would be placed, the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people. Here "prepared" means that he arranged it and made it ready for that purpose.

This is part of the historical account of the building of the temple in Jerusalem. The writer of Kings describes in detail how Solomon built a worthy place to worship God. It is not a character speaking; it is the narrator telling the work.

For today: God deserves the best place in our lives. We can prepare a space, a time, and a heart ready each day to be with him, not with what is left over, but with what is first and best.
exp.5:22:
He says that Solomon had two cherubim made inside the inner sanctuary (the most holy place, where the ark of the covenant would be), of olive wood. Each one was ten cubits high, about four and a half to five meters. A cubit was the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. The cherubim are angelic beings who, in the Bible, accompany the presence of God.

The text is a historical account of the construction of the temple in Jerusalem. The narrator describes each part of the work in detail: the gold, the chains, the altar. The cherubim would guard the ark, the place where God made his presence felt among his people. It does not say why that exact measure was chosen; it only records that the work was done with care.

God deserves the best of our effort and our attention. Today we do not have a temple of wood and gold, for God dwells in his people. We might ask ourselves: do I treat my time of prayer and of reading the Bible with reverence and care?
exp.5:23:
It says that each cherub had two wings, and that each wing measured five cubits (a cubit is the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters). So from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other there were ten cubits, about four and a half to five meters. The most holy place of the temple, where God made his presence known, is what is meant by the inner sanctuary.

Here the narrator of the book describes in detail the construction of Solomon's temple. The two cherubim, made of olive wood and covered with gold, stood in the most holy place. With their wings spread out, they gave the impression of guarding the place of God's presence. The text stresses that both were identical in measure and form.

For today: God delights in what is done with order, care, and excellence. Offer him the best of your work and your time, even in small things, as a way of worshiping him.
exp.5:27:
It says that Solomon overlaid with gold the two large figures of cherubim that stood in the inner sanctuary of the temple. The word "overlaid" here means that they were covered with gold, not that they were solid gold. Cherubim are spiritual beings who appear in the Bible near the presence of God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing the building of the temple in Jerusalem. The cherubim stood in the inner sanctuary, where the ark of the covenant was placed. The gold showed that this place was holy and that God deserved the best. The exact details of these figures are not fully known.

For today: let us give God the best of our time, affection and effort, not the leftovers. We can begin the day with a sincere prayer, made with attention and gratitude.
exp.5:31:
It says that Solomon made the two doors at the entrance to the most holy place from olive wood. On them he carved cherubim (angelic beings), palm trees, and open flowers, or flower buds. Then he overlaid them with gold, and he also overlaid with gold the carvings. The verse of the carving and overlaying words has been left out, since the verse above already makes that plain.

It is part of the description of the building of the temple in Jerusalem. The narrator tells in detail how Solomon prepared the inner sanctuary, the place where the ark of the covenant stood and where the presence of God was. The cherubim, the palm trees, and the flowers also appear in other parts of the temple. Some see in them a reminder of Eden, although the text does not explain this.

For today: drawing near to God is something great and precious. We can give him the best of our time and attention, with reverence and gratitude, because Christ opened the way for us.
exp.5:33:
The verse describes the doors at the entrance to Solomon's temple. There were two doors, made of fir tree (other translations say cypress or pine, because the Hebrew word is uncertain). Each door was made of two leaves that folded, like a folding door, which is why each one is described as having two leaves folding. The word "folding" perhaps refers to the leaves turning on their hinges.

The book of Kings relates the building of the temple with many details. The author, an Israelite historian, wants to show that Solomon built for God a house that was carefully kept, beautiful, and made with order.

For today: if in that time every last detail of a door was cared for to honor God, we too can serve Him with diligence in small things, doing well the everyday things as an offering to Him.
exp.5:34:
It says that Solomon ordered figures carved on the doors of the temple: cherubim (angelic beings), palm trees, and open flowers. Then everything was covered with gold, fitted closely to the carved work, that is, following each carved shape.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, describing the building of the temple in Jerusalem. No character is speaking. He wants to show the care and beauty with which a place for worshiping God was prepared. These same figures were on the walls of the temple. Some see in them an image of God's presence and of a garden, though the Bible does not explain their exact meaning.

For today: God deserves our best, even in the details. We can do our work and our service with diligence, as an offering to Him.
exp.5:36:
This verse says that the foundations of the temple were laid in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, in the month of Ziv. To lay the foundation means to set the base on which a building is raised. The house of the Lord is the temple in Jerusalem. Ziv is an ancient Hebrew name for the second month, roughly between April and May.

Here the narrator of the book, who records dates with care, is noting the timing. After describing the decorations and structure, he returns to the start of the work. The verses that follow say it was finished in the eleventh year, that is, after seven years of steady labor.

For today: the important things of God often begin with a firm foundation and grow with patience. If you are starting something good, such as prayer, a service, or your family, do not be discouraged by how slow it seems. Be steady and make sure the foundations are well set.
exp.6:0:
Solomon, after finishing the temple, built his own house or palace, the text says. It took him thirteen years, and he left it fully completed.
