The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who tells the story of the kings of Israel. It is not known with certainty who wrote it. Here he describes Solomon's works at the height of his splendor. Some scholars see in the thirteen years compared with seven a sign that Solomon gave more time to his own house than to God's house, although the text does not say this explicitly.

It is worth examining how we divide our time and effort. We can ask ourselves whether we give God and his work the same dedication we give to our comforts and personal projects.
exp.6:8:
This verse says that all the buildings of Solomon's palace were made of costly stones and of very high quality. They were cut with saws and to exact measure, inside and outside, from the foundation up to the highest part. The outside too, all the way to the great court, had the same finish.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. He describes Solomon's works after the building of the temple: his palace, the hall of the throne, and the house for Pharaoh's daughter. The verse does not say why he insists so much on the details. Some think he wants to show Solomon's wealth and effort.

For today: when you do your work, take care of the details, including the ones nobody sees. Doing things well, inside and out, honors God.
exp.6:9:
The verse says the foundation was made of costly stones, great stones, some ten cubits and some eight cubits long. A cubit was about half a meter, so we are talking about stones of four or five meters, though the exact measure is debated. A foundation is the base on which something is built, and costly stones are valuable ones.

This is part of the narrative in the book of Kings, which describes Solomon's buildings after the temple: his palace, his porch, and the house for Pharaoh's daughter. The author, whose name we do not know for certain, details the quality of the work to show the wealth and effort of that reign.

For today: what is seen above depends on what is placed below. It is worth caring for the foundations of our life, such as faith, integrity, and prayer, even though no one sees them. Jesus also spoke of building on the rock.
exp.6:11:
This verse describes the wall that surrounded the great courtyard of Solomon's complex. It was made with three rows of hewn stones and one row of cedar beams. The same style was used for the inner court of the house of the Lord and for the porch of the house.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. He recounts Solomon's buildings, which include his palace and the temple. Attention is paid to the materials and the measurements. Scholars do not agree on all the details of exactly how this wall looked.

For today: what is done for God deserves care, even in things almost no one sees, like a wall or a foundation. We can offer Him our daily work with order, honesty, and dedication.
exp.6:13:
This verse introduces Hiram, a craftsman whom Solomon brought from Tyre. He was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father, who had already died, was from Tyre. He worked in bronze and was full of skill in every work in metal. He came to the king and carried out all his work.

Here the narrator of the book describes the building of the temple. This Hiram is not the king of Tyre but a worker with the same name. Solomon needed someone with great skill for the bronze pieces, such as the columns that follow. A parallel text, 2 Chronicles 2:14, mentions a mother from the tribe of Dan, and it is not known with certainty how the difference is to be explained.

God uses the ordinary abilities of people for his work. If you have a talent, however simple it may seem, put it at the service of God and of others with humility and good work.
exp.6:14:
It says that Hiram, the craftsman who worked the bronze for Solomon, cast two bronze pillars. Each one was eighteen cubits high, about eight or nine meters, although the cubit varied a little. The phrase about a line of twelve cubits was a measuring cord or tape that went around the pillar, that is, its circumference. The word "cast" means they were poured into a mold.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, describing the construction of the temple and its surroundings. Hiram came from Tyre, was the son of a widow from Naphtali, and had great skill. These pillars were placed at the entrance of the temple. Later they receive names, but this verse gives only their measurements.

For today: God values gifts and work done well, even the work of someone who makes simple things. Offer your trade with dedication and honesty, because you can serve God and others there too.
exp.6:15:
This verse tells how the craftsman Hiram made two capitals of cast bronze. A capital is the decorated piece placed on top of a column, like a crown. Each one measured five cubits high, about two and a half meters, though the length of a cubit is only an approximate measure. Casting means the bronze was melted and poured into a mold.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings describes the building of the temple and its surroundings under King Solomon. He presents Hiram, the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali and a father from Tyre, as a wise and skillful man. The text gives so many details because the temple was the place of God's presence, and it was built with great care.

For today: God values good work and the abilities of each person. Offer to God your trade, whatever it is, with diligence and humility, because even what seems small or hidden can serve his work.
exp.6:16:
It describes the capitals, that is, the tops or crowns of the two bronze pillars, as decorated with nets of interwoven work and wreaths shaped like chains. There were seven of these chains on each capital.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings describes in detail the work on Solomon's temple. The two pillars stood at the entrance of the temple. The verses that follow say that the craftsman was Hiram of Tyre. The exact meaning of each decoration is not known for certain; some think they showed beauty and order, but the Bible does not explain it here.

For today: God is interested even in the details. We can do our work, large or small, with care and dedication, as for the Lord.
exp.6:17:
This verse describes the work of Hiram, the bronze craftsman, on Solomon's temple. After making the two pillars, he placed on each one an ornament of pomegranates in two rows around the bronze network, to cover the capitals, which are the decorative pieces at the top. He did the same for the second capital.

The book of Kings tells in detail how the temple in Jerusalem was built. The account is not spoken by a single character; it is narrated by the one who compiled the history of Israel. The pillars stood at the entrance of the temple. The Bible does not explain the exact meaning of the pomegranates here. Some think they symbolized abundance, but this is an interpretation.

For today: God cared even for the small details in his house. We can do what is given to us with care and excellence, whether it is great or simple, as an offering to God.
exp.6:19:
This verse describes the upper part of the two bronze pillars of the temple. Each capital, the piece that crowned the pillar, had two hundred pomegranates in two rows all around. They were above the rounded part, the belly of the pillar, next to the network of decoration.

The book of Kings tells how Solomon built the temple. The account the author writes is very detailed, and it says that the craftsman Hiram worked the bronze. The pillars, called Jachin and Boaz, stood at the entrance. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning of their names or of the pomegranates.

For today: God cares about details and beauty in what is done for Him. We can serve Him with care, even in small tasks that no one notices, doing everything with dedication and gratitude.
exp.6:21:
This verse says that the craftsman placed on the top of the columns an ornament shaped like lilies, that is, lilies or flowers. With that, the work on the two bronze columns was finished. The decorative pieces that sit on the top of a column are the ones the text refers to in this passage.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, describing in detail the building of the temple in the time of Solomon. The columns, named Jachin and Boaz, stood at the entrance. The text does not explain why they chose lilies; some think they evoked beauty and life, but that is an interpretation.

For today: God pays attention to details and to work well finished. We can do our tasks, even the small ones, with care and with a desire to honor him, and remember that finishing well is also a way of serving him.
exp.6:22:
It says that Hiram, the craftsman from Tyre, made a great basin of cast and shaped bronze. It measured ten cubits from one rim to the other (about four and a half to five meters), was completely round, and stood five cubits high. A line of thirty cubits went around it, that is, that was its circumference. The word "sea" here refers to an enormous basin of water. The numbers are approximate, and some scholars note that ten and thirty do not match exactly in mathematical terms.

The narrator of the book describes how Solomon furnished the temple in Jerusalem. After the pillars Jachin and Boaz, this great basin is described. According to 2 Chronicles 4:6, it served for the priests to wash themselves. Its size and beauty showed the care and reverence with which people were to approach God.

God deserves our best effort and respect. Today we do not need a great basin, because Christ cleanses us completely. Even so, we can approach God with a sincere heart, confessing our faults and receiving his forgiveness with gratitude.
exp.6:23:
Under the rim of the great bronze "sea" of the temple, the text says, there were ornaments shaped like small gourds, ten for each cubit (a cubit was about half a meter). They went all the way around the sea in two rows, and they were cast together with the piece, meaning they were part of the same bronze.

Here the account describes the work that Hiram of Tyre made for Solomon's temple. The "sea" was an enormous basin of water used in the temple's service. It is not God who speaks, but the narrator of the book, who records in detail how it was built. The exact meaning of the ornaments is not explained; only their beauty is emphasized.

For today: God values work done well and cared for even in the details. We can do our tasks with diligence, as for the Lord, even when no one notices.
exp.6:25:
It says the walls of the great bronze basin were a hand breadth thick. Its brim was shaped like a cup or a lily blossom, and the basin held two thousand baths. A bath was a measure of liquid, perhaps about 22 liters, although scholars are not sure of its exact amount.

The writer of Kings describes in detail the works Solomon made for the temple. This basin was a huge water container for the service of the priests (2 Chronicles 4:6). Chronicles speaks of three thousand baths, and there are several possible explanations for the difference.

For today: God deserves the best of our effort and care. Just as the temple had water for cleansing, we can come near to God with humility, asking him to cleanse us and prepare us to serve him with sincerity.
exp.6:26:
Hiram, the craftsman of Solomon, made ten bronze stands for the temple. A stand was a base or wheeled cart that served as a support. Each one measured four cubits in length, four in width, and three in height. A cubit was roughly half a meter, though its exact measure is debated.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, describing in detail the building of the temple in Solomon's time. Earlier he mentions the great bronze basin, a huge vessel of water. These stands held up the fonts or washbasins used to wash what was offered in worship. Such order and care show that serving God was taken seriously.

For today: God is interested in the simple and the practical too. If you serve in small tasks, such as preparing, cleaning, or organizing, do them with care, because that too can be worship.
exp.6:28:
This verse describes the decoration of the ten bronze stands, which were bases or carts that held the water basins of the temple. On the panels, that is, the framed sections between the moldings (the borders or edges), lions, oxen, and cherubims had been engraved. Above and below the lions and oxen were additions made of thin work, which were ornaments in the form of hanging garlands, raised out from the surface but not very deep.

The book of Kings recounts the building of Solomon's temple in Jerusalem. The narrator describes in detail the work of the craftsman Hiram of Tyre, who made these bronze objects for worship. The basins were used for washing what was used in the sacrifices. The cherubims recall the presence of God; the exact meaning of the other animals is not explained here.

For today: God delights in what is well made and in what is beautiful. We can serve him with excellence and care, even in small tasks that are little seen.
exp.6:30:
This verse describes a detail of the bronze stand (the base) that held up one of the basins or laver stands of the temple. The mouth was the round opening at the top, which sat a cubit (about 45 centimeters, roughly) down into the crown or top of the stand. That crown measured a cubit and a half. The carved figures were engraved decorations, and the framed panels that surrounded them were square, not round.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing the work of Hiram, the bronze craftsman who labored for Solomon. The text details the construction of the temple with care. Some terms are hard to understand exactly, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God cares about the details of what is done for Him. We can serve Him with excellence and care even in small things, whether at work, at home, or in the church, because nothing done with love for Him is insignificant.
exp.6:31:
It describes that each bronze stand for the temple basins had four wheels, placed beneath the frames or panels. The axles of the wheels came out of the same stand, that is, they formed one piece with it. Each wheel measured a cubit and a half, about 65 to 70 centimeters, though the exact measure is debated.

Here the narrator describes the work of Hiram, the bronze craftsman whom Solomon brought from Tyre. The text details the furnishings of the temple to show the care and excellence with which everything was made for the worship of God. The passage does not say here in detail exactly what these movable stands were used for.

For today: God pays attention to details and values work done well. What we do with care, even what no one sees, can be a way of honoring him.
exp.6:32:
This verse says that the wheels of the temple stands were made like those of a chariot. They had axletrees (the central bar), spokes (the rods), naves (the central hub where the axle goes), and felloes (the outer rims). Everything was molten, that is, bronze melted and poured into molds.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, describing in detail Solomon's work for the temple. These stands with wheels supported the bronze basins, which were used in the temple service. The author shows the care and quality of the work. Some details of these pieces are difficult to reconstruct with exactness.

For today: God values work done well, even in small things. We can serve him with diligence in what we do each day, without thinking that something is too simple to matter.
exp.6:33:
This verse describes one of the bronze stands that Hiram made for the temple. At each corner there was a piece that stuck out, the four corners each having one, like a small support or ledge. The stands were not attached afterward; these supports were part of the same piece, cast together with it.

The book of Kings tells how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. The writer gives very exact details about the items that the craftsman Hiram of Tyre made. These stands held the bronze basins used for washing. Scholars are not sure exactly how each detail looked, but the text shows the care with which everything was made.

For today: God pays attention to details and to work done well. We can serve him with diligence in small things, without thinking that anything is unimportant, and do our tasks with unity and dedication.
exp.6:34:
It says that the top of the base, that is, the bronze stand or cart that held a basin for water, had a round rim half a cubit high (about 25 centimeters). On that rim there were moldings (raised decorations) and bands (strips or borders), and everything was made from the same piece of metal, with no parts attached.

It is part of the description that the book of Kings gives of the building of the temple in the time of Solomon. The narrator describes in detail the work of the craftsmen, who made ten stands for the service of the temple. Some technical details of these verses are hard to understand exactly, and scholars explain them in various ways.

For today: God values work done well, even in small and hidden things. We can carry out our daily tasks with care and integrity, as a way of honoring him.
exp.6:35:
It says that Hiram, the craftsman, carved into the panels and the frames of the stands (the little bronze carts or bases) figures of cherubim, lions, and palm trees. He spaced them out well, according to the room in each part, and also added other decorations around them.

This is a narrative passage, not a speech. The author of the book describes the works of Solomon's temple. These ten stands held bronze basins for the service of the temple. The details show the care and beauty with which everything was made. Scholars discuss the exact meaning of some Hebrew words, but the general idea is clear.

For today: God values work done with care, even in small things. Today you can do your tasks, even when no one notices, with order and excellence, as an offering to God.
exp.6:36:
Verse 37 says that Solomon made ten stands, which were bronze bases or carts to hold the basins. All of them were cast in the same way, with the same measure and the same carved design.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings describes the building of the temple in Jerusalem. He gives detailed accounts of the temple furnishings, and the basins were used to wash items used in the sacrifices. The ten stands are said to be identical, and the text does not explain why. Some believe this shows order and care in the worship of God.

For today: God values order and care in what we do for Him. We can serve Him with steadiness and diligence, even in small tasks that no one sees.
exp.6:37:
This verse tells how Hiram, the craftsman from Tyre, made ten large bronze basins for the temple. Each one measured four cubits (about 1.8 meters, although the exact measure is debated) and could hold forty baths (about 800 liters, according to common calculations). Each basin was set on one of the ten stands, which were like carts or bases with wheels.

It is part of the historical account of the building of Solomon's temple. The narrator describes the temple's furnishings in detail. These basins were used for washing, according to 2 Chronicles 4:6, the things used for the burnt offering. The detail shows the care taken in preparing the place of worship.

For today: God values cleanliness and order in our relationship with him. We can ask ourselves what we need to wash clean in our lives, such as attitudes or habits, before coming to pray with sincerity.
exp.6:40:
It says that Hiram made two pillars of bronze for the temple. On top of each one he put a chapiter, which is the decorative piece at the top, shaped like a round bowl or a cup. He also made two networks, which is a kind of adorned mesh, to cover those chapiters.

It is part of the account of how Solomon built the temple. The narrator lists in detail the work of the craftsman Hiram, who came from Tyre. The pillars stood at the entrance of the temple. The texts do not explain their exact meaning with certainty, and some think they symbolized firmness or the presence of God.

For today: God notices the details of what is done for Him. We can serve Him with excellence in small tasks, such as preparing a lesson or cleaning the church, knowing that nothing done with love for Him goes unnoticed.
exp.6:41:
This verse describes a detail of the work of Hiram, the bronze craftsman. Four hundred pomegranates decorated the two networks, in two rows for each network. Those networks covered the two bowls that were on top of the pillars, the round parts shaped like a cup or ball at the top of the columns. A "network" here is an interwoven ornament, like a bronze mesh.

It is part of the list of what Hiram made for Solomon's temple. The account has no speaking character; the narrator carefully counts off the finished works. The two pillars stood at the entrance of the temple. The exact meaning of the pomegranates is not known for certain; some think they symbolized abundance or beauty, but the text does not explain it.

For today: God cares about details and about work done well. Do your everyday tasks with care, as an offering to Him, even when no one notices them.
exp.6:43:
This verse mentions two pieces of the temple: a "sea" and twelve oxen under it. The "sea" was an enormous bronze basin full of water, called that because of its great size. It rested on twelve ox figures.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He makes an inventory of what Hiram, the craftsman from Tyre, made for the temple of King Solomon. The details show the care with which the place of worship was prepared. According to 2 Chronicles 4:6, the water served for the priests to wash themselves. The number twelve could recall the tribes of Israel, although the text does not explain it.

For today: God is concerned with cleanliness and order in our relationship with him. We can set aside time to draw near to him with sincerity, asking him to cleanse our hearts.
exp.6:45:
This verse says that King Solomon had all the bronze objects of the temple cast in the plain of the Jordan, in clay ground between two places called Succoth and Zarthan (in other versions, Zeredathah or Zarethan). Casting means melting the metal and pouring it into molds.

Here the narrator of the book is describing the building of the temple. The objects were made by the craftsman Hiram, at Solomon's commission. That ground was probably used because the clay was suitable for making the molds, although the text does not give the exact reason. The detail shows the care and effort behind the work.

For today: serving God deserves our best effort, even in hidden or unremarkable tasks. What we do with dedication and honesty, God sees and values.
exp.6:46:
Solomon did not weigh the bronze of all the furnishings of the temple, because there were so many that it was impossible.

It is the narrator of Kings who speaks, summarizing the great work of Hiram, the craftsman from Tyre, for the temple. The objects were cast in the Jordan valley, in clay ground. The author wants to highlight the enormous abundance of material and the scale of the project. The text says nothing more about why they stopped weighing it, so it is best not to speculate.

God deserves our best, and sometimes his work goes beyond our calculations. We can serve him with generosity and devotion, without keeping petty accounts, trusting that he values the heart with which we give.
exp.6:47:
This verse says that Solomon had made all the articles that were to be used inside the temple. It mentions a golden altar and a golden table where the bread of the presence was placed, that is, the bread set before God as a continual offering.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book of Kings, who describes in detail Solomon's work when the temple was finished. Shortly before, he tells us there were so many metal objects that Solomon stopped weighing them. The account emphasizes the value, the care, and the beauty with which the place where Israel would worship God was prepared.

For today: if Solomon gave his best to the temple, we can offer God our best of time, talents, and affection, not what is left over. It is about giving with sincerity, not for show.
exp.6:48:
This verse says that Solomon placed ten lampstands of very pure gold in front of the inner sanctuary, the most holy place: five on the right side and five on the left. They had flowers (ornaments shaped like flowers), lamps, and snuffers, which were tongs for trimming the wicks and keeping the light burning.

The author of the book tells how the temple that Solomon built was furnished. Here he describes the gold objects used for worship. God does not speak here, nor does any character; it is the account of what was made. The lampstands gave light in the holy place, and the text highlights the care and richness with which everything was made to honor God.

For today: if God deserves the best, we can give Him our attention and sincere effort, even in small things, such as tending the wick of a lamp. May our prayer, our service, and our time with Him not be what is left over, but something done with care.
exp.6:49:
This verse lists more objects of pure gold for the temple: pitchers, bowls, cups, small spoons, and censers. Even those pieces, both for the inner house (the most holy place) and for the entrance of the temple, were made of gold.

It is part of the account in the book of Kings about Solomon's work. The narrator describes in detail how the temple was finished. The objects served worship: offerings, incense, and daily service. The text emphasizes the value and care given to what was dedicated to God.

For today: God takes an interest in the great and in the small. We can offer him our best in simple things, such as a sincere prayer, a job well done, or quiet service, without thinking that anything is too small for him.
exp.6:50:
This verse closes the account of the building of the temple. It says that Solomon finished all he had set out to do for the house of the Lord. Then he brought in the offerings that his father David had set apart for God: the silver, the gold, and the vessels. He placed them among the treasuries, that is, the storerooms of the temple.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who sums up Solomon's achievement after describing in detail the golden furnishings and utensils. What stands out is that Solomon did not start from scratch: he carried on the desire and the preparation of David. The Bible's books do not explain every detail, but here we see a work that passed from father to son.

For today: what we do for God often rests on the effort of others who came before us. We can give thanks for their faithfulness and, at the same time, prepare something for those who will come after, through offerings, prayer, and steady service.
exp.7:2:
This verse tells that all the leaders of Israel came to Jerusalem, and that the priests lifted the ark to carry it. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence and held the tablets of the law. The elders are the respected heads and authorities of each tribe.

Here the narrator of the book describes how King Solomon finished the temple and gathered the people. He wanted to move the ark from the city of David (Zion) to its new place in the temple. This took place in the seventh month, during a festival time. It is notable that the priests carried the ark, as the law directed.

For today: when something important must be done for God, it is good to do it together and in order, with his presence at the center. Before planning or building, ask yourself: am I giving God first place?
exp.7:4:
Here, before the ark, King Solomon and the whole congregation of Israel who had gathered with him offered sacrifices of sheep and oxen so many that they could not be counted. The people had come together around the king in a time of celebration.

The narrator of the book of Kings describes the dedication of the temple. Solomon brought the ark of the covenant to its place in the temple, and the people marked the occasion with offerings. The ark represented God's presence with Israel. The text does not give us the exact number of animals, but the image of countless offerings points to great joy and gratitude.

Today we can learn to receive God's presence with gratitude and generosity. Before asking him for anything, we can give thanks and offer him the best of our time, affection, and resources.
exp.7:5:
This verse tells that the priests placed the ark of the covenant of the Lord in its permanent place inside the temple: the inner sanctuary, which is the most holy place, the innermost and most sacred room. It was set under the wings of two cherubim, figures of heavenly beings made for that place.

The passage describes the dedication of the temple that Solomon built. After years of the ark being kept in tents and other places, it finally rests in a permanent house. The narrator of the book emphasizes that everything was done in order, with the priests in charge and all the people present, offering countless sacrifices.

For today: God deserves a central place in our lives, not a leftover one. We can ask ourselves what occupies the center of our heart and of our home, and set aside a fixed time each day to listen to him in prayer and in his Word.
exp.7:15:
Ever since the day God brought his people Israel out of Egypt, this verse recalls, he had not chosen any city among the tribes of Israel in which to build a temple where his name would dwell. He had chosen David to rule over his people.

Solomon, the king, is speaking during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He turns to the people, blesses them, and reviews what God said to his father David. He wants to show that the temple was not a human idea, but fulfills a promise and a decision of God.

For today: God is the one who chooses the place, the timing, and the manner of his work. We may make plans with a good heart, but it is wise to ask him first and to wait for his direction with humility and trust.
exp.7:17:
This verse says that God spoke to David and told him he did well to desire to build a temple for his name.

The one speaking is Solomon, on the day he dedicates the temple in Jerusalem. He explains to the people that his father David wanted to build the house, but God did not allow it; that task would fall to his son. Solomon recalls that God kept his promise. Even so, God recognized the value of David's desire, even though it was not David himself who carried it out.

For today: God looks at the heart, not only at the results. If you have wanted to serve Him and were unable to accomplish it, your sincere intention is not lost. Trust that He can use others, or another time, to complete what He began in you.
exp.7:18:
God tells David that he will not build the temple. Instead, his son, the one who will come from David's own descendants, will build it for God's name.

Solomon is speaking at the dedication of the temple. He reminds the people that David had wanted to build it and that God approved of that desire, even though the task would fall to someone else. Solomon makes clear that what the people now see fulfilled is God's promise, not simply his own accomplishment.

For today: God values the good desires of our hearts, even when we do not live to see them fulfilled. We can serve with joy, prepare the way, and trust that God will use others to finish what we began.
exp.7:24:
Solomon asks God to keep the promise he made to his father David: that a descendant of David would never fail to sit on the throne of Israel. But he adds a condition: that his children watch over their way and live in God's presence as David did. "Keep" means to make good on what was promised; "a man" means a male descendant; "walk before me" means to live with faithfulness and obedience.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple, in front of all the people. He has just acknowledged that God has been faithful to David, and now he relies on that faithfulness to ask that the promise continue. God's word becomes the foundation of his prayer.

For today: when you pray, rely on what God has already promised in his Word. And remember that his promises also call us to a faithful life, not only to receive.
exp.7:26:
Solomon asks in amazement whether God can truly dwell on the earth. He says that neither the heavens nor the heaven of heavens, the highest and most vast skies, can contain God. So much less, then, can the temple he built.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem, before the people. He has just asked God to keep his promise to David. He acknowledges that God is infinite, yet he still asks God to hear the prayers offered toward that place, where God said his name would be.

For today: God is greater than any place or idea we have of Him, and yet He wants to hear us. We can pray with humility and confidence, knowing that we do not need a special building to speak with Him.
exp.7:28:
Solomon asks that God would watch carefully over the temple, "night and day", that is, at all times. He reminds God that this is the place where God said, "My name shall be there". And he asks God to hear the prayer that his servant, meaning Solomon himself, makes in that place.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. Shortly before, he admits that even the highest heavens cannot contain God, so how much less a building. Still, he trusts that God draws near to his people and listens when they pray toward that place. His request opens a series of prayers for forgiveness and help.

For today: God does not live confined to a building, but he does want us to seek him. You can pray with confidence in any place, remembering that God is great, and yet he is attentive to your simple cry.
exp.7:31:
It says God hears from heaven and acts as a just judge. It asks that he deal with the wicked by letting the consequences of their actions fall back on their own head. And it asks that he declare the innocent right and give them what their righteousness deserves. The word "wicked" refers to the one who lives without reverence for God. To "justify" means to declare someone righteous.

King Solomon speaks here at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He is praying that God will respond when someone has a conflict with a neighbor and must swear an oath before the altar. Solomon knows that only God sees the truth of the heart, so he asks God to do justice where people cannot see it.

For today: when you suffer injustice and cannot prove the truth, hand the case over to God in prayer. He sees everything and judges with justice. That helps you not to seek revenge and to live with integrity.
exp.7:32:
If Israel's people are beaten down by their enemies because they have sinned against God, there is a way back. That way is to turn back to God, acknowledge his name, pray, plead, and make supplication in the temple.

Solomon speaks in the prayer at the temple's dedication. He is asking that God hear his people when they fail and repent. The temple is presented as a place of prayer, and the text does not say that God is confined there, since Solomon says God hears from heaven.

For today: when we fail or feel we have lost ground, we do not have to hide our error. We can return to God with humility, admit what we did, and ask him sincerely for forgiveness and help.
exp.7:33:
Here Solomon asks God to hear from heaven when the people, defeated by their enemies because of sin, repent. He pleads that God forgive that sin and bring them back to the land he gave to their fathers.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He is praying aloud before all Israel. He presents to God various cases in which the people might fail and need mercy. Here he has in mind a military defeat, and some understand it to include exile, although the text speaks of falling before the enemies and returning to the land.

For today: when we fail, God invites us to return without hiding anything. Acknowledging the mistake, asking for forgiveness, and coming back to Him opens the way to restoration. His mercy is still greater than our fall.
exp.7:35:
This verse asks that God hear from heaven, forgive the sin of his servants and of all Israel, and teach them the good way in which they should walk. It also asks that he send rain on the land he gave them as an inheritance. "Inheritance" refers to a possession that is received as a gift and passed down to the children.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple. He prays for the people, thinking of a time when there is sin and God shuts up the heavens so that no rain falls. If the people then repent, he asks that God restore them. Here rain is a sign of blessing, and its absence is a form of discipline.

For today: when you fail or go through a difficulty, do not turn away from God. Come to him sincerely, acknowledge your mistake, and ask him for forgiveness and direction. He not only forgives; he also wants to teach you how to walk well.
exp.7:39:
This verse says that God forgives and answers prayers so that the people will fear Him all the days they live in the land that God gave to their ancestors. "Fear" here means to respect God with reverence and trust, not to live in dread. The phrase about the land refers to the land itself, the ground on which they live. "Fathers" refers to the ancestors of Israel.

Solomon, the king, speaks in the prayer at the dedication of the temple. He asks that God hear whoever prays with a wounded heart, turning toward that house. His desire is that God's mercy will lead the people to live in reverence and faithfulness toward Him.

For today: when God forgives you or answers you, let that draw you closer to Him rather than toward indifference. Thank Him today for a prayer He has answered, and ask that your life show reverence and obedience to Him.
exp.7:41:
It says that the foreigner, who lives far away and is not part of Israel, will hear of the greatness of God, of his strong hand and his outstretched arm, which are ways of speaking of his power and his acts of rescue. Moved by this, he comes to pray in the temple.

Solomon is the one speaking, in the prayer when he dedicates the temple he built in Jerusalem. He asks God to listen also to the foreigners who come seeking him. In this way, the desire is that all peoples come to know and honor God, not only Israel.

For today: God has an open heart toward everyone. We can speak simply of what God has done in our lives and welcome with kindness anyone who comes seeking him, no matter where they come from.
exp.7:42:
Here it is asked that God hear from heaven, where he dwells, the prayer of a foreigner and grant what he asks. The goal is that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name, revere him as Israel does, and know that this temple belongs to him. "Fear" here means to revere and honor God. The phrase "dwelling place" refers to the place where God lives, heaven.

King Solomon speaks during the prayer at the dedication of the temple. He had heard of a great and powerful God, and he asks that the one who is not an Israelite also be able to draw near to him. From the beginning, the temple was meant to show God to the nations, not only to Israel.

Today we can remember that God hears anyone who seeks him sincerely. We can treat with respect and kindness those who come from afar or are different, and invite them to know God.
exp.7:43:
If your people go out to battle against their enemy, wherever you send them, and pray to the Lord toward the city you have chosen and toward the house I have built for your name, this verse says that God will hear them. It is the Israelites, going out to fight, who are praying while following the path God himself sends them on, facing toward Jerusalem, the chosen city, and toward the temple.

King Solomon is speaking during the prayer for the dedication of the temple. He is asking God to answer his people in many different situations: war, sin, drought, and others. Praying toward the temple showed trust in God's presence and in his promise. Solomon knows that God does not live in a building, since just before this he says that the heavens are God's dwelling place.

For today: before facing a struggle or a difficult decision, pray and ask God for direction. Trust that he listens to those who seek him with humility, even when you do not see the result right away.
exp.7:45:
It says that if the people of Israel sin against God, and God becomes angry and allows their enemies to take them captive and carry them away to another land, whether far or near, there is still hope. In the middle of that sentence stands a clear truth: there is no one who does not sin. The word "angry" means upset, and "deliver them" means letting them fall into the hands of the enemy.

King Solomon is speaking in the prayer he offers at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks that if the people fail and suffer the consequences, God will listen when they repent and pray. The verses that follow show that sincere repentance is what opens the door to forgiveness.

For today: we all fail, so we do not have to pretend we are perfect. When you make a mistake, do not hide from God or sink into guilt. Return to Him honestly and wholeheartedly, trusting that He listens.
exp.7:52:
This verse says that God chose Israel and set them apart from all the other peoples of the earth to be his own, as his inheritance, his most precious possession. God had said this through Moses when he brought their ancestors out of Egypt.

King Solomon is speaking at the end of his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He reminds God of his promise and his past care for them. He builds on what God has already done as he asks God to hear his people when they cry out to him.

For today: when you pray, remember what God has already done for you and for his people. His past faithfulness gives you confidence to ask him for help today. Learn to pray with gratitude and with firmness, relying on his promises and not only on your needs.
exp.7:54:
This verse says that Solomon, after praying, stood up and blessed all the people of Israel. He did it speaking loudly so that everyone could hear him. "Assembly" means the crowd gathered together, and "blessed" means that he asked for God's good for them and spoke words of thanks and encouragement.

Solomon, king of Israel, is speaking at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He had just prayed on his knees, with his hands stretched toward heaven, asking God to hear his people. Now he turns from speaking to God to speaking to the people. Right away he praises the LORD because He kept the promises He had given through Moses.

For today: after praying, don't stop with your own needs. Use your voice to encourage others, to remind them of God's promises, and to give thanks for what He has done. A word of blessing can strengthen your family, your church, or your friends.
exp.7:55:
Solomon praises the Lord because he has given rest to Israel, that is, peace and quiet in the promised land. He says that God fulfilled what he had said, and that not one of his promises, given through Moses, has failed; none of them was left unfulfilled.

The king speaks just after dedicating the temple and praying on his knees before the altar. He stands up and blesses the whole people aloud. He looks back and recognizes that God was faithful for centuries, from Moses until that day. Then he will ask that God stay with them and turn their hearts to obey him.

For today: when you doubt God, remember how he has been faithful to you. Write down some promises that have already come true in your life, and give thanks to him out loud.
exp.7:56:
Solomon asks that God continue with his people as he was with their ancestors. The word "forsake" in the verse above means to abandon, and "leave" repeats the same idea: that God would not let them go or move away from them.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple, which had just been completed in Jerusalem. Standing, he blesses all Israel. Before that, he recalls that God kept every promise made through Moses. For that reason he dares to ask with confidence that this faithfulness continue. The verses that follow show that he also asks for a heart inclined to obey God.

For today: when you face a change or a new season, remember how God has sustained you before and ask for his company with confidence. And, like Solomon, ask him also for a heart willing to follow him, because his presence and our obedience walk together.
exp.7:58:
Solomon asks that his words of prayer remain constantly before God, day and night. He wants God to maintain the cause of his servant, the king, and the cause of all Israel, giving them what they need "at all times, as the matter shall require." The phrase about maintaining the cause means that God would defend them and see that they receive justice.

Solomon is finishing his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has just asked that God not abandon his people and that he would incline their hearts to obey him. His desire is that all the nations would know that the Lord alone is God.

For today: we can pray with confidence, believing that God hears and answers in his time. While we wait, it is good to also ask for a faithful heart, not only for quick solutions.
exp.7:64:
This verse tells how Solomon held a great feast together with all Israel, before the Lord. It was a huge gathering, coming from the northern border of the land, at the entrance of Hamath, down to the southern border, the river of Egypt. The feast lasted seven days and then seven more days, fourteen days in all.

This is the account of the narrator of the book of Kings, after Solomon had dedicated the temple in Jerusalem. The fourteen days probably included the dedication and the Feast of Tabernacles, though the text does not explain this in detail. When it ended, the people went home joyful and thankful for what God had done for David and for Israel.

For today: God delights when his people gather to celebrate and to give him thanks. Set aside time to give thanks together, with your church or your family, remembering with joy the good things God has done.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that God showed himself to Solomon again, that is, a second time, in the same way he had done before at Gibeon. The word "appeared" here speaks of God making himself present and speaking to him. In 1 Kings 3 it is told that this happened in a dream. Here the text does not make clear whether it was also in a dream.

The narrator tells this after Solomon had finished building the temple and his palace. God answers the prayer Solomon made when he dedicated the temple. Then he reminds him that his blessing depends on walking in faithfulness, as David did.

For today: God does not stay silent before someone who prays to him sincerely. After reaching a goal, it is a good time to return to him, give thanks, and ask him to keep us faithful, because what matters is not the finished works but an obedient heart.
exp.8:3:
God tells Solomon that if he walks before Him as David did, with a sincere and upright heart, doing everything He has commanded, then a promise will come. Walk means to live and conduct oneself. Integrity of heart is honesty and loyalty without deceit. Uprightness is righteousness and justice. Statutes and judgments are the laws and rules God gave to His people.

The Lord speaks, appearing to Solomon a second time, after Solomon had finished building the temple and prayed to dedicate it. God accepts the temple and promises His presence. Then He adds a condition: the promise of the throne depends on faithfulness. The verses that follow also warn about the consequences of turning away from God and worshiping other gods.

For today: God does not look only at what we do on the outside, but at a sincere heart. Today you can ask yourself: is my obedience to God honest and steady, even when no one sees me? Ask Him for help to live consistently in your home, your work, and your decisions.
exp.8:6:
If the people turn away from God, he will remove them from the land he gave them. He will also reject the temple that he set apart for his name. Israel would become a proverb and a byword, meaning an example that others talk about and mock.

God speaks to Solomon a second time, after he had finished building the temple and dedicating it. He promises to establish his throne if he remains faithful, but he warns of the consequences of idolatry. The temple was beautiful, but it did not guarantee protection if the people's hearts drifted away from God.

For today: privileges, the church, or good customs do not replace sincere faithfulness. It is worth asking ourselves whether our hearts truly still follow God, and returning to him with humility when we have grown careless.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that if Israel turns away from God, people who see the ruins of the temple and the land will ask why that happened. The answer will be clear: they forsook the Lord, who brought their fathers out of Egypt, they took hold of other gods, worshipped them, and served them. For that reason God allowed this evil to come upon them.

God speaks to Solomon after the dedication of the temple. It is a warning: the promise depended on the people and their king remaining faithful. The temple was beautiful, but it would not protect them if their hearts went after other gods.

For today: good beginnings and religious activity do not replace faithfulness day by day. Ask yourself what things compete with God for your trust, and return to Him with gratitude, remembering what He has already done for you.
exp.8:9:
This verse marks a point in time: twenty years had passed since Solomon began building. In that time he had built two important structures, the temple and his palace.

Here the book's narrator speaks. Earlier, God had warned Solomon that if the people abandoned him, the temple would be left in ruins. Now the account picks up the story again and tells how Solomon paid Hiram, king of Tyre, with twenty cities for the materials and the gold. Hiram was not pleased with them. Scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: finishing a great work is good, but it is not enough. What matters most is staying faithful to God. Check whether, among your projects and your accounts, you still put him first.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that Hiram, king of Tyre, had sent Solomon one hundred twenty talents of gold. A talent was a very large unit of weight; the exact amount is debated, but it was a great deal of gold. The phrase "had sent" indicates that the shipment had already been made before this episode.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings. This verse appears between two scenes: Hiram is disappointed with the cities Solomon gave him, and then it is explained how Solomon gathered resources for his building projects. Hiram's gold helped with that work. Scholars do not agree on whether the cities were a payment for the gold, a gift, or something else; the text does not make this clear.

For today: promises and agreements matter. When we receive help from others, it is good to be thankful and generous, and to fulfill what we have promised with fairness, without letting the dealings become a cause of resentment.
exp.8:14:
This verse explains how Solomon paid for his great building works. It speaks of a forced levy, which here means compulsory labor that the king demanded from the people. With that labor he built the house of the Lord, his own palace, Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, and the cities of Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer. We do not know for certain what Millo was; it was probably a filling or a fortification in Jerusalem.

The author of the book, whose name we do not know, is the one speaking. After describing the arrangement with Hiram, he explains how Solomon managed to raise so many buildings. These cities protected the kingdom.

For today: even good works, such as the temple, come at a cost to people. If you have authority, take care that your projects do not abuse those who work alongside you.
exp.8:15:
This verse tells how the king of Egypt attacked the city of Gezer, captured it and set it on fire. He also killed the Canaanites who lived there and handed the city over as a gift to his daughter, who was Solomon's wife.

The narrator of the book explains how Solomon came to hold Gezer, a strategic city, and why he had to rebuild it. We do not know for certain which pharaoh this was, since the text does not give his name. This detail appears in the middle of the list of Solomon's works. It shows his power and his alliances, although marrying the daughter of a pharaoh was also a delicate step for a king of Israel.

For today: what looks like prosperity can carry hidden risks. Before accepting a gift or an alliance, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to God or pulls you away from Him.
exp.8:16:
It says that King Solomon rebuilt the city of Gezer and Beth-horon the nether. "Rebuilt" means that he repaired them or raised them up again, since Gezer had been burned. Beth-horon the nether was a city in an area on the route toward Jerusalem.

The one telling this is the author of the book of Kings, who explains how the labor and the tribute of the people were used. Gezer had been destroyed by the pharaoh of Egypt and then given as a wedding gift to the daughter who married Solomon. Solomon rebuilt and strengthened it, probably because of its strategic value for defending the kingdom.

We must take care of what already exists, not only start new things. Solomon raised up what was in ruins. Today we can ask ourselves which relationship, habit, or service needs to be restored with patience, and ask God for wisdom to do it.
exp.8:18:
This verse continues the list of Solomon's building projects. It says that he also built or fortified the cities where he kept supplies and provisions. In addition, he set up cities for his war chariots and for his horsemen. And he built whatever he wished in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout his kingdom.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings summarizes Solomon's reign after finishing the temple and the palace. He wants to show the extent of his power, his wealth, and his ability to organize a large kingdom. The verses that follow also speak of forced labor from peoples who were not Israelites.

For today: building and planning are good, but it is worth asking ourselves what we seek through them. Achievements can give us a sense of security, but only God is our true strength. Let us ask him that our projects honor him and serve others.
exp.8:19:
This verse begins to name the peoples whom Solomon put to work: the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. They were people of Canaan who continued living in the land and did not belong to the people of Israel. The sentence continues in the next verse, where it says that Solomon forced them to serve as tribute laborers, that is, with forced labor.

The narrator of the book of Kings describes Solomon's great works: storage cities, chariot cities, and cavalry cities, as well as his building projects in Jerusalem and Lebanon. It explains who did that labor. The text makes clear that the Israelites were not made into servants but held military and command posts. Some scholars see here a partial fulfillment of the command not to live among these peoples, though others note that the obedience was incomplete.

For today: power and success can become unjust if we neglect the weakest people. Let us ask God that our progress never be built at the expense of others.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that Solomon did not put any Israelites to work as slaves or in forced labor. The Israelites held other posts: they were soldiers, the king's attendants, princes, captains, commanders of the chariots, or horsemen. The servants mentioned here are the king's attendants.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, whose name we do not know. He recounts how Solomon carried out his great works with labor drawn from the peoples who remained in the land. There is a difficulty: in 1 Kings 5:13 it speaks of a levy of Israelites to work in Lebanon. Some think this was a temporary service, different from slavery, but there is no single explanation that is certain.

Today, this text invites us to look at how we treat those who work for us. No work, however good it may seem, justifies abusing people. Paying fairly and respecting the dignity of others honors God.
exp.8:24:
It says that Solomon offered sacrifices three times a year on the altar he had built for the Lord. They were burnt offerings, which were burned whole as a complete giving of oneself to God, and peace offerings, offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving. He also burned incense on the altar that was before the Lord. He did all this after he had finished the temple.

This is the account of the writer of Kings, who summarizes Solomon's work. After speaking of his great buildings and projects, the text reminds us that the temple was indeed used for worship. The three yearly feasts (Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles) are probably the ones meant, although the text does not name them. Some scholars debate how the incense fits with the role of the priests.

For today: it is not enough to build or accomplish things for God; we must worship him with consistency. Set aside regular times to give him thanks and to surrender your life to him.
exp.8:25:
He says that King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, a port near Eloth, on the shore of the Red Sea (once called the Sea of Reeds), in the land of Edom. "Ships" are the vessels, and "shore" is the edge of the sea where the land meets the water.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, the one who tells the history of Israel. After finishing the temple and his other works, Solomon expands his kingdom through sea trade. The next verse says that Hiram, king of Tyre, sent expert sailors, and they brought back a great deal of gold from Ophir. Where Ophir was is not known for certain; scholars have several opinions.

God may give us resources and opportunities, but it is wise to use them with humility and wisdom. Solomon worked with others, making use of Hiram's experience. Today we too can learn from people with more knowledge, and remember that everything we accomplish is meant to honor God and serve others.
exp.9:1:
She says that the queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with a large retinue, with camels carrying spices, a great deal of gold, and precious stones. When she met Solomon, she confidently shared with him everything she had in her heart, that is, her doubts and questions.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells that she had heard of Solomon's fame, which was tied to the name of the Lord, and wanted to test it with difficult questions. It is not known for certain where Sheba was; many place it in southern Arabia, though some suggest other regions. Her costly journey shows how much she valued wisdom.

If we truly seek answers, it is worth making an effort and being honest. We can bring to God, and to wise and trustworthy people, everything that weighs on our hearts, without pretending or hiding our doubts.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that the queen of Sheba observed two things closely: the wisdom of Solomon and the house he had built. It is the beginning of a list of things that left her deeply impressed.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The queen had traveled to Jerusalem with valuable gifts, because she had heard of Solomon's fame and wanted to test it for herself. Sheba was a distant kingdom; scholars do not fully agree on its exact location, and it is often linked with southern Arabia or with Africa. She did not settle for rumors: she wanted to see and to ask for herself.

For today: Seek the truth with humility and with a desire to learn. Ask, observe, and let wisdom teach you. And remember that Jesus said there is someone greater than Solomon (Matthew 12:42).
exp.9:4:
This verse tells what the queen of Sheba saw in Solomon's court: the food on his table, how his servants sat, the order and the clothing of those who attended him, his cupbearers (the ones who served the king's table, or his cupbearers), and the burnt offerings (offerings burned up) that he offered in the temple. She was left breathless, that is, overwhelmed and without breath from amazement.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. He tells that the queen traveled from Sheba to test Solomon with hard questions. When she saw his wisdom and his kingdom, she understood that what she had heard was true.

For today: the queen noticed the order, the service, and the worship as signs of wisdom. We can ask ourselves whether our lives, in our daily routines and in the way we worship God, show something of his goodness to those around us.
exp.9:6:
She says she did not believe the reports about Solomon until she came and saw them with her own eyes. When she arrived, she found that she had not even been told half. The king's wisdom and prosperity far exceeded the report she had heard.

The queen of Sheba, who traveled from far away to meet Solomon and test him with hard questions, has just seen his table, his servants, his clothing, and his sacrifices at the temple, and she was amazed. Her praise ends by turning to the LORD, who set Solomon on the throne.

For today: do not rely only on what others say about God. Draw near to Him, read His Word, and seek Him personally. Whoever knows Him closely discovers that what they had heard was only a small part.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that the queen of Sheba blesses God, because He took pleasure in Solomon and set him as king over Israel. She affirms that God has always loved Israel and for that reason gave them a king. The king's task is to do judgment and justice, that is, to govern with uprightness and give each person what is due to them. "Delighted in you" means that God accepted you gladly, and "throne" is the seat of the king.

She is the queen of Sheba, a foreign visitor who came to test Solomon with difficult questions. After seeing his wisdom and his kingdom, she is amazed. She acknowledges that what she had heard was small compared with what she saw. Her praise of the Lord is a recognition that this greatness comes from God.

For today: whoever holds authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, should remember that it is a charge from God, and use it to act with justice and uprightness.
exp.9:9:
This verse tells that the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon a very generous gift: one hundred and twenty talents of gold, a great quantity of aromatic spices, and precious stones. The word "spices" here refers to spices and perfumes, which were worth a great deal in that time. A talent was a unit of weight; scholars calculate it was about 30 to 35 kilograms, though the exact figure is debated. The text emphasizes that never again came such an abundance of spices.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Kings. The queen had travelled to test Solomon's wisdom, and she was so impressed that she praised God for having placed him as king. Her gift expresses respect and gratitude, and it was also a form of courtesy between rulers.

For today: when we recognize what God has given us through others, gratitude should be accompanied by generosity. We can joyfully give time, help, or resources to honor the one who has blessed us.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and asked for. Besides that, he gave her gifts that came from his own generosity as a king. Afterward she returned to her own country with her servants. The word "gave" in the verse reflects the same idea of a king giving freely from his own generosity.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. He has just told of the visit of the queen of Sheba, who came to test Solomon's wisdom with difficult questions and was amazed. This verse closes her visit. The account then goes on to show Solomon's riches. It does not say exactly what she asked for, so it is not right to invent it.

For today: Solomon gave generously to the one who came seeking wisdom. God is also generous with those who seek him sincerely. We can ask him for wisdom and also learn to be generous toward others.
exp.9:15:
This verse tells that Solomon had two hundred shields made, which were large shields, made with plates of gold beaten out until they were thin layers. Six hundred shekels of gold were used in each shield. A shekel weighed about 11 grams, although exact calculations vary.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking, not Solomon. He is describing the enormous wealth of the kingdom at its best. These shields were kept in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, and they were more for display than for battle. The account shows the greatness of Solomon, but it also prepares the reader to see how that wealth would become a trap.

For today: Enjoy with gratitude what God gives you, but do not put your security in what looks valuable. Ask yourself which things give you a sense of strength, and surrender them to God.
exp.9:16:
It says that King Solomon had three hundred small shields made of hammered gold, beaten out into thin sheets. Three pounds of gold went into each one (in Hebrew, the unit is minas; its exact weight is calculated in different ways). He kept them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a building in his palace.

The account is told by an author we do not know, and it aims to show Solomon's great wealth and fame. These shields were more for luxury and ceremony than for battle. The text does not criticize them here, but it does show the splendor of a kingdom that would later be divided.

Today, this verse reminds us that gold and prestige shine, but they do not last. We can enjoy what God gives us without placing our security in it. Today, decide to trust God more than your possessions.
exp.9:17:
This verse tells that King Solomon had a very large throne made of ivory, which is the hard, white material from elephant tusks. Then he covered it with the finest gold, that is, gold of the highest quality. It was a unique and very luxurious throne.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings describes the wealth and fame of Solomon after the visit of the queen of Sheba. The gold shields and the throne show his power and splendor. The text simply reports it; other passages, such as Deuteronomy 17:16-17, warn kings against accumulating too much.

We can enjoy and give thanks for what God gives us, but we should take care that riches or prestige do not take the place that belongs to Him. Ask yourself today: what is it that truly holds my heart?
exp.9:19:
It says that on the six steps of Solomon's throne there were twelve lions, six on each side, one on each step. The text stresses that no other kingdom had a throne like it. The steps are the stairs leading up to the throne, and the phrase about the one side and the other means on one side and on the other.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking, not Solomon. He is describing the splendor of Solomon's reign, with ivory, gold, and riches brought from far away. The lions are often understood as a symbol of royal power and authority, although the text does not explain their meaning. It is a scene of glory, but the book later shows that Solomon turned away from God.

For today: greatness, wealth, and power impress us, but they do not replace a faithful heart. Ask God to place your trust in him and not in what you have or achieve.
exp.9:21:
It says that Solomon had large ships that sailed the sea, together with those of Hiram, king of Tyre. Every three years they returned from Tharshish loaded with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Today it is not known for certain where Tharshish was; some think of Spain, others of other distant lands.

It is the narrator of the book of Kings who speaks. He is showing Solomon's enormous wealth: the ivory throne, the gold dishes, and now trade with distant lands. The following verse clarifies that his greatness was a blessing from God, and that his wisdom attracted the whole world.

For today: everything we have, whether much or little, comes from the hand of God. We can thank him and use it wisely to bless others, without setting our hearts on riches.
exp.9:23:
This verse says that people from all the known world wanted to come before Solomon to hear his wisdom. The phrase about seeking an audience with him, meaning being in his presence, is not used in the verse above, so I will simply say that they came to seek an audience with him, that is, to be in his presence. The text makes clear that this wisdom was not only his own: God had put it in his heart.

It is the narrator of the book of Kings who speaks, describing the splendor of Solomon's reign. Earlier he mentions Solomon's riches and his ships; afterward, the gifts that were brought to him and his great army. It shows that God fulfilled what he had promised Solomon (1 Kings 3:12). Some note that the account also prepares the way for warnings about his later downfall.

For today: true wisdom is a gift from God. We can ask for it with humility (James 1:5) and use it to serve and bless others, not to show off.
exp.9:24:
Here, year after year, people from many places brought gifts to Solomon. They were objects of gold and of silver, clothing, weapons, perfumes and spices, horses and mules. Mules are beasts of burden. Gifts are presents.

The biblical account goes on describing the greatness of Solomon's reign. The verses before explain that the people of the land sought to hear his wisdom, which God had placed in his heart. The gifts show the prestige he had. The verses that follow speak of his chariots and horses, which sets the scene for seeing also the dangers of so much wealth and power.

For today: everything good we have, whether talent, work or possessions, comes from God and should be used with humility. True wisdom is worth more than riches, and we should take care that what we receive does not draw us away from Him.
exp.9:25:
It says that Solomon gathered a large force of war chariots and cavalry. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen. He stationed them in special cities for the chariots and also kept some with him in Jerusalem. The horsemen are those who ride on horseback.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, recounting the greatness of Solomon. It comes after the account of his wisdom and his riches. But the Law said that the king should not multiply horses or return to Egypt for them (Deuteronomy 17:16), and yet the text goes on to say that they were brought from Egypt. The text does not condemn it here, but it shows a warning sign.

For today: security and success can become a trap if they begin to replace trust in God. Ask yourself what you are leaning on most: your resources or God. Give thanks for what you have, but place your trust in Him.
exp.9:26:
It says that in Solomon's time silver was as common in Jerusalem as stones on the road. Cedars, a very valuable wood, were also as plentiful as the sycamore trees that grew everywhere in the fields.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He wants to show the enormous wealth of Solomon's kingdom, which came from gifts from other peoples and from trade. It is a way of saying that God kept His promise to bless him. But the text goes on to horses and chariots brought from Egypt, something the law of Moses warned kings not to do (Deuteronomy 17:16). For that reason many readers see here a warning sign.

For today: abundance can be a blessing from God, but it can also be a temptation to trust in what we have instead of in Him. Let us honestly ask ourselves where our hearts truly rest.
exp.10:0:
King Solomon, in addition to marrying the daughter of the Pharaoh of Egypt, loved many foreign women: women of Moab, Ammon, Edom, and Sidon, as well as Hittite women.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings. After describing Solomon's glory and wisdom, the account changes tone and shows his fall. The verses that follow explain that God had already warned Israel not to join themselves with these peoples, because they could turn their hearts toward other gods. The text points out that these marriages led Solomon to turn away from God.

For today: success and wisdom do not protect us from going astray. We should guard what influences we let into our hearts and obey God in small decisions, before they become great ones.
exp.10:2:
It says that Solomon had seven hundred wives of royal rank and three hundred concubines, who were secondary women within his household. The text states that these women turned his heart, meaning they led it away from the right path, drawing him away from God little by little.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who is evaluating Solomon's life. God had warned Israel not to join itself with peoples who worshiped other gods. Many royal marriages sealed political alliances, but here the account shows that those decisions came at a very serious spiritual cost, even for the wisest king.

For today: pay attention to the influences and relationships that most shape your heart. No one is so strong that they cannot be turned away little by little. Ask God for wisdom to choose well, and stay close to Him every day.
exp.10:5:
This verse says that Solomon did what God considered evil. He did not follow the Lord completely, as his father David had done. The phrase about going fully after the Lord means that he did not follow him with his whole heart, in a whole and steady way.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is evaluating the life of Solomon. In his old age, his many foreign wives gradually led him to worship other gods, such as Ashtoreth and Milcom. Afterward he built places of worship for them. The author compares him with David, not because David was perfect, but because his heart remained directed toward God.

For today: a divided heart rarely falls all at once. Examine which close influences are slowly pulling you away from God, and decide today to follow him with steadiness and not only at certain times.
exp.10:7:
He says that Solomon not only built places of worship for Chemosh and Molech, but also did the same for all his foreign wives. They burned incense and offered sacrifices to their own gods. A high place was an elevated site where worship took place, and the foreign women were wives from other peoples.

Here the narrator of the book, who tells the story of Israel, speaks. He explains how Solomon, already old, turned away. Earlier it says that his wives turned his heart. God had commanded the kings not to follow other gods, and so the account shows that this choice had serious consequences.

For today: let us take care with what we tolerate and support. Solomon did not only turn away himself; he allowed others to worship what drew him away from God. Today we can ask ourselves what influences we let in little by little, and return to God with sincerity.
exp.10:9:
This verse says that God had given Solomon a clear command: not to follow other gods. But Solomon did not keep what the Lord commanded him. The word "other" here refers to the gods of foreign nations, and "Lord" is the name of God.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, who explains why God became angry with Solomon. His foreign wives had led him to allow the worship of their gods, and his heart gradually turned away from God. This was serious because God had appeared to him twice. That is why the consequence follows: the kingdom would be divided.

For today: knowing what God says is not enough; we must obey him. Let us watch which things and which influences are winning our hearts, because drifting away usually begins little by little.
exp.10:10:
God speaks to Solomon and tells him that, because he did not keep his covenant and his commandments, he will take the kingdom away from him and give it to one of his servants, that is, to one who serves him.

The Lord speaks after Solomon, now old, allowed his many foreign wives to turn his heart toward worshiping other gods. God had already appeared to him twice and had warned him plainly. Even so, the judgment comes with mercy: it would not happen during Solomon's lifetime, because of the promise made to David. Later, the kingdom was divided.

For today: our hearts can drift away little by little, without our noticing. Let us be careful about the people we keep close and about what takes first place in our lives. Let us return to God soon and sincerely, for He is patient and wants to restore us.
exp.10:15:
This verse describes a detail from the past. It says that Joab and all Israel stayed six months in Edom, until they had cut off every male in that nation. Some scholars think it refers to the men old enough to fight, because Hadad and others escaped.

Context: the narrator of the book explains why Hadad became an enemy of Solomon. Years earlier, when David subdued Edom, Joab led a very violent campaign. Hadad, from the Edomite royal family, fled to Egypt as a boy. The text presents him as an adversary whom God allowed because of Solomon's unfaithfulness.

For today: violence leaves wounds that can last for generations. This invites us to seek peace, not hold on to resentment, and to remember that our decisions can affect others for a long time.
exp.10:17:
It says that Hadad and the men who fled left Midian and came to Paran. There they took other men with them and went on to Egypt, where the pharaoh received him very kindly. He gave him a house, appointed him provisions, and even gave him land. The phrase about appointing provisions means that he gave him a regular supply for living.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He tells how God allowed Hadad, a prince of Edom who survived Joab's campaign, to later become an adversary of Solomon. Earlier, Hadad had fled as a boy. The text does not explain every detail of his journey, but it shows that Egypt welcomed him.

For today: even when someone loses their home or family, God can open unexpected doors. It also reminds us that our decisions have consequences; Solomon turned away from God, and adversaries arose. It is wise to walk in faithfulness.
exp.10:19:
Adad the Edomite married the sister of Queen Tahpenes. She gave birth to Genubath, and the queen weaned him, that is, she raised him in Pharaoh's house. So Genubath grew up as one of the king's own sons.

The narrator of the book explains how God allowed adversaries to rise against Solomon, because Solomon had turned away from Him. Adad had fled as a boy when Edom was destroyed. In Egypt he was well received and started a family. About Genubath we know nothing more; the Bible mentions only this fact.

For today: God sees and uses long, hidden processes, in unexpected places. Trust that He governs history, and live faithfully, because our decisions also have consequences that become visible over the years.
exp.10:23:
It says that Rezon gathered a band of men and became their captain, after David defeated those of Zobah. Then they went to Damascus, settled there, and made him king.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He explains how God allowed Solomon to have adversaries, because Solomon turned away from Him by following other gods. Rezon had fled from his master, the king of Zobah, and now ruled in Damascus. He was a threat to Israel throughout Solomon's reign.
