For today: our decisions have consequences, even though they may take time to show. If we live in peace and success, let us not forget to thank God and to follow Him faithfully. When a difficulty comes, we can ask ourselves humbly whether there is something we should correct before Him.
exp.10:30:
Here the prophet Ahijah tells Jeroboam to take ten of the twelve pieces of the torn cloak. It is a sign of what God will do: he will take the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and give Jeroboam ten tribes.

The prophet Ahijah speaks in the name of God. Solomon had turned away from the Lord and had allowed the worship of false gods such as Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Molech. For this reason the division would come. God would leave one tribe to the family of David, because of the promise he made to David and because of Jerusalem, the city he chose.

For today: God sees when we give to other things the place that belongs only to him. Today you can ask yourself what things compete for your heart, and put him first again, knowing that he keeps his promises.
exp.10:32:
God says he is going to take ten tribes away from Solomon and give them to Jeroboam. The reason is that the people left him and worshiped false gods: Ashtoreth (also called Astarte) of the Sidonians, Chemosh of the Moabites, and Molech of the Ammonites. The words translated as "statutes" and "judgments" refer to his laws and commands. God compares this with David, who had remained faithful to him.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Ahijah, who delivers this message to Jeroboam. Earlier, Solomon had built places of worship for the gods of his foreign wives. Because of this, the kingdom is divided, though God preserves one tribe for the sake of David and Jerusalem.

For today: faithfulness to God does not stay in words; it shows in what we put first. Ask yourself what things compete for your heart, and ask God for help to return to him with sincerity.
exp.10:33:
God says that he will not take the whole kingdom away from Solomon while he lives. He will keep him as prince, that is, as the one who rules, all the days of his life. He will do this for the sake of David his servant, whom he chose, because David kept his commandments and his statutes.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ahijah to Jeroboam. Solomon had turned away from God and worshiped foreign gods, under the influence of his wives. Because of this, the kingdom would be divided. Even so, God shows mercy: the punishment would not come during Solomon's lifetime, but in the time of his son, out of honor for David's faithfulness.

Today we see that God is just, but also patient and faithful to his promises. Our decisions can affect our children, for good or for harm. Living faithfully to God leaves a spiritual inheritance that blesses those who come after us.
exp.10:35:
He says that God will leave one tribe to the son of Solomon, so that David, His servant, may always have a lamp before Him in Jerusalem. The lamp stands for a line of descendants that continues and keeps his memory alive. Jerusalem is the city that God chose to put His name there, that is, to be the place of His presence and worship.

God speaks through the prophet Ahijah to Jeroboam. Solomon had turned away from God, and for that reason the kingdom would be divided. Jeroboam would receive ten tribes. Even so, God does not abandon the promise He made to David. Some understand that the "one tribe" is Judah, and that Benjamin remained joined to it; the Bible tells it in different ways.

God corrects sin, but He also keeps His promises. If you have failed today, do not think that God has forgotten you. Return to Him with confidence.
exp.10:39:
This verse tells us that Solomon wanted to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam got up and fled to Egypt, where King Shishak received him. He stayed there until Solomon died. The word "sought" here means that Solomon tried or looked for a way to do it.

The one speaking in the earlier context is God, through the prophet Ahijah, who had promised Jeroboam that he would be king over ten tribes of Israel if he obeyed the Lord. Solomon found out and reacted violently. The text does not say how he found out, nor does it give more details. God had announced that he would divide the kingdom because of Solomon's unfaithfulness, but he also promised not to leave David's family forever.

For today: when God says something, resisting it with force or pride does not change his purpose. It is better to humble ourselves, listen, and obey him sincerely.
exp.11:0:
Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, went to Shechem. The verse notes that this place name appears in the verse as "Shechem," and that all Israel had gathered there to make him king. To make him king means to proclaim him and formally recognize him as the ruler. The phrase all Israel refers to the tribes of the people, represented by their leaders.

The narrator describes what happened after Solomon's death. Rehoboam was the heir, but the people still had to accept him. Shechem was an important place in Israel's history, and the gathering there shows that his reign depended on the approval of the tribes. What follows in the account reveals that tension existed, and that this tension would bring serious consequences.

For today: having authority is not enough; you also have to earn people's trust. If you lead a family, a job, or a church, listen with humility and seek to serve, not just to command.
exp.11:1:
This verse says that Jeroboam, son of Nebat, heard that all Israel had gathered in Shechem to make Rehoboam king. Jeroboam was in Egypt, where he had fled to escape King Solomon.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Solomon had died, and his son Rehoboam was about to be crowned. Earlier, 1 Kings 11 tells how Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, and for that reason Jeroboam took refuge in Egypt. The news reaches him there, and afterward the people send for him to speak with Rehoboam.

For today: God can watch over and prepare a person through years of waiting or exile. If you are in such a season, do not think that God has forgotten you. Trust and stay alert, but act with humility and wisdom when your opportunity comes.
exp.11:7:
He abandoned the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and asked the advice of the young men who had grown up with him and who now stood in his service. This verse says that he set aside the counsel of the older men, that is, the mature and experienced men who had advised him well. Instead, he asked the opinion of the young men, who were with him since childhood and were now serving him.

The people of Israel had just asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burdens that Solomon, his father, had placed on them. The elders, who had served Solomon, advised him to be a servant to the people and to speak to them with kind words. But Rehoboam preferred to listen to his young friends. The text does not explain all of his reasons, but what follows shows that this decision led to the division of the kingdom.

Today, it is wise to seek wise counsel, not only the kind that pleases us. Let us ask God for humility to listen to mature, honest people of good reputation, even when their words make us uncomfortable.
exp.11:8:
Rehoboam asks the young men he grew up with: "What answer should we give this people, who asked me to lighten the yoke that my father put on them?" A "yoke" was the wooden piece placed on oxen to make them pull a load; here it is a way of speaking about heavy labor and taxes.

Rehoboam, son of Solomon, has just become king. The people asked him for lighter treatment. First he listened to the elders, who advised him to serve the people with kind words. But he set that advice aside and sought the counsel of his young friends, who gave him a harsh answer.

Before deciding, it is worth asking ourselves whom we are listening to and why. Good counsel usually comes from someone with experience who seeks our good, not from someone who only tells us what flatters us or hardens our hearts.
exp.11:9:
The young men who grew up alongside Rehoboam tell him what to say to the people. The people were asking for relief from the burden, which is the heavy load of labor and taxes. His advisers suggest he speak harshly: "my little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins," meaning he will be stronger and more severe than Solomon.

Rehoboam had just been made king. The people, together with Jeroboam, asked him for gentler treatment. The elders had advised him to serve the people, but he left them and listened to his friends from his youth, who spoke with pride and without experience.

For today: before deciding something important, seek the counsel of wise and mature people, not only of those who tell you what pleases you. Humility and kindness build up; pride divides and destroys.
exp.11:10:
This verse says that Rehoboam, the new king, promises his people a heavier load than that of his father Solomon. The "yoke" is the wooden piece placed on oxen for work; here it means heavy labor and taxes. The "whips" were blows with a lash, and the "scorpions" were probably whips with metal points or knots that wounded more severely (some explain it this way, though it is not certain).

Rehoboam speaks to the people, who were asking for relief after the years of Solomon. He had listened to the elders, but preferred the advice of the young men he had grown up with. With these words he responds harshly and proudly, and this provoked the division of the kingdom.

For today: when you have authority at home, at work, or in the church, listen with humility and be kind. Good advice and a gentle word can care for others, while harshness can break relationships that are then very hard to repair.
exp.11:11:
This verse tells us that on the third day, Jeroboam and all the people came back to Rehoboam, just as the king had asked them to do.

Rehoboam had just become king after the death of his father Solomon. The people asked for relief from the heavy burdens. Rehoboam asked for three days to think, and he consulted the older men and the young men he had grown up with. Now the day has come to give his answer. What follows shows that he set aside the counsel of the older men and spoke harshly.

For today: before you answer someone who asks you for help or makes a claim on you, take time, but use it well. Seek God in prayer and listen to wise counsel, not only to the advice you like or the advice that agrees with you.
exp.11:12:
This verse says that King Rehoboam answered the people harshly. He set aside the counsel of the elders, that is, the older, experienced men who had served his father. The word "harshly" here means with rough words and without compassion.

The people, led by Jeroboam, asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burdens that Solomon had placed on them. The elders advised him to serve the people with kindness, but he preferred the advice of young men his own age. The text adds that God allowed this to fulfill what He had already announced about the division of the kingdom. So the decision was Rehoboam's responsibility, and it also fit within God's plan.

Today we can learn to listen to wise counsel, especially from people with experience and the fear of God. Before deciding, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are seeking humility and service, or only pride and control.
exp.11:13:
Rehoboam, the new king, follows the advice of the young men and answers harshly. He says that his father Solomon made the people's burden heavy, but that he will make it even heavier. "Yoke" refers to the burden of labor and taxes. The "whips" were common lashings, and the "scorpions" were probably whips with metal points or thorns, though some think it is only an image of greater pain.

Rehoboam speaks before Jeroboam and the people, who were asking for relief. He rejected the advice of the elders, who suggested serving the people with kindness. The text says that God allowed this to fulfill what He had announced, and the kingdom was divided.

For today: before responding with pride or anger, listen to wise counsel and remember that ruling well means serving, not crushing.
exp.11:14:
It says that King Rehoboam did not listen to the people, who were asking him for fairer treatment. The text explains that this came about by the Lord's ordering, that is, something God allowed and directed, so that the word He had spoken through the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat would be fulfilled.

The narrator of the book describes the moment when the kingdom is divided. Rehoboam, son of Solomon, rejected the advice of the elders and followed that of the young men, and he answered harshly. Earlier, Ahijah had told Jeroboam that God would divide the kingdom because of Solomon's sins. The Bible does not say that God forced Rehoboam to be proud; it shows that God works even through free and mistaken human decisions.

For today: before deciding, listen humbly to wise counsel, especially from people with experience. And trust that God continues to guide history, even when people fail.
exp.11:16:
This verse says that, although the northern tribes left, Rehoboam continued to rule only over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah. Rehoboam ruled over them. In other words, his kingdom was greatly reduced.

The people had asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burdens that Solomon had left them, but he did not listen to them. Then the northern tribes rejected the house of David and departed. The text says this came about by the LORD's doing, fulfilling what he had said through the prophet Ahijah. This does not remove the blame for Rehoboam's bad decisions; the account shows both things.

For today: listen humbly to those who depend on us. Harshness and pride can cost us relationships and valuable things. Let us ask God for a heart willing to serve and not to dominate.
exp.11:17:
He says that Rehoboam, the king, sent Adoram, the man in charge of collecting the tribute (the taxes and forced labor), to speak with the people. But all Israel stoned him, and he died. Then Rehoboam hurried to get up into his chariot and fled to Jerusalem.

The people had already rebelled because Rehoboam rejected their request to lighten the burden and answered them harshly. By sending the very man in charge of the tribute, the king chose the person most connected with what the people hated. The text does not explain his reason, but the result was the division of the kingdom.

For today: When someone brings us a complaint born of pain, listening with humility can prevent breaks in relationships. Answering with harshness or stubbornness usually makes everything worse, as Proverbs 15:1 says.
exp.11:20:
This verse tells how Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, came to Jerusalem and gathered the people of Judah and Benjamin. He assembled a hundred and eighty thousand chosen men, who were warriors, that is, select soldiers. His aim was to fight against Israel and to bring the kingdom back under his rule, that is, to put back under his command the tribes that had broken away.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had been divided: ten tribes made Jeroboam their king, and only Judah, together with Benjamin, remained with Rehoboam. He reacted with force, not with humility. But the next verse shows that God intervened through the prophet Shemaiah.

For today: when something breaks and hurts us, our first reaction is often to fight to regain control. Before we act, let us stop and listen to God and ask him for wisdom. A conflict is not always resolved by force.
exp.11:24:
It says that Jeroboam, the new king of the northern kingdom, rebuilt the city of Shechem, in the hill country of Ephraim, and settled there. Then he went out and also strengthened or built up Penuel. The word "built" here means building again or making stronger; it is not made clear whether the cities had been destroyed or whether he only improved them.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just been divided into two kingdoms, and God had prevented Rehoboam from fighting against them. Jeroboam begins to build up his kingdom, but the text that follows shows his fear: he does not trust God's promise and seeks security through his own plans.

We can work hard, but without letting fear direct our decisions. Before we build or make plans, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are trusting in God or only trying to secure ourselves on our own.
exp.11:25:
He said in his heart, without telling anyone, "Now the kingdom might return to the house of David."

Jeroboam had just been made king of the ten tribes of the north, and God himself had given him that kingdom. Even so, he did not trust God's promise, and he feared losing his power. The people were to go up to Jerusalem to worship, and he was afraid their hearts would turn back to Rehoboam. So later he made two golden calves.

When fear rules the heart, we try to protect ourselves with our own solutions, even when we stop obeying God. Today we can bring our fears to God in prayer and trust that He keeps what He promises.
exp.11:26:
What it says: Jeroboam thinks that if the people keep going up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord, their hearts will turn back to Rehoboam, king of Judah. He fears they will kill him and that the people will again join Rehoboam.

Context: The speaker is Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom, after the tribes separated from the house of David. God had promised him a kingdom (1 Kings 11:37-38), but he let fear and his own plan guide him. As we will see shortly, his fear led him to make golden calves and turn the people away from true worship.

For today: When fear of losing what we have takes hold of us, we may make decisions that harm others and draw us away from God. Let us trust his promises instead of protecting our position with shortcuts.
exp.11:27:
This verse tells that King Jeroboam, after taking counsel, had two golden calves made. He told the people that going up to Jerusalem to worship was too much for them. He presented the calves as the gods who brought them up out of Egypt.

Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom, Israel, after the kingdom was divided. He feared that if the people went to the temple in Jerusalem, they would return to obeying King Rehoboam and would kill him. So he invented a convenient religion to protect his power. The text calls it an occasion of sin.

Today we can ask whether some of our religious decisions are made out of fear or convenience, rather than obedience to God. Whoever seeks their own security before the truth ends up leading others away from God.
exp.11:28:
He placed one of the two golden calves in Beth-el and the other in Dan. The word "set" in this verse means that he installed them as places of worship. Beth-el was at the southern end of the northern kingdom, and Dan at the northern end.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After the kingdom was divided, Jeroboam ruled the northern tribes. He feared that if the people kept going to the temple in Jerusalem, they would return to King Rehoboam and he would be killed. Out of fear and political convenience, he created a false religion. With his words, he also mixed the memory of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt with idols.

For today: when the fear of losing something presses on us, we can justify shortcuts that lead us away from God. Trusting his promises is worth more than protecting our position with crooked solutions.
exp.11:29:
This verse says that what King Jeroboam did became a sin for the whole people. The people walked all the way to Dan to worship before one of the golden calves. "Became a sin" means it caused sin, that is, it led many people into wrong.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jeroboam ruled the northern tribes, which had separated from Judah. He feared that if the people kept going up to the temple in Jerusalem, they would return to the king of Judah. So he invented a more convenient and political religion, with calves, altars, and priests that God had not established.

For today: be careful about shaping faith to suit our convenience or our fears. When a decision that seems practical draws us away from what God has said, it can drag others along with it. Let us seek to obey God, even when it costs us.
exp.11:31:
This verse tells that King Jeroboam set up a religious festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, similar to the one celebrated in Judah (probably the Feast of Tabernacles, which was one month earlier). He himself offered sacrifices on an altar at Bethel, directed to the golden calves he had made. He also appointed priests for the high places, which were places of worship on hills or elevated sites.

The book narrates this as history; no character is speaking. After the kingdom was divided, Jeroboam ruled the northern tribes. He feared that the people would keep going to Jerusalem and return to the king of Judah. For this reason he built his own religious system, with dates, places, and priests of his own invention.

For today: it is easy to adapt faith to our own convenience, especially when we are afraid of losing something. We should ask ourselves whether we worship God as He asks in His Word, or as is more comfortable for us.
exp.12:0:
Suddenly, while Jeroboam was standing beside the altar to burn incense, a man of God came from Judah to Bethel. He had been sent by the word of the LORD. The phrase "man of God" refers to a prophet, a messenger who speaks for God.

Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom, Israel. He had set up an altar and a form of worship of his own at Bethel, separate from the temple in Jerusalem, probably so that the people would not go back to Judah. The prophet arrives without invitation to deliver a message from God, which continues in the following verses. The text does not give his name.

God speaks even when royal power and religion are organized against his will. Today we can ask ourselves whether our way of worship follows what God has said, or only what suits us. Listening to his Word with humility is always better.
exp.12:3:
This verse tells how King Jeroboam became angry when he heard the prophecy against his altar at Bethel. He stretched out his hand and gave the order to seize the man. But his hand dried up, that is, it was left paralyzed, and he could not pull it back to himself.

The narrator describes what happened after a man of God, sent from Judah, announced that a king named Josiah would destroy that altar. Jeroboam had set up that worship so that the people would not go up to worship in Jerusalem. God answered with an immediate sign that showed who held the authority.

Today we can learn that nothing is gained by resisting God or by silencing his message in anger. When a word makes us uncomfortable, it is wiser to pause, examine the heart, and turn back to God with humility.
exp.12:4:
This verse tells that the altar at Bethel was split in two and the ashes that were on it were poured out onto the ground. It happened just as the man of God had announced in the name of the Lord. The man of God means a prophet, and the sign is a visible proof that his word came from God.

King Jeroboam had set up that altar to worship in a way different from what God commanded. A prophet, whose name the text does not give, came and spoke against the altar. When the king tried to arrest him, his hand dried up. The sign of the broken altar confirmed that the message was from God.

For today: when God speaks in his Word, what he says comes to pass. We can trust it and obey it with humility, without doubting it or wanting to bend it to our own plans.
exp.12:6:
Here the king Jeroboam invites the prophet to his house. He offers him food and a gift. "Man of God" means a man sent by God, a prophet. "Come home" is the invitation in the verse, so the phrase is simply translated.

The prophet had come from Judah to speak against the altar that Jeroboam built at Bethel. God had just confirmed his message by breaking the altar and healing the king's hand. Now the king seems grateful and wants to make a friend of the prophet. We do not know whether his intention was sincere or whether he was looking to benefit from the prophet's reputation. But the prophet already had a clear command from God.

For today: sometimes temptation comes in the form of kindness, gifts, or praise. We can be thankful for what is good, but God's word must weigh more than any offer. It is wise to remember clearly what God has told us and not exchange it for comfort or for the sake of pleasing people.
exp.12:8:
Here the man of God explains why he refuses King Jeroboam's invitation. God gave him a clear command: not to eat bread, not to drink water, and not to return by the same way he came.

The speaker is a prophet from Judah, whose name is not mentioned. He had just announced God's judgment against the false altar that Jeroboam set up in Bethel. Refusing the food and the gift showed that he could not be bought or have fellowship with that place. Some see in the command a sign of total separation; the Bible does not explain this in more detail.

Today, obeying God may cost us attractive offers. Before accepting something, let us ask: does this agree with what God has told me in his Word?
exp.12:9:
He says that the man of God obeyed the command he had received and went away by a different road from the one he used to reach Bethel. The word "went" in the verse is the one that matters here, and Bethel is a town in the northern kingdom of Israel.

The man of God came from Judah and had spoken against the altar that King Jeroboam had set up in Bethel. God had told him not to eat, not to drink, and not to return by the same road. The king invited him to his house, but he refused, because his instruction came from God. Here we see him carrying out that instruction with firmness.

When God gives us a clear direction in his Word, it is wise to obey it even when something attractive or more comfortable is offered to us. Faithful obedience requires attention and steadiness until the end, not only at the beginning.
exp.12:11:
This verse tells how the old prophet of Bethel asks his sons which way the man of God went, the man who came from Judah. They point out the exact road. The old forms of the words are not used here; the verse itself speaks plainly of the way he went. A "man of God" is a prophet or servant of God.

The old prophet lives in Bethel. His sons have just told him what the man of God did and said to King Jeroboam. God had commanded that man to go back by a different road, without eating or drinking there. The old prophet wants to catch up with him. The Bible does not say here why, but what follows shows that he will seek him out through a deception.

For today: not everyone who speaks of God or seems close to Him helps us obey Him. When God has already given us a clear instruction, we should not change it because of another person's opinion, even if that person seems respectable. Let us ask for wisdom and measure everything against what God has already said.
exp.12:12:
It says that the old prophet from Bethel told his sons to prepare his donkey. The word for putting the saddle on the animal is not needed here; the sons did what he asked. They saddled the donkey, and the old prophet mounted it and went out after the man of God.

The old prophet lived in Bethel. His sons had told him what the man of God from Judah had said to King Jeroboam. He wants to catch up with him. The text does not explain his motives here, but what follows shows that he will deceive him (v. 18). God had commanded the man from Judah not to eat or drink there.

For today: not everyone who speaks in a religious tone tells the truth. When God has given you a clear instruction, do not change it because another person invites you, even if the invitation seems pious. Test everything against what God has already said.
exp.12:15:
Here the man of God, who had come from Judah, refuses the invitation of an old prophet. He tells him that he will not return with him, nor eat bread or drink water in that place.

The one speaking is the prophet sent by God to Bethel to announce judgment against the altar of King Jeroboam. God had commanded him not to eat, not to drink, and to return by another way. For this reason he answers with firmness: he is obeying a clear instruction. The following verse shows that the old prophet had lied to him.

For today: when God has spoken clearly, we should not exchange his word for the opinion of someone else, even when it sounds religious or convincing. It is wise to compare everything with what God has already said.
exp.12:17:
Here an elderly prophet from Bethel tells the man of God who came from Judah that he too is a prophet, and that an angel ordered him to bring him home to eat and drink. The last sentence makes clear that it was a lie.

The man of God had received a clear command from the Lord: not to eat or drink in that place, nor to return by the same way. He had already resisted King Jeroboam. Now the elderly prophet uses a supposed angelic revelation to contradict what God had already said. The text does not explain why he lied.

For today: no new word, even when it comes from someone respected and sounds spiritual, should lead us to disobey what God has already said clearly. Let us compare everything with Scripture and with what we know of his will, and ask for wisdom before we act.
exp.12:18:
This verse tells us that the man of God who had come from Judah went back with the other prophet, entered his house, and ate bread and drank water. That was exactly what God had forbidden him to do in that place. The word "went back" means that he turned around and returned the way he had come.

God had commanded this man not to eat or drink in Bethel, nor to return by the same road. An old prophet from Bethel told him that an angel had spoken to him, but the text makes clear that he was lying. The man of God chose to believe a person rather than remain firm in what God had already told him. Soon after, God himself corrected him at that same table.

For today: if someone says they speak on God's behalf but contradicts what God has already made clear in his Word, we should not follow them. Let us test everything by Scripture and prayer, even when the one speaking to us seems very spiritual.
exp.12:19:
As the two men sat at the table, the word of the Lord suddenly came. It came through the same prophet who had deceived the other man to make him turn back.

The man of God had received a clear command: he was not to eat or drink in Bethel. The old prophet lied to him, saying that an angel had spoken to him. The man of God believed him and disobeyed. Now God uses that same liar to announce judgment. This is striking, and the Bible does not explain why God spoke through him.

Today, when someone tells us that God has said something that contradicts what God has already clearly commanded us, we must stop and think. Let us test everything by what God has said, and not exchange his word for a voice that suits us or merely sounds religious.
exp.12:20:
This verse tells how God spoke through the old prophet, the same man who had deceived the man of God. This prophet cried out, that is, he spoke with a loud voice. He said that the man from Judah had disobeyed the mouth of the Lord, that is, he had not obeyed what God had said. God had commanded him not to eat or drink there.

God had told the man from Judah not to eat bread or drink water in Bethel. An old prophet invited him to his house and lied to him, saying that an angel had given him permission. The man believed him. While they were eating, God spoke through the very prophet who had deceived him and announced the punishment for the disobedience.

When God gives us clear instruction, no voice, however respectable it may seem, should change it. Let us compare every counsel with what God has already told us in His Word.
exp.12:22:
This verse tells something simple: the man of God finished eating and drinking in the house of the old prophet, and the old prophet saddled the donkey for him. "Saddle" here means putting the saddle, that is, the mount, on an animal so that it can travel.

The man of God came from Judah and had a clear command from Jehovah: not to eat or drink in Bethel. The old prophet deceived him by saying that an angel had given him a different instruction. The text does not explain why he lied. It may look like a kind gesture, but the punishment announced is already on its way.

For today: when God speaks clearly to us, we should not replace his word with the opinion of another person, even if that opinion seems pious or kind. It is wise to compare everything with what God has already said.
exp.12:23:
He says that the man of God, after eating where God had forbidden him, went back on his way, and a lion met him on the road and killed him. The strange thing is that the body was left lying there, and both the donkey and the lion stayed beside it, without the lion devouring it.

The narrator tells what happened to a prophet from Judah whom God sent with a clear command: not to eat or drink in that place. An old prophet deceived him by saying that an angel had spoken to him, and the man believed him. Many see in the lion a sign that this was God's judgment, and not a simple accident.

For today: when God has spoken to us clearly, let us not allow another voice, even one that sounds religious or convincing, to turn us away from that obedience.
exp.12:27:
This verse says that the old prophet went out and found the body of the man of God lying on the road. Beside the body stood the donkey and the lion. What is strange is that the lion did not eat the body or hurt the donkey.

The man of God was coming from Judah with a clear command from the LORD: not to eat or drink in that place. An old prophet deceived him, saying that an angel permitted him to eat, and he believed it. Because he disobeyed, a lion killed him. The narrator emphasizes that the lion stayed still, as a sign that this was God's judgment and not a simple accident.

For today: if God has already spoken clearly, do not change it for someone else's opinion, even if it sounds pious or comes from a respected person. Always compare what you hear with what God has already said.
exp.12:28:
It says that the old prophet took up the body of the man of God, set it on his donkey, and brought it back. Then he returned to his city to mourn for him and bury him. The word "mourn" here means to grieve and wail over a dead person.

The narrator tells what happened after this prophet disobeyed God. The old prophet had deceived him with a false word claiming to come from an angel, and the man of God died from a lion. The lion did not devour the body or harm the donkey, something many understand as a sign that God was at work. The old man now gives him a dignified burial.

Today, this invites us to obey what God has already told us clearly, even when someone we greatly respect says otherwise. It also shows us the value of accompanying with respect and compassion someone who has fallen.
exp.12:31:
The old prophet of Bethel says that what the man of God cried out by the word of the Lord will surely come to pass. He refers to the altar at Bethel and to the shrines of the high places, that is, places of worship on the hills.

The elderly prophet of Bethel, who had deceived the man of God, speaks here, and the man of God died for disobeying. Now, as he buries him, he acknowledges that his message was true. "Samaria" probably refers to the northern kingdom. Even so, Jeroboam did not change, as the following text shows.

For today: God's word does not depend on people accepting it. It is wise to obey it with humility, without letting other voices lead us astray. And if God corrects us, let us not harden our hearts as Jeroboam did.
exp.12:32:
This verse says that Jeroboam, the king of Israel, did not change after everything that had happened. He kept to his evil way and again appointed priests for the high places, which were places of worship built on the hills. He chose them from among the common people, regardless of whether they were from the tribe of Levi. Whoever wanted to be one was set apart as a priest.

The narrator of the book tells this after a prophet, a man of God, announced the judgment of the LORD against the altar at Bethel. Even with that warning, Jeroboam hardened his heart. God had commanded that the priests be Levites, so this was a serious act of disobedience. The following verse says that this led to the ruin of his house.

For today: when God corrects us or warns us, let us not harden our hearts. Turning back in repentance in time, and returning to his Word, is better than continuing on a path we know is wrong.
exp.12:33:
It says that what Jeroboam did, appointing as priests of the high places anyone who wanted to be one, became a sin that dragged his whole family down with him. That is why his house was "cut off and swept from the face of the earth": that is, destroyed and wiped out completely.

The one telling this is the author of the book of Kings, who sums up the end of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom. God had spoken to him through a prophet, but he did not repent. Instead of turning back to God, he kept on with his invented religion, paying no regard to what God had established for the priesthood.

For today: when God corrects us, it is an opportunity to change. A hardened heart can harm those who come after us as well. Let us ask for the humility to obey in time.
exp.13:0:
This verse says that at that time Abijah, the son of King Jeroboam, became sick. It is a simple sentence that opens the story. The phrase used here means that the illness laid him in bed, perhaps seriously.

The narrator of the book of Kings speaks here. Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom, Israel, and he had led the people into idolatry with golden calves. When his son falls ill, the king does not seek God sincerely. He sends his wife, in disguise, to consult the prophet Ahijah, because he trusted his word, though not his God.

For today: in a crisis, let us not seek God only when everything becomes complicated. Let us draw near to Him sincerely and without disguises, in good times as well.
exp.13:1:
Jeroboam asks his wife to get up, disguise herself so that no one will know she is his wife, and go to Shiloh. There lives the prophet Ahijah, the same man who years earlier told Jeroboam that he would be king over this people. Disguise means changing one's appearance, so that she will not be known to be Jeroboam's wife.

The speaker is King Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom, Israel. His son Abijah is sick, and he wants to know whether the boy will recover. It is striking that he trusts the prophet of God, yet does not want it known who his wife is. Many think he feared that Ahijah, or the people, would reject her because of idolatry. The text does not say this with certainty.

For today: when we are in trouble, we sometimes seek God while hiding the truth of our lives. God sees beyond any disguise. We can come to Him with sincerity, just as we are.
exp.13:2:
Here Jeroboam tells his wife to take a simple gift to the prophet Ahijah: ten loaves, a few dry or hard small cakes, and a jar of honey, that is, a small container. With these she was to ask him what would happen to their sick child.

Jeroboam speaks, worried because his son Abijah is very ill. He wants an answer from God, but he sends his wife in disguise, perhaps so that no one would know he was consulting the prophet, whom he had ignored before. The gift was modest, the kind one would bring to a man of God. God, however, had already told Ahijah everything.

For today: it is easy to seek God only when a crisis arrives, and to do it in disguise or halfheartedly. We can come to Him with sincerity, just as we are, and not only in moments of anguish, for He already knows our hearts.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that Jeroboam's wife did as her husband had told her. She got up, traveled to Shiloh, and came to the house of the prophet Ahijah. Ahijah could no longer see, because in his old age his eyes had grown dim.

The narrator tells what happens after Jeroboam, king of the northern kingdom, asked his wife to disguise herself. His son was sick, and he wanted a word from the prophet, but without anyone knowing who she was. It is striking that he tried to hide her identity before a man of God. The next verse shows that God let Ahijah know who she was anyway.

For today: we cannot disguise ourselves before God. When we are in need, it is better to come to Him honestly, without masks, trusting that He already knows us.
exp.13:4:
This verse says that God told the prophet Ahijah, before she arrived, that the wife of King Jeroboam would come to ask him about her sick son. It also said she would come in disguise, pretending to be another woman, and that God would give him the words to answer her.

Jeroboam was king over the northern tribes, and he had turned away from God. Even so, when his son fell ill, he wanted to know what would happen, and he sent his wife in disguise, perhaps so the prophet would not recognize her. Ahijah was already old and nearly blind, but God told him everything in advance. So we see that no one can hide from Him.

For today: there is no point in pretending before God. He knows our hearts and our needs. We can come to Him honestly, without masks, trusting that He receives us with truth and also with grace.
exp.13:6:
God tells Ahijah to carry a message to Jeroboam. God reminds him that it was He who lifted him up from among the common people and made him ruler over Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ahijah, who was blind from old age but had been warned by the Lord. The king's wife came in disguise to ask about her sick son. God exposes her and begins to explain why judgment is coming: Jeroboam received an honor he did not deserve, but he responded with idolatry.

Everything we have, whether work, influence, or responsibilities, is a gift from God. Today we can ask ourselves: am I using what He has given me with gratitude and faithfulness, or am I using it to move away from Him?
exp.13:14:
He says that God will shake Israel like the wind shakes a reed in the water: an unstable people, without firmness. God will uproot them from the good land he gave to their ancestors and scatter them across the river, that is, the Euphrates. The reason is that they made groves, that is, images and posts for worshiping the goddess Asherah, which offended God.

The prophet Ahijah of Shiloh speaks to Jeroboam's wife, who went in disguise to ask about her sick son. God announces judgment because Jeroboam led the people into idolatry. Only the child will receive a proper burial, for in him there was something good.

For today: what we put in place of God leaves us unstable like a reed. Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our heart, and return God to his place as our firm rock.
exp.13:17:
Here is what the verse tells us: Jeroboam's sick son died, they buried him, and all Israel mourned for him. Mourning means grieving, with weeping and sorrowful songs, over someone who has died. Everything happened exactly as the LORD had spoken through His servant, the prophet Ahijah.

The narrator of the book describes the end of this scene. The wife of King Jeroboam, in disguise, had gone to ask Ahijah about her sick son. The prophet told her that the child would die as soon as she entered the city. According to the text, something good was found in him before God, and for that reason he received a worthy burial and the mourning of the people, while the house of Jeroboam would suffer judgment for its sin.

For today: God keeps his word, both his warnings and his promises. This invites us to take it seriously, to correct our path in time, and to trust that he sees the good that is in every heart.
exp.13:18:
This verse says that the rest of Jeroboam's life, his wars, and the way he ruled were recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." That expression does not refer to the Bible, but to court records that we no longer have today.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings. He has just told of the death of Jeroboam's son, as the prophet Ahijah had foretold. Now he closes the account of this king with a summary, as he does with other kings. What matters to the author is not his political achievements, but that he turned away from God.

For today: our lives will also be summed up one day. It is worth asking ourselves what will leave the deeper mark, what we accomplished or whether we were faithful to God.
exp.13:20:
This verse says that Rehoboam, son of Solomon, began to reign in Judah at the age of forty-one and ruled for seventeen years in Jerusalem. It recalls that the Lord chose that city to put his name there. It also mentions his mother, Naamah, who was an Ammonitess.

The text is the account of the narrator of the book of Kings. After speaking of the end of Jeroboam's reign in the north, he turns his attention to the southern kingdom. He introduces Rehoboam and emphasizes that Jerusalem was the city chosen by God. Then the following passage shows that Judah turned away from God with idols and high places.

God can give us a good place and a good inheritance, but that does not replace a living faith. Today we can ask him to help us not to live by religious habits, but to obey him sincerely every day.
exp.13:26:
This verse says that King Rehoboam had shields made of metal (the word is usually understood to mean bronze) to replace the gold shields that Shishak had taken away. He handed them over to the captains of the guard, that is, the soldiers who watched over the entrance to the palace. The word "committed" in the verse means that he gave them to these men for safekeeping.

This is a historical account from the book of Kings, so the one speaking is not a character but the narrator. Judah had turned away from God, and Shishak, king of Egypt, plundered Jerusalem. Rehoboam did not recover what had been lost; he put something less valuable in its place. The bronze shields served to keep up an appearance of greatness, and they were carried out on solemn occasions to the temple.

For today: when we lose something valuable because of our mistakes, it is tempting to disguise the loss. It is better to return to God with sincerity and not settle for appearances.
exp.13:28:
This verse is a closing formula. The author says that anyone who wants more details about Rehoboam and everything he did can look them up in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah," a record of the kings that we no longer have as a separate book today. The phrase "the rest of the acts" refers to everything else.

The narrator of Kings summarizes each reign and points to other sources. Rehoboam, son of Solomon, lost much of the kingdom and saw Egypt carry off the treasures of the temple. Shields of bronze, according to the earlier account, replaced those made of gold. It is a sober summary of a life marked by loss and war.

For today: our lives will also be summed up in a few lines. Rather than trying to impress, it is wise to live today faithfully before God, for He knows every detail, and what we do matters.
exp.14:0:
This verse says when Abijam began to reign over Judah: in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam, king of Israel, the northern kingdom. The phrase that appears in the original wording is an older way of writing a word that is spelled the same way today, so no further comment is needed here. Abijam was the son of Rehoboam and the grandson of Solomon.

It is part of the book of Kings, a historical account with no single personal speaker. The author places each king of Judah in relation to the kings of Israel, because the people were already divided into two kingdoms. The verses that follow say that he reigned a short time and that his heart was not wholly devoted to God, unlike David. Some names, such as Abijam and Maachah, appear in other forms in other passages, and that can be explained in several ways.

For today: what we inherit from our parents shapes us, but it does not have to decide our path. We can ask God for a whole heart, one that truly follows him and not merely out of habit.
exp.14:1:
Abijam, king of Judah, ruled in Jerusalem for three years. The verse names his mother, Maacah, described as the daughter of Abishalom.

The narrator of Kings, whose name we do not know, introduces each king with basic facts: how long he reigned and who his mother was. Then he judges his spiritual life. There is some uncertainty about Abishalom: he could be Absalom, David's son, or an ancestor with a similar name. In the Bible, "daughter" can sometimes mean granddaughter or a female descendant. The verses that follow say that Abijam continued in the sins of his father and did not have a wholehearted heart toward God.

For today: what matters most is not how long our life or our position lasts, but where our heart is turned. Let us ask God for a sincere and devoted heart, because our example shapes those who come after us.
exp.14:2:
This verse says that Abijam, king of Judah, repeated the same sins that his father Rehoboam had committed before him. His heart was not whole with God, that is, it was not undivided or fully loyal to Him, as David's heart was, David being his ancestor. Here "father" can also refer to an ancestor.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who judges each king according to his faithfulness to God. Abijam reigned over Judah for a short time, and the text sums up his life with a single idea: he followed bad examples. Even so, the next verse shows that God, out of love for his promise to David, kept his line alive and protected Jerusalem.

For today: what we see at home shapes us, but it does not have to decide our path. Let us ask God for a whole heart, and choose carefully which examples to follow and which to leave behind.
exp.14:3:
Even though King Abijam (son of Rehoboam) was not faithful to God, the Lord showed mercy for David's sake. The word "lamp" means a line of descendants that keeps the light burning, that is, that David's family would continue to reign. God gave him a son to rule after him and protected Jerusalem.

The narrator of the book of Kings explains why the kingdom of Judah continued in spite of the sins of Abijam, who copied the mistakes of his father. The reason was not his own merit but God's promise to David and the faithfulness David showed in his life, with the exception of the case of Uriah.

For today: God's goodness often sustains us beyond what we deserve. This is not an excuse to sin, but an invitation to give thanks, to turn back to Him, and to live in such a way that we leave a good spiritual inheritance to those who come after us.
exp.14:4:
This verse says that David did what pleased God and obeyed his commands all his life. There was only one great failure: what he did with Uriah the Hittite. "Right" means correct, just. "Matter" here means the affair or the event.

The one who tells this is the author of the book of Kings, whose name is not given. He speaks of King Abijam of Judah, who followed the sins of his father and did not have a wholehearted heart toward God. By contrast, he recalls David. For David's sake, God kept his dynasty and protected Jerusalem. He refers to the episode of Uriah, whom David had put to death so that he could take his wife.

For today: God values a faithful heart, but he does not hide our serious mistakes. If we fail, let us seek forgiveness and not repeat the wrong. Our lives leave a mark on those who come after us.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that Asa reigned in Jerusalem for forty-one years. It also names his mother, Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom. It is possible that Maachah was actually his grandmother, since in the Bible the word "mother" is sometimes used for a grandmother. It is also not known for certain whether this Abishalom is the son of David.

The author of the book of Kings, who is not named, summarizes the history of the kings of Judah and Israel. Here he presents Asa with basic facts: how long he reigned and what family he came from. This prepares the account that follows, which says that Asa did what was right before God and removed idolatry from the land.

For today: our family influences us, but it does not decide who we will become. Asa came from a family with bad examples, and yet he chose to obey God. You too can choose a better path.
exp.14:14:
He brought in the things his father had dedicated, and the things he himself had dedicated, to the house of the Lord: silver, gold, and vessels. That is, he returned and added valuable offerings to the house of God.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing Asa's reign in Judah. Shortly before, Asa had removed his mother Maacah from the position of influence she held because of her idol, and he destroyed it. Although he did not take away the high places, his heart was wholly with God. This verse shows that his faith was also expressed in what he gave. Then come the wars with Baasha, and some scholars think these offerings were later used for other matters of the kingdom.

For today: our faith is not only about removing what is wrong; it is also about giving God our best with gratitude, whether time, money, or talents.
exp.14:17:
This verse tells how King Asa took all the silver and gold that was left in the treasures of the temple and of his own palace. He gave them to his servants so that they would take them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus. The sentence the verse quotes is simply the account of the giving and the sending of those treasures.

It is the narrator of Kings who tells these events. Baasa, king of Israel, had fortified Ramah in order to block Judah's way. Instead of asking God for help, Asa chose to buy the support of Syria, so that it would attack Israel. This passage does not say that God approved of this; in 2 Chronicles 16 Asa is rebuked for relying on the king of Syria.

When pressure comes, it is easy to look for quick, human solutions. Before acting, we can pray and ask ourselves whether we truly trust God or only our own resources.
exp.14:18:
This verse says that King Asa reminds Ben-hadad, king of Syria, that there was already a treaty between their fathers and between them. He sends him a gift of silver and gold, and asks him to break his alliance with Baasha, king of Israel, so that Baasha will withdraw and leave him alone.

Asa, king of Judah, speaks here. Baasha was building Ramah to block the way into Judah. Asa felt pressured, and he took the gold and silver out of the temple and the palace to buy Syria's help. It worked in the short term, but the text does not present it as an act of trust in God. Later, in 2 Chronicles 16, a prophet rebukes him for relying on the king of Syria instead of the Lord.

For today: when pressure comes, before looking for shortcuts or human solutions, pray and ask God for direction. Quick exits may resolve things today, but they can cost the trust God wants to build in you.
exp.14:20:
This verse says that when Baasha, king of Israel, learned that Ben-hadad had attacked his cities, he stopped building the fortress of Ramah and went to live in Tirzah. Tirzah was then an important city in the kingdom of Israel, and it was where his residence was.

The narrator tells what happened after King Asa of Judah sent silver and gold to Ben-hadad, king of Syria. Baasha was fortifying Ramah to pressure Judah. Seeing his northern cities attacked, he had to halt the work. Later, the Bible shows that Asa trusted in a human alliance and not in God (2 Chronicles 16:7-9).

Today we can learn that a quick solution may work, but it does not always come from faith. Before acting in the face of a problem, it is wise to pray and to seek God's guidance first.
exp.14:22:
This verse closes the reign of Asa, king of Judah. It says that his deeds, his strength, his works, and the cities he built are recorded in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah," an official record that we do not have today. At the end it adds a personal detail: in his old age he was diseased in his feet. It does not explain what illness this was.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes each reign and points to other sources. Just before this, it is told how Asa checked Baasha, king of Israel, and used the materials from Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah. Then comes his death and the reign of his son Jehoshaphat.

For today: our works and achievements matter, but weakness and old age also come. We can serve God faithfully in every stage and accept our limitations with humility.
exp.14:24:
Nadab, son of Jeroboam, began to reign over the northern kingdom, Israel, in the second year of Asa, king of Judah. He reigned only two years. Perhaps these were not two full years, since that was how time was usually counted back then.

The author of Kings, who is not named, records who was reigning in each kingdom and when. Here he switches from the kingdom of Judah to the kingdom of Israel. The verses that follow explain why this reign was so short: Nadab imitated his father's sins and was killed by Baasha.

Today it reminds us that our example influences those who come after us. Nadab followed his father's evil way and ended badly. We can ask ourselves what we are teaching through our lives, and ask God for help to break bad patterns and leave a legacy of faith.
exp.14:25:
Nadab, king of Israel, did what the Lord considers evil. He followed the example of his father Jeroboam, walking in his way, that is, living as he did. So he kept up the sins with which Jeroboam had led the whole people into sin.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes the reign of Nadab. He judges the kings by their faithfulness to God. The sin of Jeroboam, according to 1 Kings 12, was making golden calves to worship and turning the people away. Nadab reigned only two years, and the following text tells how Baasa killed him.

Today: our example influences others, especially in the family. Let us think about which habits we are passing on, and ask God to help us correct what is wrong and leave a path others can follow without stumbling.
exp.14:28:
As soon as Baasa began to reign, he killed the whole family of Jeroboam. No one was left alive, until the house of Jeroboam was wiped out completely. This happened just as the Lord had said through the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Baasa had killed Nadab, son of Jeroboam, and taken the throne. The text explains that this fulfilled an earlier word from God (1 Kings 14:10-11), because of the sins of Jeroboam, who led Israel into idolatry. The Bible does not say that Baasa was righteous; he acted with violence and ambition.

For today: our decisions, good or bad, affect others, especially those who follow us. Let us ask God for help to live with integrity and to guide others toward Him.
exp.14:29:
This verse explains why Jeroboam's family died. It says it was because of the sins Jeroboam committed and the sins by which he made Israel sin. It also mentions his provocation, that is, his actions that offended and angered God.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings, not a character. He explains that Baasa killed Nadab, Jeroboam's son, and wiped out his family, fulfilling what God had said through the prophet Ahijah. Earlier, Jeroboam had led the people into false worship (1 Kings 12:28-30).

For today: our decisions affect others, especially if we lead someone, as in the family, at work, or in the church. Let us ask God to help us guide others toward Him, not away from Him.
exp.14:30:
This verse closes the account of the reign of Nadab, king of Israel. It says that the rest of his deeds are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel," that is, a record of the kings of that time.

The one speaking is the author of Kings, whose name we do not know. He uses this formula to end the reign of each king and to send the reader to other sources. That book has not been preserved, and it is not the biblical book of Chronicles. The passage just before this one speaks of Baasha, who wiped out the family of Jeroboam, and the text presents this as the fulfillment of God's word because of the sins of Jeroboam.

For today: our choices leave a mark. It is worth living in a way that what is remembered of us honors God and blesses others.
exp.15:0:
God spoke to Jehu, son of Hanani, with a message aimed against Baasha, king of Israel. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" simply means that God himself sent a message. The word "saying" introduces what follows: a serious warning.

The one speaking is God, and he does so through Jehu, a prophet. Baasha came to the throne by violence, yet God reminds him that he had raised him up from the dust, that is, from a lowly condition. Even so, Baasha followed the evil path of Jeroboam, which had led the people into idolatry. For this reason God announces judgment on his family.

For today: everything we have, our work, our position, or our influence, is a gift from God and not something we have earned on our own. Let us use with humility and faithfulness what he has entrusted to us, and take care not to lead others down the wrong path.
exp.15:1:
God speaks to Baasa, king of Israel. He reminds him that he raised him up from the dust, that is, from a humble condition, and made him ruler over his people. Even so, Baasa followed the evil way of Jeroboam, led the people into sin, and angered God.

The prophet Jehu, son of Hanani, carries this message. Baasa came to the throne after wiping out the family of Nadab, the son of Jeroboam. But he repeated the same sin of idolatry that Jeroboam had started. That is why, in the verses that follow, God announces that his family will suffer the same end.

For today: everything we have, whether position, work, or influence, is a gift from God. If we lead others, our example matters a great deal. We can ask ourselves: am I using what God gave me to lead others toward Him or away from Him?
exp.15:10:
As soon as Zimri became king and sat on the throne, he killed all the household of Baasha. He left no male alive, neither relatives nor friends.

The narrator of the book explains that Zimri killed King Elah while Elah was drinking to excess. He then wiped out the dynasty of Baasha, and the following text says this fulfilled what God had announced through the prophet Jehu. The passage does not approve of Zimri's violence; it only shows that God judged the sins of Baasha and Elah. Zimri reigned only seven days.

God does not overlook injustice, even though he may be slow to act. But we must not excuse the evil that others commit. Today we can examine our lives with humility, turn away from sin, and entrust justice to God, without taking revenge with our own hands.
exp.15:11:
This verse says that Zimri completely wiped out the family of Baasha. Everything happened just as God had announced it through the prophet Jehu.

The book of Kings records this as a historical event. Baasha was king of Israel, and he had done evil, leading the people into sin. God warned him through Jehu that his family would be removed (1 Kings 16:1-4). Zimri killed Ela, the son of Baasha, and then destroyed his relatives. The text does not approve of Zimri's violence; it only shows that God's word was fulfilled.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he is also faithful to his word. This invites us to live with humility, to listen to his warnings, and not to use our influence to lead others down the wrong path.
exp.15:13:
This verse closes the account of the reign of Elah, king of Israel. It says that his other deeds and all that he did are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." That name refers to court records, which are not preserved today.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. It is a formula he uses to end the account of each king. Just before this, he tells how Zimri killed Elah and all the household of Baasa, as the LORD had warned through the prophet Jehu, because of their sins and their idols.

For today: our lives also remain in God's memory. It is better to live with humility and faithfulness than to leave a famous name without obedience.
exp.15:14:
This verse says that Zimri began to reign over Israel in the twenty-seventh year of Asa, king of Judah. His reign lasted only seven days, and he ruled from Tirzah, the capital of the northern kingdom. Meanwhile, the army of Israel had camped around Gibbethon, a city of the Philistines, to besiege it.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. He tells how the house of Baasha fell, because of its sins and because it led Israel into idolatry. Zimri seized the throne by violence, and the army quickly rejected him by making Omri king. The text does not say that Zimri was approved by God.

For today: power gained through violence and without God does not last. Let us seek to serve with integrity and trust that God sustains what is done with righteousness.
exp.15:16:
It says that Omri, the commander of the army, left the camp at Gibbethon, where Israel was fighting against the Philistines, and went up with the whole army against Tirzah. The word "besieged" means they surrounded the city in order to attack it. Tirzah was then the capital of the northern kingdom, and Zimri was there.

This is not a character speaking; it is the account from the book of Kings. Zimri had killed King Elah and proclaimed himself king, but he lasted only seven days. When the army learned of this, it made Omri king, and he marched to take back the capital. The text shows that power seized through violence does not last.

For today: let us not seek position or success by unjust or impatient means. What is built on betrayal collapses soon. Rather, let us trust in God and act with integrity, even if it takes longer.
exp.15:18:
This verse explains why Zimri came to such a tragic end. It says he died because of his sins: he did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, followed the bad example of King Jeroboam, and, like him, made the people of Israel sin.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who judges the lives of the kings according to their faithfulness to God. Zimri had taken the throne by force, but he reigned only seven days. When Omri laid siege to the city of Tirzah, Zimri set the palace on fire and died inside it. The text wants to show that his end was the result of his way of life.

For today: our decisions affect others, for good or for harm. It is worth asking ourselves what example we are setting and whom we are following. Let us ask God to guide us in right paths.
exp.15:20:
After Zimri's death, the people of Israel were split into two camps. Half wanted to make Tibni, son of Ginath, king, and the other half backed Omri.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. Israel, the northern kingdom, was going through a crisis: Zimri had seized the throne by force and held it for only a few days. Without a clear leader, the people divided. Little is known about Tibni's background, and the text does not explain why people followed him.

For today: when a firm and wholesome guidance is missing, people divide easily. Let us seek peace and ask God for wisdom before taking sides in conflicts.
exp.15:22:
This verse tells us the year when Omri began to reign over Israel: the thirty-first year of King Asa of Judah. Omri reigned twelve years in total, and he spent the first six of them in Tirzah, which was the capital at that time. "Reigned" means that he ruled as king.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recording the history of the kings. Israel had come through days of chaos: several kings had fallen quickly, and the people were divided. Omri came to power in the middle of that crisis. The dates help us place his reign alongside that of Judah. Some scholars explain in different ways how these years are counted.

For today: a person may have power and success in the eyes of others, but what truly matters is how he or she lives before God. Let us ask him to give us a faithful heart, not only achievements.
exp.15:23:
This verse tells how King Omri bought a hill from a man named Shemer, paying two talents of silver, a large amount of silver. There he built a city and named it Samaria, after Shemer, who had owned the hill.

It is the narrator of the book of Kings who speaks. After a civil war over the throne, Omri was left as king and moved the capital to a new site. Samaria would remain the capital of the northern kingdom for a long time. But the account goes on to make clear that Omri did evil in the sight of God. His great political work did not please the Lord.

For today: a person can have success, power, and great projects and still fail before God. Before building something large, ask yourself whether your life is faithful to Him.
exp.15:26:
This verse says that the rest of Omri's life, everything he did and his feats of power, was recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. The word "might" refers to his achievements and exploits, above all military and political ones.

The author of the book of Kings uses this formula to close the reign of each king. It points to an official record that we no longer have today. Here it contrasts with the verse before: although Omri was powerful, God judged him as worse than his predecessors, because he followed the sin of Jeroboam and idolatry. What counts before God is not success but faithfulness.

For today: do not measure your life only by achievements, fame, or power. Ask yourself whether what you do pleases God, because He sees beyond what is written in human books.
exp.15:33:
In the time of King Ahab, this verse tells us, a man named Hiel, from Bethel, rebuilt the city of Jericho. When he laid its foundation, his firstborn son Abiram died, and when he set up its gates, his youngest son Segub died. The firstborn is the eldest son, and the youngest is the last and most recent son.

The author of the book of Kings tells this story to show how Israel was turning away from God under Ahab, who set up altars to Baal. Joshua had pronounced a curse on anyone who would rebuild Jericho (Joshua 6:26). The text does not explain the details of the deaths; many believe they were a judgment for disobedience, although it does not say how they happened.

For today: God's words are serious and trustworthy. They are worth hearing with respect and not taking lightly, trusting that his Word is fulfilled.
exp.16:2:
God tells Elijah to leave that place, to head east, and to hide himself by the brook Cherith, which is before the Jordan. A brook is a small stream of water. The exact location of Cherith is not known with certainty.

The LORD speaks. Elijah had just announced to King Ahab that there would be no rain, and that put him in danger. God sends him to hide, and in the verses that follow, He promises to look after him with water and food.

For today: sometimes God does not ask us to do something great, but to obey a simple step and wait in quiet places. Trust that the one who gives you an instruction also knows how to sustain you. Obey today what you already know He is asking of you, even when you cannot see the whole way ahead.
exp.16:3:
God tells Elijah that he will be able to drink water from the brook, and that he has already given the order to the ravens so that they will bring him food there. "Commanded" means that God has already given them instructions.

The LORD, the God of Israel, speaks to his prophet Elijah. Elijah had just announced to King Ahab that there would be no rain, and for that reason he was to hide beside the brook Cherith. There he would be kept away from danger, and God would take care of him. Scholars do not know for certain where that brook was, although the text places it near the Jordan.

God often cares for us step by step, not always with great provisions. Elijah received bread for each day. Today we can trust that God knows what we need, obey him even when we do not understand everything, and thank him for daily provision.
exp.16:6:
After some days, the brook at Cherith ran out of water. The reason is simple: there had been no rain in the land.

Here the narrator tells what happened to Elijah. He had obeyed God and had stayed by the brook, where God was feeding him through ravens. That drought came from the word Elijah himself had announced to King Ahab (17:1). In other words, Elijah was not exempt from the consequences of what was happening in the country. Right away God gives him new instructions: go to Zarephath.

Obeying God does not always keep us from things drying up. Sometimes a source runs out, like a job or a season of life, and that does not mean God has abandoned us. It may be that He is preparing us for the next step. We can keep trusting and wait for His next direction.
exp.16:9:
Elijah obeys God and travels to Zarephath. When he arrives at the city gate, he finds a widow gathering sticks. He calls out to her and asks for a little water in a cup so that he may drink.

God had told Elijah to go to Zarephath, a town in the region of Sidon, outside Israel, because a widow there would provide for him. There was a famine in the land. What is surprising is that God chooses a poor woman who is a foreigner. She does not yet know anything about this plan, as her words show later.

God often guides us one step at a time. Elijah obeyed without seeing the whole road ahead. Today we can trust God and take the next step we know he is asking of us, even when we do not understand everything. We can also remember that God can use simple, humble people.
exp.16:12:
Elijah tells the widow not to be afraid and to go ahead and do what she had planned. But he asks her to first make him a small cake, baked in the ashes, and bring it to him. After that she can cook for herself and her son.

Elijah speaks during a time of drought, and God sent him to Zarephath. The widow has just told him that she has only a handful of flour and a little oil left, and that she was going to prepare one last meal before dying. Elijah asks her for faith, and the next verse explains that God had promised the supply would not run out.

For today: when what you have feels very small, you can take a first step of trust in God through obedience and generosity, without giving up on being wise. He can care for you in ways you do not expect.
exp.16:14:
The verse tells us that the widow of Zarephath did what Elijah asked of her. She first made the cake for the prophet, and after that, there was food every day for Elijah, for her, and for her household.

Elijah speaks in the middle of a drought. God sent him to a poor widow who had only a little flour and oil, and she was getting ready to prepare her last meal with her son. Elijah asks her to trust God's promise: the flour and the oil would not run out until the rain returned. She decides to believe and to act.

For today: faith shows itself in concrete steps of obedience, even when the resources seem few. God does not always give us everything at once, but He can provide what is needed for each day while we trust in Him.
exp.16:18:
Elijah asks the widow to hand him her dead son. She was holding him in her lap, that is, on her legs, cradled in her arms. Elijah takes him and carries him up into the upper room, where he himself was staying, and lays him on his own bed.

The prophet speaks to the widow of Zarephath, who had welcomed him into her house. She, full of grief, believed that her son's death was a punishment for her sins. Elijah does not argue with her; he acts. He takes the child to a secluded place to pray to God freely.

When grief crushes us and we have no answers, we can do what Elijah did: carry the burden to a quiet place and bring it before God with sincerity, without pretending or keeping silent about what we feel.
exp.16:19:
Elijah cries out to God with a sincere complaint. He asks whether God has also brought suffering upon the widow who is taking him in, by taking away her son.

Elijah speaks in the house of the widow of Zarephath, who had cared for him in a time of famine. Her son has just died, and she fears it is a punishment for her sins. Elijah, distressed, takes the child to his room and brings his grief before God. We do not know exactly what Elijah was thinking, but his prayer is honest and comes from compassion.

For today: when pain confuses you, you can speak to God with complete frankness. He is not offended by your sincere questions, and He listens to anyone who cries out to Him in faith.
exp.16:23:
The woman tells Elijah that now she knows he is a "man of God", that is, a man who speaks on God's behalf. She also acknowledges that the word of the Lord (the name of God in this version) is truth when it comes from Elijah's mouth.

The widow of Zarephath, who had hosted Elijah in a time of famine, speaks here. Her son died, and Elijah prayed to God for him. God listened, and the boy came back to life. On receiving her son alive, the woman confesses her faith. She had already seen the supply of flour and oil, but this time God showed her his power over death.

For today: faith often grows when we see God at work in the midst of pain. We can remember the times he has sustained us, and trust that his word remains true even when we do not understand everything we are going through.
exp.17:0:
After many days, God spoke to the prophet Elijah in the third year. He told him to go and present himself before King Ahab, and He promised that He would send rain on the earth.

The one speaking is God, and He gives the command to Elijah. Earlier, Elijah had announced a drought in Israel (1 Kings 17:1). Now the land is suffering from hunger. The "third year" is counted from that time; Jesus mentioned three and a half years (Luke 4:25). God acts to end the drought, but first Elijah must face the king.

For today: when God tells us to do something difficult, we can obey even without yet seeing the result. He keeps what He promises, in His time, and asks us to trust Him in the meantime.
exp.17:3:
It says that when Queen Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah took one hundred of them, hid them in caves, fifty to each cave, and also gave them bread and water to keep them alive.

Here the narrator of the book explains why Obadiah, the steward or manager of Ahab's palace, was a man who feared God. Although he worked for a wicked king, he secretly protected the servants of God. The scene takes place during a severe famine in Samaria, before Elijah appears before Ahab.

For today: we can serve God faithfully even in difficult places, such as at work or at school. Sometimes his work is done quietly, through acts of courage and care toward other believers, and God sees each one of them.
exp.17:4:
Here King Ahab orders Obadiah, his steward, to travel through the land and search all the springs and streams. He hopes to find grass to keep the horses and mules alive, so that they will not lose all their animals.

We are in the third year of a severe drought. Ahab, king of Israel, is concerned with saving his animals, not with the people or with turning back to God. Obadiah, by contrast, was a man who feared the LORD, and he had secretly protected one hundred prophets when Jezebel was hunting them down. He lived faithfully in a dangerous setting.
