For today: we can serve God with integrity even in difficult places, as Obadiah did. And it is worth examining our priorities: Ahab took care of his horses, but ignored the spiritual root of the problem.
exp.17:5:
So they divided the land between them to cover it on foot: Ahab went one way alone, and Obadiah went another way alone. This verse tells how King Ahab and Obadiah split up the territory to search for water and pasture. Each one left by his own path, going in different directions.

It was a time of severe drought in Israel. Ahab, the king, was trying to save his horses and mules. Obadiah, his steward, was a man who feared God, and he had hidden one hundred prophets from the persecution of Jezebel. This separation sets up the meeting with Elijah in the next verse.

For today: sometimes God places us on what look like ordinary routine paths, where we are looking for everyday things, and there he meets us. Be faithful in your daily tasks, even in difficult surroundings, as Obadiah was, because God can use you at any moment.
exp.17:12:
Obadiah, the one in charge of Ahab's household, reminds Elijah of something he did. When Jezebel was killing the Lord's prophets, he hid one hundred of them in caves, fifty to a cave, and gave them bread and water.

Obadiah speaks with fear. Elijah asks him to tell Ahab that he is there, but Obadiah is afraid that the Spirit of the Lord will carry Elijah away, that Ahab will not find him, and that Ahab will kill him. So he defends his faithfulness to God with this example, even though he works for a wicked king.

For today: God can have faithful servants in difficult places. If today you are called to serve God in a hostile environment, doing good quietly, with wisdom and generosity, also counts before Him.
exp.17:17:
Elijah answers King Ahab that he has not brought trouble or confusion upon Israel. Rather, the guilty party is Ahab himself and his family, because they abandoned the commandments of the Lord and followed the Baals, which were the false gods of the Canaanites. Here "trouble" means bringing misfortune or disturbing the nation.

The prophet Elijah speaks before Ahab, who accuses him of being the cause of the drought and the crisis the people were suffering. Elijah does not defend himself with evasions; he returns the accusation with courage and points to the root: idolatry. He then asks Ahab to gather all of Israel at Mount Carmel.

For today: when problems come, it is wise to examine honestly whether we have drifted away from God, instead of blaming others. And if we must speak the truth, let us do so with courage and respect, trusting that God sustains those who are faithful to him.
exp.17:18:
Elijah asks King Ahab to gather all the people of Israel at Mount Carmel. He is also to bring the 450 prophets of Baal and the 400 prophets of the groves, who were prophets tied to the worship of Asherah, a pagan goddess. It is said that they "eat at Jezebel's table" because she provided for them and supported them.

Elijah speaks boldly after Ahab accused him of troubling Israel. Elijah replies that the real problem is that the king and his family abandoned the commandments of God to follow the Baals. Now Elijah wants a public meeting so that the people can decide whom they will serve.

Today we can ask ourselves to whom we are giving our loyalty. God invites us to stop living divided and to follow him with sincerity.
exp.17:19:
Elijah had accused Ahab of abandoning the commandments of the LORD and following the Baals, false gods. For that reason he asked for a public gathering. The account goes on to say that there Elijah would challenge the people to decide whom they would serve. Ahab obeys, although the text does not explain his reasons; it may have been because of the drought or because of Elijah's authority, but this is not stated.

God sometimes places us before a decision that we can no longer keep postponing. Today it is worth asking ourselves honestly: whom am I really following? Asking God for the courage to choose Him clearly is a good first step.
exp.17:20:
Elijah approaches all the people gathered there and asks them how long they are going to hobble between two ideas or options. He puts it plainly: if the Lord is God, follow him; if Baal is God, then go after him. The people stay silent and do not answer him at all.

Elijah, a prophet of God, speaks on Mount Carmel before Israel. King Ahab had gathered everyone, along with hundreds of prophets of Baal. The people worshiped the Lord, but they had also mixed in the worship of Baal. Elijah confronts them so that they will stop wanting both and make a decision before the test with the two bulls.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we tell God yes while still being guided by other things, such as money, fear, or the approval of others. God invites us to a sincere and steady faith. Today you can give God a concrete decision in an area where you have been wavering.
exp.17:21:
Elijah reminds the people that he is the only prophet of the Lord left in sight, while Baal has four hundred and fifty prophets. The numbers make clear that he is at a great disadvantage.

Elijah speaks on Mount Carmel, before King Ahab and all Israel. The people worshiped Baal and at the same time claimed to follow the Lord, so they kept silent in answer to his question. Elijah does not say he is the only believer in the whole country (later the text mentions Obadiah and other prophets in hiding), but the only prophet of the Lord present there. With this he prepares the test by fire.

Today, following God can sometimes leave us in the minority. We do not need the majority to support us in order to be faithful. Decide today where your loyalty lies and live it out with simplicity and courage, trusting that God answers.
exp.17:22:
Elijah proposes a simple test. Two bulls will be given: the prophets of Baal choose one, cut it into pieces, and lay it on the wood, but without lighting any fire. Elijah will prepare the other one in the same way.

Elijah speaks before all the people of Israel, who were divided between worshiping the LORD and worshiping Baal. He was the only prophet of the LORD who showed himself, facing 450 prophets of Baal. With this test he wants the people to see with their own eyes who the true God is, and to stop doubting.

For today: God does not ask us for a half-hearted faith. If there is anything that competes with Him in your heart, today you can choose to follow Him without a divided mind, trusting that He answers.
exp.17:24:
Elijah tells the prophets of Baal to choose one of the two bullocks and to dress it first, because they are many. Then they are to call on their gods, but without putting fire under the wood.

Elijah speaks in a public contest before all the people of Israel, who were divided between the LORD and Baal. He proposes a clear test: the God who answers with fire is the true one. He lets the prophets of Baal go first, so that no one can doubt what happens.

For today: let us not fear the truth when it is examined honestly. We can trust that God is real and faithful, and live with integrity, without tricks or pretense, letting Him speak for Himself.
exp.17:28:
It says that midday passed, and the prophets of Baal kept on prophesying, that is, shouting and acting out in a religious frenzy, until the time of the evening sacrifice, the offering presented to God in the temple. Even so, there was no voice: no answer, no one responding or paying attention.

Here the narrator describes the most tense moment of the challenge on Mount Carmel. Elijah had proposed a test before all Israel: the god who answered with fire would be the true one. The prophets of Baal had been crying out for hours, and Elijah had already mocked them. Their silence shows that Baal was nothing.

For today: it is easy to place our trust in things that promise a great deal and never answer, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Today you might ask yourself what you are truly trusting in, and turn your heart back to the living God, who does listen.
exp.17:29:
Elijah invites all the people to come near, and the people draw close to him. Then he repairs the altar of the Lord, which had been broken down or was in ruins.

Elijah speaks on Mount Carmel, in the contest with the prophets of Baal. They spent hours shouting without receiving any answer. Now Elijah calls the people so that they can see up close what he is about to do. Repairing the altar suggests a return to true worship, which Israel had neglected. Some believe it also shows that God does not compete from disorder, but invites us to restore what had been abandoned.

For today: if prayer, the Bible, or communion with God has been neglected in your life, do not wait until you feel perfect. Begin by repairing a small "altar": a simple and sincere daily time with God.
exp.17:33:
Elijah tells them to fill four jars with water and pour it over the offering and the wood. Then he asks them to do it again, and once more, three times in all. "Fill" is the word the verse uses for this action, and a burnt offering was the sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar.

Elijah, a prophet of God, confronts the prophets of Baal before all Israel on Mount Carmel. The people were hesitating between serving the LORD and serving Baal. By soaking the altar, Elijah makes it impossible for the fire to be a trick or a coincidence. If the fire falls, it can only come from God. Some think the water came from the nearby sea, but the text does not say so.

For today: trusting God sometimes means setting aside our backup plans and safety nets, so that if He acts, it is clear that the work was His and not ours.
exp.17:34:
This verse says that the water Elijah had poured out was so much that it ran all around the altar and filled the trench that surrounded it. The trench is a channel dug around the altar.

Elijah is on Mount Carmel, facing the prophets of Baal and all the people. It was a contest to see who the true God was. By soaking the sacrifice, Elijah made any trick or human explanation impossible: if fire fell, it could only come from the LORD.

For today: sometimes we doubt that God can act in situations that seem hopeless. This passage encourages us to trust Him without seeking shortcuts or human supports, and to bring our needs to Him in faith, knowing that He can answer.
exp.17:37:
This verse tells that God answered with fire from heaven. The fire consumed everything: the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and even the dust. It also "licked up" the water that filled the trench around the altar, meaning it dried it up completely.

Elijah had challenged the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. The people of Israel were divided between worshiping the Lord and Baal. Elijah prayed that God would show who the true God was, and the fire was the answer. The people acknowledged the Lord and turned back to Him.

For today: God does not compete with modern idols, such as money or success. We can pray with confidence and simplicity, and return to Him with our whole heart, without dividing our loyalty.
exp.17:39:
Elijah orders that the prophets of Baal be seized so that none of them escapes. The people catch them, Elijah takes them down to the brook Kishon, and there he puts them to death.

Elijah speaks just after God sent fire from heaven on Mount Carmel and the people acknowledged that the Lord is God. Baal was an idol whose worship had drawn Israel away. The law of Moses commanded severe punishment for idolatry (Deuteronomy 13; 18:20). It is a difficult episode, and it is not presented as a model for how to treat others today. It was a judgment within the particular history of Israel.

For today: it is not enough to be moved before God and say that the Lord is God. We must remove from our lives whatever competes with Him, such as pride, money, or any habit that takes His place.
exp.17:40:
Elijah tells King Ahab to go up and eat and drink, because the sound of a heavy rain can already be heard. The word for "heavy" in this passage means abundant.

The prophet Elijah is speaking. There had been a long drought, and on Mount Carmel the people had just acknowledged that the LORD is God. Elijah speaks in faith, before seeing any signs. Afterward he himself goes up to pray with humility. Some think Ahab had been fasting during the trial, but the text does not say so, so we cannot be certain.

For today: sometimes God gives you a promise before you see the result. Trust Him, and in the meantime keep praying with patience, as Elijah did when he told his servant to look seven times.
exp.17:41:
This verse shows two scenes at once. Ahab goes up to eat and drink, while Elijah climbs to the top of Carmel. There he bows down to the ground and puts his face between his knees. It is a posture of deep, humble, and focused prayer.

This happens after the confrontation on Mount Carmel, when God answered with fire and the people once again acknowledged him. Elijah had already announced that a great rain was coming after years of drought. Ahab busies himself with eating; Elijah, on the other hand, devotes himself to prayer. The text does not give the words of his prayer, so it is better not to invent them.

For today: when God gives us a promise, praying with humility and patience is the way to wait for its fulfillment. Keep praying, even when you do not yet see signs.
exp.17:42:
Elijah tells his servant to go up and look toward the sea, that is, the Mediterranean Sea. The servant goes, looks, and comes back saying there is nothing. Elijah does not give up and tells him to go again seven times.

Elijah speaks after the great contest on Mount Carmel and after three and a half years of drought. He has already announced that rain is coming, and now he prays with humility, bowed low to the ground. He sends his servant to look for the sign that God will answer.

For today: when you pray and still see no answer, do not lose heart. Keep praying in faith and watch for what God is doing, even when the progress seems small, like that little cloud.
exp.18:0:
This verse says that Ahab, the king of Israel, told his wife Jezebel everything Elijah had done. The most serious part for her was that Elijah had killed all the prophets of Baal with the sword (that is, with a sword).

This happens right after the great confrontation on Mount Carmel (chapter 18), where God answered with fire and the people once again acknowledged him.

The one speaking here is the narrator. Ahab reports to Jezebel, who promoted the worship of Baal and persecuted the prophets of the Lord. Her violent response will show how a spiritual victory can bring strong opposition.

For today: after a moment of great faith, threats and weariness may come. Do not be surprised; rest in God and do not make decisions moved only by fear.
exp.18:2:
It says that Elijah, seeing that his life was in danger, got up and fled to save himself. He came to Beersheba, a place in the territory of Judah, and there he left his servant.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Elijah had just won a great victory on Mount Carmel. But Queen Jezebel sent him a message threatening him with death. Some think Elijah was afraid and lost heart; others think he was seeking protection. The text shows his exhaustion and his fear.

For today: after a great effort, tiredness and fear can make everything look dark. Do not be ashamed of that. Rest, eat, and seek God sincerely, as Elijah did, the one whom God cared for with tenderness.
exp.18:3:
Elijah walked alone for a day into the wilderness and sat down under a juniper tree, a shrub that gives some shade. Tired and without spirit, he asked God to take his life. He said it was enough and that he could bear no more, and he said he was not better than his fathers, meaning that he did not feel himself more capable than those who had died before him.

Elijah had just won a great victory on Mount Carmel, but Jezebel threatened him with death, and he fled in fear. He left his servant at Beersheba and continued alone. He speaks with God in the midst of his exhaustion and his fear. God does not rebuke him here, but instead sends him rest, food, and water.

When you are exhausted or discouraged, you can tell God how you feel with honesty. He cares also for your body and your spirit, and He can use rest and the help of others to lift you up.
exp.18:5:
He looked and saw, right beside his head, a round bread baked on hot coals, and a jar of water. He ate, drank, and lay down to sleep again. A "cake" here is a flat bread, and "coals" are the embers of the fire. "Head" is the place where he rested his head.

The narrator tells us that Elijah was fleeing from Queen Jezebel, who wanted to kill him. He was exhausted and discouraged, and he asked God to take his life. God did not rebuke him: he sent an angel to touch him and give him food. Afterward, Elijah received strength for a long journey to Mount Horeb.

When you are very tired or sad, God also cares about your basic needs. Resting, eating, and asking for help is not a lack of faith; sometimes it is the first step toward God lifting you up again.
exp.18:6:
The angel of the Lord came back a second time, touched Elijah, and told him to get up and eat, because the journey still ahead of him was long. The phrase about the rest of the way is simply the journey still to be covered, and the word for touched means that the angel laid a hand on him.

Elijah was running from Queen Jezebel, who wanted to kill him. He was exhausted, discouraged, and wanted to die, so he fell asleep under a broom tree, a shrub of the desert. The one speaking here is the angel of the Lord, sent by God. Before saying anything about his discouragement, God gave him rest, bread, and water. With that food Elijah walked forty days to Mount Horeb, where God spoke to him.

God knows our limits and cares for us with patience. When you are worn out, do not scold yourself: rest, eat, and accept the help God places near you. He knows the road is long and provides for you to keep going.
exp.18:8:
Elijah arrived at Mount Horeb and spent the night in a cave. There God spoke to him and asked him a question: "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

Elijah was fleeing from Queen Jezebel, who wanted to kill him. He was tired, afraid, and felt alone. God had strengthened him with food and led him to the mountain where Moses had encountered God. God's question does not seek information, since He already knew everything. It seeks for Elijah to open his heart and say what he feels.

When you are exhausted or discouraged, do not hide what you feel. God asks you with tenderness, and He wants you to speak with Him honestly, because He listens to you and cares for you.
exp.18:9:
Elijah answers God's question by saying that he has been very zealous, that is, that he has a burning love and a strong desire to honor the Lord. He says that Israel has forsaken God's covenant, thrown down his altars, and slain his prophets with the sword. According to him, he alone is left, and they seek his life to take it away.

Elijah speaks from a cave on Mount Horeb, where he fled from Queen Jezebel after his great victory on Carmel. He is tired, afraid, and discouraged. God asks him what he is doing there, not because God does not know, but so that Elijah may express what is in his heart. Then God answers him with a still, small voice, not with wind, earthquake, or fire.

For today: when you feel alone and exhausted, tell God honestly what you are feeling. He listens to you with tenderness, and he can speak to you with calm, reminding you that you are not as alone as you think.
exp.18:10:
God tells Elijah to go out of the cave and stand on the mountain, because the Lord was about to pass by. First a great and strong wind came, tearing apart the mountains and breaking the rocks, but the Lord was not in the wind. Then came an earthquake, and the Lord was not there either.

Elijah was fleeing from Queen Jezebel, feeling alone and afraid, even though he had served God with great zeal. He had hidden in a cave on Mount Horeb (also called Sinai). God asks him what he is doing there, and Elijah tells him of his pain. Then God makes himself known to him.

When we are tired or afraid, let us not expect God to always speak with shouting or great signs. Many times he speaks to us in calm. Let us quiet the noise for a moment, pray, and listen for his gentle voice.
exp.18:11:
It says that after the earthquake came a fire, but God was not in the fire. Then came a still, small voice, meaning a soft sound, like a whisper or a gentle breeze. The Hebrew of this expression is translated in several ways, but all of them point to something very quiet.

Elijah, the prophet of Israel, fled to Mount Horeb because Queen Jezebel wanted to kill him. He felt alone, tired, and discouraged. God passes by him, and the forces of nature are not what God uses to speak to him. When Elijah hears the whisper, he covers his face and goes out of the cave.

For today: when you are exhausted or discouraged, do not always expect something spectacular. Look for moments of stillness to pray and read the Bible, because God often speaks with calm and closeness.
exp.18:12:
Elijah hears the gentle, quiet sound, that is, a soft whisper. Then he wraps his face in his mantle, goes out, and stands at the entrance of the cave. There a voice asks him: "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

Elijah was fleeing from Queen Jezebel and was on Mount Horeb, deeply discouraged. After the wind, the earthquake, and the fire, God draws near to him in a calm sound. Covering one's face is usually understood as a sign of reverence before the presence of God. God himself asks him the question, and with it invites him to express what he carries inside.

God does not always speak to us with noise or with great signs. When we are tired or afraid, we can be still, draw near to him, and tell him honestly what we feel. He listens and also guides us.
exp.18:15:
God tells Elijah to anoint two people: Jehu, son of Nimshi, as king over Israel, and Elisha, son of Shaphat, from Abel-meholah, as the prophet who will take his place. To anoint someone means to pour oil over them to show that God has set them apart for a task.

The LORD speaks with Elijah, who is discouraged and fleeing from Jezebel. Elijah believes he is alone and that all is lost. God answers with a plan: he will raise up kings and a successor prophet to judge idolatry. He will also remind Elijah that seven thousand faithful people still remain. The text does not say that Elijah personally anointed Jehu; later, that is done by one of Elisha's disciples.

For today: when you feel alone or worn out, remember that God is still at work and does not depend on you alone. Faithfully do what is yours to do, and trust that he is also preparing others.
exp.18:16:
God tells Elijah that a severe judgment is coming upon Israel. Whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, king of Syria, will be killed by Jehu, the future king of Israel. And whoever escapes Jehu will fall by the hand of Elisha. The word "sword" here means a sword, that is, war and punishment.

The Lord speaks to Elijah, who had fled in despair and felt alone after confronting the idolatry of Baal. God gives him concrete tasks: to anoint two kings and Elisha as his successor. The judgment for idolatry is serious, but the following verse makes clear that God preserves seven thousand faithful people. Scholars debate how exactly each detail of this prophecy was fulfilled.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also cares for his own and does not leave us alone. When you feel tired or discouraged, trust that God is still at work and has a plan, even when you cannot see all of it.
exp.18:17:
This verse says that God preserved for himself seven thousand people in Israel who had never bowed down before Baal, the false god, nor kissed him as a sign of worship. The word "bowed" means that they bent down or knelt. Kissing the image was another way of giving it worship. Some understand the number seven thousand literally, and others as a figure that expresses a complete and sufficient group.

God speaks to Elijah, who was discouraged and believed he was the only faithful one left. God gives him new tasks: to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha. Furthermore, he answers him tenderly that he is not alone, for there is a faithful remnant that God himself watches over.

When you feel alone in your faith, remember that God sees many more faithful people than you can see. Ask him for strength to remain firm, and seek the company of other believers who encourage you.
exp.18:18:
Elijah leaves that place and finds Elisha, son of Shaphat, plowing the field. He had twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he himself was driving the last pair. Elijah passes by him and throws his mantle over him.

Here the narrator speaks. God had just told Elijah, who was tired and discouraged, to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place, and that there were still seven thousand faithful people left in Israel. Throwing the mantle over him seems to be a sign of calling and of sharing in his mission, though the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God often calls us in the middle of our daily work. Elisha responded by leaving what was comfortable and giving himself completely. Ask yourself what God is asking of you today, and respond with willingness.
exp.18:20:
Elisha says goodbye to his former life. He takes a pair of oxen, kills them, and uses the wood of the plow to cook the meat. Then he gives it to the people so they can eat. After this, Elisha gets up, follows Elijah, and serves him.

Elijah, the prophet, had just thrown his cloak over Elisha, a gesture that many understand as a call to become his successor. Elisha was a farmer with resources, since he plowed with twelve teams of oxen. By burning his working tool and celebrating with the people, he made clear that he did not intend to turn back. The text does not say everything Elisha thought, so that reading is a common interpretation.

When God calls us, following him may require leaving behind comfortable and familiar things. Think about what ties you to your past, and take a concrete step toward what God is asking of you, with gratitude and service.
exp.19:3:
Ahab says to Ben-hadad, "According to your word, my lord the king, I am yours, and all that I have." It is an answer of submission. Ahab agrees to become a vassal of Ben-hadad.

Here speaks Ahab, king of Israel. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had surrounded Samaria with a great army and demanded silver, gold, wives and children. Ahab answers out of fear, wanting to avoid war. Soon we see that Ben-hadad asks for even more, and the submission did not bring peace. The Bible does not say here that Ahab sought God's counsel before answering.

For today: when we feel afraid, we may give in too much and surrender what we should not. Before responding to pressure, let us pray, seek wise counsel, and remember that God is our true refuge.
exp.19:4:
The messengers of Ben-hadad, king of Syria, came back with another message. This time the king demanded that Ahab give him his silver, his gold, his wives, and his children. The verse notes that this was no longer just a request for submission but a clear demand.

Ben-hadad was besieging Samaria with a large army. At first Ahab, king of Israel, agreed to submit in order to avoid war. But Ben-hadad, seeing his weakness, hardened his terms and threatened to plunder the palace and the houses of his servants. Then Ahab consulted the elders, and they saw that this king was only looking for harm.

When we give in again and again to someone who keeps pressing us, sometimes they only increase their demands. Let us ask God for wisdom to know when to yield and when to say enough, seeking the counsel of sensible people, as Ahab did with the elders.
exp.19:5:
Ben-hadad, king of Syria, sends word to Ahab that the next day, at this same time, he will send his servants to search the palace and the houses of Ahab's officials. They will take with their hands whatever they find of value and carry it away.

The speaker is Ben-hadad, king of Syria, who had Samaria under siege with a large army. Ahab had already agreed to submit and to give him whatever he asked. Now Ben-hadad hardens his terms and demands to plunder everything. So Ahab consults the elders, and they tell him not to yield. What seemed like a negotiation was in fact a threat of total looting.

For today: when someone keeps demanding more and is never satisfied, it is wise to pause and seek counsel. Giving in again and again out of fear does not bring peace. Let us seek God's guidance and that of prudent people before we decide.
exp.19:7:
They say that the elders of Israel and all the people answered the king: "Do not listen to him, do not give in to what he asks." It is a clear and firm rejection of the enemy's demand. The elders are the respected leaders of the community.

King Ahab of Israel is in Samaria, surrounded by Ben-hadad, king of Syria. Ben-hadad had already asked for his silver, his gold, his wives and his children, and Ahab had agreed. But now he threatens that his servants will search the whole house and take everything of value. Ahab consults the leaders, and they tell him no. It was no longer a simple negotiation, but an unlimited plundering.

For today: there are moments when giving in once more is no longer peace, but opening the door to abuse. Seek advice from wise people and hold firmly to what is right.
exp.19:8:
This verse says that the king of Israel (Ahab) answers the messengers of Ben-hadad, king of Syria. He accepts what the Syrian king asked for at the first, but refuses the new demand. The word "servant" here is a humble way of speaking before a stronger king. "Messengers" are the men sent with the message.

Ben-hadad had laid siege to Samaria. First he asked for silver, gold, wives and children, and Ahab gave in. Then he demanded that his men search the city and take away everything of value (v. 6). The elders advised not to obey, and Ahab listened to them. The Bible does not say in detail why that second demand was the limit, but it was a much more serious demand.

For today: giving in on what can be given does not mean giving in on everything. It is wise to recognize where the line is that we must not cross, and to seek the counsel of prudent people before deciding, as Ahab did with the elders.
exp.19:12:
A prophet came to King Ahab with a message from God. His name is not given here. He asked Ahab, "Do you see this entire great army?" God was promising to put that massive army into Ahab's hand that very day, so that Ahab would know that the Lord is God.

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had surrounded Samaria with a large army and demanded that the city surrender. While he was drinking with other kings and felt secure, God acted. It is striking that he did so through Ahab, a king who was not faithful to him. Many see this as a sign of God's mercy toward his people, and also as an opportunity for Ahab to acknowledge him.

When problems seem enormous, God is still greater. We can trust that he is at work, even when we cannot see how, and we can recognize his hand when he helps us.
exp.19:16:
These verses tell how the young men who served the governors of the provinces were the first to go out from Samaria to fight. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had posted lookouts, and someone reported to him that some men had come out of the city.

This is part of the war between Aram and King Ahab of Israel. Samaria was under siege by a huge army. A prophet had announced that God would give Israel the victory through a small group. Meanwhile, Ben-hadad was drinking and felt secure, not taking so small an enemy seriously.

For today: God can work through small resources, and pride and excessive confidence make us careless. Trust God even when you feel weak, and do not feel invincible when everything seems to be in your favor.
exp.19:17:
Verse 18 records the order of Ben-hadad, king of Syria, when he is told that some men are coming out of Samaria. He does not know whether they come for peace or for war, and he orders that they be taken alive in either case. The word translated "take them alive" in the verse above is the key phrase here, and it means that they are to be captured, not killed.

The speaker is Ben-hadad, who was besieging Samaria. According to the text, he was drinking and drunk together with thirty-two allied kings. His overconfidence and carelessness contrast with what follows: Israel, though small, comes out and wins. The text presents this victory as the work of God (vv. 13-14).

For today: self-confidence and carelessness can leave us unprepared. Let us live with sobriety and attention, and remember that God can act even when we seem few and weak in the face of our problems.
exp.19:19:
Each Israelite soldier struck down the enemy he was facing. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, escaped on a horse together with some of his horsemen.

Context: Ben-hadad had besieged Samaria with a large army and felt confident. God, through a prophet, promised victory to King Ahab. The young servants of the district leaders went out first, and Ben-hadad, who was drinking, gave the order to capture them alive. The victory came from God, although Ahab was not a faithful king.

For today: God can give victory even when we seem few or weak. Trust in his help, but do not relax after a triumph. The prophet warned that the enemy would return, so keep watch and prepare yourself with humility.
exp.19:20:
It says that the king of Israel (Ahab) went out to fight and defeated the cavalry and chariots of the Syrians. He caused a great slaughter among them.

This account is not a speech but a narrative. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had laid siege to Samaria with great force and demanded everything. A prophet announced that God would give Israel the victory, so that they would know that He is the Lord. First the young men of the district governors went out, and then the army. Although Ahab was a king whose faith was doubtful, God acted for His own glory and out of mercy toward the people.

For today: when a problem seems bigger than you, remember that victory does not depend on your resources but on God. Trust in Him, take the step that is yours to take, and give thanks to Him when you come through.
exp.19:21:
A prophet approached the king of Israel, who at that time was Ahab, and advised him to prepare himself well. He told him to take courage, to think carefully, and to see what he ought to do, because the king of Syria would attack again when the year came around.

Israel had just won a battle against Ben-hadad, king of Syria. The prophet, who is not named here, speaks on God's behalf. He had already announced that victory earlier, so God does not abandon Israel after winning. He warns the king that the threat is not over. The Syrian servants, in the next verse, are already planning a new strategy.

After a success, it is easy to become overconfident and let your guard down. God invites us to be wise: to give thanks for the victory, but to stay alert, prepared, and dependent on Him for what is coming.
exp.19:23:
This verse is military advice. The servants of the king of Syria tell Ben-hadad to take the thirty-two allied kings away from their posts as commanders of the army and put captains in their places, that is, officers in charge.

The advisers of Ben-hadad are speaking after they have been defeated by Israel. They believed that the God of Israel had power only in the mountains, and so they propose fighting on the plain. Their idea was also to organize the command of the army better. That idea shows that they did not know the God of Israel well, and later in the text it shows that He is Lord over the valleys too.

For today: when we fail, it is wise to review what we can improve. But let us be careful not to blame God or shrink Him in our minds. He governs in every place and in every circumstance.
exp.19:24:
Here the advisers of King Ben-hadad of Syria tell him to raise a new army, equal to the one he lost: the same horses and war chariots. They propose fighting Israel again, but on the plain, that is, on level and open ground. The king listened to them and did just that.

These are the servants of Ben-hadad speaking, after Israel defeated them in the hills of Samaria. They thought that the God of Israel was a god of the mountains, like the gods of other peoples, and that on the plain he would have no power. The text shows that they misunderstood who God is. Later, a prophet announces to Ahab that the Lord will show that he rules in every place.

Today, we sometimes believe that God acts only at certain times or places, such as in church or in easy times. This passage invites us to trust that the Lord is present in everything: at work, at home, and in trials.
exp.19:25:
This verse says that when the year had come around again, Ben-hadad, king of Syria, counted and reviewed his soldiers once more. Then he went up to Aphek to fight against Israel again.

The narrator now tells what happened after Syria's first defeat. Ben-hadad's advisers told him that the God of Israel was a god of the hills, so this time he wanted to fight on the plain. He thought the LORD had limits. What comes next is that God will send a prophet to tell Ahab that he will win, so that they will know that the LORD is the Lord.

For today: let us not think that God is small, or that He acts only in certain places or at certain times. He is present in our good days and in our hard ones. We can trust that He is still Lord, even when the problem seems bigger than we are.
exp.19:28:
This verse tells how the two armies camped facing each other for seven days without fighting. On the seventh day the battle began, and the Israelites killed one hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in one day. The old numbers are sometimes debated, but the text wants to stress a huge victory.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. The Syrians, led by Ben-hadad, believed that the God of Israel had power only in the hills. So a prophet, a man of God, promised King Ahab that God would give them the victory, so that they would know that the LORD is God. Israel was small, like two little flocks of goats, and yet God acted.

For today: God is not limited to certain places or certain situations. When you feel small before a large problem, trust that God also rules over that season of your life, and wait for his help with patience.
exp.19:35:
He said that a prophet warned his companion that, because he had not obeyed the word of the Lord, a lion would attack him as soon as he left him. And so it happened.

A prophet asked another man to strike him, as part of a symbolic act to confront King Ahab. Ahab had made an alliance with Ben-hadad instead of acting on what God had indicated. The companion refused, and for that reason received this punishment. Some see here a severe judgment; others, a lesson that every word of God must be taken seriously.

For today: when God shows us clearly what we should do, obeying at once is an act of trust. Let us not think that partial or late obedience is of no importance.
exp.19:37:
This verse says that the prophet went out and placed himself on the road, waiting for the king of Israel. So that the king would not recognize him, he covered his face with ashes.

The prophet belonged to the company of the prophets and was obeying a command from God. Ahab, king of Israel, had let Ben-hadad, king of Syria, live, though God had given him into his hands. The wounded, disguised prophet tells an invented story, as a parable, so that the king himself will pass judgment. In this way the king condemns himself without realizing it, just as happened with David and Nathan.

For today: God sometimes speaks to us through simple examples so that we can see our own failings. Let us ask him for a humble heart, to hear his correction and obey him without excuses, before it is too late.
exp.19:38:
He says that a prophet in disguise, with a wound and a cloth over his eyes, stood in the king's path and cried out to him. He told how, in the middle of the battle, a man brought a prisoner to him and said, "Keep this man; if he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a weight of silver."

The prophet has no name in this passage. With this made-up story, he sets a trap for King Ahab, who had let go Ben-hadad, king of Syria, whom God had delivered into his hands. The king judges himself without realizing it.

For today: before judging others harshly, examine your own life with humility. Ask God to show you whether you have disobeyed in anything, and correct your path in time.
exp.19:39:
This verse says that the so-called soldier was busy with many things, and the prisoner he was supposed to guard escaped. Then the king of Israel answers him that the punishment is already decided, and that he himself said it. "Busy here and there" means he was going back and forth, occupied with many tasks. "Judgment" is the punishment that is pronounced.

It is King Ahab speaking, after defeating Ben-hadad of Syria and letting him go under a covenant. A disguised prophet tells him an invented story so that Ahab will pass judgment on himself. Without realizing it, the king condemns his own disobedience, since God had given Ben-hadad into his hand and he let him go.

For today: it is easy to see clearly the mistakes of others and to be lenient with our own. Today we can ask God for humility to apply to our own lives the same measure we use with others, and to obey him without letting distractions lead us astray.
exp.19:40:
He quickly pulled the bandage off his face, the cloth that had been covering his eyes as a disguise. When the king of Israel saw his face, he recognized that the man was a prophet.

The prophet told the king an invented story so that King Ahab would give his own verdict. Ahab had let Ben-hadad, king of Syria, go free, though God had delivered him into Ahab's hands to be destroyed. By pronouncing his own sentence, Ahab condemned himself. Then the prophet announced God's judgment.

For today: it is easy to see the faults of others and be harsh with them, while being blind to our own. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his Word and let it correct us, without excuses, before it is too late.
exp.20:1:
Ahab asks Naboth to sell him his vineyard or exchange it for another. He wants to use it as a vegetable garden, because it lies right next to his palace. He offers him two options: give him a better vineyard in its place, or pay him in money what it is worth.

Ahab is the king of Israel, and he speaks with Naboth, a man of Jezreel who owns that vineyard. The offer seems fair, but Naboth refuses, because it was the inheritance of his fathers. The law of Moses taught that family land should be kept within the family (Leviticus 25:23). Ahab asks for something that was not his to have.

That something is possible or seems fair does not mean we should demand it. When someone says "no" to what we desire, let us learn to respect that answer and not covet what belongs to another. Let us ask God for a heart content with what we have.
exp.20:5:
Ahab explains to Jezebel why he is sad. He tells her that he asked Naboth for his vineyard, offering to buy it for money or, if Naboth preferred, to give him another vineyard in exchange. Naboth refused.

Ahab is the king of Israel, and he speaks with his wife. His account is partial: he leaves out that Naboth refused because that land was an inheritance from his fathers, something the law of Moses protected (Leviticus 25:23). Ahab does not rebel openly, but he sinks into anger, and that opens the door to Jezebel's wicked plan.

When something is denied to us, we can become bitter or accept the limit with humility. If we keep brooding over our anger, others can take advantage of it to push us into doing wrong.
exp.20:7:
Jezebel writes letters in the name of King Ahab, seals them with his signet ring, and sends them to the elders and leaders of Jezreel, the city where Naboth lived. The seal served as the official signature, so the letters seemed to carry the king's authority.

Ahab was bitter because Naboth refused to sell him his vineyard, which was an inheritance from his family. Instead of accepting that refusal, Jezebel takes control. She acts without Ahab giving the order, but he does not stop her. The verses that follow show that she is preparing a false trial to kill Naboth.

Today we can learn not to use our influence or our position to take something away from another person. When we hear a just no, we should respect it. And if we have power, let us ask God for humility to use it justly.
exp.20:8:
This verse tells what Jezebel's letters said. They ordered that a fast be proclaimed, that is, a solemn gathering in which the people went without food to seek God. They also commanded that Naboth be set in a place of honor and in plain view of everyone.

Jezebel writes in the name of her husband, King Ahab, and uses his signet ring as the official seal. Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard, but Naboth refused to sell it. Jezebel uses a religious ceremony as a disguise to prepare an unjust murder. Naboth seemed to be honored, but it was a trap.

For today: let us be wary of anyone who uses religion to cover up injustice. And let us make sure that our practices of faith are always accompanied by truth, justice, and respect for our neighbor.
exp.20:10:
This verse tells us that the elders and the nobles of Naboth's city carried out exactly what Jezebel had ordered. Her orders are described as being in the letters she had sent them. "Nobles" here refers to the important men or leaders of the town. They did just what the letters said.

King Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard, but Naboth refused to sell it because it was the inheritance of his family. Then Jezebel, Ahab's wife, wrote letters sealed with the king's seal to falsely accuse Naboth and have him put to death. The text does not say that the leaders protested; they simply complied.

Local leaders were supposed to uphold justice, but they gave way before power. Today, when someone in authority asks us to take part in a lie or an injustice, let us remember that obeying does not free us from guilt. Let us ask God for the courage to speak the truth and to defend the innocent.
exp.20:13:
This verse tells us that the city's leaders sent word to Queen Jezebel that Naboth was already dead. The word "stoned" means he was killed by having stones thrown at him, a punishment for those accused of blasphemy.

The ones speaking here are the elders and nobles of Jezreel. Jezebel had written them letters asking them to arrange a false trial against Naboth. He had refused to sell his vineyard to King Ahab, because it was the inheritance of his fathers. Using lying witnesses, they accused him so that Ahab could take the land.

For today: this account invites us to distrust injustice, even when it seems legal or comes with a religious appearance. God sees what is hidden. We can defend the truth, refuse to take part in lies, and care for those who have no power.
exp.20:15:
This verse says that when Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to Naboth's vineyard in Jezreel, to take it for himself. The word "went down" simply means he traveled down to the vineyard, and "take possession" means to make something his own. Notice that Ahab does not ask how Naboth died.

The narrator tells what happened after Jezebel's plan. She had false charges brought against Naboth and had him stoned, because he refused to sell the vineyard he inherited from his fathers. Ahab took advantage of that crime. Soon after, God sends Elijah to confront him, and so we see that God looks upon injustice.

For today: it is not enough to avoid doing evil directly. If we benefit from an injustice and stay silent, we also bear responsibility. Let us ask God for the courage to ask questions, to reject what is unjust, and to act with integrity.
exp.20:18:
God tells Elijah to confront King Ahab with two things: "Have you murdered and also taken possession?" That is, he killed an innocent man and then seized his land. Next comes the announcement of punishment: dogs will lick Ahab's blood in the same place where they licked Naboth's.

God speaks through the prophet Elijah. Naboth refused to sell his vineyard, which was a family inheritance. Then Queen Jezebel had him falsely accused, and he was killed, and Ahab went to take the land. God sees the injustice and does not let it pass. About how this word was exactly fulfilled, the text continues to tell more later on.

For today: do not take advantage of others or stay silent in the face of abuse. God sees what is hidden, and at the same time he offers repentance to those who acknowledge their wrongdoing.
exp.20:22:
God himself also spoke about Jezebel, the wife of King Ahab: the dogs would devour her beside the wall of Jezreel. The verse of this word is a reference to the outer defenses of the city. It is a very harsh and specific sentence of judgment.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Elijah. Ahab and Jezebel had had Naboth put to death so they could take his vineyard. God judges them for that injustice and for leading Israel into idolatry. The text points out that Jezebel urged Ahab to do evil. Later, in 2 Kings 9, the fulfillment of this word is recounted.

For today: God sees injustice, even when the one who commits it has power. We can trust that he will judge with justice, and we must be careful not to abuse others or to encourage anyone to do wrong.
exp.20:23:
What the verse says: God announces that the descendants and relatives of Ahab who die will be humiliated. Those who die in the city will be eaten by dogs, and those who die in the field, by the birds of the air. In that time, being left without burial was a great dishonor.

Context: The prophet Elijah speaks on God's behalf. Ahab, together with his wife Jezebel, had had Naboth killed so that he could take his vineyard. Besides this, he had led Israel into idolatry. God thus announces a just judgment on his house, as he had already done with the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha.

For today: Our decisions affect others, especially those we lead. God sees injustice, even when it seems that no one will stop it. Today we can seek to act with honesty and respect what belongs to others, remembering that God also offers forgiveness to one who repents, as he later showed with Ahab.
exp.20:24:
He says that no one was as wicked as Ahab, because he "sold himself" to do evil in the sight of God. That is, he gave himself over completely to sin, like someone who sells himself into slavery. And his wife Jezebel pushed him on and encouraged him to do it.

This verse is a note from the book's narrator. It comes after Ahab and Jezebel had Naboth killed so they could take his vineyard. God sent the prophet Elijah with a judgment against them. The narrator explains why the judgment was so severe: Ahab let himself be dragged into evil, and idols led him to live like the nations God had driven out. Even so, the text that follows shows that Ahab humbled himself.

For today: let us be careful about who influences our decisions, and if we have done wrong, let us humble ourselves quickly before God, who responds to a repentant heart.
exp.20:25:
This verse says that Ahab was extremely detestable in God's sight, because he followed idols just as the Amorites did. The Amorites were the peoples who lived in Canaan, and God had driven them out of the land before the Israelites arrived.

Here the author makes a comment, like a note in parentheses, to sum up Ahab's life. He had just ordered Naboth killed so that he could take his vineyard, and God, through Elijah, announced judgment on his house. The text notes that Jezebel, his wife, pushed him to do wrong, but Ahab was still responsible for his actions.

For today: bad influences can push us, but they do not take away our responsibility. It is worth thinking about whom we listen to and, like Ahab later, humbling ourselves quickly before God when we fail.
exp.20:27:
This verse says that God spoke again to the prophet Elijah, the Tishbite. The word "Tishbite" tells us that Elijah came from the place called Tishbe. It is only an introduction: God is about to give a message.

The one speaking is the LORD. He has just pronounced judgment on Ahab for taking Naboth's vineyard and for his idolatry. Ahab reacted with grief: he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and fasted. God notices this change and answers Elijah. Although Ahab was very wicked, his humbling received a response of mercy, and the punishment was delayed.

For today: God sees repentance, even when it comes late or is imperfect. If you have failed, do not wait: acknowledge your wrong with humility before God. He is patient and compassionate, and he always listens to a sincere heart.
exp.20:28:
God asks Elijah whether he has noticed that Ahab humbled himself before Him. Because of that humility, God decides not to send the punishment announced during Ahab's lifetime, but to postpone it until the days of his son.

God is speaking, addressing Elijah. Ahab had allowed Naboth to be killed so that he could take his vineyard, and Elijah announced a severe punishment to him. Hearing it, Ahab tore his clothes, put on mourning clothes, and fasted. His repentance seems to have been real though limited, and God responded with mercy. The Bible does not say he was forgiven completely, only that the punishment was delayed.

For today: when you recognize a fault, do not make excuses. Humble yourself sincerely before God and seek to correct what you did wrong. He receives a repentant heart with mercy.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that three years passed without war between Syria (the Syrians, also called Arameans) and Israel. It was a time of calm after many conflicts.

Here no character is speaking; the narrator of the book of Kings simply reports the events. He presents this period of peace as the start of a new part of the story. In the verses that follow, King Ahab of Israel wants to recover the city of Ramoth Gilead, and that decision leads to a new war. The Bible does not say why there was this truce, so it is better not to invent an explanation.

For today: peaceful times are a gift, but they are also an opportunity to decide wisely. Before undertaking something new, it is good to pray and seek counsel, rather than being carried along by pride or impatience.
exp.21:8:
Here the king of Israel, Ahab, gives an order to a eunuch, that is, an officer of his court. He tells him to bring Micaiah, son of Imlah, quickly.

Ahab and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, wanted to know whether they should go to war against the Syrians. Jehoshaphat asked to consult a prophet of the LORD. Ahab acknowledged that Micaiah existed, but he despised him because he never told him what he wanted to hear. Jehoshaphat asked him not to speak like that, and then Ahab sent for him.

Many times we prefer voices that agree with us, even when the truth is uncomfortable. Today we can ask God for humility to listen to his Word, and to sincere people, even when they do not flatter us.
exp.21:9:
This verse describes a solemn scene. Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were sitting each on his throne, wearing their royal robes, in the open area near the entrance of the gate of Samaria. There, all the prophets were prophesying before them.

The king of Israel wanted to go to war against the Syrians to recover Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat asked to consult God, and Ahab gathered his prophets, who announced victory. Shortly before, Jehoshaphat had asked to hear Micaiah, a prophet whom Ahab did not want to listen to because he did not tell him what he wished to hear.

Today, we can learn not to surround ourselves only with voices that tell us what we want to hear. Honest advice, even when uncomfortable, can protect us. It is wise to measure every word against the Scriptures and to pray for wisdom.
exp.21:10:
This verse tells us that Zedekiah, the son of Chenaanah, made himself horns of iron. With them he put on a dramatic display for the king, declaring in the name of the Lord that Israel would gore the Syrians until they were destroyed.

He is one of the prophets at the court of King Ahab. Ahab and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, wanted to know whether they should attack Ramoth-gilead. All the prophets announced victory, and Zedekiah confirmed it with a dramatic action. But Jehoshaphat asked to hear another prophet, Micaiah, who said something very different. The text shows that many voices agreed, but that did not make them true.

For today: do not settle for what sounds strong or pleases the majority. Compare what you hear with the Word of God, and seek faithful counsel, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.21:13:
Micaiah says he swears by the living God, and that he will speak only what God himself tells him. In other words, he will not say what the king wants to hear or what the others are saying, but only what he receives from the Lord.

Micaiah is a prophet of the Lord. King Ahab wants to attack Ramoth-gilead, and four hundred prophets promise him victory. The messenger asks Micaiah to join the chorus and say the same thing. But Micaiah answers with this oath, showing that his loyalty is to God, not to the king. Later, his first answer sounds ironic, since the king himself notices that he is not speaking in earnest.

Today we can learn to be faithful to the truth even when everyone thinks differently. Before we speak, let us ask God for wisdom and seek what his Word says, without adapting the message to please others.
exp.21:18:
This verse says that the prophet Micaiah asks the king to hear the word of God. It tells that he saw the LORD sitting on his throne, surrounded by all the host of heaven, that is, the heavenly beings who serve him. They stood at his right hand and at his left.

Micaiah speaks as a prophet of the LORD before Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. The king's prophets had promised him victory, but Micaiah announces the truth, even though it is unwelcome. With this vision he shows that his message comes from the God who rules and who is above kings.

For today: God still sits on his throne, even when the world seems confused. We can listen to his word with humility, even when it is not what we want to hear, and trust that he rules with justice.
exp.21:28:
It says that the king of Israel, Ahab, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, marched together toward Ramoth-gilead to fight. The word for "went up" is used because the land of Israel is described as an ascent. Jehoshaphat is the same name as Josafat, and Ramoth is the same town as Ramot, a city east of the Jordan.

It is the narrator who tells what happened. Shortly before, the prophet Micaiah had warned that God would not bless this war. Ahab had him put in prison, and Micaiah replied that if Ahab returned in peace, God had not spoken through him. Even so, the two kings went ahead, as if the warning did not matter.

For today: hearing God is not enough if we then do not obey. Before making a major decision, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek wise counsel from the Word, even when the truth is uncomfortable and does not match our plans.
exp.21:29:
Here King Ahab of Israel proposes a plan to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah: he will dress as an ordinary soldier so that he will not be recognized, while Jehoshaphat will wear his royal robes. To disguise oneself means to change one's appearance so as not to be identified. Ahab did this and went into the battle.

Ahab is the one speaking. Shortly before, the prophet Micaiah had warned him that the war would end badly, and Ahab did not want to believe him. Now he tries to protect himself with cunning, and in doing so leaves Jehoshaphat more exposed, since the king of Syria had ordered his forces to attack only the king of Israel. So the plan was selfish and showed distrust in the word of God.

For today: we cannot hide from what God has already said. Instead of looking for tricks to escape the truth, it is better to listen with humility and obey, even when it costs us.
exp.21:30:
This verse tells how the king of Syria (Aram) gave a military order to his thirty-two captains who commanded his chariots. He told them not to waste time with the common soldiers, but to attack only the king of Israel, whether small or great.

The narrator describes the battle of Ramoth-gilead. Ahab, king of Israel, disguised himself so he would go unnoticed, and he let Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, wear the royal clothing. Syria wanted to end the war by eliminating the leader. The captains mistook Jehoshaphat for Ahab, but when they heard him cry out, they saw their error. The text does not explain all of Jehoshaphat's reasons, but it shows the danger of allying with Ahab.

For today: we cannot hide from our problems behind disguises, nor let others carry our risk. It is wise to act with honesty, to take care with our alliances, and to call on God in danger.
exp.21:32:
This verse tells us that the Syrian captains, when they got a close look at Jehoshaphat, realized that he was not the king of Israel and stopped chasing him. The phrase "turned back from pursuing him" means that they pulled away and no longer attacked him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The king of Syria had ordered his forces to attack only King Ahab of Israel. Ahab had disguised himself, but Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, was wearing his royal clothing and was mistaken for him. Jehoshaphat cried out, and the Bible does not explain in detail how, but it became clear that he was not Ahab. Soon after, an arrow shot at random struck Ahab, just as God had announced.

For today: even in dangerous situations that we ourselves bring about, God can care for us with mercy. Let us call out to Him and seek to walk with greater wisdom.
exp.21:33:
It says that a Syrian soldier shot an arrow without aiming at anyone in particular, at random, and yet it wounded the king of Israel at a weak point, between the joints of his armor. The king, who was Ahab, ordered his chariot driver: "Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am wounded."

The context is that Ahab, king of Israel, had disguised himself so that no one would recognize him, while Jehoshaphat went out in royal clothing. In this way he tried to escape the prophecy of Micaiah, which announced his defeat. Here Ahab speaks, wounded and afraid. What seemed to be chance fulfilled the word of God.

For today: we cannot hide our lives from God or escape His truth with disguises. It is better to hear His warning with humility, before it is too late.
exp.21:34:
It says that the battle grew very fierce that day. King Ahab, wounded by an arrow, stayed standing in his chariot facing the Syrians, and at evening he died. His blood ran down into the bottom of the chariot.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Ahab had ignored the warning of the prophet Micaiah and disguised himself so he would not be recognized. An arrow shot at random, without aiming at anyone in particular, struck him. In this way the word of God announced earlier was fulfilled.

For today: no one can hide from God or escape his word through disguises or cleverness. It is better to hear correction in time, even when it hurts, and to turn back to him with humility.
exp.21:36:
This verse sums up the end of King Ahab in few words. After he was wounded in battle, he died, and his body was carried back to Samaria, the capital of Israel, where they buried him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. Ahab had ignored the warning of the prophet Micaiah and went to war against the Syrians, trying to hide in disguise. Even so, an arrow struck him. The text shows that what God had said came to pass, as seen in the next verse, when the dogs lick up his blood.

For today: the word of God is fulfilled, even when we try to avoid it or find ways to escape. Instead of hardening the heart, it is better to listen in time, correct our course, and obey him with humility, while there is still opportunity.
exp.21:37:
They washed the war chariot of King Ahab in a pool in Samaria, together with his weapons. The dogs licked up the blood that had been left behind, just as God had said before.

The narrator of the book tells of the end of Ahab, king of Israel, who died in battle. Earlier, the prophet Elijah had announced that dogs would lick up his blood, because of his injustice toward Naboth (1 Kings 21). Some scholars note that the place does not fully match what was said then, and they explain this in different ways. Even so, the text stresses that the word of God was fulfilled.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, and his word does not fail. This invites us to live with humility and not to abuse anyone, trusting that God is just.
exp.21:40:
This verse says that Jehoshaphat, son of Asa, began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab, king of Israel. "Jehoshaphat" and "Ahab" are the names as they appear in the verse you are reading. "Judah" was the southern kingdom, and "Israel" the northern one.

The author of the book of Kings goes through the reigns of both kingdoms one by one. Here he changes subject: he finishes with Ahab and introduces Jehoshaphat. Scholars note that the dates of the kings are hard to fit together, and there are different explanations, so one should not claim more than the text says. What matters is that the account introduces a king who, according to the verses that follow, followed the LORD.

For today: God cares that his work continues from one generation to the next. We can ask ourselves what example of faith we leave to those who come after us, as Asa left it to Jehoshaphat.
exp.21:41:
The verse says that Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign over Judah, and that he ruled twenty-five years in Jerusalem. It also names his mother: Azubah, daughter of Shilhi. The word "was" appears here spelled in an older way.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, whose author is not known for certain. He presents each king with his age, the years of his reign, and the name of his mother, before he evaluates how the king governed. Here the scene shifts: Ahab, king of Israel, dies, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, is introduced, who will follow the path of his father Asa.

For today: God pays attention to the details of a life, even the simplest ones, such as family and the years we are given. What matters is how we live that time. Jehoshaphat did what was right, though he left something unfinished. Let us ask God for steady faithfulness and the courage to complete what we have begun.
exp.21:42:
It says that Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, followed the example of his father Asa. He did not turn away from that path and did what pleased God.

The narrator of the book of Kings is speaking here, summarizing how Jehoshaphat's reign went. He measures each king against a faithful model. The following verse makes clear that not everything was perfect: the high places, where the people offered sacrifices, were not taken away. So the text presents a good king, but one with limitations.

For today: we can learn from those who went before us in the faith, following the good we saw in them. But it is also wise to ask God to show us the areas we have not yet fully surrendered to him.
exp.21:47:
This verse says that at that time Edom had no king of its own. Instead of a king, there was a deputy, an older-style word that here means governor or representative, someone who ruled on behalf of another.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings gives a brief historical detail. Many understand that Edom was under the control of Judah, and that is why a deputy governed it. This detail helps explain why Jehoshaphat was able to set up his ships at the port of Ezion-geber, which lay nearby. The Bible gives no further details, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God cares even for the small details of history. Let us learn to read the whole Bible with attention and humility, knowing that every detail, though it may seem minor, has its place in the account of how God works among the nations.
exp.21:48:
King Jehoshaphat of Judah built a fleet of ships, large vessels made for long voyages at sea. He wanted to send them to Ophir, a region famous for its gold, though no one knows for certain where it was. But the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber, Judah's port on the Red Sea, and never set sail.

The writer of the book of Kings sums up the reign of Jehoshaphat here, a king who on the whole pleased God. This trade plan failed. The parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 20:35-37 explains that Jehoshaphat had joined forces with Ahaziah, king of Israel, and that a prophet told him God would destroy the work because of that alliance.

Before we join with someone in a project, it is wise to ask whether that partnership is sound. A good plan can fail when we team up without seeking God's guidance.
exp.12:21:
This verse says that the man of God turned back and ate bread and drank water in the place where God had told him not to. Because he disobeyed, the message is that his body would never reach the tomb of his family. The phrase "the tomb of your fathers" refers to the burial place where his ancestors were laid to rest.

The one speaking is another prophet, the old man who lived in Bethel, who had earlier misled the man of God into coming to his house. Now, while they sit at the table, a word from the LORD comes to him, and he announces it as judgment. God had given this man a clear command, and he left it behind because he believed another person. The text does not explain everything, but it shows that God's command weighed more than any other voice.

For today: when God has already spoken clearly in his Word, do not change your obedience because someone with a religious appearance tells you something different. Test everything against what God has said.
exp.5:19:
This section describes the inner sanctuary, the most holy room of the temple, where the ark of the covenant would be placed. It was a room shaped like a cube, about 9 meters on each side (20 cubits). Solomon overlaid its inside with the purest gold. He also overlaid the altar of cedar.

The author of the book of Kings tells how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. This room was the most sacred, because it was where God's presence would be among his people. For that reason every detail was cared for, and the gold showed its holiness and its worth.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not what is left over. Today we can draw near to Him through Christ, so give Him your time, your attention, and your heart with reverence and gratitude.
exp.1:36:
If you go out and cross the Kidron Valley, which lies east of the city, you will die. Solomon makes this plain: "Know for sure that you will die." The guilt would rest on Shimei alone, because he would have chosen to disobey a clear command. "Your blood will be on your own head" means exactly that: the responsibility would be his and no one else's.

King Solomon is speaking. His father David had been cursed by Shimei while fleeing from Absalom. Later David spared Shimei's life, but Solomon now sets a limit: Shimei must stay in Jerusalem, where he could be watched. Shimei accepted the condition and so was fully warned. Later he broke it by going to Gath.

For today: when we accept a commitment, we must keep it seriously. God and other people set limits to protect us, and when we ignore them, the consequences often come from our own choices.
exp.1:5:
Solomon is told to act with wisdom where Joab is concerned. The phrase "gray head" refers to an old man's gray hair, and "Sheol" is the place where the dead are laid. The sentence means that Joab should not die peacefully in old age, but should face justice for his crimes.

David, already old and near death, gives instructions to his son Solomon, who will be the new king. He reminds him that Joab, commander of his army, killed Abner and Amasa in a time of peace, shedding blood unjustly. Some understand these words as a desire for justice; others also see a political matter of security for the kingdom. The Bible does not explain all of David's reasons.

For today: justice matters, and serious actions do not disappear with time. But we can also learn to ask God for wisdom before deciding, without letting ourselves be carried away by resentment.
exp.19:9:
Ben-hadad, king of Syria, sends another message to Ahab. He swears by his gods, in words that amount to saying, "May the gods punish me if I do not carry out this threat." He says Samaria will be so completely destroyed that there will not be enough of its dust to give a handful to each of his men. The words "and ever so severely" show that the threat is pressed even harder than it first sounds.

Ben-hadad had laid siege to Samaria and had demanded from Ahab his silver, his gold, his wives, and his children. Ahab at first agreed, but when Ben-hadad also asked to search all the houses, the elders advised him to resist. Then Ben-hadad answered with this threat full of pride.

For today: speaking with arrogance and trusting in our own strength is dangerous. As the next verse shows, it is not wise to boast before the battle. It is better to act with humility and place the outcome in God's hands.
exp.11:6:
The elders advise Rehoboam to be a servant to the people, that is, to treat them with humility and serve them. If he responds to them with kind words, they will remain loyal to him for as long as he lives. In the phrase "if you will be," the wording points to a choice Rehoboam is being asked to make, and "if you will respond by speaking kind words" describes the way he should answer them.

The elders had served Solomon, Rehoboam's father. The people, gathered in Shechem, asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burdens that Solomon had placed on them. Rehoboam asked them for three days and sought counsel. These older men, with their experience, recommended gentleness. However, the text that follows shows that Rehoboam did not listen to them.

Whoever has authority, whether in the home, at work, or in the church, wins more hearts by serving and speaking with kindness than by imposing themselves. Jesus also taught that the greatest is the one who serves. Before deciding, it is worth listening to wise people with experience.
exp.3:31:
This verse says that Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, or wise sayings, and that his songs numbered a thousand and five. The word "composed" means that he created or wrote these works. "Proverbs" are wise sayings, comparisons or short sayings. "Songs" are the poems he wrote to be sung. Today we keep only a part of this: the book of Proverbs and some psalms, such as Psalms 72 and 127, are attributed to him.

The narrator of the book tells how God kept his promise to give Solomon wisdom (1 Kings 3). His fame spread far, and people from many nations came to hear him. The numbers show how much God gave him, although some scholars think they may also be a way of expressing abundance.

For today: wisdom grows when it is used and shared. Ask God for wisdom (James 1:5) and use it to encourage and teach others with simple, useful words.
exp.13:25:
It says that Shishak, king of Egypt, seized the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace. "He took everything" means that he carried off all of it. He also took the gold shields that Solomon had made. "Sodomites" refers to men who were prostitutes in pagan worship.

This is the account in the book of Kings, which tells the history of Israel. Before this event, Judah had turned away from God with pagan practices. In the fifth year of Rehoboam, Egypt invaded Jerusalem. The text presents this loss as a consequence of that unfaithfulness. Afterward Rehoboam made shields of bronze in place of the gold ones, a cheaper imitation.

When we turn away from God, we can lose what is valuable and be left with appearances. Today we can ask ourselves: am I tending my relationship with God, or am I only keeping up the facade? Returning to Him sincerely is worth more than any treasure.
exp.12:1:
A prophet, described as a "man of God," speaks directly to the altar as if it were a person. He declares that a son named Josiah will be born to the house of David. On that altar, Josiah will sacrifice the priests of the high places (places of worship on the hills) who burn incense there. He will also burn human bones on it.

The prophet comes from Judah, the southern kingdom, to Bethel, in the northern kingdom. Jeroboam had set up a rival worship site there, competing with the temple in Jerusalem, so that the people would not return to Judah. God sends this message to condemn that false worship. The prophecy is fulfilled about three centuries later, in the time of King Josiah (2 Kings 23:15-16).

God sees every religion that departs from his word, even when it seems useful or convenient. Today we can ask ourselves: does my way of worshiping follow what God said, or what is comfortable for me? And we can trust that his promises and warnings come true, even when they take a long time.
exp.11:23:
God tells Rehoboam, through the prophet Shemaiah, that he and his army must not go to war against the northern tribes. They are to go back home, because "this is my doing," that is, this division comes from God. The words "so they listened" and "turned back" show that the people obeyed.

The Lord speaks through Shemaiah, the man of God. After Solomon's death, ten tribes broke away from Rehoboam and followed Jeroboam. Rehoboam had gathered a large army to take back the kingdom by force. God stops the war, since the division was the result of Solomon's sins and of Rehoboam's harshness. The Bible says nothing more about how each soldier felt.

For today: sometimes we want to fight to get our way, even against relatives or brothers and sisters in the faith. Obeying God may mean stopping, lowering the sword, and letting him govern the situation.
exp.1:8:
David tells Solomon not to let Shimei go unpunished. The words "do not hold him guiltless" mean Solomon should not treat him as free of blame. "For you are a wise man, and you know what you ought to do to him" is a statement that Solomon will know how to act toward him. "Bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood" refers to Shimei's old age and speaks of a violent death.

David is about to die and gives his final instructions to his son, the new king. Years earlier, Shimei had cursed him as he fled from Absalom. Later, David had sworn that he would not put him to death. Bible students understand this in different ways: some see a measure of prudence meant to protect the kingdom, while others see a grudge that is hard to justify.

Today, do not carry resentment to the end of your life. Seek to forgive, and make sure your words and promises are sincere.
exp.17:31:
Elijah builds an altar with stones in honor of the Lord. Then he digs a trench around the altar, large enough to hold two seahs of seed. A seah was a unit of dry measure for grain, roughly seven to thirteen liters depending on how it is calculated. Here "seed" is what is sown, and the trench is a channel dug into the ground.

We are on Mount Carmel. Elijah, a prophet of God, confronts the prophets of Baal before all Israel, who had been divided between the two. Elijah repairs the fallen altar and uses twelve stones to remind the people that they belong to one God. The trench serves so that the water poured out later will be clearly seen.
