For today: when our spiritual life has been neglected, we can begin by repairing what has fallen, with simplicity and trust in God, without shortcuts. He deserves to be sought with order and sincerity.
exp.12:10:
It says that a certain old prophet was living in Bethel at that time. His sons told him everything the man of God had done that day in Bethel, and they also told their father the words he had spoken to King Jeroboam. "Now" simply introduces the story and moves it forward in time, and "man of God" refers to a man sent by God, a prophet.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. A prophet from Judah had just announced judgment against the false altar at Bethel, and he had obeyed God's command not to eat or drink there. The Bible does not explain why this old man lived in Bethel or why he had not spoken before. What follows shows that his interest in the prophet will have serious consequences.

For today: when God gives you a clear instruction, do not change it because of another person's opinion, even if that opinion seems very spiritual. Always compare what you hear with what God has already told you.
exp.10:22:
The passage says that God raised up an opponent against Solomon: Rezon, the son of Eliada. This man had fled from his master, Hadadezer, king of Zobah. The phrase "raised up" means to bring someone forward or allow them to rise. An adversary is someone who opposes another or sets himself against them.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Solomon had turned away from God by following other gods, and for this reason God allowed enemies to come against him. Rezon settled in Damascus, became king of Syria, and opposed Israel during Solomon's reign. The text presents this as a consequence of disobedience, though it does not explain every detail of how God acted.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously. When we notice that we have drifted away from Him, let us not wait for greater troubles to come. Let us return soon, with humility, and ask Him to help us obey Him.
exp.21:25:
This verse records the order of King Ahab of Israel: take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son. "Return him" means hand him back to these officials, and the order is to throw the prophet into prison.

Ahab gives this command because Micaiah had announced to him, on behalf of God, that his war against Ramoth-gilead would end badly. The other prophets had promised him victory, and Zedekiah even struck Micaiah. Instead of heeding the warning, the king prefers to punish the messenger. Beyond what the text says, it is not known with certainty who Amon and Joash were.

For today: when the truth makes us uncomfortable, we should not silence it or attack the one who speaks it. Let us ask for humility to listen to correction, even when it hurts, because it may save us from serious mistakes.
exp.1:38:
It says that three years passed, and two of Shimei's slaves ran away to Gath, where Achish, son of Maacah, was king. Someone told Shimei where they were. "Slaves" here means people owned by Shimei, who served in his household. "Ran away" means that they escaped.

The narrator tells what happened after Solomon had set a condition for Shimei: he was to live in Jerusalem and not cross the Kidron valley, under penalty of death. Shimei had agreed and obeyed for a time. Years earlier Shimei had cursed King David, and that is why Solomon was keeping watch over him. This news tests his promise. Going to Gath meant crossing the Kidron.

For today: when we give our word, temptations often come later, dressed up as good reasons. Think before giving in to a small loss, because it can cost you something much greater. Ask God for help to keep what you have promised.
exp.2:10:
God tells Solomon that he is pleased with his request. Solomon did not ask for a long life, for wealth, or for the death of his enemies. Instead, he asked for discernment to administer justice, that is, the ability to listen carefully and decide fairly.

God speaks at Gibeon, in a dream Solomon had at the beginning of his reign. God had offered to give him whatever he wanted. Solomon was young and felt the weight of leading a large people, so he asked for help to serve well, not to benefit himself.

For today: before asking God for something, examine your motives. We can ask him for wisdom to treat with justice and patience those who depend on us, at home, at work, or in the church. God delights in hearts that seek to serve.
exp.18:7:
He got up and ate and drank what God had provided through an angel. Strengthened by that food, he walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God. Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, according to many scholars. The bread mentioned in the account is a flat loaf baked on hot coals.

Elijah was fleeing from Queen Jezebel, who wanted to kill him. He was exhausted, discouraged, and wished to die. God did not rebuke him first but cared for his body with rest and food. Then He led him to the mountain where God had revealed Himself to Moses. There God would speak to him.

For today: when you are tired or discouraged, do not despise the simple things, such as sleeping, eating, and resting. God often takes care of us first in the basics, and then speaks to us with greater clarity.
exp.6:29:
Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles, and a basin rested on four supports, with wreaths at each side. The verse describes the stands themselves, which were carts of bronze built to hold a large basin, called a laver. The supports that held the basin up were set at the four corners of the stand and were cast from the same piece as the stand. The wreaths at each side were decorative pieces that were part of the design.

This is not God speaking, but the narrator of the book, who describes in detail the works that the craftsman Hiram of Tyre made for Solomon's temple. These basins were used for washing what was used in the sacrifices, and the wheels made it possible to move them.

For today: God pays attention to details and to what supports the service to Him. Let us do even the small and hidden tasks with care and faithfulness.
exp.16:20:
Then he stretched himself out over the child three times and cried out to the LORD, "O LORD my God, please let this boy's life return to him!" The word "stretched" describes how he lay over the boy, and "life" refers to the child's life itself.

The prophet Elijah is the one speaking. He is staying in the house of a widow from Zarephath, who had cared for him in a time of hunger. Her son died, and she felt that God was punishing her. Elijah, confused and hurt, carries the child to his room and prays with sincerity. The text does not explain why he stretched himself out three times, and some see it as a sign of persistence in prayer.

We can bring our pain and our questions to God with complete honesty. Elijah did not pretend or hide his anguish; he prayed persistently and trusted that God listens. When something overwhelms us, let us speak to Him without fear.
exp.5:35:
This verse describes how Solomon built the inner courtyard of the temple. It had three rows of dressed stone and one row of trimmed cedar beams. A "courtyard" is an open yard around the temple, and "dressed" refers to stone that has been shaped with tools.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, recounting in detail the building of the temple in Jerusalem. This is not a speech but a historical record. These details show the care and order with which the work was done for God. Scholars are not entirely certain how this wall looked exactly, but the general idea is a solid and well-made wall.

For today: God values what we do with care and perseverance, even in the details that almost no one sees. We can offer Him our work, study, or service with excellence and patience, knowing that He looks at the heart and not only at the result.
exp.21:23:
Zedekiah, one of King Ahab's prophets, went up to Micaiah and struck him in the face. Then he demanded, with scorn, which way the Spirit of the LORD had gone when He left him to speak to Micaiah. "Struck" means hit, and "face" is the front of the head.

Micaiah had just said that the LORD had allowed a lying spirit to be in the king's prophets, and that the LORD had decided disaster would come upon Ahab. Zedekiah, who had told Ahab what he wanted to hear, felt accused and answered with violence instead of weighing the message. Micaiah replied that Ahab would see it on the day of disaster. Some understand the "lying spirit" as a divine permission to judge; the text does not fully explain this.

When a word from God makes us uncomfortable, let us not silence it with pride or anger. Let us examine it with humility and in the light of the Bible.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that Hiram provided Solomon with all the timber he wanted. The Hebrew word behind "cypress" is one that many scholars connect with the cypress or the pine, though this is not known with complete certainty.

Hiram was the king of Tyre, and Solomon was preparing to build the temple. Solomon had asked him for cedar wood from Lebanon, and Hiram agreed to send it by sea on rafts. In return, Solomon would provide wheat and oil for Hiram's household. The text adds that God gave wisdom to Solomon, and that there was peace between the two kings.

Today we can learn that good work often moves forward through fair agreements and cooperation. Keep your commitments, treat with respect those who help you, and recognize that God can use many people to carry out his plans.
exp.21:52:
Ahaziah, king of Israel, did what was evil in the Lord's eyes. He followed the bad example of his father Ahab, his mother Jezebel, and Jeroboam, the king who led Israel into sin. The phrase about walking in the same way means that he lived just as they did. He served and worshiped Baal, a false god of Canaan, and in this way he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking, not a character. He sums up the reign of Ahaziah, which lasted only two years, and judges it by how faithful he was to God. This kind of judgment is repeated for many kings of Israel. It shows that sin was passed down from generation to generation, and that the throne was taken by someone who did not learn from the mistakes of his parents.

For today: all of us receive influences from our family, good and bad. We can ask ourselves which habits we imitate without thinking, and ask God for help to follow Him, not only what we learned at home.
exp.17:2:
King Ahab summoned Obadiah, the man in charge of the palace. Obadiah was a high-ranking official who managed the royal household. We are told that Obadiah greatly feared the LORD, meaning he had a deep and sincere reverence for God, and this showed in the way he lived.

The narrator introduces Obadiah while a severe famine grips the land after years without rain. God is about to send Elijah to meet Ahab. The verses that follow explain that Obadiah, serving under Ahab and Jezebel, secretly protected a hundred prophets of the LORD. It is a detail that shows his courage.

For today: One can serve God in difficult places, even while working for people who do not honor him. Today we can live with faithfulness and courage in our work or surroundings, doing good with wisdom, even when no one notices.
exp.7:27:
Here Solomon asks God to listen to him. He asks God to regard his prayer and plea, so that God will hear the cry and the prayer. A "prayer" is a humble request, and a "plea" is a request made with urgency. Solomon presents himself as God's "servant," someone who recognizes that he depends on God.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has just acknowledged that not even the highest heavens can contain God, much less a building. Even so, he asks that God hear the prayers offered toward that place, because God had promised to put his name there. His request rests on God's faithfulness to his word.

God is great and above all things, yet he still listens to you. You can pray with humility and without fear, trusting that God cares about what you say today.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that King Solomon gave orders that very large and valuable stones be quarried for the foundation of the temple, along with stones already dressed and shaped. "Costly stones" are expensive stones of good quality. "Dressed stones" are stones worked and cut so that they would fit well together.

The account tells how Solomon prepared the building of the temple. Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing the king's orders. Solomon organized thousands of workers and worked together with Hiram, king of Tyre, who provided timber and workers. The foundations were the base of the whole work, and that is why firm, good material was chosen.

For today: what is built well begins with a solid foundation. We can devote time and effort to grounding our lives in the Word of God and in prayer, even though this is not often seen, because what comes after depends on it.
exp.0:39:
All the people followed Solomon, playing flutes and filling the streets with cheering and celebration. Their joy was so loud and so strong that it seemed the ground itself was splitting open. The phrase "the earth was split" is an exaggerated way of saying the noise was enormous.

This is part of the larger story. David was now very old, and his son Adonijah had declared himself king without David's approval. So Nathan the prophet, Zadok the priest and Benaiah took Solomon down to Gihon, as David had commanded. There they anointed him as king. The people celebrated, and their noise carried all the way to the feast Adonijah was holding, as the story goes on to show.

For today: God deserves our sincere joy. Just as the people rejoiced over the anointed king, we can praise Christ, our King, with gladness, without shame or fear of what others think.
exp.6:20:
This verse tells how Hiram, the craftsman who worked for Solomon, set up two great bronze pillars at the entrance of the temple. The porch is the covered entryway. He gave the pillar to the south the name Jachin, and the pillar to the north the name Boaz. "Set up" means raised or stood upright.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is describing in detail the construction of the temple in Jerusalem. The names are often explained as "he establishes" (Jachin) and "in him is strength" (Boaz), though some scholars debate their exact meaning. Many think they served as a reminder that God sustains his people and his house.

For today: before you come to worship, remember that your stability and strength come from God. You might begin your day or your prayer by saying: "Lord, you sustain me."
exp.14:6:
This verse closes the account of the reign of Abijam, king of Judah. It asks whether the rest of his deeds and all his accomplishments are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, official court records that we do not have today. It also records that there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam, king of Israel. The phrase "slept with his fathers" is a way of saying that he died.

The writer of Kings summarizes the reign and points to other records for more detail. Earlier, he explained that, for the sake of David, God kept the royal line in Judah in place despite Abijam's sins. The division between the two kingdoms continued to cause conflict.

For today: our lives also leave a record. It is worth asking ourselves what will be said about us. Let us do what is right before God each day, without living only on what others did before us, and let us seek peace wherever we can.
exp.15:25:
This verse says that Omri, king of Israel, followed the same path of wickedness as Jeroboam, son of Nebat. He copied Jeroboam's sins, the sins that Jeroboam led the people of Israel into. The phrase "provoking the LORD" means that he angered God. The "worthless idols" were false images that the people worshiped in place of the true God.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, judging each king according to his faithfulness to God. Jeroboam had set up golden calves so that the northern kingdom would not go up to worship in Jerusalem (1 Kings 12). Omri, although he was a powerful king and founded Samaria, is judged mainly for turning away from God.

For today: success or power are worth nothing more than faithfulness to God. It is worth asking ourselves which examples we follow, because what we imitate can draw us closer to God or pull us away from Him.
exp.14:10:
And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done. Here the verse uses "father," but in the Bible this word can also mean an ancestor, since Asa was a descendant of David. "Right" means just, and what pleases God.

The book of Kings tells this story through a narrator who reviews the history of the kings of Israel and Judah. He judges each king by how faithful he was to God. Asa ruled Judah for forty-one years, and the verses that follow give examples: he removed practices of idolatry and destroyed the idol made by his mother, even though that cost him a confrontation with his own family.

Today, this text invites us to obey God even when it is hard. Sometimes doing what is right requires uncomfortable decisions, even with people we love. Let us ask God for the courage to put him first.
exp.0:48:
This verse says that Adonijah's guests were frightened when they heard the news. All of them got up and scattered in every direction. The guests at the banquet were the people invited to the feast, and the verse's description of them arising in terror and scattering simply means they each left on their own path.

The narrator recounts what happened at the banquet of Adonijah, son of David, who had proclaimed himself king without David having decided it. Then news arrived that David, now an old man, had made Solomon king. The guests understood that supporting Adonijah now was dangerous, and they abandoned him at once.

Plans that rest on pride and on the support of people can collapse quickly. It is worth asking ourselves whether our goals seek God's will or only our own benefit. What God sustains endures; everything else may last only for a moment.
exp.11:3:
The people of Israel ask Rehoboam, the new king, to make their burden lighter than the one his father Solomon placed on them. A "yoke" is the wooden frame placed on oxen for pulling loads; here it stands for a heavy load of labor and taxes. "Forced service" is labor that people are required to do. They promise that if he lightens that load, they will serve him.

Jeroboam speaks on behalf of the whole assembly of Israel, gathered in Shechem to make Rehoboam king. Solomon had required much labor and tribute from the people for his great building works. Jeroboam had fled to Egypt, but they had called him back to speak for them. The request is respectful, and Rehoboam asks for three days to consider his answer.

For today: whoever holds authority should listen humbly to those who depend on him. At home, at work, or in church, asking for counsel and caring for others, rather than weighing them down, honors God.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that there was war between the houses of Rehoboam, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel, during all the days of Abijam's life. The phrase "all the days of Abijam's life" shows that the conflict lasted for the whole of his reign.

The book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel and Judah. When Solomon died, the kingdom was divided into two. Rehoboam ruled the south and Jeroboam ruled the north. The verse names Rehoboam's house, and the surrounding context speaks of Abijam, his son, who reigned in his place. Whatever the exact details, the point is clear: the division brought lasting hostility between brothers of the same people.

For today: divisions that are never healed become a habit and are passed down to children. If there is a conflict with a relative or a brother in the faith, seek reconciliation soon, before it becomes part of your life.
exp.2:13:
God tells Solomon that, along with wisdom, riches and honor, he offers him a promise: a long life. But he attaches one condition: that Solomon walk in God's ways and keep his statutes and commandments, just as David his father did. "Statutes" are the rules God gave his people. "I will prolong your days" means giving him a long life.

God speaks in a dream at Gibeon. Solomon, the new king, did not ask for wealth or fame, but for an understanding heart to govern with justice. God was pleased and gave him more than he asked. This promise depends on his faithfulness. The Bible shows that David was not perfect, but he sought God sincerely and repented.

For today: the gifts and opportunities God gives us are not enough on their own. What matters is continuing to walk with him each day. Ask him today to help you obey him in one specific decision.
exp.10:16:
Hadad was still just a young boy when he escaped from Edom with some Edomite men who had served his father. They fled to Egypt. Our reader's verse says Hadad had "fled to Egypt," so the verse keeps that wording and drops any comment on the older word "fled."

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He explains why Hadad later became an opponent of Solomon. Years earlier, Joab had attacked Edom very harshly, and Hadad survived. In Egypt the pharaoh welcomed him. Some scholars think the account of the slaughter is summarized, so not all the details are clear.

For today: wounds and injustices that are never healed can keep bearing bitter fruit for years. Today we can seek peace, avoid revenge, and ask God to help us forgive and not leave roots of enmity behind.
exp.17:27:
They shouted even louder and cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom, until the blood gushed over them. Cutting themselves means cutting into the skin.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. Elijah had challenged the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel to see who was the true God. After Elijah's mockery, they redoubled their effort and their pain to get Baal's attention, but there was no answer at all.

Today we can learn that we do not need to strain or suffer to win God's attention. He is not like a silent, distant idol. We can pray with simplicity and confidence, knowing that God hears his children.
exp.12:7:
Here the man of God gives King Jeroboam a firm answer. He tells him that even if the king gave him half of his possessions, he still would not go with him, nor would he eat bread or drink water in that place. Here "half your possessions" refers to the king's wealth and estate, and "bread" stands for food in general.

A prophet from Judah had come to Bethel to speak against the false altar that Jeroboam had set up. The king reached out to seize him, and his hand dried up; then it was healed through the prophet's prayer. Grateful, the king invited him to eat, but God had already commanded him not to eat, not to drink, and to return by another way.

For today: when God has given us a clear instruction, no gift, flattery, or offer should make us hesitate. Obeying God is worth more than any reward.
exp.0:52:
This verse tells that King Solomon summoned Adonijah, who had been holding on to the horns of the altar. Adonijah came and bowed down before the king, as a sign of submission. Solomon told him, "Go to your home."

Adonijah, Solomon's brother, had tried to make himself king without David's approval. When Solomon was proclaimed king, Adonijah became afraid and sought refuge at the altar. Solomon gave him a conditional chance: if he proved loyal, he would live. Here he lets him go in peace, although later events would show more.

For today: mercy offers a new opportunity, but it calls for humility and loyalty. If someone asks us for forgiveness, we can extend grace; and if we have failed, let us come near with humility.
exp.20:14:
Jezebel learns that Naboth has been stoned to death. Then she tells Ahab to get up and take the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, the one Naboth would not sell to him. "Take possession" means to take it as your own. "Refused to give it for silver" means he would not sell it. She says this coldly: since Naboth is no longer alive, the vineyard is now free for the taking.

Jezebel, Ahab's wife, is the one speaking. He wanted that vineyard, but Naboth refused because it was the inheritance of his fathers (1 Kings 21:3). Jezebel set up a false trial with two lying witnesses, men who were wicked and worthless. In this way she used the appearance of law to carry out a murder.

Today, this passage warns us against pursuing what we want at any cost. Something can look legal and still be unjust. Let us ask God for an honest heart, one that respects our neighbor and does not use power to take advantage of others.
exp.5:32:
Solomon made door frames of olive wood for the entrance to the temple, the main hall that stood before the most holy place. The upright sides of each frame are called posts. The verse says these posts were four-sided, and scholars note that the exact meaning of this word is not entirely certain.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who tells how Solomon built the house of God. He describes the wood, the gold, and the carved figures of cherubim and palm trees in detail, because the temple was the place where Israel drew near to God. The names of some of the woods are uncertain.

For today: God cares about care and dedication. We can serve Him faithfully in small things, such as a sincere prayer or a task done well, remembering that coming near to Him is a privilege.
exp.19:32:
The passage tells how Ben-hadad's servants were watching closely for any sign of hope. The word "grasped" means they took hold of it right away. When Ahab said "He is my brother," they seized on it at once and replied, "Yes, your brother Ben-hadad." Ahab ordered that he be brought, and he had him come up into his chariot, a gesture of honor.

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had attacked Israel and was now defeated. His servants, dressed in sackcloth and ropes as a sign of humiliation, sought his life. Ahab, king of Israel, spoke lightly and treated an enemy as a brother. Afterward he made a covenant with him, and a prophet rebuked him, because God had given Ben-hadad into his hand.

For today: measure your words and decisions by what God says, not only by what seems kind or convenient. Mercy is good, but it must go hand in hand with obedience and wisdom.
exp.17:44:
This verse tells how, while Elijah and his servant were waiting, the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain began to fall. Then Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel.

After three and a half years of drought, Elijah had prayed and trusted that God would send rain. He had seen only a small cloud, but he believed the promise. The account tells us the rain came, and Ahab went to Jezreel, as Elijah had advised him to do.

For today: sometimes God begins to answer with small signs. If He has given you a promise, keep praying with patience and attention, and do not despise humble beginnings. When the full answer comes, remember to thank Him.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that Solomon sat on the throne of his father David and that his kingdom was firmly established. The phrase "firmly established" means that his rule was very secure and strong.

The narrator of the book, who is not named, is describing the passage from one reign to the next. David has just died after ruling for forty years. Before he died, he had left instructions for Solomon. Yet the next verse shows that Adonijah, another son of David, was still trying to do something. So the firmness of the kingdom is seen gradually, not all at once.

For today: God can give us stability, but it is kept through obedience and wisdom. If we receive a responsibility, it is good to ask God for direction and to act with integrity, rather than relying only on our own strength.
exp.11:22:
This verse is God's command to his prophet Shemaiah: he is to tell Rehoboam, the son of Solomon and king of Judah, along with all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and the rest of the people.

God speaks, and he does so through Shemaiah, called "the man of God." Rehoboam had gathered an army of one hundred eighty thousand men to fight against the northern tribes, which had separated from the kingdom. God intervenes before there is a war between brothers. In the verses that follow, we see that the people obeyed and went home.

For today: before entering into a conflict, especially with relatives or brothers and sisters in the faith, it is wise to stop and listen to God. Sometimes obeying means putting down the fight and going home.
exp.17:8:
Obadiah asks Elijah, "How have I sinned?" He does not understand why Elijah is asking him to do something so dangerous. He believes that if he tells Ahab that Elijah is there, he himself will end up dead. Here "your servant" is Obadiah speaking of himself with humility, and "handing over" means putting someone into another person's power.

The speaker is Obadiah, a man who was in charge of Ahab's household but who feared God. Three years of drought had passed, and Ahab was searching for Elijah everywhere. Elijah asks him to tell the king that he is there. Obadiah fears that the Spirit of the Lord will carry Elijah off to another place and Ahab will kill him for failing to find him.

For today: when God asks us to do something that frightens us, we can honestly express our fear. Then, as Obadiah did, we can trust and obey.
exp.7:40:
This verse begins a sentence that is completed in the verses that follow. It speaks of the foreigner, that is, someone who is not one of Israel's people and who has come from a distant land because of God's name. Here "because of Your name" means that he is drawn by the fame and character of the Lord.

The one speaking is Solomon, in his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has already asked God to hear Israel. Now he includes foreigners too. He asks that God answer their prayers so that all the peoples may know God and revere him.

For today: God has an open heart toward those who come from afar seeking him. We can imitate him by warmly welcoming those who are new to our church or community, such as migrants or visitors, and by helping them feel at home so that they may come to know the Lord.
exp.7:9:
This verse tells how, when the priests came out of the Holy Place after setting the ark of the covenant in its place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD.

The account in the book of Kings describes the day Solomon dedicated the first temple in Jerusalem. The priests had just placed the ark in the most holy place. The cloud, which in other passages of the Bible accompanies God's presence, showed that He accepted that house. The text says the priests could not continue ministering because of it.

For today: God is not impressed only by what we build, but desires to dwell among those who seek him with reverence. Before serving, take a moment to pray and acknowledge his presence.
exp.0:4:
He says that Adonijah, David's son by Haggith, began to puff himself up and declared, "I will be king!" To show that he was king, he acquired chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run ahead of him, as an escort that announced his importance.

The narrator tells this when David is already very old and weak. Adonijah is one of the older sons still living, and he wants the throne for himself, without David having appointed him. The text makes clear that his father never corrected him, and that Adonijah had the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. It does not say that God had chosen him.

For today: wanting something is not the same as receiving it from God. Before seeking a place of honor, it is good to ask ourselves whether we want it out of pride, or whether we are waiting for God's timing and calling.
exp.13:19:
This verse says that Jeroboam was king of Israel for twenty-two years. The phrase "rested with his fathers" is a way of saying that he died. After his death, his son Nadab became the new king.

The author of the book of Kings closes here the account of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom. Earlier, the story tells that God, through the prophet Ahijah, had announced judgment on his house for leading the people into idolatry. By mentioning Nadab, the account shows that the dynasty continued, but under that warning.

For today: our life is short, and what weighs most is not the years or the positions, but what we leave behind through our decisions. Ask yourself what you are sowing in your family and in those who follow you, and seek for it to be a legacy of faithfulness to God.
exp.10:18:
It says that Hadad, the young Edomite who fled to Egypt, was very well received by the Pharaoh. So highly did he think of him that he gave him in marriage to the sister of Queen Tahpenes, his own wife. The phrase "such great favor" means that he was well liked and received kindness. In this verse, "in marriage" simply states that the Pharaoh arranged for Hadad to wed the woman.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He tells how God allowed Hadad to rise up as an adversary against Solomon, because of Solomon's disobedience. Hadad had escaped as a boy when Joab destroyed the males of Edom. In Egypt he grew up under protection and came to be connected by marriage to the royal family. The Egyptian names and details are understood in various ways, but the account emphasizes his position.

For today: God can use unexpected places and people who are outsiders to accomplish his purposes. We can trust that he governs history, and we should obey him without taking our own well-being for granted.
exp.21:46:
King Jehoshaphat removed from the land of Judah the men who still took part in prostitution connected with pagan worship. The word "sodomites" in older texts refers to men given over to this practice in idolatrous shrines, and the verb "swept" means that he cleared them out completely, the way someone cleans a house. His father Asa had already begun that cleansing.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing Jehoshaphat's reign. He wants to show that this was a king who sought to please God, although he had flaws, such as allying himself with Israel. Some details of these practices are not known with complete precision.

For today: it is not enough to inherit good faith or good examples from our parents. We must keep cleansing our lives of whatever dishonors God, with humility and perseverance, leaving nothing hidden away.
exp.10:38:
God says he will humble the descendants of David because of Solomon's sin. The word "humble" means to bring low or weaken, and "descendants" refers to the children and later generations of David. But the verse ends with hope: this humbling will not last forever.

It is God speaking, through the prophet Ahijah, addressing Jeroboam. Solomon had turned away from the Lord by following false gods, and for that reason the kingdom would be divided. God offers Jeroboam the northern kingdom, on the condition that he obey Him. Even so, God remembers his promise to David and leaves the door open to restoration.

For today: God disciplines, but he does not cast off his own. If you are facing consequences for mistakes, remember that his correction seeks to heal, not to destroy. Return to Him with confidence.
exp.7:10:
When the priests came out of the holy place, a cloud filled the temple, and they could not stand there to serve. The Berean wording makes the point plainly: the cloud was so thick that the priests could not keep carrying out their duties. "To minister" here means serving in the tasks of worship. The cloud signaled that the glory of the LORD, that is, his majestic and holy presence, had filled the house of the LORD.

The passage describes the moment when Solomon finishes the temple and the ark of the covenant is brought to its place. It is not spoken by a character but by the narrator of the book. The cloud recalls when God led Israel in the wilderness. Solomon's response mentions the darkness, and many understand this as a sign that God is holy and cannot be controlled.

Today we can remember that worship is not about our own agenda but about God himself. Before we serve, it is good to stop, be quiet, and let his presence fill us with reverence and humility.
exp.3:8:
This verse names another of Solomon's twelve governors: Ben-deker, the son of Deker. The verse names his father but not the governor himself. He was in charge of several towns: Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan. In these names, "Beth" means "house of."

The book of Kings presents an official list of Solomon's administration. Each governor was responsible for supplying food to the king and his household for one month of the year. The text gives no further details about this man, and we do not know with certainty where all these places were.

For today: God notices simple and orderly work. Even if you are not well known, your faithful service, month after month, sustains others. Do your part with responsibility and honesty, as serving the Lord.
exp.4:12:
Solomon's men were pressed into labor for the kingdom. This verse says that King Solomon gathered a labor force from all Israel, meaning men required to work for the kingdom. He drew together thirty thousand of them. Here the point is that the labor itself was demanded, not money.

This is part of the account in the book of Kings, which tells the story of Solomon. He was preparing to build the temple, and for that reason he made an alliance with Hiram, king of Tyre, who supplied timber from Lebanon. The men worked in shifts: one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram oversaw this work. Later on, some Israelites felt that this burden was heavy.

For today: serving God and others requires organization and a fair sharing of the load. If you lead something, take care that no one is left exhausted and that everyone gets rest.
exp.0:25:
Here the prophet Nathan tells King David that Adonijah made a great feast and invited many, but did not invite Nathan, nor the priest Zadok, nor Benaiah, nor Solomon. The word "invited" in this context means guests who were asked to come to the feast, and the humble way of speaking to the king is "your servant," as the verse itself shows.

Nathan speaks before David, who is now very old. Adonijah, one of his sons, was declaring himself king without David having decided it. Nathan points out who was left out: precisely those who supported Solomon. In this way he wants David to see what is happening and act. The Bible says nothing more about Adonijah's reasons, but the fact that he left them out suggests he was trying to secure his power.

For today: when someone seeks their own advantage, they tend to surround themselves only with those who approve of them. Let us ask God for humility to listen also to those who tell us the truth with respect.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that Solomon answered Hiram by sending him a message. The phrase "relayed this message" means that he sent messengers carrying his words, like a letter or a spoken message. What follows is the content of that message.

Hiram, king of Tyre, had sent his servants to congratulate Solomon, since he had always held David in high regard. Now Solomon replies with respect and begins to explain his plan: to build the temple for the Lord. With this reply, Solomon seeks Hiram's help, since Hiram had timber and skilled workers.

For today: when a good relationship is nurtured with gratitude, it can open doors to serve God. Respond kindly to those who reach out to you, and think about how your friendships can help you do good.
exp.3:23:
Solomon ruled over everything west of the Euphrates River, from Tiphsah, a city on the river, to Gaza, near the Mediterranean Sea. The kings of that whole area were under his authority. "Everything west of the Euphrates" names the region he controlled, and "all the kingdoms" means the rulers of those lands. That is why he had peace on every side of his borders.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, not Solomon. He describes the high point of Solomon's reign. The verses before it talk about the abundant food of his household, and the verses after it describe a people living in security. The author shows that God kept his promises of blessing. But the book also tells how Solomon later turned away from God.

For today: peace and abundance are gifts from God. If you have calm in your life today, use it to serve others and remain faithful to God, without forgetting him.
exp.6:18:
This verse describes the top section of the two bronze pillars that stood at the entrance of the temple. The capitals are the decorative pieces that crowned each pillar, and the portico is the covered entrance. It says they were shaped like lilies, and that this part was four cubits high, or about two meters (the exact length of a cubit is debated). Some understand the measurement to refer to the height of that lily-shaped section.

Here the narrator tells how Solomon, with the help of the craftsman Hiram of Tyre, built the temple. God does not speak, nor does any character; it is a detailed description. The pillars were called Jachin and Boaz. Scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of those names or of the lily design.

For today: God cares about beauty and care in what is offered to Him. We can serve Him with diligence, even in small tasks that no one notices, doing them with dedication and gratitude.
exp.3:3:
This verse continues the list of King Solomon's chief officials. Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was in charge of the army. Zadok and Abiathar are named as the priests. The word "princes" used elsewhere in this list refers to senior officials, not to the king's sons, so it is best read as those holding positions of responsibility.

The writer of the book presents how the kingdom was organized at the start of Solomon's reign. This list shows order, stability and peace after the difficult years of David. Abiathar is mentioned alongside Zadok, even though Solomon had earlier removed him from the priesthood (1 Kings 2:26-27). Some think that here the text names those who in general held that office; the passage does not fully explain this.

For today: God values order and faithful service. Whether in the church, at work or at home, doing your part well helps others live in peace and security.
exp.21:12:
What it says: The messenger who went to get the prophet Micaiah advises him to speak the same way as the other prophets. He tells him that all of them, in complete agreement, are announcing favorable things to the king. He asks that Micaiah's words be like theirs and that he also speak favorably.

Context: King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah wanted to know whether they should attack Ramoth-gilead. About four hundred prophets had already promised victory. Jehoshaphat wanted to hear a prophet of the LORD, and Ahab called Micaiah, whom he did not like to hear because he always announced hard things. The messenger wants to spare him trouble.

For today: The majority is not always right. Before following a popular opinion, or staying silent out of fear of conflict, let us seek what God really says in his Word, and speak with honesty and love.
exp.20:4:
Jezebel, the wife of King Ahab, comes to where he is and asks why he is so sullen and why he refuses to eat. Here, "eat" refers to food in general. "Sullen" describes his mood, and his refusal to eat shows that Ahab was deeply dejected.

Ahab had shut himself in his bed, with his face toward the wall, because Naboth refused to sell him his vineyard. Naboth was obeying the law of God, which protected family inheritance in Israel. Jezebel asks, but it soon becomes clear that her answer will be unjust and violent. She speaks like someone who will solve the problem at any cost.

When something is denied to us, we can fall into anger and self-pity. Instead of letting desire rule us, let us bring our frustration to God and accept fair limits, without seeking shortcuts.
exp.5:30:
This verse tells that Solomon made, at the entrance to the inner sanctuary (the most holy place, where the ark of the covenant was), doors of olive wood. The doorposts were five-sided. The text does not explain exactly what that shape looked like; some think of a frame with five sides, while others understand it as a design that took up a fifth part of the wall.

The passage describes the building of the temple in Jerusalem. The narrator describes in detail how every part was cared for and decorated with cherubim, palm trees and flowers, because that place represented God's presence among his people.

For today: God deserves our best, even in the small details. We can offer him our work, our time and our prayer with care and reverence, not halfheartedly or just to get it done.
exp.9:0:
This verse tells us that the queen of Sheba heard that Solomon was famous, and that his fame was connected with the name of the LORD, that is, with God. So she came to test him with difficult questions. The phrases "when she heard" and "to test him" are the only words that need care here, and they simply mean what the verse says: she had heard the reports, and she came to examine him.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Solomon had already built the temple, and his wisdom was well known. It is not known with certainty where Sheba was; it is usually linked with southern Arabia, though some propose other regions. The queen wanted to check with her own eyes whether what was said was true.

For today: when you hear about the wisdom of God, do not rely only on what others say. Come with sincere questions, look for answers in the Bible and in people who live with faith, and let God speak to you.
exp.10:27:
This verse says that Jeroboam was a brave and capable man. Solomon noticed him, saw that he was a young man who worked hard, and put him in charge of the whole labor force of the house of Joseph, that is, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, who were descendants of Joseph. The phrase "mighty man of valor" means someone strong and courageous, and "young man" refers to a youth.

Here the narrator of the book tells how a rival to Solomon arose. Jeroboam was a servant of the king who rebelled, and the text presents him as someone with real ability. Later, the prophet Ahijah announces that God will divide the kingdom. In this way we see that Solomon himself promoted the one who would later become his adversary.

For today: talents and positions of responsibility are a gift that we should use with humility and faithfulness to God. Jeroboam was capable, but capability without obedience is not enough. Let us ask God for a faithful heart, not just ability.
exp.11:2:
This verse says that the people of Israel sent for Jeroboam, who was living in exile in Egypt. He came with the whole assembly, and together they went to Rehoboam to speak with him. The phrase about sending for him means "they sent word asking him to come."

After Solomon's death, Rehoboam went to Shechem to be made king. Jeroboam had fled from Solomon, and now the people seek him out as their spokesman. What follows is a complaint: they ask that the heavy burden of labor and taxes be lightened. The Bible does not say in detail how this group was organized, only that they came forward together.

For today: when you have a fair complaint, present it with order and respect, seeking dialogue. And if you are called to lead, listen with humility before you answer, because a wise word can prevent great divisions.
exp.19:14:
This verse tells how Ahab counted his forces. First he gathered the young officers who served the district governors, and there were 232 men. Then he gathered the rest of the Israelite troops, which came to 7,000 in all. Here "assembled" means he gathered them and counted them. They were very few.

A prophet who spoke for God had promised Ahab victory over the huge Syrian army of Ben-hadad, which had surrounded Samaria. God said he would do this so that Ahab would know that he is the LORD. Ahab, a king who was not faithful, counted how many he had and saw that, humanly speaking, they were not enough.

For today: sometimes our resources seem few compared to the problem. Counting what we have is not wrong, but trust does not rest on the amount, but on God keeping what he promises. We can take the step of obedience even when we feel small.
exp.11:18:
This verse says that the northern tribes of Israel broke away from the family of King David, and that this division has lasted up to the time the book was written. "Rebelled" means they separated and withdrew their loyalty.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. He summarizes what happened after Rehoboam, son of Solomon, refused to ease the people's burdens. Israel stoned Adoram, the official in charge of the forced labor, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem. The people felt weighed down, and the kingdom was split in two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south.

For today: harsh words and pride can break what took years to build. If you lead a family, a workplace, or a church, listen with humility and treat with kindness those who depend on you.
exp.2:16:
Here, one of the two women begins to tell King Solomon her case. She says that she and the other woman live in the same house, and that she gave birth while the other woman was in the house.

This takes place just after Solomon asked God for wisdom in a dream and then worshiped in Jerusalem. Two women, described as prostitutes, come before the king to settle a dispute over a baby. The one speaking is the first woman, and she presents her version of events. The text does not yet say who is right.

For today: before judging a situation, let us listen with patience and not settle on a single version. Let us ask God for wisdom, as Solomon did, to discern with justice and compassion.
exp.3:28:
This verse says that God gave Solomon wisdom and sound judgment. It also gave him deep insight and an understanding beyond measure. The comparison with the sand on the seashore suggests something vast, too great to count.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Earlier he described how the governors supplied the king's table and the horses. Now he explains where Solomon's ability to rule such a great kingdom came from: not from himself, but from God. The verses that follow compare him with the wise men of other peoples.

For today: wisdom is a gift from God, and we can ask for it with humility. Before making important decisions in the family, at work, or in the church, pray and ask God to give you understanding and a heart willing to learn.
exp.10:3:
When Solomon was already old, his foreign wives gradually turned his heart toward the gods of other nations. The phrase "his heart was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God" does not mean he was without sin, but that his loyalty to God was no longer whole and undivided, and so his heart was split between God and other gods, unlike his father David's.

This is a narrative written by the biblical author, not a spoken conversation. It explains why Solomon's kingdom ended badly. God had warned Israel not to make marriage alliances with certain peoples, because such ties would draw them away from Him. Solomon did not obey, and those alliances cost him his faithfulness. Even so, David also fell seriously at times; the comparison points to David's lasting desire to return to God.

For today: close influences shape the heart over time, often without our noticing. Take care with your relationships and habits, and ask God for a faithful heart all the way to the end of life.
exp.13:21:
This verse says that the people of Judah did what displeases the Lord. By the sins they committed, they provoked him to jealous anger more than their ancestors had. The reader's wording makes this plain: their sins stirred up God's jealous anger, going beyond anything their fathers had done.

The author of the book of Kings, who summarizes the history of the kings, is the one telling this. We are in the reign of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, in Judah, the southern kingdom. The next verse explains the sin: they set up high places, pillars, and sacred images, and followed the practices of the nations that God had driven out of the land. It is a warning: Judah had Jerusalem, where God placed his name, and still they turned away.

For today: having privileges, such as a good Christian upbringing or knowing the Bible, does not protect us from drifting away from God. Today we can ask ourselves what things we have allowed in our hearts that compete with him, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.21:45:
The narrator says that the other things King Jehoshaphat did, such as his achievements and the wars he fought, are recorded in another book: the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Here "deeds" means bold acts or important accomplishments.

The author of Kings sums up Jehoshaphat's reign and points the reader to another record for more detail. That record was probably an official court archive, and it has since been lost. It is not the same as our books of Chronicles, though some scholars think the two may be related. Kings focuses on each king's faithfulness to God rather than on every detail of his rule.

In the end, what matters most in our lives is not the list of our achievements but whether we walk faithfully with God. Ask yourself today: what do I want to be written about my life?
exp.0:37:
This verse tells how Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, together with the Cherethites and Pelethites (the king's personal guard), went down and set Solomon on King David's mule and escorted him to Gihon.

The phrase "set Solomon on King David's mule" simply means they had him mounted on the mule.

Adonijah, another son of David, had declared himself king on his own authority. So David, now old, ordered that Solomon be anointed. Having him ride on the royal mule publicly showed that David backed him as his successor. Gihon was a spring near Jerusalem. The account says nothing more about why that place was chosen.

God works through faithful people who support his purpose without seeking the spotlight. Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah acted with courage and obedience. Today we might ask ourselves: am I willing to support what God wants to do, even when I am not the one at the center of attention?
exp.1:13:
Adonijah tells Bathsheba that he has something to tell her, and she replies, "Say it." It is a brief and courteous exchange. "I have something to tell you" simply means "I have a matter to raise" or "something important." "Say it" means "speak, I am listening."

It is Adonijah, the older brother of Solomon, who had earlier tried to make himself king. Now Solomon already reigns, and Adonijah approaches Bathsheba, the king's mother, saying that he comes in peace. She gives him the opportunity to speak. What follows shows that his request had a dangerous background, although the Bible does not say here everything he was thinking inside.

For today: it is not enough for words to sound kind. It is wise to listen carefully, but also with wisdom, and to look at true intentions. Let us ask God for discernment to treat everyone with respect, without being naive.
exp.16:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Elijah again. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to Elijah" means that the LORD gave him a message. It is a very common expression in the Old Testament for when God communicated with his prophets. The name "the LORD" refers to God.

The one speaking is God, and he speaks to Elijah. The brook where Elijah had been drinking had dried up because of the drought. God did not leave him without guidance: he gave him new instructions. What follows is that he sends him to Zarephath, a place outside Israel, where a widow would provide for him.

Today, when a source of provision runs dry in our lives, such as a job or a help we had been counting on, we can still trust that God guides. We can pray, read his Word, and be willing to obey, even when the next step is not the one we expected.
exp.2:4:
One night at Gibeon, the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream, and God said, "Ask, and I will give it to you!"

The narrator tells us that Solomon loved God and followed the example of his father David, although he offered sacrifices at the high places, which were places of worship on the hills. Gibeon was the most important of these, and there Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings, offerings burned completely. Now God answers with a surprising invitation. Solomon was a young king who had just inherited the throne.

For today: God invites us to speak with him honestly. Before asking, it is good to consider what we truly need most, and not only what we desire most. God listens with love.
exp.2:25:
Here we see two women arguing over a living baby. The true mother, moved deeply with compassion for her son, would rather give him up than see him killed: "Please, my lord, give her the living baby. Do not kill him!" The other woman answers coldly: "He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!"

King Solomon had to settle the case without witnesses. He had asked God for wisdom, and his test with the sword revealed who truly loved the child. What follows shows that Israel recognized in this judgment a wisdom that came from God.

For today: true love seeks the good of the other, even when it costs giving up what is our own. Before arguing or defending my rights, I can ask myself what is best for the person involved, and ask God for wisdom.
exp.21:26:
Here King Ahab of Israel gives an order about the prophet Micaiah: that they should put him in prison and feed him only bread and water as punishment. He wants this to continue until he returns safely from the battle.

Ahab was preparing to attack Ramoth-gilead together with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Four hundred prophets had promised him victory, but Micaiah announced that the war would go badly. Ahab did not like this truth and, instead of reflecting on it, punished the messenger. Micaiah replied that if Ahab returned safely, then God had not spoken through him.

For today: let us not run from uncomfortable truths. Sometimes God uses a correction to care for us. It is better to hear it with humility than to silence the one who tells us.
exp.0:1:
This verse tells how David's servants proposed a solution for his old age. They asked that a young virgin be sought who would attend to the king, care for him, and lie by his side to keep him warm. In the wording this explanation is based on, the phrase "keep him warm" speaks of giving warmth to the body, and "young virgin" refers to a young girl. There is no talk of a marriage or sexual relationship; the following text makes clear that the king did not know her.

The speakers are David's closest servants. David was already very old, and although they covered him with clothing, he could not stay warm. The servants wanted to look after his health. This scene also sets up the conflict over who would be the next king, which continues in the chapter.

For today: caring for the elderly is a duty of love and respect. We can accompany the older people in our family or church with attention, time, and practical help, always with dignity and purity.
exp.19:41:
God, through a prophet, speaks to the king of Israel. Because the king let slip from his hand a man whom God had devoted to destruction, his own life and his people will now stand in that man's place. The word "devoted" means set apart by God's command to be destroyed. The phrase "let slip from your hand" means he let him go free.

It is a disguised prophet who speaks, and he used a parable so that the king would pronounce his own sentence. King Ahab had defeated Ben-hadad, king of Syria, but instead of carrying out what God wanted, he made a covenant with him and let him go. When the prophet removed the bandage from his face, he showed that the king had judged himself.

Today, this invites us to obey God fully, without trimming his instructions to suit our convenience. When he corrects us, it is better to listen with humility, like someone who recognizes his mistake, and not to leave angry as Ahab did.
exp.6:42:
This verse is part of a list of the bronze objects made for the temple. The "stands" were bronze carts or bases with wheels, and the "basins" were large water containers set on top of them. There were ten of each.

Here no one is speaking. The writer of the book is recording in detail the work on Solomon's temple. The craftsman Hiram, from Tyre, made these pieces. According to other passages, the basins were used to wash what was used in the sacrifices. The text shows that everything in worship had a purpose and was made with care.

For today: God is interested in the details of what we offer him. Even simple tasks, like washing and preparing, can be done with dedication and excellence, as service to him.
exp.0:15:
Bathsheba bowed down low, with her face toward the ground, to show respect to King David. Then David asked her, "What is your desire?" In other words, he wanted to know what she needed from him. Her bowing was a way of presenting herself to him with honor.

David was now very old and weak. Nathan the prophet had advised Bathsheba to go in and speak with the king, because Adonijah had declared himself king without David knowing it. She came to remind him of the promise that Solomon would reign. The text does not say when or how David made that promise, but she affirms that he made it.

Today we can learn to present our needs with respect, clarity, and courage. When something important is at stake, it is good to speak with humility, but without staying silent. And in prayer, we can draw near to God with confidence.
exp.8:12:
King Hiram of Tyre went to see the twenty cities that Solomon had given him in Galilee, and he was not pleased with them. He asked Solomon, "What are these towns you have given me, my brother?" Calling him "my brother" was a friendly way for allied kings to speak to one another. Hiram then gave the region the name "the Land of Cabul," and that name is still used, as the account puts it, to this day, meaning until this account was written down.

Hiram had sent Solomon cedar wood, cypress wood and a great deal of gold to build the temple. Solomon paid him back with these cities. The exact meaning of "Cabul" is uncertain; some think it sounds like "worthless" or "like nothing," but this is not known for sure.

When we receive a gift or a payment we did not expect, it is good to respond with gratitude and respect. If something disappoints us, we can speak honestly and kindly, taking care to protect the relationship.
exp.0:12:
Nathan tells Bathsheba to go to King David and remind him of a promise: that he had sworn to her that her son Solomon would reign after him and sit on his throne. Then she is to ask the king, "Why has Adonijah become king?"

Nathan, the prophet, speaks with Bathsheba because Adonijah had made himself king without David's knowledge. This put the lives of Bathsheba and Solomon in danger. The Bible does not say here when David made that promise, but Nathan and Bathsheba present it as a real promise from the king. Nathan plans to back it up afterward with his own testimony.

For today: when there is injustice or danger, acting wisely and in time is a form of responsibility. We can speak with respect, remember the truth, and lean on trustworthy people, asking God for direction instead of staying silent out of fear.
exp.20:12:
Two worthless men came in and sat down across from Naboth, then lied in front of everyone, saying that he had cursed God and the king. The word "scoundrels" describes people who are dishonest and wicked. When these men testified against him, they gave false evidence before the crowd. Then they took Naboth outside the city and stoned him to death.

Jezebel, the wife of King Ahab, had sent letters to the elders to arrange this false trial. Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard, but Naboth refused to sell it to him, since it was the inheritance of his family. Jezebel used the appearance of law, a fast and witnesses, to cover up a murder. The two accusers met the rule requiring two witnesses, but they were false.

Today we can remember that what is legal is not always just. If we are asked to stay silent or to support a lie that harms someone, we must refuse. God sees injustice, even when it is well disguised.
exp.7:37:
This verse is part of a prayer addressed to God. It says that whatever prayer or petition the people of Israel make, each person knowing their own afflictions and spreading out their hands toward the temple, is worth bringing before God. The words "each knowing his own afflictions" refer to the inner pain or suffering that each person carries. Spreading out the hands was a common posture of prayer.

King Solomon is speaking during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks that when the people go through hunger, sickness, or attacks from enemies, God will hear them from heaven. The temple was a place to pray toward, not a house that could contain God (v. 27).

For today: you do not need perfect words or a special place to pray. You can honestly bring to God whatever hurts most inside you, trusting that he knows your heart and listens.
exp.6:3:
This verse describes the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a large building that Solomon constructed. It had three rows of high windows, and the windows in each row faced those in the others, arranged in three tiers. In this way light and air came through the building.

This is no speech. It is the account of the writer of Kings, who describes the works of Solomon. It comes after the description of the temple and before other buildings of the palace. Scholars are not sure what this building was used for: perhaps a royal hall, an armory, or a storehouse. The text gives only its measurements and its design.

For today: God and wise people take care of the details. A well-planned house lets light in. We can ask ourselves what "windows" to open in our lives, such as prayer, the Word, and sincere friends, so that light comes in and we do not live shut in.
exp.21:17:
King Ahab, the king of Israel, here complains to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, that Jehoshaphat had already been warned: Micaiah never prophesies good for him, but only bad. The word "prophesy" here means speaking on behalf of God.

The context is that Ahab wants to attack Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets had promised him victory, but Jehoshaphat asked to hear a prophet of the LORD. Micaiah first spoke with irony, and Ahab forced him to tell the truth. Then Micaiah announced that Israel would be scattered like sheep without a shepherd. Ahab does not ask whether the message is true; he only complains that he does not like it.

For today: let us not measure truth by how pleasant it sounds. Sometimes God uses hard words to care for us. Let us ask for humility to listen to correction, even when it hurts, and to examine our hearts before rejecting the one who speaks to us sincerely.
exp.6:38:
This verse tells where Hiram placed the bronze furnishings for the temple. The "stands" were bronze stands with wheels that held the water basins. He put five on the south side of the temple and five on the north. The "Sea" was a huge bronze basin of water; he put it on the south side of the temple, at the southeast corner.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, describing in detail the building of Solomon's temple. Hiram, a bronze craftsman, made these pieces for the house of the LORD. The text shows order and care. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact use of these pieces, although they are connected with the cleansing of what was used in the sacrifices.

For today: God cares about order and diligence in what we do for Him. Even small, little-seen tasks can be done with dedication, as service to God.
exp.4:13:
This verse describes how Solomon organized the men he drafted for work. He sent them to Lebanon in monthly shifts of 10,000 men, so that each group spent one month cutting timber there and then two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of this forced labor.

The author of the book recounts how Solomon prepared the building of the temple. God had given him wisdom, and there was peace with Hiram, king of Tyre, who supplied the cedars. The text shows a well-thought-out order. Later, this system of heavy labor caused discontent among the people (1 Kings 12).

For today: wisdom also shows in organizing work well, with fair rest. If you lead others, look after their strength and their families, and remember that serving God should never be an excuse for mistreating people.
exp.10:31:
This verse says that one tribe will remain to Solomon's family. God keeps it for two reasons: for the sake of David, his faithful servant, and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city He chose out of all the tribes of Israel. The verse names Jerusalem directly, so the reader can see that the city itself is central to God's promise here.

God speaks through the prophet Ahijah, who speaks to Jeroboam. Solomon had turned away from the Lord and worshiped false gods, so the kingdom would be divided, with ten tribes given to Jeroboam. Even so, God does not completely abandon his promise to David. Some explain that the "one tribe" is Judah, and that Benjamin was joined to it, but the text here only says "one."

For today: God punishes sin, but he is also faithful to his promises. If you are suffering the consequences of a mistake today, do not think that everything is lost; return to God, who remains faithful.
exp.0:45:
It says that Solomon has already become king in fact. He is no longer just a promise: "Solomon has taken his seat on the royal throne," that is, he is already carrying out the role of king. The word "moreover" shows that this adds to what came before: they set him on the king's mule and anointed him at Gihon.

Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, speaks and brings the news to Adonijah and his guests. Adonijah had proclaimed himself king on his own, without David having decided it. While they were celebrating, David had Solomon crowned. The noise of the city was the celebration for Solomon, and for Adonijah it was bad news.

For today: God carries out his plans even when others try to get ahead or take control. We can trust that his timing and his will prevail, and we do not have to force things with our own strength.
exp.12:25:
The old prophet of Bethel heard about the death of the man of God and recognized who it was. He said the man died because he disobeyed the command of the Lord, and that the lion carried out what the Lord had spoken.

The old prophet speaks here, the same one who had earlier deceived the man of God into eating in his house, even though God had forbidden him to do so (1 Kings 13:9, 18-19). Now he acknowledges the word of the Lord that was fulfilled. The text does not explain everything that was in his heart, but it shows that the word of God does not fail.

Today, this invites us to obey what God has already told us plainly, even when someone with a good reputation suggests something else. It is wise to always test any advice against the Word of God.
exp.21:16:
Micaiah describes what he saw: all Israel scattered across the hills, like sheep without a shepherd. The LORD says that these people have no master, meaning they have no lord or leader, and that each one should go home in peace.

Micaiah is a prophet of the LORD. King Ahab asks him whether he should attack Ramoth-gilead. At first Micaiah answers with irony, repeating what the other prophets say. Ahab presses him to tell the truth. Then he speaks: the vision suggests that Ahab will die in the battle and the army will be left without its leader. Some think that "master" refers to the king, and that is the most common reading.

Today, God asks us to value the truth even when it hurts. Before following any leader or popular decision, it is wise to listen to the Word of God with honesty. And Jesus, the good shepherd, never leaves his people without guidance.
exp.21:49:
Ahaziah, king of Israel, proposes to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, that his servants sail together with Jehoshaphat's servants in the ships. "Ships" means boats, and turning down an offer means not accepting it. Jehoshaphat said no to the offer.

The one making the offer is Ahaziah, son of Ahab, who ruled the northern kingdom. Jehoshaphat's ships had been wrecked at Ezion-geber, and the text does not clearly say why he turned down the help. Chronicles tells us that Jehoshaphat had made an alliance with Ahaziah and that a prophet rebuked him for it. For that reason many think he learned the lesson, though the passage in Kings does not explain this.

For today: after a failure, it is wise to stop and ask God whether an alliance or a business venture brings us closer to Him or pulls us away. Sometimes saying "no" to an attractive offer is a form of wisdom and obedience.
exp.0:41:
It says that as Adonijah was still speaking, Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, suddenly arrived. Adonijah welcomed him warmly: "Come in, for you are a man of valor. You must be bringing good news." The phrase "a man of valor" means a brave and capable person.

Adonijah had declared himself king with a banquet, backed by Joab and Abiathar, even though David was still alive. Hearing the noise of the city, he and his guests assumed the news would be good for them. But Jonathan would bring the opposite: David had named Solomon king. Adonijah spoke with confidence, not knowing that his plan had already failed.

For today: we can make plans and feel very secure, but it is wise to seek God's will and not rely only on our own ambitions. What God has determined comes to pass, even when we expect something else.
exp.17:7:
"It is I," Elijah answers, in just a few words. Then he tells Obadiah to go and say to his master, King Ahab, "Elijah is here!"

The prophet Elijah speaks with Obadiah, a man who looked after the palace of Ahab and who, according to the text, feared God greatly. There was a great drought, and the king was searching for Elijah everywhere. Obadiah is frightened because announcing Elijah could put him in danger, as becomes clear in what follows. Elijah speaks firmly and without hiding.

For today: when God calls us to show our face, we can do it with simplicity and without fear. Trusting that He sustains us helps us to be honest and firm, even when the situation is difficult.
exp.14:15:
This verse says that Asa, king of Judah, and Baasha, king of Israel, were at war with each other throughout their reigns. It does not mean that battles happened every day, but that there was ongoing hostility and continual clashes between the two kingdoms. The phrase "throughout their days" simply means for the whole time that both of them ruled.

The account in Kings is a narrative, not a person speaking. After the kingdom was divided, Judah and Israel remained as peoples who were related but also enemies. Just before this, it is said that Asa's heart was fully devoted to the Lord, though he did not remove the high places. Soon after, Baasha fortifies Ramah, and Asa seeks help from the king of Syria using the treasure of the temple. So we see that a faithful life can coexist with struggles and difficult decisions.

For today: even when we love God, conflicts may last a long time. Before looking for hasty ways out, let us pray and ask for wisdom so that we can act with trust in Him.
exp.9:13:
Each year, 666 talents of gold came to Solomon. The word "income" here means yearly revenue or tribute. A talent was a unit of weight, roughly 30 kilograms by the most common calculations, although scholars do not fully agree on the exact figure.

The narrator of the book of Kings, whose author is unknown, describes Solomon's great wealth right after the visit of the queen of Sheba. This gold came from taxes, trade and tribute, as the following verses say. The account shows how God blessed Solomon, but it also sets up the contrast with his fall, since the law warned kings not to accumulate too much gold (Deuteronomy 17:17).

For today: material blessing can be a gift from God, but it can also be a test. Ask him to give you gratitude and generosity, and that your heart not depend on what you have.
exp.13:23:
There were male shrine prostitutes in Judah during the reign of Rehoboam. The Hebrew word (qedeshim) most likely refers to men given over to prostitution connected with pagan worship, although scholars do not all agree on its exact sense. The text adds that the people imitated the detestable practices of the nations that the LORD had driven out before Israel.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells this as part of his assessment of Judah's spiritual condition. After Solomon's death, the people set up altars, sacred pillars, and Asherah images on the high places. They mixed their lives with the worship of Canaan. Because of this, not long afterward, the king of Egypt invaded Jerusalem and carried off the treasures.

For today: when we copy without thinking what the people around us do, we drift away from God little by little. Ask yourself which customs you have adopted without examining them in the light of his Word.
exp.7:21:
This verse tells us that Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord, in front of the whole assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven. The words "at once" are not in the verse, so we will leave them out. The gathered people of Israel are the crowd that stood by and watched. Spreading out the hands was a posture of prayer.

Solomon has just finished the temple and set the ark of the covenant in its place. He has already spoken to the people, reminding them that God kept his promise to David. Now, as their leader, he prepares to pray in public. What follows is a prayer of dedication for the temple, in which he praises God for being faithful to his covenant.

For today: before we ask for anything, we can do as Solomon did and pause to remember how God has been faithful. Praying with humility and gratitude, even in the presence of others, strengthens our confidence in him.
exp.11:32:
He offered sacrifices on the altar he had set up in Bethel, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month. He chose that month and that date on his own, a month of his own choosing, that is, without God having commanded them. He arranged a festival for the Israelites and went up to the altar to burn incense, a task that belonged to the priests.

The one telling the story is the author of Kings, and he judges Jeroboam. After the kingdom was divided, Jeroboam feared that the people would keep going up to Jerusalem and would return to the king of Judah. So he created his own religion, with calf idols, priests who were not from the tribe of Levi, and a festival parallel to the one God had established (Judah celebrated its festival in the seventh month).

For today: it is dangerous to adapt faith to our own convenience. We should ask ourselves whether we worship God as He directs in His Word or as is comfortable for us.
exp.7:53:
This verse tells us that Solomon finished praying and making his requests to God on behalf of the people. He had been kneeling before the altar with his hands spread out toward heaven, and then he got up. The phrase "it came to pass" and the word "supplication," meaning a humble request, help us understand the sense of the verse.

Solomon had just dedicated the temple in Jerusalem. He spoke as a king, but also as someone who interceded for his people.
