His prayer recalled that God had chosen Israel and brought them out of Egypt. When he rose, he moved from asking to blessing the congregation and acknowledging that God had kept his promises.

For today: pray with humility and surrender, and then rise with confidence. We can bring our needs before God and afterward give thanks, remembering that he is faithful to his word.
exp.11:5:
This verse tells us that King Rehoboam, son of Solomon, did not answer the people right away. He consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime. He asked them how he should respond to the people. The "yoke" is a wooden frame placed on oxen; here it stands for heavy loads and hard labor.

The people of Israel had gathered with Rehoboam to make him king. They asked him to lighten the hard labor and the taxes of Solomon's time. Rehoboam asked for three days to think it over, and his first step was to seek advice from people with experience. That was wise.

For today: before deciding something important, ask advice from wise and experienced people. But asking is not enough; you also need to be willing to listen and to follow the good counsel you receive, even when it is not what you hoped to hear.
exp.20:9:
Jezebel ordered that two worthless men be seated across from Naboth. They were to accuse him falsely, saying that he had cursed God and the king. After that, they would take him outside the city and stone him to death.

The word for testify means that they would give testimony in court. Cursed means that he had spoken against God and the king.

Jezebel writes letters, using King Ahab's seal. Naboth had refused to sell his vineyard, because it was the inheritance of his family (1 Kings 21:3). Ahab became sad, and Jezebel decided to take the vineyard from Naboth through a false trial that appeared to be legal.

For today: injustice sometimes disguises itself as legality. This invites us always to tell the truth, not to join in slander, and to defend those accused without cause, trusting that God sees everything.
exp.13:10:
This verse says that people from Jeroboam's family who die will be denied a proper burial. Those who die in the city will be eaten by dogs, and those who die in the field will be eaten by the birds of the air. It was a very harsh way of speaking about disgrace and judgment. And it ends by saying that this comes from God: "For the LORD has spoken."

The prophet Ahijah, speaking on God's behalf, is addressing Jeroboam's wife, who came in disguise to ask about her sick son. God accuses the king of making idols of cast metal, that is, metal melted and poured into a mold, and of turning his back on Him. Because of this, his family would be wiped out.

For today: God takes faithfulness seriously. We can examine what things have taken His place in our hearts, and return to Him with humility, trusting that He also sees the good in us.
exp.10:25:
This verse introduces Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, who was an Ephraimite from the town of Zeredah. He served under Solomon. His mother, Zeruah, was a widow. The verse says that he rebelled against the king, which means he turned against Solomon.

The narrator of the book of Kings explains how God allowed opponents to rise up against Solomon, because Solomon had turned away from the Lord by worshiping other gods. After speaking of Hadad and Rezon, the narrator now introduces Jeroboam, who would become king over the ten northern tribes.

For today: Jeroboam had talent and received an opportunity, but that does not guarantee a good ending. If God gives us responsibilities, let us ask him for humility and faithfulness to use them well, without letting ambition draw us away from him.
exp.0:30:
Bathsheba bows facedown to the ground and shows homage to King David. Then she says, "May my lord King David live forever!" The phrase "homage" here is a gesture of honor, and "live forever" was a common way of wishing the king a long life, not a literal idea that he would never die.

Bathsheba speaks after David, now very old, promises her that her son Solomon will reign. Before this, Adonijah had declared himself king on his own. She had asked David to keep his word. Her gesture expresses gratitude and relief at this answer.

Today we can learn to receive God's answers, and those of the people who help us, with gratitude and humility. It also reminds us to speak with respect to those who have authority, while boldly asking for what is just.
exp.12:29:
This verse says that the old prophet laid the body of the man of God in his own tomb, and that they lamented over him with the cry, "Oh, my brother!" The words "Oh, my brother!" are the wording of the verse above.

The narrator then tells what follows the disobedience of the man of God from Judah. He had been given the command not to eat or drink in that place, but the old prophet of Bethel deceived him and led him to turn back. Then a lion killed him. The old prophet treats him as a brother, mourns him, and buries him with honor. Afterward he acknowledges that the word of the Lord against the altar of Bethel will surely come to pass.

For today: God takes his word seriously, and we should not trade it for the voice of others, even when they sound religious or convincing. We also see compassion: even in the face of someone's error, we can mourn with respect and not with mockery.
exp.20:19:
Ahab sees Elijah standing in the vineyard he has just taken and asks him angrily whether he has found him, calling him "my enemy." Elijah answers that he has, and gives the reason: Ahab has sold himself to do evil in the sight of the LORD. The word "sold" describes someone handed over completely to sin, like a slave to it.

God had sent Elijah after Ahab, and Ahab's wife Jezebel had urged him on. Naboth had been murdered so that Ahab could take his vineyard. Ahab sees Elijah as an enemy, but the prophet is only bringing God's message about the injustice that was done.

For today: sometimes we are bothered by the one who confronts us with the truth. Instead of seeing that person as an enemy, we can ask whether God is speaking to us through them, and respond with humility and repentance.
exp.16:16:
After these things, God had provided flour and oil for the widow of Zarephath, and then her son became seriously ill. "The woman who owned the house" is the widow herself. "His sickness grew worse and worse" means he got much worse, and "no breath remained in him" means he stopped breathing. It is understood that the child died.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Elijah was living in this widow's house, and she had welcomed him in faith in the middle of the drought. That is why, when the child dies, she reacts with grief and guilt, and thinks that the prophet's presence has brought her sin to God's remembrance. The text does not explain why this misfortune happened.

For today: faith does not spare us from all suffering. When an unexpected pain comes, we can bring it to God honestly, as this woman did, without pretending that everything is fine.
exp.12:30:
After he had buried the man of God, the old prophet of Bethel told his sons that when he died, they should bury him in the same tomb, with his bones laid beside those of that man.

The old prophet of Bethel is the one speaking. He had deceived the man of God, who disobeyed the Lord's command and died for it. Even so, the old man recognizes that what that man announced against the altar at Bethel would come to pass. Asking to be buried in that tomb was a way of identifying himself with the true word. Scholars disagree about how truly repentant he was.

For today: let us not wait to see the consequences before taking God's word seriously. Let us listen to it and obey it now, even when others ignore it, as Jeroboam did.
exp.15:8:
This verse tells that Zimri, a servant of King Elah, plotted against him. Zimri commanded half of the chariots. Elah was in Tirzah, the capital, getting drunk in the house of Arza, the steward of the royal household there. A conspiracy is a secret plan to bring someone down.

The narrator of the book relates how what God had announced through the prophet Jehu against the house of Baasha, because of its wickedness, was fulfilled. Elah, son of Baasha, reigned only two years. His carelessness and drunkenness left the door open to the plot. The text does not say that God approved Zimri's violence; it only shows that the announced judgment was fulfilled.

For today: lack of self-control leaves us vulnerable. Let us ask God for sobriety and wisdom, and live alert, without letting pleasures lull us to sleep in what matters most.
exp.3:29:
It says that Solomon's wisdom was greater than that of all the men of the East, and greater than all the wisdom of Egypt. These were two places known in that time for their wise men and their teachings.

The narrator of the book, who is not named, describes the reign of Solomon. Earlier he says that God gave him wisdom, understanding and a large heart, that is, a broad and capable mind. The author wants to show that this wisdom was a gift from God, not only a human achievement. Afterward he mentions his proverbs and his songs, and his fame among the nations.

For today: if we need wisdom, we can ask God for it with humility, as Solomon did. Furthermore, we can use what He gives us to serve others well, not to show off.
exp.7:49:
Solomon asks God to forgive his people when they have sinned against Him and to forgive all the wrongs they have done against Him. He also asks that God would grant them compassion in the eyes of their captors, so that those who hold them will show them mercy. The "transgressions" are the times the law of God is broken.

Solomon speaks in the prayer of dedication of the temple. He knows that the people may fail and be taken captive. So he pleads that, if they repent with all their heart and pray facing the land and the temple, God will hear them. The words that follow remind us that Israel is God's people, rescued from Egypt.

For today: when you fail, do not hide from God or sink into guilt. Return to Him sincerely, acknowledge your mistake, and trust in His mercy. He remains a Father ready to forgive and to restore.
exp.7:6:
This verse describes how the cherubim were placed in the most holy place. They were two large figures with their wings spread out over the place of the ark, so that they overshadowed the ark and its poles.

The text is narrative, not a speech. It tells of the day when Solomon dedicated the temple and the priests brought the ark to its place. The cherubim mentioned here were enormous and stood in the temple. The passage emphasizes that the ark was protected and covered, as a sign of the holiness of God's presence.

God deserves respect and reverence. Today we can approach him with confidence, but without taking him lightly. One practical way is to set aside a quiet moment to pray, with a humble and grateful heart, remembering that we stand before a holy and near God.
exp.12:5:
King Jeroboam, whose hand had become paralyzed, asks the prophet to intercede with the Lord his God and pray for him, so that his hand will be restored. The prophet prays, and the king's hand is restored to him as it was before. "Restored" means given back or healed, and "as it was before" means it returned to its former condition.

Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom, and he had set up an altar at Bethel to draw the people away from Jerusalem. A prophet, called "the man of God," announced judgment against that altar. When the king ordered him seized, his hand dried up. Now the king, humbled, asks for help. The Bible does not say that he truly repented.

For today: God can show us his power and his mercy, but what matters is answering him with a sincere heart. It is not enough to ask for relief in the moment of trouble; we also need to turn to God and obey him.
exp.3:18:
This verse mentions Geber, son of Uri, who was governor of the land of Gilead, a region that had once included the territories of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and of Og, king of Bashan. "Governor" here refers to an official appointed by the king. The verse also says there was one governor in the land of Judah, so Geber's post is one of a small number of appointed leaders overseeing different parts of the kingdom.

Context: the narrator of the book of Kings, who is not named, lists the twelve officers Solomon appointed to supply his household and his government, each serving one month a year. This list shows a well-organized kingdom with plenty of provision, as the following verse says.

For today: God uses ordinary people in concrete, orderly tasks. Faithfully do what you have been entrusted with, even when no one notices; steady service also sustains the good of others.
exp.1:40:
When Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had returned, the report reached the king, and he learned that Shimei had left the city. Gath is a Philistine city.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. Solomon had ordered Shimei not to leave Jerusalem, on pain of death, and Shimei had agreed to that condition. Shimei was the man who had earlier cursed King David. Three years later, Shimei went to look for two of his servants who had run away, and so he broke what he had promised. Many believe Solomon acted justly; others see in this account a harsh political decision. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: when we give our word, we must keep it, even when an excuse seems reasonable and no one would notice. God and people value faithfulness in small things.
exp.2:6:
Solomon speaks to God and reminds him that it was he who made him king in place of his father David. He calls himself "only a little child," that is, a young man without experience. The phrase "not knowing how to go out or come in" describes his lack of know-how for leading and managing the affairs of daily life.

Solomon speaks at Gibeon, where God appears to him in a dream and says, "Ask what I shall give you." He has just acknowledged God's faithfulness to David. Now, instead of asking for riches or power, he humbly admits that the task of governing a people so great is far too much for him.

For today: when you face a responsibility that is bigger than you are, do not pretend to have everything figured out. Acknowledge your limits before God and ask him for wisdom. That humility opens the door to his help.
exp.19:0:
He says that Ben-hadad, king of Aram, assembled his entire army, and that thirty-two kings accompanied him with their horses and chariots. He marched up to Samaria, the capital of Israel, surrounded it, and waged war against it. "Marched up and besieged" means that he encircled the city to shut it in and put pressure on it.

It is a historical account. Ben-hadad was the king of Aram, and Ahab ruled Israel. The thirty-two kings were probably lesser rulers allied with him. The text does not explain why he attacked, but the next verse shows that he wanted to dominate Israel and demand its wealth and family.

For today: when troubles surround you that seem larger than you are, remember that visible strength does not decide everything. God still governs, and you can come to Him with humility and confidence.
exp.9:2:
This verse says that Solomon answered all the questions of the queen of Sheba. Nothing was too difficult for the king to explain to her. "Answered" means he responded to each question she brought, and the phrase "nothing was too difficult" refers to the matters she raised.

The narrator tells us that the queen of Sheba, from a distant land, heard of Solomon's fame "in the name of the LORD." She traveled to Jerusalem with gifts to test him with difficult questions. She shared everything she had in her heart. Then the text shows that she was amazed. Many understand that his wisdom was a gift from God.

For today: when you have doubts or serious questions, bring them honestly to God and seek counsel from wise and faithful people. Speaking openly, without hiding what you carry in your heart, opens the way to receive light and direction.
exp.17:23:
Elijah proposes a simple test. The prophets of Baal will call on their god, and he will call on the LORD. The God who answers by fire is the true God. "Call on" means "call out to" or "ask for help." "Answers" means "responds." The people replied, "What you say is good," meaning the proposal seemed fair to them.

Elijah speaks before Israel gathered on Mount Carmel, in the time of King Ahab. The people were divided, wanting to serve the LORD and Baal at the same time. Elijah, who felt alone before 450 prophets of Baal, wants them to see clearly who the living God is, so that they will stop hesitating.

Today we too can fall into a divided faith, trusting in God and in other things at the same time. This verse invites us to ask where we truly place our trust, and to sincerely decide to follow the God who does listen.
exp.4:10:
Each year Solomon gave King Hiram a large amount of wheat and of pure olive oil. The measures used for grain and oil were large units, though their exact size is uncertain. The food for Hiram's household refers to the house and court of the king. Some scholars note that the figure for the oil differs in other ancient texts.

The speaker is the narrator of the book. He explains how Solomon paid for the cedar and cypress wood that Hiram sent him to build the temple. Hiram had asked for food in exchange, and Solomon kept his word. The passage shows that God gave Solomon wisdom, and there was peace and an alliance between the two kings.

For today: keep your agreements and pay fairly what you owe. Peace and trust grow when we are punctual and generous in what we have promised.
exp.13:24:
This verse says that in the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign, Shishak, king of Egypt, attacked Jerusalem. Rehoboam was the son of Solomon and had been king of Judah for five years when this happened. The attack reflects the military reality of the time, since Jerusalem sits on high ground and an army had to march up to reach it.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, telling the story with a spiritual perspective. Just before this, the text describes how Judah copied the idolatrous practices of the nations around them. The passage presents this attack as a consequence of that unfaithfulness, though this verse does not say it in these exact words. It then goes on to tell how Shishak carried off the treasures of the temple and of the palace.

For today: what we put in God's place ends up costing us dearly. It is good to examine what we truly trust in and to return to God before we lose everything.
exp.5:20:
Solomon covered the inside of the temple with pure gold. He also extended gold chains across the front of the inner sanctuary, the most holy place, and that inner room was overlaid with gold as well. The verse notes that this innermost room was the place where God's presence was understood to dwell, the most sacred space in the temple.

This is the narrator of the book of Kings, describing the building of the temple in Jerusalem. The inner sanctuary was the innermost room, where the ark of the covenant was to be kept. The text emphasizes the gold and the separation of that place to show that the holiest thing was located there. Scholars do not agree on the exact purpose of the chains, whether they served as a barrier or as an ornament.

For today: God deserves our best, not what is left over. Today we can give him the best of our time, our attention, and our hearts, with reverence and gratitude.
exp.9:7:
Here the queen of Sheba says that Solomon's men and servants are blessed and happy, meaning very content and fortunate, because they are always near the king, standing before him continually and hearing his wisdom every day.

The queen of Sheba speaks here; she had traveled from very far away to meet Solomon. She had heard of his fame and did not believe it, but when she saw him she found that he was even greater than she had been told. Afterward she blesses the LORD, the God of Israel, for having placed Solomon as king.

Today we can value the privilege of hearing God's wisdom. If we set aside time each day to read his Word and listen to him in prayer, we too will stand before him and grow in wisdom.
exp.11:30:
He says that Jeroboam, king of Israel, built shrines on the high places, that is, small places of worship set on raised ground. He also appointed priests from every class of people, even though God had set apart the descendants of Levi for that service.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After the kingdom was divided, Jeroboam feared that his people would keep going to the temple in Jerusalem, in Judah, and would return to the other king. So he set up golden calves in Bethel and Dan and arranged his own religion, with priests and feasts suited to his own convenience.

For today: we should not shape our faith to our comfort or convenience. God deserves to be worshiped as He has revealed Himself, not as is most useful or easy for us.
exp.16:1:
This verse says that God spoke to Elijah. "A revelation from the LORD came to Elijah" means that God made his message known to Elijah. "The LORD" is God's name in this translation, and the colon introduces what God told him.

Elijah had just told King Ahab that there would be no rain or dew. It was a hard message for a king who had turned away from God. Now God gives Elijah instructions: to hide by the brook Cherith, where God would care for him. God not only sends his servant to speak, he also guides and sustains him.

For today: before taking the next step, seek God's direction in prayer and in his Word. He knows what is coming and He cares for you, even in times of waiting.
exp.20:20:
He says that God will bring disaster upon Ahab and will wipe out his descendants. Words that mean to eliminate completely are used here, so the meaning is total destruction. The phrase about cutting off every male in Israel, both slave and free, is understood to mean that no one will escape, whoever they are.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Elijah. King Ahab of Israel had allowed his wife Jezebel to have Naboth killed so that he could take his vineyard. Elijah brings God's judgment for that murder and for his injustice. Ahab calls him "enemy," but Elijah answers that the real problem is that Ahab has sold himself to doing evil.

For today: God sees injustice, even when it is committed with power and in secret. This invites us not to take advantage of the weak and to examine our hearts honestly, seeking God's forgiveness before sin hardens us.
exp.9:27:
It says that King Solomon's merchants bought horses in Egypt and in Kue and brought them back. The phrase "royal merchants" refers to the king's traders. The verse names Kue as a second source for the horses, and the place is uncertain today, with some scholars suggesting Cilicia.

The author of the book of Kings describes Solomon's greatness and wealth, with chariots, horsemen and a great deal of silver. He does not openly criticize him here, but the Law of Moses warned the king not to multiply horses or return to Egypt to get them (Deuteronomy 17:16). Many readers see in this a warning sign.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security. Having resources is not wrong, but trusting in them more than in God is dangerous. Let us ask him for wisdom to use what we have without ceasing to obey him.
exp.5:21:
This verse tells us that Solomon overlaid with gold the whole interior of the temple, until everything was completely finished. He also covered with gold the entire altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary, which is the most holy place, the innermost room where the ark of the covenant was kept. The phrase "until everything was completely finished" means that the work was carried through to its end.

It is part of the description of the building of the temple in Jerusalem. The author of the book of Kings, whose name we do not know, relates in detail how Solomon prepared a worthy house for the presence of God. The gold shows the honor and holiness of that place.

For today: God deserves our best, and not just a part of it. We can ask ourselves whether we give him our time, our heart, and our decisions completely, down to the very last corner, and not only the areas that are comfortable for us.
exp.3:7:
This verse begins the list of the twelve governors of Solomon. The first one named is Ben-hur, who was in charge of the hill country of Ephraim, in the center of Israel. The Bible does not give his own name here; it only says whose son he was.

This is the account in the book of Kings, which describes how Solomon organized his kingdom. Each governor had to supply food to the king and his household for one month of the year. The text does not say who the narrator is. Some believe Ben-hur may have been someone well known, but that is not certain.

God uses good organization and shared work. No one carries the whole load alone; each person does his or her part. In your family, your church, or your work, faithfully do the task that falls to you, even though no one notices it, for God does see it.
exp.17:11:
Obadiah, the steward of Ahab's palace, tells Elijah that he is afraid of what will happen if he obeys. He believes the Spirit of the LORD may carry Elijah off to some unknown place, and that when Ahab cannot find him, Ahab will kill Obadiah. His words "I, your servant, have feared the LORD from my youth" show how long his faith has been part of his life.

Elijah asks Obadiah to tell Ahab that he is there. Obadiah had already searched for Elijah without success, and Ahab had looked for him everywhere. Obadiah reminds Elijah that he is a faithful believer, for he hid one hundred prophets during the persecution by Jezebel. He is afraid because he has already seen Elijah disappear before. The Bible does not say how Elijah was carried away, so the text only shows what Obadiah was thinking.

For today: true faith can live alongside fear. When God asks you for something difficult, you can be honest with Him about your fears and still take the step of obedience, trusting that He will sustain you.
exp.17:38:
When all the people saw this, they fell facedown and shouted twice, "The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!" That is, they confessed that the LORD alone is the true God. Falling facedown was a sign of respect and surrender.

The prophet Elijah had challenged the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. For a long time the people of Israel had wavered between serving the LORD and serving Baal. Elijah prayed that God would show who the true God was. When the fire fell, the people stopped doubting. Those speaking here are the Israelites who witnessed the event.

For today: God does not want a divided heart. Think about which things compete with God in your life, and today decide to put Him first with a sincere prayer.
exp.15:21:
In the struggle for the throne of Israel, the followers of Omri proved stronger than the followers of Tibni, son of Ginath. Tibni died, and Omri became king. The phrase "proved stronger" means that Omri's side came out on top.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells how the northern kingdom fell into chaos after Zimri rebelled and died. The people split into two camps. The text does not explain how Tibni died, so we do not know whether it was in battle or in some other way. With Omri a dynasty began that the text later judges to be very evil in God's eyes.

For today: that a group wins does not prove that it is right or that God approves of it. Before following a leader, it is worth asking whether his path pleases God, not only whether he is strong or popular.
exp.9:5:
She speaks directly to King Solomon. She tells him that the report she heard in her own country about his words and wisdom was true. The word "words" here points to what he said and taught, along with the wider reports about his kingdom.

The queen had traveled from far away, and she had just seen Solomon's wisdom, his palace, his table, his servants, and his offerings in the temple. She was overwhelmed, that is, amazed and left without words. Now she speaks to confirm that the reports were accurate. Scholars do not agree on the exact location of Sheba, but the text shows that she came from a distant land.

For today: do not rely only on what others say about God or about wisdom. Come near, look, and check for yourself. Seek the Word of God with an open heart, and you may discover that it is far more than you were told.
exp.8:10:
This verse explains that Hiram, king of Tyre, had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress logs and all the gold he wanted, for the building of the temple and the palace. In return, Solomon gave him twenty towns in the land of Galilee.

The writer of Kings records this exchange after the twenty years of construction. The passage explains why Solomon handed over those towns. The next verse shows that Hiram was not pleased with them, and the text does not fully say why. Some think the towns were of little value.

For today: fulfill your duties and commitments with honesty and generosity, and gratefully acknowledge the help others have given you. But remember that no wealth or human dealing can replace faithfulness to God.
exp.15:4:
The verse says that the rest of Baasha's story, along with his accomplishments and his might, is not told in full here because it is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. The word "might" refers to his power or his accomplishments as king. That book is not the Bible we have; it was an official record that is not preserved today.

The writer of the book of Kings summarizes Baasha's reign. Just before, God had announced through the prophet Jehu that his family would be destroyed, as Jeroboam's had been, because of his wickedness and for provoking God. Here the author closes the reign with a common formula and moves on to his death.

For today: even if someone has power and accomplishments, what truly remains is how they lived before God. Ask yourself today: would my life please God, beyond what others see or remember?
exp.7:11:
Solomon recalls that God had said he would dwell in the thick cloud. The word "cloud" describes a dense cloud that covered the presence of God, not anything evil.

Solomon speaks at the completion of the temple, when the cloud filled the house and the priests could not continue serving. He interprets that cloud as a sign that God accepted the place. God had already shown himself in a cloud at Sinai and in the tabernacle (Exodus 19:9; 20:21), and Solomon connects what is happening with that history.

For today: God is near, but he remains greater than our understanding. We will not always understand everything, and that does not mean he is absent. We can approach him with confidence and with reverence, and trust him even when we cannot see clearly.
exp.5:25:
This verse says that each cherub measured ten cubits in height. A cubit was roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 centimeters, so they would have been close to four and a half meters tall.

The book of Kings tells here how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. The narrator gives precise measurements of the two cherubim made of olive wood that were placed in the most holy place, where the ark of the covenant was kept. These beings represented the presence and the glory of God. The details show the care and order with which the work was done. The Bible does not explain exactly what the cherubim looked like.

For today: God cares about what is done with order and diligence. We can serve him with dedication even in small tasks, knowing that he values faithfulness in the details.
exp.10:41:
This verse says that Solomon ruled in Jerusalem over all the people of Israel for forty years. It is the final summary of his reign. The word "ruled" refers to his time as king, and "Jerusalem" is the city of Jerusalem.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, whose name we do not know. He closes the story of Solomon with a brief note, right after telling that Solomon wanted to kill Jeroboam, who fled to Egypt. Solomon had received much wisdom from God, but he ended his life far from him. The number forty may be an exact figure or a way of expressing a complete period; the Bible does not make it clear.

For today: our years are also limited and will have an end. What matters is not only how much time we have or how many gifts we receive, but whether we remain faithful to God to the end. Ask him today for a heart that always obeys him.
exp.10:24:
Rezon was Israel's enemy for the entire reign of Solomon. His hostility added to the trouble that Hadad had already caused. Rezon ruled over Aram, which is Syria, and he did so with hostility toward Israel. The phrase "was Israel's enemy" means that he opposed Israel and brought them trouble.

The narrator of the book tells us that Solomon turned away from God because of his marriages to foreign women and because he worshiped other gods. For this reason God allowed enemies to rise up who took away the peace of his reign. Some scholars see small difficulties in the wording of this verse, but the overall message is clear.

For today: when we neglect our relationship with God, we begin to lose our peace little by little. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but we can ask ourselves whether we have drifted away from Him. Let us return with humility, because God remains merciful.
exp.3:14:
Ahimaaz was in charge of the territory of Naphtali, one of the tribes of Israel. He had married Basemath, a daughter of King Solomon.

The passage is part of a list that the author of the book of Kings records. It names the governors whom Solomon placed over twelve districts to supply food for the king and his household throughout the year. That Ahimaaz married a daughter of the king shows that he had a close relationship with the royal court. Nothing more is known about him with certainty. Some think he may be the same Ahimaaz mentioned in other passages, but this is not certain.

For today: God uses ordinary tasks, such as organizing and serving faithfully. Do your daily work well, even when no one notices, as something you offer to the Lord.
exp.4:4:
Solomon says that he has decided to build a temple to honor the Lord his God. This is what the Lord had already told his father David: that his son, placed on the throne after him, would be the one to build the house.

The phrase "a house for the Name of the LORD" means a place set apart to honor God.

Solomon writes to Hiram, king of Tyre, to ask for cedars of Lebanon. He explains that David could not build the temple because he was busy with wars. Now, with peace throughout the kingdom, Solomon sees that this is the right time to fulfill God's promise.

God keeps His promises in His own time, even when it seems slow to us. Solomon waited for the time of peace and acted on what God had said. Today we can ask ourselves: what has God shown me that I should do? Let us trust His timing, but when the opportunity comes, let us take the step with faith and obedience.
exp.7:16:
King David, the father of Solomon, had a sincere desire to build a temple to honor God. The phrase "it was in the heart of my father David" means that he truly wanted it, that it was his intention and his longing. A house for the Name of the LORD means a temple where God would be worshiped.

The one speaking is Solomon, during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. In front of all the people, he acknowledges that God kept what He promised. Although David was not able to build the temple, God approved his desire and entrusted the work to his son. Solomon wants the people to see the faithfulness of God.

For today: God looks at the heart, not only at the results. Perhaps you have a good desire that you were not able to fulfill, and God values it. Keep serving with love, and rejoice when others finish what you began.
exp.18:1:
Jezebel sends a messenger to Elijah with a very serious threat. She swears an oath: "May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the lives of those you killed." In other words, she is calling on her gods to punish her if she does not carry it out. She says that by this time tomorrow Elijah will be like the prophets he put to death.

Jezebel, queen of Israel and wife of Ahab, worshiped Baal. Ahab had told her what Elijah had done on Mount Carmel, where the prophets of Baal were killed. She reacts with fury and a threat of death. Some think she wanted to frighten him into fleeing rather than kill him at once, but the text does not make this clear.

Even after a great victory, a threat can make us tremble and want to give up. When fear reaches you, do not hide it: bring it honestly to God, as Elijah did, and rest in his care.
exp.10:26:
This verse introduces the reason Jeroboam rose up against King Solomon. Solomon had built the supporting terraces and repaired the gap in the wall of the city of his father David. The phrase "his rebellion against the king" means that Jeroboam turned against Solomon's rule. Supporting terraces were probably a fill or fortification work in Jerusalem, although this is not known for certain.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells how God allowed adversaries to rise against Solomon because of his turning away. Jeroboam was one of his servants. The text does not detail how repairing the gap in the wall led to his rebellion; some think it was because of the forced labor or the burden of the building projects, but this is an interpretation.

For today: power and great works must not make us forget the people who work under our authority. If we lead, let us treat those who serve with us with justice and humility.
exp.8:20:
These descendants of the peoples who lived in Canaan, the ones the Israelites were unable to devote to destruction, remained in the land. Solomon conscripted them as forced laborers, and that is still their situation as the account is written.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks. He explains how Solomon got workers for his great building projects without placing that burden on the Israelites. This shows that Israel did not finish what God had commanded years earlier (Deuteronomy 7). Some see here power and success; others, incomplete obedience.

For today: it is not enough to start well in obeying God; things left half-done tend to come back as burdens. Ask God for help to finish honestly what He has asked of you, even when it is costly.
exp.14:11:
King Asa cleared Judah of religious immorality. The "male shrine prostitutes" here are men who gave themselves to prostitution as part of pagan worship. The "idols" were the images and impure practices that had come down from earlier generations.

The book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel and Judah, and its narrator evaluates each one according to his faithfulness to God. Asa reigned in Judah after kings who had filled the land with idolatry. The text says he did what was right, like David, though he was not perfect: the high places remained standing. Even so, his heart was sincere toward God.

For today: God invites us to remove from our lives whatever displaces him, even when it is an inherited custom. Let us do it with courage, even within the family, and without becoming discouraged if some areas still need to change.
exp.7:44:
Here, Solomon asks God to hear their prayer and plea from heaven, and to uphold their cause. That is, he asks God to act justly on their behalf and to defend what is right for them. The word for plea names a humble and sincere request, and upholding their cause means acting with justice on their side.

King Solomon speaks in the prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks God to attend to his people in various situations: when they go out to battle on the path that God himself sends them, and when they pray facing the city and the temple. Solomon does not ask for an automatic victory, but that God hear and act justly. Later he speaks of sin and repentance.

For today: when you face a struggle, pray with humility and trust that God hears you and is just. Ask him for guidance to walk his way, and leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.17:6:
Here is what the verse says: as Obadiah was walking along the road, Elijah suddenly came up to him. Obadiah recognized him, threw himself facedown on the ground as a sign of respect, and asked, "Is it you, my lord Elijah?" The phrase "suddenly met him" describes Elijah appearing right in front of Obadiah.

Obadiah was the manager of King Ahab's household, but he feared the Lord and had protected prophets of the Lord. There was a severe drought, and the king had sent him out to look for water and grass for the animals. Elijah, whom Ahab had been searching for some time, now appears. Obadiah speaks with surprise and reverence, and also with some fear, as the following verse shows.

For today: one can serve God in difficult places, as Obadiah did in the palace. God can put us in the path of people we need to meet. And when we feel fear, we can show respect and honesty, and ask God for courage to act rightly.
exp.7:60:
So let your heart be fully devoted to the LORD our God, as it is this day, to walk in His statutes and to keep His commandments. The word "fully" points to a heart that is complete and whole, without being divided or half-hearted. "Statutes" are God's rules, and "commandments" are His orders. The phrase "as it is this day" means: as things stand now, at this very moment.

Solomon speaks at the end of his long prayer at the dedication of the temple, before all Israel. He has just asked that God protect them and that the nations know that the LORD alone is God. Then he asks that their lives respond to that prayer, and afterward everyone offers sacrifices.

For today: faith is not only an exciting moment, but a constant surrender. Ask God for a sincere heart and decide today on one concrete act of obedience, without waiting to feel ready.
exp.20:21:
God says that Ahab's family will meet the same end as the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, two kings of Israel whose families were completely destroyed. The phrase "because you have provoked My anger" means that Ahab's wickedness angered God, and "caused Israel to sin" means that he led the people into sin through his bad example.

The prophet Elijah speaks for the LORD. Ahab had just taken Naboth's vineyard, and Naboth had been killed through a scheme of Jezebel. Elijah confronts him and announces God's judgment for that injustice and for his idolatry.

For today: our decisions influence others, especially if we have authority. God sees injustice, but he also forgives those who repent. Let us ask him to help us live with integrity and to be a good example.
exp.5:9:
It says that Solomon built side rooms along the temple, all the way around it. Each one was five cubits high, about two and a quarter meters. These rooms were attached to the temple by beams of cedar.

The narrator describes how the temple in Jerusalem was built. These rooms probably served to store objects and treasures of the temple, though the text does not make this clear here. Right after, God speaks to Solomon: he reminds him that what matters most is not the building, but obeying him. His promise to David depended on that faithfulness.

For today: take care of the details of your life with diligence, but do not forget what is central. God looks for a heart that obeys him, more than things done well on the outside. Ask him today for help to live out his Word.
exp.3:30:
He was wiser than all men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, who were themselves known for their wisdom. The word "wiser" is used here for the comparison, and the phrase "his fame spread" describes how his reputation reached the nations around Israel.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, not Solomon himself. He wants to show that Solomon's wisdom was a gift from God, as the verse before it says. The four men named appear to have been recognized wise men in Israel, though the Bible gives few details about them, and some scholars debate exactly who they were.

For today: true wisdom is a gift from God, and we can ask for it with humility. Moreover, the one who receives it should not boast, but use it to serve and bless others.
exp.9:11:
This verse tells that Solomon used a very fine wood to make steps for the temple of the LORD and for the royal palace. He also made lyres and harps, stringed musical instruments, for the singers. Scholars are not certain what kind of wood it was. Whatever it was, it was rare: never before had such wood been brought in, and none like it has been seen since.

The text is a historical narrative. It follows the account of the visit of the queen of Sheba, and it shows the wealth and order of Solomon's reign. The wood came in the ships of Hiram, which also brought gold from Ophir. The best was set apart for the house of God and for music.

For today: let us give God our best, not what is left over. Our time, talents, and resources can help make worship beautiful and sincere.
exp.0:11:
Nathan tells Bathsheba to come and let him advise her. His aim is to help her save her own life and the life of her son Solomon. The word "save" here means to keep safe, and his advice is a concrete and urgent plan.

Nathan, the prophet, speaks in the middle of a crisis. David is very old, and Adonijah, another of his sons, has declared himself king without David knowing it. Adonijah did not invite Nathan or Solomon. If Adonijah strengthened his power, Bathsheba and Solomon could be in danger. Nathan proposes that she remind the king of his promise, and that he will confirm her words. The Bible gives no further detail about Adonijah's motives.

For today: when a situation becomes serious, do not sit with your arms folded. Seek the advice of someone wise and faithful to God, and act with care and in good time, trusting that God keeps his promises.
exp.10:21:
Pharaoh asks Hadad, "What have you lacked here with me that you suddenly want to go back to your own country?" Hadad replies, "Nothing, but please let me go."

Hadad was a young man from the royal family of Edom who fled to Egypt when David and Joab conquered his land. Pharaoh had treated him very well. When he learned that David and Joab had died, Hadad wanted to return. The following text says that God raised him up as an adversary to Solomon. For that reason his desire to go back was not just homesickness; the Bible presents it within God's plan.

One can have comfort and yet feel the call to return to where one belongs. Let us ask God for wisdom to distinguish between what is comfortable and what He truly asks of us.
exp.14:19:
Ben-hadad listened to King Asa's request. He sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of the kingdom of Israel. They conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and the whole land of Naphtali, including the region of Chinnereth. "Listened" means that he agreed to what Asa asked; "conquering" means that he attacked and won.

The account tells what Asa, king of Judah, did. Baasha, king of Israel, was building Ramah to block his way. Asa took silver and gold from the temple and the palace and sent them to Ben-hadad so that he would break his alliance with Baasha. The text only narrates the event, but in the next chapter (2 Chronicles 16) a prophet rebukes Asa for relying on Syria and not on God.

For today: under pressure, it is tempting to look for quick, human solutions. Before acting, let us ask God for wisdom and trust Him first.
exp.13:11:
It says that Jeroboam's wife must get up and go back home, and that as soon as she sets foot in the city, the child will die. The child is young, and the words "go home" are the key phrase here. It is painful news, yet it carries a sign of mercy.

The prophet Ahijah speaks for God. Jeroboam, king of Israel, had led the people into idolatry. His wife disguised herself to go to Shiloh to ask about the child's health. Ahijah, though blind from age, had received a word from God and recognized her. The child would die, but he would be the only one of that family to receive an honorable burial, because in him was found "something good."

For today: God sees the good that is in every heart, even in the midst of an atmosphere of sin. We can seek to honor him sincerely, even when those around us do not, trusting that he notices and values it.
exp.18:19:
Elisha leaves the oxen he was plowing with and runs after Elijah. He asks permission to kiss his father and mother goodbye, and promises that afterward he will follow him. Elijah answers, "Go on back," and adds, "for what have I done to you?" The phrase "Please let me" is a polite request, and "ran after" means he hurried to catch up with him.

Elijah has just thrown his cloak over Elisha, a gesture that many understand as a call to become his successor. Elijah's reply can be understood in more than one way: perhaps he leaves Elisha free to decide, or he reminds him of the seriousness of what is happening. Elisha responds with a clear action: he sacrifices the oxen and serves Elijah.

Today, when God calls us, it is good to respond with determination and to leave behind what holds us back, without lovingly neglecting our family.
exp.20:6:
Jezebel asks Ahab whether he is really the king, since he is sulking because he has not gotten the vineyard. She tells him to get up, eat some food, and cheer up, because she will get the vineyard for him herself.

Ahab was bitter because Naboth, following God's law about family inheritance, refused to sell his land. Jezebel, who was a foreigner and did not respect that law, speaks with contempt and suggests that a king should simply take what he wants. What follows shows that she will use lies and violence.

When something is refused to us, we may react with anger and look for unjust shortcuts. Today is a good time to accept a "no," to trust God, and not to listen to voices that push us to run over others.
exp.7:51:
It says that Solomon asks God to keep his eyes open, that is, to pay close attention, to his prayer as God's servant and to the pleas of all Israel. He wants God to listen to them whenever they call to him. A prayer of this kind is a humble plea, and to "call" means to cry out to God and ask for his help.

Solomon is speaking at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. His long prayer asks God to listen to the people when they pray toward that place, even when they have sinned or are in exile. He relies on the fact that Israel is God's own people, the nation he brought out of Egypt.

For today: you can pray with confidence, knowing that God invites his people to call on him. When you feel far away or have failed, do not stay silent; come near with humility and sincerity, and remember that his care does not depend on your perfection, but on his faithfulness.
exp.7:13:
King Solomon turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel. While he did this, the people stood where they were. The "assembly" means the crowd gathered together. Here, to "bless" means he asked God for His favor on them.

Solomon had just finished the temple, and the presence of God had filled the place with a cloud. Earlier he had directed his gaze toward the sanctuary; now he turns toward the people to bless them. Later, in his prayer, he will acknowledge that God fulfilled the promise made to his father David. That the people stood shows respect and attention in that solemn moment.

For today: when God gives us something good, we should not keep it only for ourselves. We can use it to bless others with words of encouragement, prayer, and gratitude toward God.
exp.16:17:
The widow of Zarephath speaks to Elijah with grief and anger. Her words "What have you done to me?" express her hurt and confusion. She asks whether he has come to remind her of her iniquity, meaning her wrongdoing, and to cause the death of her son. She believes her son's death is a punishment for her failings.

The speaker is the woman who had housed Elijah during the drought, and God had kept her flour and oil from running out. Now her son has died. In her grief, she connects the prophet's presence with God's judgment. The text does not say which wrong she had in mind, so we should not invent one.

When suffering comes, it is not always a punishment for something we have done. Even so, we can be honest with God, as she was, and as Elijah was, who immediately cried out to God. Bring your pain and your questions to Him with sincerity.
exp.13:29:
There was war between Rehoboam, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel, throughout the whole of their reigns. "Throughout their days" means continually, with no lasting peace between them. Rehoboam was the son of Solomon; Jeroboam ruled the ten tribes of the north.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking, summarizing the reign of Rehoboam. After the kingdom was divided, the two peoples stood opposed to each other. The text mentions this alongside other sad events, such as the loss of the temple treasures, which is told in the preceding verses. In this way it shows the cost of the division and of turning away from God.

For today: conflicts that are allowed to grow can last for years and wear down families and churches. Seek reconciliation with someone today, beginning with humility and a sincere conversation.
exp.21:4:
In this verse, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, asks the king of Israel, Ahab, to first seek the word of the LORD. To inquire means to ask or seek counsel, and the word of the LORD is what God says about the matter.

Ahab wanted to recover the city of Ramoth-gilead and asked Jehoshaphat to join him in the war. Jehoshaphat had already said yes, but he stopped before moving forward. We notice that his desire to hear from God came after he had committed himself. Then Ahab's four hundred prophets approved the plan, but Jehoshaphat was not at peace and asked for a prophet of the LORD.

For today: before making an important decision, let us seek God's voice in prayer and in his Word. And if something does not give us peace, let us not be afraid to ask more questions, even when everyone says yes.
exp.15:30:
And as if it were not enough for Ahab to walk in the sins of Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, the king who had set up golden calves for worship in Israel, he went further: he married Jezebel, the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and then proceeded to serve and worship Baal, a god of fertility and rain worshipped by the Canaanite peoples. The phrase "as if it were not enough" means that Ahab treated the sins of Jeroboam as though they were something he could easily add to.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, evaluating each king according to his faithfulness to God. It explains why Ahab is presented as the worst up to that point. His marriage to Jezebel also had a political side, since it sought an alliance with Sidon, but the text emphasizes the spiritual result.

For today: when we downplay a small sin, the heart grows accustomed to it and then dares to do more. It is wise to take small things seriously and to be careful about who we associate with.
exp.5:14:
He says that Solomon lined the inside walls of the temple with cedar paneling, from the floor all the way up to the ceiling. In the verse, the floor is the floor of the temple, and he covered that floor with cypress boards.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing the building of the temple in Jerusalem. Shortly before, God had promised Solomon that he would dwell among his people if Solomon remained faithful to him. The author details the work to show that the temple was built with care and with the best materials, as a place to meet with God.

For today: God deserves our best, even in things no one sees. We can take care with what is hidden, such as our prayer, our honesty, and our character, because the Lord looks at the heart.
exp.7:62:
Solomon offered peace offerings to the LORD: 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. These were sacrifices of fellowship and thanksgiving, and part of the meat was shared as a meal before God. With this, the king and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD, that is, they set it apart for God's use. These numbers are very large, and some scholars think they might be rounded or symbolic figures; the text does not make this clear.

The narrator tells what happened after Solomon finished building the temple in Jerusalem. Shortly before, the king had prayed and blessed the people, asking that their hearts be whole, that is, complete and faithful to God. Then came this great celebration, which lasted fourteen days.

For today: dedicating something to God is not only a special act, but also living with a faithful heart. We can give thanks with generosity and joy, and share our blessings with others.
exp.11:15:
It says that when King Rehoboam refused to listen to them, the people of Israel answered with a words of rejection: "What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse?" By saying this, they meant that they no longer felt connected to David's family. The word for "tents" means tents or homes, and their call "To your tents, O Israel!" meant that each person should go back to their own home. Then each one returned to his home, and the unity of the kingdom was broken.

The passage speaks of the people of Israel, weary of the heavy burdens placed on them by Solomon. They asked Rehoboam for relief, but he followed the advice of the young men and answered them harshly. The text says that God allowed this turn of events to fulfill what he had announced through the prophet Ahijah.

For today: whoever holds authority should listen with humility and treat others with kindness. A harsh word can break relationships that took years to build. Before answering, it is wise to ask God for wisdom.
exp.18:4:
It says that Elijah lay down under a broom tree, a shrub of the desert, and fell asleep. Suddenly an angel touched him and said to him, "Get up and eat." The words "lay down" and "suddenly" show that he stretched out and that the angel came right away.

Elijah was fleeing from Queen Jezebel, who wanted to kill him. He was exhausted, afraid, and so discouraged that he asked to die. The narrator tells the scene, and the angel speaks on God's behalf. God does not scold him; first he tends to him with care, giving him rest and food.

When you are tired and discouraged, God does not demand more from you all at once. Take care of your body: rest, eat, and ask for help. Sometimes the first step of faith is to do the simple thing in front of you, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.2:27:
This verse says that all of Israel heard about the decision Solomon had made. When they saw it, they stood in awe of him, because they recognized that God had given him wisdom to administer justice. Here, "stood in awe" means that they respected and honored him deeply, not that they were afraid of him as of a tyrant.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. Earlier, two women were arguing over a living baby. Solomon proposed cutting it in two, and so he discovered who the true mother was: the one who was willing to give up the child so that it would live. Shortly before this, Solomon had asked God for an understanding heart to govern his people well.

For today: wisdom is not only intelligence, but also compassion and justice. Before deciding something difficult, we can ask God for wisdom with humility, and listen carefully to what is in people's hearts.
exp.14:13:
This verse says that King Asa did not remove the high places, which were raised places where people offered sacrifices, sometimes to the LORD and sometimes to other gods. Even so, his heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his life. "Fully devoted" here does not mean without sin, but complete, sincere, and loyal to the LORD. "But" introduces this contrast with the high places left standing.

This is the account of the writer of Kings about Asa, king of Judah. It tells that Asa made reforms: he removed idolatry, including that of his grandmother or mother Maacah, and burned her idol. But the narrator notes that something was left uncorrected. Some scholars think the high places were used to worship the LORD in ways that were not allowed; others, that they were mixed with pagan worship. The text does not fully clarify this.

We can truly love God and still have areas we have not surrendered. Let us ask him to show us what our high place is, and have the courage to remove it.
exp.10:1:
These women were from the nations that the LORD had told the Israelites about. He had said, "You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods." Yet Solomon clung to these women in love. The verse shows that he held fast to them even though God had given a clear warning.

The narrator of the book of Kings explains why Solomon, so wise, ended up turning away from God. The warning is connected with what God commanded in the law, in Deuteronomy 7:3-4. Here it is not said only that it was a political mistake, but a problem of the heart.

For today: take care what wins your heart. Close relationships and customs can draw us closer to God or pull us away little by little. Ask for wisdom and listen to his Word before the drift becomes great.
exp.7:29:
Solomon asks God to hear his prayer and also the prayer of all the people of Israel. When they pray toward this place, the temple, he asks that God hear them from heaven, which is God's dwelling place, that is, where God lives. And he asks for something more: that God, when he hears, forgive.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple he has just built in Jerusalem. He knows God cannot be contained in a building, so he asks that God's name and attention be present there. He asks for forgiveness because he knows the people will often fail.

For today: when you pray, do not stop at asking for things. Ask also for forgiveness with sincerity, trusting that God hears from heaven and desires to restore you.
exp.8:5:
God warns Solomon and his people: if you or your children turn away from following him, stop keeping his commandments and his statutes, and go off to serve and worship other gods, there will be consequences. "Statutes" are the rules God gave them. "Other gods" are the gods of other peoples.

God speaks to Solomon a second time, after he finished building the temple and dedicated it. Earlier, God had promised to establish his throne if he walked with integrity, as David did. Now God shows him the other side: God's promise is serious, but so is the people's responsibility to remain faithful to him.

Today, we might ask ourselves what things are taking God's place in our hearts. You don't need a statue to have an idol; it is enough to put money, success or pride above him. Let us return to him with humility each day.
exp.17:10:
Obadiah, the steward of Ahab's palace, speaks to Elijah. He repeats Elijah's command with astonishment: "Go, tell your master that Elijah is here!" The word "master" here refers to King Ahab, and Obadiah himself is the one who serves him. He considers this task dangerous and almost absurd.

Here Obadiah speaks, a man who feared God but worked for a wicked king. Ahab had searched everywhere for Elijah during the drought. Obadiah fears that if he tells the king and Elijah then disappears, the king will kill him. Earlier he had hidden one hundred prophets, and that is why he recalls his faithfulness.

For today: when God asks us to do something that frightens us, it is normal to feel fear and to express it honestly. But let us remember that God has already seen our past faithfulness and can sustain us in the next step of obedience.
exp.19:36:
This verse says that a prophet, after the first man refused to strike him, looked for another man and asked him for the same thing: "Strike me, please!" This time the man did obey. He struck him and wounded him.

A prophet, one of the sons of the prophets, was acting on God's command. He wanted to disguise himself as a wounded soldier so that he could appear before King Ahab. Through a parable, he would make the king see that he had let Ben-hadad, king of Syria, go free, though God had given that man into his hand. The first man disobeyed and suffered the consequences; this second man obeyed.

For today: when God speaks to us clearly, obeying promptly is the right thing to do, even when his command seems strange or hard to understand. Let us trust that his word has a purpose.
exp.8:27:
Solomon sent a fleet, and his sailors sailed to Ophir. From there they imported 420 talents of gold and delivered it to the king. The talent was an ancient unit of weight; it amounted to several tons of gold. Where Ophir was located is not known with certainty, and scholars have placed it in different places.

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of Solomon. He explains that the king built ships at Ezion-geber, beside the Red Sea, with the help of Hiram, king of Tyre, and of his skilled sailors. The text shows Solomon's wealth and alliances at the height of his reign. Later, the same book tells that his heart turned away from God.

For today: prosperity can be a blessing, but it is not a guarantee of faithfulness. If God gives you success or resources, use them with gratitude and generosity, and do not let them displace God from your heart.
exp.16:11:
She answers Elijah with an oath: "As surely as the LORD your God lives," she has no bread at all. All she has left is a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. She is gathering a couple of sticks to take home and make one last meal for herself and her son, and then they expect to die.

She is a widow from Zarephath, a town outside Israel. A severe drought has come, and God had sent Elijah to her there. Her oath, "As surely as the LORD your God lives," shows that she recognizes the God of Elijah, even though she does not call him her own. She explains her poverty because Elijah had asked her for bread.

For today: when you feel that only the bare minimum is left to you, be honest with God about your need and take the next step of obedience. He often gives us what we need day by day, rather than all at once.
exp.19:13:
Here Ahab asks the prophet how the victory will come. God answers that it will be by means of the "young officers of the district governors," that is, the young assistants or soldiers of the regional governors. When Ahab asks who will start the battle, the answer is: "You will." So Ahab must take the first step.

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had Samaria under siege with a huge army and felt secure, drinking with his allies. A prophet, whose name is not given here, brings Ahab a word from the Lord: God would deliver that great multitude so that Ahab would know that the Lord is God. Ahab was an unfaithful king, but God still acted with mercy toward Israel.

For today: God can use small means and unexpected people, but He usually asks us to take a step of obedience. Trust His promise and take today the step you already know is yours to take.
exp.0:13:
He tells Bathsheba that, while she is still speaking with King David, he will come in after her and confirm her words. This means he will back up what she has said, supporting her words before the king.

The one speaking is the prophet Nathan. David is now very old, and Adonijah has declared himself king without David knowing it. Nathan wants to protect the lives of Bathsheba and Solomon, whom Adonijah might see as a threat. According to the text, David had promised that Solomon would reign. So Nathan prepares Bathsheba and agrees with her to act together.

For today: when something difficult but necessary has to be said, it is wise not to go alone. Seeking honest support and acting with order, respect, and truth can help a just cause be heard.
exp.3:22:
This verse continues the list of what was needed each day to feed Solomon's court: ten fattened oxen, twenty range oxen that grazed in the open pastures, and one hundred sheep. There was also venison, including deer, gazelles, and roebucks, along with fattened poultry.

The author of Kings is not named with certainty. He wants to show the greatness and peace of Solomon's kingdom. Such a large amount of food every day reflects his wide rule, the tribute he received, and the stability of the people, who lived safely "under his vine and under his fig tree."

For today: God often gives abundance and peace so that we may serve with gratitude, not to show off. If you have what you need today, give thanks, and think about whom you can share with from what God has given you.
exp.1:22:
Solomon makes a solemn oath before the LORD. He says, "May God punish me, and ever so severely," a strong way of saying: "May God punish me if I do not carry out what I say." Solomon declares that Adonijah, in making this request, has made it at the expense of his own life, that is, he has staked his life on it.

The speaker is King Solomon, answering his mother Bathsheba, who had carried Adonijah's request. Solomon understood that asking for Abishag, who had cared for King David, was a step toward the throne, and Adonijah had already tried to reign before. Some scholars see here a real threat; others think Solomon acted with political harshness. The text only shows that Solomon saw it as treason.

For today: our words and requests carry weight and consequences. Before we ask or speak, it is wise to ask ourselves humbly what is really in our hearts.
exp.3:32:
This verse says that Solomon spoke and taught about all of nature. Here "spoke" means he taught with order and knowledge, like a teacher. It covers everything from the cedar in Lebanon, a huge and majestic tree, down to the hyssop growing in the wall, a small, humble plant. He also taught about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.

The narrator of the book, who is not named, describes the wisdom God gave Solomon. Earlier it says he surpassed the wise men of his time, and afterward it says that people from many nations and kings came to hear him. The text wants to show that his wisdom was broad and famous.

For today: creation deserves our attention and respect. We can learn to observe with curiosity both the great and the small, and see in them the work of God. Asking God for wisdom also includes valuing what is simple.
exp.11:4:
Rehoboam, the new king, answers the Israelites: "Go away, and come back to me in three days." The word "return" is the ordinary way of saying "come back." And the people went away, waiting for his answer.

Rehoboam, son of Solomon, is the one speaking. Jeroboam and all Israel ask him to lighten the heavy burdens his father placed on them, and they promise to serve him. Rehoboam does not answer right away, but gives himself time. Then he asks advice from the elders, who advise him to serve the people with kind words.

Before answering an important matter, it is wise to pause and seek sound counsel. Asking God for direction and listening to mature people helps us avoid deciding out of pride or haste. But we should also accept good advice when it comes.
exp.19:31:
The servants of Ben-hadad, king of Syria, wrapped sackcloth around their waists and put ropes around their heads, showing surrender and humility. They went to Ahab and asked him to spare their king's life. Ahab replied warmly: "Is he still alive? He is my brother."

Ben-hadad had attacked Samaria and had been defeated. His servants advised him to ask for mercy, since Israel had a reputation for merciful kings. Ahab, without seeking the Lord's guidance, treated an enemy as a brother. Afterward, a prophet rebuked him for letting Ben-hadad go (v. 42).

Asking for forgiveness with humility is valuable, and mercy is admirable. But before making important decisions, it is wise to seek God's guidance and not simply follow our sympathy or convenience.
exp.1:37:
Shimei accepts King Solomon's order and promises to obey it. He says the sentence is fair, meaning the terms seem reasonable to him. Because he agrees, he is allowed to stay and live in Jerusalem for a long time.

Solomon had just taken over the kingdom. Shimei was the man who had cursed King David when David was fleeing from Absalom (2 Samuel 16). Solomon does not kill him, but he restricts him: he could not cross the brook Kidron. That order gave him an opportunity and a clear warning. Later Shimei broke it, as the text that follows shows.

Promising is easy; keeping a promise requires steadfastness. We can say "yes" to God with good words, but what matters is staying faithful when time passes and excuses appear. Let us ask Him for help to keep what we promise.
exp.7:23:
Solomon tells God that he has kept the promise he made to Solomon's father David. The word "servant" here means someone who serves God. God spoke the promise with his own mouth, and what he spoke he has now carried out with his own hand. The phrase means that God himself made real what he promised. The verse says the promise has been fulfilled "this day," meaning it can still be seen today.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple, in front of all Israel, with his hands stretched out toward heaven. David had wanted to build a house for God, and God promised him that his son would reign and build the temple. Now, with the temple finished, Solomon acknowledges that God was faithful. Then he asks that God continue to keep what was promised about David's throne.

For today: when you doubt God, remember the times he has already kept his word to you. Giving thanks for that past faithfulness strengthens your confidence for what you are still waiting for.
exp.7:59:
This verse says that the final purpose of Solomon's prayer is that all the peoples of the world may know that the LORD is the only true God. "The LORD" is the name of God; "There is no other!" means that no other God exists who is equal to him.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has asked that God turn the hearts of Israel to obey him and that he care for his people in every need. Solomon understands that Israel's faithful life would serve as a witness before the other nations. He then urges the people to be faithful in heart, and sacrifices are offered.

For today: the way we live can show others who God is. Today, be honest, kind, and faithful in your work or your family, and ask God that your life may honor him before others.
exp.14:12:
This verse says that King Asa removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother, a post of great influence in the palace. The reason was that she had made a detestable Asherah pole, an object used in false worship. Asa chopped the pole down and burned it in the Kidron Valley, a valley near Jerusalem.

This passage is part of the account in the books of Kings, which judges each king by how faithfully he followed God. Asa ruled Judah and worked to clear the kingdom of idolatry. The account notes that he did this even within his own family, which must have been costly. Even so, it makes clear that the high places were not entirely removed.

For today: following God sometimes calls for hard decisions involving people we love. We can respect family, but without letting anything take the place that belongs to God in our lives.
exp.15:15:
This verse tells that the people of the army camped near Gibbethon heard that Zimri had plotted against the king and struck him down. That same day, while they were still in the camp, all Israel proclaimed Omri, the commander of the army, as king. The word "conspired" in this verse refers to a secret plan to overthrow someone.

The account is told by the author of Kings, not by one of the characters. Israel was at war with the Philistines when the news arrived. Zimri had taken the throne by force, and the soldiers did not accept him. They chose their own commander, which led to a civil war. The text shows the chaos of a kingdom that had turned away from God.

For today: power taken by violence or deceit does not bring lasting security. Zimri reigned only seven days. Let us seek to serve with honesty and trust in God, rather than forcing our way forward by unjust means.
exp.21:43:
This verse says that, although Jehoshaphat did much good, he did not remove the high places, which were raised sites where people offered sacrifices and burned incense. The people kept worshiping there. The word "still" means "even then" or "continuing."

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is summarizing Jehoshaphat's reign. He praises his faithfulness to God, but points out one failure. Scholars explain that some high places were used to worship the LORD in unauthorized ways, and others may have been mixed with idols. The text does not give details. In 2 Chronicles 17:6 it says Jehoshaphat removed the high places, so perhaps he did so only in part or was unable to keep them gone.

For today: a good life can have one point that we keep leaving unresolved. Ask God to show you which high place you need to remove, and take one concrete step this week.
exp.0:3:
Abishag was a young woman of remarkable beauty. She cared for King David and served him, but he had no sexual relationship with her.

David was by then very old and could not keep warm under the covers. For that reason his servants suggested finding a young woman to attend him. The account shows how weak the king had become, and it prepares for what follows: Adonijah takes advantage of that weakness to try to seize the throne. Some believe the text also makes clear that Abishag was not a wife in the full sense, though the passage gives no further detail.

For today: caring for the elderly is a worthy and honorable task. Even when someone no longer has strength, they deserve respect, companionship and attention. And whoever holds power over others must act with integrity and clear boundaries.
exp.6:1:
It says that Solomon built another large building, called "the House of the Forest of Lebanon." It was one hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so it would have been about 50 by 25 meters and some 15 meters high. It had four rows of cedar pillars supporting cedar beams. It was called this because of the large amount of Lebanon cedar that was used.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. After describing the construction of the temple, he describes Solomon's other works. Scholars are not sure of its exact use; it may have served as an armory (Isaiah 22:8 mentions a "house of the forest") or as a hall of government.

For today: Solomon spent seven years on the temple and thirteen on his own house. We can ask ourselves whether we give God and his work the principal place, before our own comforts.
exp.21:21:
This verse tells of a spirit's reply, offering to deceive Ahab. It says he will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all the king's prophets. God answers him: "You will surely entice him and prevail," meaning you will win him over and succeed. Then God tells him to go and do it.

The prophet Micaiah is speaking, describing a vision of heaven. Ahab's prophets had promised him victory at Ramoth-gilead, but Micaiah explains that those words were a deception. God allowed judgment on a king who had already rejected his truth. Scholars debate how to understand this scene, but it is clear that God rules even over what seems evil.

For today: do not trust a message just because it is pleasant or because many people repeat it. Compare what you hear with the Word of God, and pray for discernment.
exp.0:35:
