Benaiah answers King David with the word "Amen." In the Berean Standard wording, he replies, "May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, so declare it." He accepts the king's command and asks the LORD, the God of David, to confirm that decision. With that answer he expresses his desire that God himself would support what David has commanded.

David is very old, and his son Adonijah has proclaimed himself king without David's authorization. Benaiah, captain of the king's guard, speaks with loyalty, and David charges him, together with Zadok and Nathan, to anoint Solomon. His response shows that he supports the decision, but it also acknowledges that God is the one who has the final word.

For today: when we make plans or accept a responsibility, we can obey with determination and at the same time pray that God would confirm them. In this way we act faithfully, without relying only on our own strength.
exp.13:15:
God says he will give Israel over to their enemies because of the sins of Jeroboam. The verse points out that Jeroboam did not only sin himself, but also caused the whole people to sin. "Give over" means that God will allow Israel to be defeated or left to face the consequences of its wickedness.

The prophet Ahijah speaks on God's behalf to the wife of Jeroboam, who had gone in disguise to ask about her sick son. Jeroboam had made idols and had turned the people away from worshiping the true God. The message is a judgment: his house would fall and the people would be carried into exile. Later, the history of Israel shows that this came to pass.

Our decisions influence others, especially if we have authority or are an example. We can ask ourselves: does my way of living draw others closer to God or push them away from Him? Let us ask God for an obedient heart.
exp.16:15:
This verse says that the widow's flour and oil did not run out, just as God had promised through Elijah. The "jar" held the flour, and the "jug" held the oil. The words "exhausted" and "did not run dry" mean that the supply never reached an end, even as it was being used.

The narrator recounts what happened after Elijah, during a drought, arrived at Zarephath. There he asked a widow for bread when she had only the last of her supplies for herself and her son. Elijah promised her, on God's behalf, that her food would not run out until the rain returned. She obeyed, and God kept His word.

God often gives us what we need for today, not a pantry full forever. When you are in need, trust Him and take the next step of obedience, even when what you have seems small. He is faithful to sustain you day by day.
exp.10:36:
God tells Jeroboam that he will take him and that he will reign over Israel. The phrase "you shall reign over all that your heart desires" means that Jeroboam will have rule over whatever his heart wants, and it refers to the power he will hold. "I will take you" means that God chooses him and places him in that position.

The prophet Ahijah of Shiloh speaks in God's name. Solomon had turned away from God and worshiped other gods, so the kingdom would be divided. Jeroboam receives ten tribes, and David's family keeps one, because of the promise made to David and because of Jerusalem. This promise carries a condition: to obey God, as the next verse says.

For today: what God gives us is not only for us to enjoy, but so that we remain faithful to him. Let us ask that our desires be aligned with his will, because his blessing calls for an obedient heart.
exp.1:1:
David tells his son that he is about to go the way of all the earth, a way of speaking about death, which comes to every human being. Then he encourages him: "be strong" means be strong and courageous, and "prove yourself a man" means act like a mature and responsible man.

The speaker is King David, now old and near the end of his life. He is giving his final instructions to Solomon, who will succeed him on the throne of Israel. As the following verses show, that strength is not about political power, but about obeying God and following his law with all the heart.

For today: true strength does not consist in appearing powerful, but in being faithful to God when we take on responsibilities. Today you can ask God for help to obey him in a specific decision you have pending.
exp.14:27:
In the third year of Asa's reign over Judah, Baasha killed Nadab, king of Israel, and then took the throne in Nadab's place. Baasha succeeded Nadab as king.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the history of the kings. Nadab had followed the evil path of his father Jeroboam, and his death came through a conspiracy during the siege of Gibbethon. The following text explains that this fulfilled what God had said through the prophet Ahijah about the house of Jeroboam.

For today: our decisions leave a mark, and sometimes the next generation repeats what it saw. We can ask God to help us break bad examples and walk in obedience, without thoughtlessly imitating what others taught us.
exp.10:13:
God allowed an enemy to rise up against Solomon. That enemy was Hadad, a man from the royal line of Edom. The verse says the LORD "raised up" this adversary, which means God brought him forward. The phrase "Hadad the Edomite" identifies him as coming from Edom.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. Solomon had turned away from God by worshiping other gods under the influence of his foreign wives. Because of this, God announced consequences for him: the kingdom would be divided, though not in his days, for the sake of David. The verses that follow explain the source of Hadad's resentment: Joab had destroyed the males of Edom in the days of David.

For today: God loves us and corrects us, but our decisions bring consequences. If we have turned away from Him, let us return soon, before our problems grow.
exp.21:24:
Micaiah answers Zedekiah that he will soon see it, on the day when he goes to hide in an inner room. An "inner room" is a private room inside a house, and the picture of going from one inner room to another suggests that he will keep searching for a hiding place, full of fear.

Micaiah is a prophet of the LORD and speaks before Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Zedekiah, one of the prophets who told the king what he wanted to hear, struck him and questioned whether Micaiah spoke on God's behalf. Micaiah does not defend himself in anger, but points out that time will show who was right. The text does not say when this came to pass.

For today: we do not need to win every argument or respond with violence when others scorn us for speaking the truth. We can speak with firmness and gentleness, trusting that God, in time, makes clear what is true.
exp.17:45:
It says God gave Elijah a special strength. Elijah "tucked his cloak into his belt," that is, he pulled up his robe and fastened it so that he could run without tripping. So he ran ahead of King Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Rain had just fallen after three years of drought, and this came after Elijah's challenge on Mount Carmel. Jezreel was a good distance away, and the Bible does not clearly say why Elijah ran: some think he wanted to honor the king, others that it was a sign that God was acting through him.

For today: when God calls you to a task, he can also give you the strength to carry it out. Get ready, tighten your belt with prayer and order, and take the next step trusting in his help.
exp.15:2:
God says he will completely remove the family of Baasha, leaving nothing behind, much like someone clearing out a house from top to bottom. "Family" here means those who come after him: his children and descendants. God will also do to Baasha's house what he did to the house of Jeroboam, whose family was wiped out.

God speaks through the prophet Jehu, son of Hanani. Baasha was king of Israel, the northern kingdom. God had lifted him up from humble beginnings, but he followed the evil way of Jeroboam, led the people into sin, and angered God.

For today: everything we have, whether a position, a talent, or an opportunity, is a gift from God. We should use it with humility and gratitude, and take care that our example does not lead others down the wrong path.
exp.17:1:
So Elijah obeys God's command and goes to present himself before King Ahab. The text notes that the famine was severe in Samaria, the region of the northern kingdom, where Ahab ruled.

God had spoken to Elijah in the third year of the drought. He told him to present himself to Ahab, and that afterward He would send rain. The narrator makes clear that the situation was very hard. Elijah does not go on his own initiative, but because God commands it, even though Ahab regarded him as an enemy.

Obeying God can bring fear, especially in difficult times. Even so, Elijah trusted God's word and went. Today we can take the step God shows us, trusting that He knows what He is doing and keeps what He promises.
exp.11:21:
This verse says that God spoke to a man named Shemaiah. He is called "the man of God," a way of saying that he was a prophet, someone known for carrying messages from the Lord. "But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God" means that a message from God came to him. The name of the Lord is the name Jehovah.

Rehoboam, king of Judah, had gathered 180,000 soldiers to fight against the northern tribes, which had separated and made Jeroboam their king. Before the war could begin, God intervenes through Shemaiah. What follows is the message: do not fight against your brothers. The people obeyed and went home.

For today: God knows how to stop what we have already set in motion. Before entering a conflict, especially with family members or brothers and sisters in the faith, it is good to stop and listen to God in his Word and in prayer. Sometimes obeying means turning around.
exp.2:19:
According to this woman, the other one got up in the middle of the night while she was sleeping, took her living baby from her side, and laid him in her own bed. Then she put the dead child at this woman's side.

The wording in this verse is plain: "got up" describes the other woman rising, "took" describes her taking the child, and "laid" describes placing him in her own arms. The speaker addresses the king with humble respect, calling herself his servant.

The speaker is one of two women who came before King Solomon to settle a dispute. They lived alone in the same house, and both had a newborn baby. She accuses the other of switching the babies. There were no witnesses, so Solomon had to discern the truth. What follows in the chapter shows how God gave him wisdom to judge.

For today: when there are conflicts without clear proof, let us not be quick to believe the first version we hear. Let us ask God for wisdom, listen calmly, and seek the truth with justice.
exp.7:48:
It says that God hears from heaven, the place where he dwells, the prayer and petition of his people who have turned back to him in repentance. And he does not merely hear them: the phrase "uphold their cause" means that he will do them justice, that is, he will take up their cause and act on their behalf. A "petition" is a humble and sincere request.

It is spoken by King Solomon as he dedicates the temple he built in Jerusalem. In his prayer he imagines that Israel will sin and be carried off captive into enemy lands. He asks God that if the people repent with their whole heart and pray turned toward the land and the temple, God will hear them and forgive them. He says this as a request, not as something that has already happened.

For today: there is no place or situation so far away that God cannot hear you. If you have done wrong, return to him sincerely, acknowledge your fault, and pray with confidence. He listens to the one who humbles himself.
exp.5:8:
It says that Solomon finished building the temple and roofed it with beams and planks of cedar. The verse tells us he was the one doing the building, and it describes the roof as made of cedar beams and planks. Cedar roofs of this kind are made with beams and planks of wood, often with sunken, decorated panels.

The narrator of the book of Kings, an author who is not named, tells how the temple in Jerusalem was raised. Shortly before, he explains that the stones arrived already cut, so no iron tools were heard at the site. Then he describes the side chambers, and right after that God speaks to Solomon. The account shows the care and order of the work.

For today: God values that we finish with care what we begin for Him. Today we can dedicate our work, our service, and our responsibilities to Him with steadiness, without leaving them half done.
exp.14:23:
This verse tells of the death of Asa, king of Judah. "Rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died. He was buried in the city of his father David, that is, Jerusalem, and his son Jehoshaphat took his place as king.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing the lives of the kings of Judah and Israel. After recounting Asa's deeds, his cities, and his sickly old age, he closes his story simply. This shows that the kingdom passes from fathers to sons, and that David's line continues in Judah, while in Israel the kings follow one another in another way, as we see next with Nadab.

For today: our lives also have an end, and others will continue what we leave behind. It is worth living so that what we pass on to our children and to those around us is faith, a good example, and faithfulness to God.
exp.10:20:
This verse tells that Hadad, a young Edomite who had taken refuge in Egypt, learned that King David had died (the phrase "had rested with his fathers" is a way of saying he died) and also that Joab, the commander of the army, was dead. Then he asked the Pharaoh to let him go so he could return to his own country.

Hadad had fled from Edom as a boy, when Joab destroyed many of his men. In Egypt he grew up well treated and related to the Pharaoh's family. With the death of David and Joab, he saw that those who had caused his pain were no longer there, and his heart turned back to his homeland. Afterward, the text presents him as an adversary whom God allowed to rise against Solomon.

For today: even when we are comfortable in another place, the desire to return to our roots can be strong. It is wise to examine whether our longings seek healing and doing good, or whether they hold on to resentment, and to ask God for wisdom in deciding.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that above the foundations and the walls, the building also had costly stones, cut to size, and cedar beams. "Costly stones" are stones of great value, and "cut to size" means they were shaped with care to fit exactly.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He describes the buildings of Solomon, in this case the palace and its courts, after telling of the work on the temple. His interest is to show the splendor and order of his reign. Some scholars note that Solomon devoted much more time to his palace than to the temple, though the text does not explain the reason.

For today: what we do deserves care and right measure. Whether at work, at home, or in serving God, let us do it with diligence and honesty, without neglecting what is not seen, such as the foundations of our character.
exp.4:17:
This verse describes how Solomon's workers and Hiram's workers labored together. They quarried the stone and prepared the timber and stone for the construction of the temple. "Prepare" means to get the materials ready and shape them, and the stone was cut before it was used. The verse names the Gebalites alongside the builders, and their exact role is not entirely clear.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings. He tells how Solomon prepared to build the temple with the help of Hiram, king of Tyre. Earlier, the overseers and the large stones for the foundations are mentioned. The author wants to show that this work was done with order and effort.

For today: the important things of God often require preparation, patience, and teamwork. Value those who serve alongside you, even when they are very different from you, and do your part with care.
exp.7:30:
If a person sins against their neighbor, and is required to take an oath to settle the matter, and comes to swear that oath before the altar in this temple, Solomon asks that God hear and act. The verse given here is simple: the person is being accused of wrongdoing, and the oath is the way they are called to prove what they say.

Solomon speaks during the prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He names various situations in which the people would turn to God in that place. Here he asks that, when there are no witnesses or clear proof of an offense, God be the judge who uncovers the truth. The verses that follow ask that He condemn the guilty and vindicate the innocent.

For today: God sees what no one else sees, and He cannot be deceived. If there is injustice in your life, whether you caused it or suffered it, bring it to God with sincerity. Be honest in your word, and trust that He judges with justice.
exp.5:28:
Here the writer says that Solomon had carvings of cherubim, palm trees and open flowers cut into all the walls of the temple, both on the inside and on the outside. "Carved" means cut into the surface so that the figures stand out in relief. "Open flowers" refers to flowers in bloom or buds. "Temple" is the building meant here by the word "house."

The book of Kings tells how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. The narrator describes its beauty in detail to show that it was set apart for God. The cherubim recall God's holy presence, and the palm trees and flowers suggest life and beauty, perhaps like a garden. Some scholars see here a reference to Eden, though the text does not say so directly.

For today: God values beauty and care when we serve him. We can offer him our work, our homes and our church with diligence and gratitude, not for appearance, but to honor him.
exp.10:11:
God tells Solomon that he will indeed take the kingdom away from him, but not while Solomon is still alive. The word "nevertheless" in the verse means that God's judgment is qualified by his loyalty to David, and "tear it out of the hand of your son" means that the kingdom will be divided and taken from his line. The punishment will fall on Solomon's son, not on Solomon himself.

The Lord speaks. Solomon, now old, had turned away from God by following the gods of his many foreign wives, even though God had commanded him not to. For this reason God announces that he will divide the kingdom. Even so, he keeps his promise to David, Solomon's father, and leaves one tribe for his descendants.

For today: our decisions have consequences that can reach our children. Let us guard our faith, for it will leave its mark on our family. And let us trust that God is just, but also faithful to his promises.
exp.21:22:
It says that the LORD allowed a deceiving spirit to speak through the prophets of King Ahab, and that the disaster coming upon him has already been determined. "Determined" means decided or settled. "A lying spirit" is a spirit that deceives.

Micaiah, a prophet of the LORD, speaks before Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Four hundred prophets were promising him victory in the war. Micaiah describes a vision of heaven to show that this message was false. Ahab had already rejected the truth, and God allows his deception to lead him to judgment. Interpreters explain in various ways how to understand this scene, but all agree that God rules and is just.

Today: do not seek only the voices that tell you what you like. Ask God for humility to hear the truth, even when it hurts, and test every message against the Bible.
exp.7:47:
This verse describes a people who, while held prisoners in an enemy land, turn back to God with all their heart and all their soul. "Turn back to You" means they return to God, and "pray to You in the direction of the land" means they would pray facing the land God gave their fathers, the city God chose, and the house built for his Name.

King Solomon speaks in the prayer at the dedication of the temple. He imagines that Israel will sin and be taken captive. He asks that, if the people truly repent, God will hear their prayer. We do not know in detail how that direction of prayer was practiced, but the temple was a sign of God's presence among his people.

For today: if you feel far from God because of your mistakes, you can return to him no matter where you are. No special place is needed; a sincere heart that acknowledges its failure and trusts in his mercy is enough.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that the rest of what Zimri did, including the plot he carried out to seize power, is written in "the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel." That is a closing phrase, like saying: "for more details, see the official records." Treason is a secret plan to overthrow someone.

The speaker is the author of Kings, who uses this formula at the end of the account of each king. Zimri killed King Elah and reigned only seven days. When the army laid siege to the city, he burned himself in the palace. That book of chronicles is not the Bible; it has been lost, and we do not know exactly what it contained.

For today: power taken through betrayal does not last long. In the end, what matters is how we live before God, since our deeds are recorded before Him. Let us ask Him to guide our decisions.
exp.3:33:
This verse says that men of many nations came to listen to Solomon's wisdom. Messengers also came, sent by the kings of the earth, because the news of his wisdom had reached their lands.

The book of Kings was written by an author we do not know for certain. Here the narrator summarizes the greatness of Solomon's reign. Earlier he mentions Solomon's proverbs, his songs, and his knowledge of plants and animals. This wisdom is presented as a gift from God, as is told earlier in this same chapter, and as something that brought Israel respect among the nations.

Today we can ask God for wisdom to live with humility and honesty. A wise, simple, and just life can awaken interest in others, without our needing to boast. James 1:5 invites us to ask for it with confidence.
exp.16:22:
This verse tells how Elijah took the child, who had already been brought back to life, and carried him down from the upper room into the house. He handed him to his mother with a short statement: "Look, your son is alive." The "upper room" is the room where Elijah had been staying.

The narrator describes what Elijah did after praying. The widow of Zarephath had given the prophet a place to stay, and her son died suddenly. Elijah cried out to God, and the child came back to life. Now Elijah returns the son to his mother, and in the next verse the woman acknowledges that the word of the Lord in Elijah's mouth is true.

For today: when God answers our prayers, we can share the joy with others and bear witness simply. May our lives help others trust in God.
exp.15:27:
It says that King Omri died, using the phrase "rested with his fathers," an old way of speaking about death. He was buried in Samaria, the city he himself had made the capital, and his son Ahab took the throne.

No one speaks here in the first person; it is the account of the author of the book of Kings. It summarizes Omri's reign and evaluates it: he followed the sin of Jeroboam, that is, idolatry. With this verse his story is closed and Ahab's is opened, who, according to the text, would do even more evil than those before him.

For today: what we do leaves a mark on those who come after us. Omri left his son a throne, but also a bad example. Let us consider what we are leaving to our children and to those who watch us: a sincere faith and a path of obedience to God.
exp.15:29:
Ahab, the son of Omri, is said in this verse to have been king of Israel for twenty-two years, ruling from Samaria, the capital. The Bible states that he did evil in the sight of the LORD, that is, in the eyes of God, and that he did more evil than all who were before him. To do evil here means that he knowingly disobeyed God.

The book of Kings tells this story through a narrator who judges each king by his faithfulness to God, not by his political power. Omri had already been a wicked king, and now his son goes further. The verses that follow explain why: Ahab married Jezebel, worshiped Baal, and built a temple and an altar to Baal in Samaria.

For today: let us be careful not to treat as a small matter what we consider minor. Ahab began by taking sin lightly, and he ended up very far from God. Let us ask God for a sensitive and obedient heart, starting with the small things.
exp.12:26:
Here the old prophet of Bethel asks his sons to saddle the donkey for him. The sons obey at once.

The old prophet had deceived the man of God from Judah into disobeying the direct command of the Lord not to eat or drink in that place. When he learns of the man's death, he recognizes that God's word has been fulfilled. Now he goes out to look for the body so he can give it a proper burial.

For today: God's word is clear, and we should not exchange it for the opinion of others, even when they sound spiritual or have prestige. And if we have failed, or have influenced someone for the worse, it is good to acknowledge it and act with humility.
exp.9:20:
It says that all the drinking cups King Solomon used were gold, and that all the tableware of the building called the House of the Forest of Lebanon, part of his palace, was pure gold. No silver was used, because silver was regarded as worth almost nothing in his day. "Drinking cups" here means the cups or containers he drank from, and the statement that silver was accounted as nothing means that it was not considered valuable.

The one telling this is the narrator of the book of Kings. He wants to show how much wealth Solomon had, right after describing his throne and the visit of the queen of Sheba. The verses that follow explain that the gold came through sea trade. Some see this as a blessing from God; others notice that it also sets the stage for the later warnings about his heart.

For today: abundance can be a gift, but it is not what matters most. Let us use what we have with gratitude and generosity, without letting it master us.
exp.13:9:
God says he is going to bring disaster upon the family of Jeroboam. He will cut off all of his males, both slave and free, in Israel. The verse describes this in very blunt terms, and God compares his judgment to burning away dung: removing everything until nothing is left.

God speaks through the prophet Ahijah, who addresses the wife of Jeroboam, who came in disguise to ask about her sick son. Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom, had made idols and led the people away from God. That is why he receives this harsh judgment.

Today: God has given us much, and we should not repay him with our backs turned. Examine what things are taking the place of God in your life, and return to him with all your heart, as David did.
exp.15:9:
Zimri went in, struck down King Elah, and killed him. This happened in the twenty-seventh year of Asa's reign over Judah. Afterward Zimri became king in his place. The words "struck down and killed" show that this was a murder, not a battle.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings tells what happened. Elah was the son of Baasha and was reigning over Israel. Zimri was his servant and the commander of half his chariots. While Elah was drunk, Zimri seized the opportunity to plot against him. The next verses say that this fulfilled the word of God against the house of Baasha, spoken by the prophet Jehu. That does not approve Zimri's betrayal; it shows that God judges sin.

For today: let us take care of our lives and our responsibilities. Elah was careless and became drunk, and he lost everything. Let us ask God for sobriety and wisdom so that we may live attentively.
exp.12:2:
That day the man of God gave a sign, saying, "The LORD has spoken this sign: 'Surely the altar will be split apart, and the ashes upon it will be poured out.'" This sign would show that God had really spoken: the altar would split apart and the ashes on it would spill out onto the ground.

The context is that Jeroboam, king of the northern kingdom, had set up an altar at Bethel so that the people would worship there, away from the temple in Jerusalem. A prophet from Judah came with a message from God against that altar. Because the prophecy about Josiah would not come true until much later, this immediate sign showed that the message was true.

For today: God does not stay silent in the face of false worship or pride. We can trust His word, even when some promises or warnings take time to come true. Today you can ask yourself whether you are worshiping God as He teaches, or as it is more comfortable for you.
exp.0:7:
This verse names the important men who did not support Adonijah. "Would not join Adonijah" means they refused to side with him or back his attempt to make himself king. Among them are Zadok the priest; Benaiah, the military leader; Nathan the prophet; and David's mighty men, that is, his trusted men and his most distinguished warriors. About Shimei and Rei the Bible says little, so we do not know more about them.

The narrator tells us that David was already old. Adonijah, one of his sons, began to act as if he were already king, supported by Joab and Abiathar. This verse shows that other leaders who were loyal to David and to God refused to join him.

For today: we do not always have to follow whoever has the most influence or the most support. Before joining a cause or a leader, it is wise to ask whether it is just and whether it honors God, even if we end up in the minority.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, sent messengers to Ahab, king of Israel, who was inside Samaria. "Then he sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel" means that he sent men to deliver a message to the king. The message itself follows in the next verse.

The one sending the messengers is Ben-hadad. He had already surrounded the city with a huge army and thirty-two allied kings. Before attacking fully, he wanted to pressure Ahab with a threatening message. He hoped Israel would surrender out of fear and hand over its riches and its family.

For today: sometimes fear makes us give in to whoever intimidates us, even before a fight begins. Before responding to strong pressure, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask God for wisdom to act with calm and faith, not only out of fear.
exp.6:12:
King Solomon sent for a man named Huram, who lived in Tyre, a city on the coast of Phoenicia. To send for him meant that Solomon had him brought to Jerusalem. This Huram is not the king of Tyre but a craftsman who shared the same name.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Solomon had already built the temple and his palace, and now he needed someone skilled in working bronze for the furnishings of the temple. The verses that follow explain that this man was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and that his father was from Tyre. He was very skilled and wise in his trade.

For today: God uses people's talents and preparation for his purposes. Develop well what you know how to do and offer it with humility, because it can serve to bless others and honor God.
exp.7:1:
This verse tells us that all the men of Israel came together to King Solomon in the seventh month, the month of Ethanim. It was a special feast. "Men" here means the men of the nation, and "came together" means that they gathered in one place.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Solomon had already finished the temple, and now he called the leaders of the people to bring the ark of the covenant from the city of David into the temple. Many think the feast was the Feast of Tabernacles, but the text does not name it, so this is not entirely certain.

For today: God deserves to be worshiped in community. Seek to meet together with other believers, not only to fulfill an obligation, but to give God first place and to celebrate together what he has done.
exp.17:32:
Elijah arranged the wood on the altar, cut the bull into pieces, and placed it on the wood. "Arranged" means "set in order" or "put in place," and "bull" here refers to a young bull that was offered as a sacrifice.

Elijah is a prophet of God, and he stands on Mount Carmel before the people of Israel and the prophets of Baal. The people were divided between worshiping the LORD and worshiping Baal. Elijah rebuilt the altar with twelve stones, reminding everyone that all the tribes are one people of God, and he prepared everything carefully so that it would be clear who the true God is.

For today: when we come to God in prayer, let us do our part with order and obedience, and then trust that He answers. Elijah prepared everything in faith, without shortcuts, and left the result in God's hands.
exp.12:16:
Here the man of God, who had come from Judah, explains why he cannot accept the invitation to eat. God had told him not to eat bread or drink water in that place, and not to return by the way he came. The phrase "the way you came" simply means the road he had traveled to get there.

The speaker is a prophet sent to Bethel to denounce Jeroboam's altar. His command was clear and strict, and perhaps it showed that God did not want fellowship with that place. An old prophet invites him to his home. It will later be seen that he lied to him, and that the man of God left a sure word for a voice that sounded religious.

For today: when God has already spoken clearly in his Word, do not exchange it for someone's opinion, even if that person seems very pious. Always compare what you hear with what God has already said.
exp.0:10:
Nathan the prophet goes to speak with Bathsheba, the mother of Solomon. He asks her whether she has heard that Adonijah, the son of Haggith, has become king, and that our lord David does not know it. The phrase "has become king" means that Adonijah was already acting as king, even though David was still alive.

Nathan speaks because Adonijah held a great feast and invited almost everyone, but left out Nathan, Solomon, and those loyal to David. It was a move to seize the throne. Nathan wants to protect the lives of Bathsheba and Solomon, and to remind David of his promise that Solomon would reign.

For today: when you see that something unjust is advancing quietly, do not stay silent. Act with wisdom, look for the right moment and the right words, and speak with someone who can help set it right.
exp.21:6:
Jehoshaphat asks whether there is still a prophet of the Lord here through whom they might seek guidance. "Still" in the verse above means "yet" or "still," and "inquire" means "seek guidance." He is not satisfied with what they have just heard.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, is visiting Ahab, king of Israel. Ahab has already gathered about four hundred prophets, and all of them promised victory. But Jehoshaphat senses that something does not sound sincere, or that a faithful voice from God is missing. The Bible does not explain in detail why he doubted, so we can only note his caution.

For today: it is not enough to hear words that please us or that many people repeat. Before deciding something important, let us seek the truth of God in his Word, with prayer, and with sincere people who speak to us even when it is not the most comfortable thing.
exp.15:32:
Then he set up an Asherah pole, the verse says, using the name of a wooden pole or sacred tree tied to worship of a false goddess. It was probably a wooden post or sacred tree used in that worship, although scholars explain it in different ways. With this, Ahab provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger more than all the kings of Israel before him.

The narrator of the book of Kings, whose author is not known for certain, judges Ahab as king of the northern kingdom. He married Jezebel, a princess of Sidon, and introduced the worship of Baal in Samaria. The text shows that Israel's sin went from bad to worse.

Today, a small compromise with what displeases God can open the door to something greater. It is wise to examine our influences and relationships honestly, and to ask God to keep us faithful to Him in small things.
exp.19:30:
Ben-hadad's servants, the advisers to the king of Syria, come up with a plan to save his life. They say that the kings of Israel have a reputation for being merciful, meaning they are ready to show compassion. So they suggest putting on sackcloth (rough cloth worn as a sign of grief and humiliation) and ropes around their waists and heads (a sign of surrender), and going out to the king of Israel. They say, "Perhaps he will spare your life."

These are the advisers of Ben-hadad, who had been defeated by Israel and was running away and hiding. They look for a way out by appealing to mercy. Ahab, king of Israel, ends up sparing him. The Bible later shows that this decision was criticized by a prophet (1 Kings 20:35-43).

For today: humility and mercy are powerful, but they also need wisdom. Let us sincerely ask God for forgiveness, and when it falls to us to forgive, let us ask him for discernment.
exp.21:27:
Micaiah says to King Ahab, "If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me." Then he adds, "Take heed, all you people!" as if calling everyone present to be witnesses of what he is saying.

Ahab, king of Israel, had imprisoned Micaiah for telling him that the battle at Ramoth Gilead would end badly. The other prophets had promised him victory. Micaiah stakes his own word on the outcome: if Ahab comes back safely, then Micaiah has spoken falsely. Ahab, even so, disguises himself in the battle, as if he wanted to avoid what had been said.

For today: God's truth does not depend on whether we like it or on whether most people approve of it. Let us seek to listen to his Word with humility, even when it makes us uncomfortable, rather than looking only for voices that tell us what we want to hear.
exp.1:34:
This verse tells us that Solomon appointed Benaiah son of Jehoiada as commander of the army, in Joab's place, since Joab had been put to death. He also appointed Zadok the priest in place of Abiathar. To "appoint" someone means to place them in a position of authority.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings. Solomon is securing his kingdom at the beginning of his reign. Joab had supported Adonijah, and Abiathar had too, when they tried to take the throne. Earlier, Solomon had sent Abiathar home to Anathoth (2:26-27). Leaders who were not loyal are replaced by others who were. Some also see here the fulfillment of what was said about the house of Eli, though the text does not state this in this verse.

For today: loyalty and integrity matter in those who lead. We can ask God to help us be faithful people, and also to choose wisely those who guide us.
exp.21:35:
As the sun was setting, the cry rang out through the army: every man was to go back to his own city and his own land. The word "cry" here refers to a call shouted aloud so that everyone could hear it. With this, the battle came to an end.

The text does not say who gave the order. King Ahab had already died by then, struck by an arrow shot at random. Without him, the army was left without a leader and had no reason to keep fighting. This is how what the prophet Micaiah had warned came true: Ahab would not return in peace, even though he disguised himself and tried to avoid the fate that had been announced.

For today: no human plan can outwit the word of God. We may ignore his warnings, but we cannot change them. Today is a good day to listen to him with humility and to obey him.
exp.1:17:
Bathsheba replies to Adonijah, "Very well. I will speak to the king for you." In other words, she agrees to carry his request to her son Solomon. To speak to the king for someone means to make their case before a person who has authority.

Bathsheba is the mother of King Solomon. Adonijah, Solomon's older brother, had wanted to be king, but Solomon was the one chosen. Now Adonijah asks that she get Abishag for him as a wife. From the context, many believe his request hid a political intention, but the text does not say whether Bathsheba saw it that way or ignored it.

For today: before helping someone or speaking on another person's behalf, it is wise to ask ourselves what lies behind their request. Speaking up for others is good, but let us do it with wisdom, and pray for discernment.
exp.13:16:
Jeroboam's wife left Shiloh and went back to Tirzah, which was then an important city in the northern kingdom. As soon as she stepped over the threshold of the house, the boy died. The "boy" here is her young son.

Ahijah, a prophet of God, had spoken with her. She had disguised herself to ask about her sick son, but the prophet recognized her. He announced judgment on Jeroboam's house because of its idolatry. This verse shows that God's word was fulfilled just as He had spoken it.

God does what He says, and His word deserves our trust and respect. We also see that the sin of a leader affects his family. Today we can seek God with sincerity, without pretending or hiding anything, and ask Him for help to guide those in our care well.
exp.1:43:
Solomon tells Shimei that he knows very well, deep in his own heart, all the wrong he did to David, the king's father. He says that the LORD will bring that wrong back upon Shimei's own head. The words "bring back" and "head" here refer to Shimei bearing the consequences of his actions.

Solomon is speaking at the beginning of his reign. Years earlier, Shimei had cursed and thrown stones at David as David fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 16). David spared his life at that time, but Solomon set a condition: Shimei must not leave Jerusalem. Shimei promised to obey, but he broke that promise, and so Solomon pronounces judgment. Some see justice here; others see a political decision on Solomon's part.

For today: our words and promises carry weight. If God gives us a second chance, let us value that grace, keep what we have promised, and not harden our hearts.
exp.3:1:
This phrase begins a list of Solomon's chief officials. Here "chief officials" refers to leaders who held authority in the government, not to the king's sons. Azariah, son of Zadok, is named first and is identified as the priest. In the Bible, "son" can sometimes mean a descendant, so it is not certain whether he was a direct son or a grandson.

The narrator of the book of Kings, who is unnamed, shows how the kingdom was organized once Solomon reigned over all Israel. It is significant that the list begins with a priest: it shows that religious life had an important place in the government. How Azariah is related to Zadok and to Abiathar, who is mentioned later, is explained in different ways by scholars.

For today: good leadership relies on faithful counselors and puts God first. We can apply this at home, at work, or in church, seeking guidance in prayer and from wise people.
exp.19:11:
Ben-hadad, king of Syria, hears Ahab's reply while he and the allied kings are drinking in their tents. Then he gives an order to his servants: "Take your positions." Some understand this as getting ready to attack. They station themselves against the city of Samaria.

Ben-hadad had threatened to destroy Samaria. Ahab answered him with a saying: the one who only puts on his armor should not boast of victory, but the one who has already won and is taking it off. Ben-hadad becomes angry and gives the order to attack. Afterward, God will send a prophet to Ahab with a promise of victory.

For today: do not make important decisions out of pride or with a clouded mind. Before acting, stop, listen with humility, and remember that God governs beyond appearances.
exp.12:14:
Here an elderly prophet from Bethel invites the man of God, who had come from Judah, to come home with him and eat some bread. The phrase "Come home with me" is an invitation to stay as a guest, and "eat some bread" means to share a meal. The word "saddle" refers to putting the saddle on the donkey.

The man of God had received a clear command from God: not to eat or drink in that place, nor to return by the same road. The old prophet seeks him out and extends the invitation. Later the text says he lied (v. 18), although the Bible does not fully explain why he did so.

For today: a kind invitation, or even the voice of someone with a reputation for piety, does not change what God has already told us clearly. It is wise to test all advice against the Word of God and to remain firm in obedience.
exp.0:46:
This verse says that the servants of King David came to congratulate him because Solomon was already king. They prayed that God would make Solomon's name more famous than David's, and his throne greater than David's throne. Then David, who was weak in his bed, bowed in worship of God.

Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, speaks and tells Adonijah what happened. Adonijah had proclaimed himself king on his own, but David, already old, had chosen Solomon. Jonathan explains the festive noise in the city: Solomon had just been anointed.

For today: David did not cling to his position or feel envy. He rejoiced that another would continue the work, and he gave thanks to God. We can learn to bless those who come after us, and to trust that God continues to guide his plan.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the servants of King David searched throughout Israel for a beautiful girl, and found Abishag the Shunammite, from the town of Shunem. They brought her to the king. The word for the girl is "beautiful," and the phrase for the land is "throughout Israel."

The narrator tells us that David was very old and could not get warm. His servants proposed this solution to care for him. The text clarifies that Abishag attended to him and that the king had no intimate relationship with her. This prepares the account that follows, when Adonijah tries to seize the throne while David is weak.

For today: caring for the elderly is an important duty. But it also reminds us that the weakness of a leader can open the door to selfish ambitions. Let us care for our elders with respect, and ask God to keep us from seeking power by taking advantage of others.
exp.21:44:
This verse says that Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, made peace with Ahab, or with the king who ruled Israel at that time. The word "peace" here means there was an agreement or a good relationship between the two kingdoms, which had earlier been in conflict. The name is spelled Jehoshaphat in this version.

This is part of the narrator's summary of Jehoshaphat's reign. The text praises him for following his father Asa and doing what was right, but it also notes that the high places were not removed. This peace sounds positive, though other passages in Scripture, such as 2 Chronicles 19:2, show that this closeness with Israel also brought trouble.

For today: seeking peace is good, but it is wise to do it with discernment. We can be people who build bridges, while also taking care that our alliances do not pull us away from what God asks of us.
exp.15:5:
It says that King Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah, which was then the capital of the northern kingdom. The phrase "rested with his fathers" is a biblical way of saying that he died. His son Elah became king in his place.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings. He summarizes the end of Baasha's reign, which was an evil one. Shortly before, God had announced through the prophet Jehu that his family would face judgment for their wickedness. Although Baasha's death seems peaceful, the text shows that God's warning still stood.

For today: Even when a person ends their life without being punished right away, God does not overlook what we do. It is wise to live with humility, to listen to his correction, and not to trust in power or in years of calm.
exp.5:37:
This verse says that the temple was finished in the eleventh year of Solomon's reign, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month. It was completed in every detail and according to every specification. The phrase "in every detail" refers to all the parts and features of the work. When the text says "was finished," it means the work was brought all the way to completion. And the verse sums it up: Solomon built the temple in seven years.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who records the history of Israel. Earlier he said that the foundations were laid in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv. That is why the count comes to seven years. The author wants to show that the work was carried through to completion and done in good order.

For today: God values steadiness. A great work is done step by step, with patience and care, without leaving details half-finished. We can serve him this way in our families, our work, or our church, trusting that he rewards faithfulness.
exp.21:31:
This verse says that the chariot commanders of the Syrian army saw Jehoshaphat, dressed as a king, and said, "Surely this is the king of Israel!" They turned to attack him, but Jehoshaphat cried out. The phrase "cried out" simply means that he called out loudly. The text does not say what he cried out, but the next verse shows that the commanders realized their mistake and stopped.

Ahab, king of Israel, disguised himself so that he would not be recognized, and left Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, in royal clothing. The king of Syria had ordered his commanders to seek only Ahab. Many understand that Ahab put Jehoshaphat at risk in order to save himself. Some see in Jehoshaphat's cry a call to God, since 2 Chronicles 18:31 says that God helped him, although this passage does not make that clear.

For today: when we end up in trouble because of unwise alliances, we can still call out to God. And it is wise to think carefully about whom we join ourselves with.
exp.10:42:
This verse tells us that Solomon died. "Rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he passed away. He was buried in Jerusalem, called "the city of his father David," and his son Rehoboam became the new king.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who sums up Solomon's life. Earlier he says that Solomon reigned forty years and that his deeds were recorded in another book, which is no longer preserved. This ending comes after Solomon turned away from God because of his foreign alliances and wives. With Rehoboam begins a difficult period for the kingdom.

For today: no one remains forever, not even the wisest or most powerful. What matters is how we live and what we leave to those who come after us. Let us ask God to keep us faithful to the end.
exp.0:14:
This verse tells us that Bathsheba went to see King David in his bedroom. He was already very old, and a young woman named Abishag, from Shunem, was serving him and taking care of him. The phrase "bedroom" refers to a private room where the king rested, and "from Shunem" tells us the town she came from.

The prophet Nathan advised Bathsheba to go to the king. Adonijah had declared himself king without David knowing it, and Solomon had been left out. Nathan asked her to remind David of his promise that Solomon would reign, and that Nathan himself would come in afterward to support her words. According to the text, David had made that promise, although this passage does not say when.

When something important is at risk, it is wise to act with care and not stay silent. It also helps to seek the advice of trusted people and to speak with respect and with the truth.
exp.19:33:
Ben-hadad, king of Syria, offers to return the cities his father took from Ahab's father. He also allows Ahab to set up his own marketplaces in Damascus, just as his father did in Samaria. Ahab accepts, makes a treaty with him, and sends him away.

Ben-hadad had attacked Israel, but God had given Ahab the victory. Then Ben-hadad, defeated, humbled himself and asked for mercy. Ahab called him "brother" and negotiated for political advantage. According to what follows, God did not approve of that decision, since Ahab let go an enemy whom God had delivered into his hand.

For today: before making deals or forgiving quickly, let us seek what God wants and not only what suits us. Goodwill without obedience can lead us to wrong decisions.
exp.0:26:
Here the prophet Nathan asks King David whether he is the one who ordered what is happening. "Thing done" means a matter or deed carried out. "Your servant" is Nathan speaking with respect. He asks whether David decided, without letting him know, who would be the next king.

Nathan speaks with King David, who is now very old. Adonijah, one of his sons, has declared himself king and has held a feast with many important guests. He did not invite Nathan, nor Solomon. Nathan asks this question so that David will react, since it had been said that Solomon would reign. In this way, the Bible shows that Nathan acts with prudence.

For today: when you see that something important is going the wrong way, do not stay silent. Speak with respect, with clarity, and at the right moment, seeking that justice be done and what is right be fulfilled.
exp.3:27:
This verse says that the officials of the kingdom brought barley (a grain) and straw for the horses and the other horses. Each one did this according to the quota assigned to him. Although the phrase "to the required place" is brief, it is not clear whether it refers to the king or to the place where the horses were kept.

The author of the book, who is not named in the text, describes how Solomon's government worked. Twelve governors took turns, one month each, to supply the king, his table, and his horses. The account shows a well-organized kingdom, and right away it says that God gave Solomon wisdom.

For today: wisdom also shows in small, orderly tasks. Faithfully carry out the responsibility that falls to you, even when no one applauds it. God uses those who do their part with steady consistency.
exp.10:12:
God tells Solomon that, although the kingdom is going to be divided, he will not take it away completely. He will leave one tribe for Solomon's son. "Tear away" means to divide or pull apart. "Chosen" means picked out. God gives two reasons: his love and faithfulness to David, his servant, and the place he himself chose, Jerusalem.

The LORD speaks to Solomon after Solomon turned away from God by following other gods, under the influence of his foreign wives. The punishment is the division of the kingdom, but God softens it: it will not happen during Solomon's lifetime, and it will not be total. The tribe is traditionally thought to be Judah, although the text does not name it here. Benjamin is also linked with Judah in other passages.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he does not stop being faithful to his promises. If you are facing consequences of your mistakes today, remember that God can discipline and still show mercy. Return to him with humility.
exp.20:16:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Elijah. The phrase "the Tishbite" tells us that Elijah came from a place called Tishbe. It is a short phrase, but it opens God's response to what has just happened.

The LORD speaks here, and he does so after a very unjust event. Jezebel had Naboth killed so that she could take his vineyard, and Ahab went to claim it. God does not stay silent: he sends Elijah to confront the king and tell him that his sin will have consequences.

For today: God sees injustice, even when no one speaks out and the powerful seem to get away with it. This encourages us to be honest and to stand up for the weak. It also reminds us that we can trust God to listen and that one day he will bring about justice.
exp.19:6:
Here the king of Israel, Ahab, calls together the leaders of the land and asks them to see something clearly: Ben-hadad is not seeking peace but looking for trouble. He first demanded Ahab's wives, children, silver, and gold, and Ahab agreed. Now Ben-hadad also wants his servants to search through all the houses. "Please take note and see" means "consider this carefully and look closely."

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had Samaria under siege. Ahab had given way to him out of fear, but the new demand was too much. So he consults the elders, and they tell him not to obey. Some scholars see here a weak king who finally leans on his people; the Bible does not detail his reasons.

For today: giving in again and again to someone who abuses their power does not bring peace. It is wise to seek the counsel of sensible people and to set limits when a demand goes beyond what is fair.
exp.2:8:
Here he says that Solomon asks God for an understanding heart, that is, a heart that knows how to listen and learn. With it he wants to govern the people justly and to tell good from evil. He recognizes that the people are very great and that no one could govern them alone. Calling himself "servant" here is a humble way of speaking about himself.

Solomon speaks as a king who has just succeeded his father, David. God appeared to him in a dream at Gibeon and offered to give him whatever he asked. Solomon describes himself as a young man, since he felt young and inexperienced for so great a task. God was pleased that he did not ask for riches, long life, or victory over his enemies.

For today: before asking for success, let us ask God for a humble and understanding heart. If you have a responsibility, at home, at work, or in the church, recognize that you need his wisdom and ask for it with simplicity.
exp.7:50:
It says that Israel belongs to God: they are "Your people" and "Your inheritance," that is, his dearly loved possession. God himself brought them out of Egypt, which is described as "the furnace for iron," a furnace where metal is melted down. It is an image of intense suffering and harsh slavery.

The passage records Solomon speaking in the prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He is asking that, if the people sin and end up captive, God will hear their prayer and show mercy. Solomon does not rely on how good the people are, but on what God has already done: he rescued them and made them his own.

For today: when you fail and feel far from God, pray by remembering what he has already done for you. His past faithfulness is a firm reason to return to him with confidence and ask for his forgiveness.
exp.16:0:
Suddenly the prophet Elijah appears, the Tishbite from the settlers of Gilead, east of the Jordan. He tells King Ahab that, as surely as the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at his word. The phrase "before whom I stand" shows that Elijah sees himself as a servant who stands in the service of God.

Ahab was king of Israel and had led the people to worship Baal, a god believed to have power over the rain. Elijah speaks as a messenger of the Lord, not out of his own pride. His announcement challenges that false belief. The Bible says very little about Elijah's background. The next verse shows that God himself guides him after this announcement.

Today we can learn that speaking with courage begins with living "before God." If we seek first to please Him, we will have the steadiness to tell the truth with respect, even when it is difficult or unpopular.
exp.10:14:
This verse explains why Hadad, the Edomite, became an enemy of Solomon. It tells how, earlier, when David was in Edom, Joab, the commander of the army, had gone to bury the dead and had struck down every male in Edom. "Commander of the army" means the leader of the army. "Males" are the men.

The writer of the book explains where this adversary came from. Hadad was of the royal family of Edom and, as a boy, escaped to Egypt. God allowed this enemy to rise because Solomon had turned toward other gods. The text does not say that God approved of everything that happened in that war; it only reports the events.

For today: our decisions, good or bad, can have consequences that reach far and take time to appear. It is wise to live faithfully before God and act with justice, knowing that violence and sin leave wounds that last for years.
exp.19:15:
They marched out at noon while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk. Ben-hadad was the king of Syria, and the thirty-two kings had come to help him. The tents were the temporary shelters of the army's camp.

The story picks up after a prophet told Ahab that the LORD would give Israel the victory through the young servants of the provincial governors. Syria had Samaria under siege. The Israelites were few, but they went out trusting in the word of God, while the enemy felt so secure that it became careless.

For today: excessive confidence in our own strength makes us lower our guard. By contrast, whoever obeys God, even when small, can advance in peace. Ask Him for humility and direction.
exp.17:13:
Obadiah tells Elijah that he does not understand what he is asking. Elijah wants him to go and tell his lord, King Ahab, that Elijah is here. Obadiah thinks this would be like handing himself over to death. The word "lord" here means master or boss, and the words about being killed mean that Ahab would have him put to death.

The one speaking is Obadiah, the manager of Ahab's palace, who feared God and had hidden one hundred prophets during Jezebel's persecution. Ahab had spent years searching for Elijah without finding him. Obadiah fears that if Elijah disappears again, the king will punish him. Elijah promises that he will appear before Ahab that very day, and so he does.

For today: obeying God can frighten us, and it is normal to feel that fear. Obadiah had already shown faith by what he had done, but he still needed confidence. We can ask God for courage, knowing that he keeps his word when he calls us to take a hard step.
exp.5:29:
This verse says that Solomon covered the whole temple floor with gold, both in the inner rooms and in the outer ones. The floor is the ground you walk on, and the phrase "inner and outer sanctuaries" refers to the two main parts of the building: the holy place and the most holy place, which is the inner sanctuary.

It is part of the historical account of the building of the temple in Jerusalem. The writer describes in detail the wealth and care with which the house of God was made. The cherubim, the palm trees and the flowers decorated the walls, and gold covered almost everything. Scholars do not fully agree on the symbolic meaning of these details, but they clearly show reverence toward God.

For today: God deserves our best, not what we have left over. We can ask ourselves which part of our time, talent or affection we give to him generously and with care.
exp.15:6:
This verse explains why God sent a message of judgment against Baasha, king of Israel, and against his family. The word "Moreover" links it to the story before it, and "because of all the evil he had done in the sight of the Lord" means that God judged Baasha according to what he had done. Baasha did evil, provoked God's anger with the work of his hands, and his house would end up like the house of Jeroboam, whom Baasha himself had struck down.

The narrator of the book of Kings sums up Baasha's life and explains, before the account of his death, why his dynasty would come to a bad end. The prophet Jehu, son of Hanani, had already brought that message of judgment. Baasha came to the throne by wiping out the family of Jeroboam, but he fell into the same sins as that family.

For today: it is not enough that others fail for me to feel righteous. God looks at our own works, so it is worth asking ourselves whether we repeat the very things we criticize.
exp.2:0:
Solomon formed an alliance with Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, by marrying his daughter. He brought her to live in the City of David (Jerusalem) while he finished building his palace, the house of the LORD, and the wall around the city.

The alliance was a family tie between two rulers, and the marriage was how Solomon sealed it. The verse makes clear that Solomon brought his new wife into the city, where she lived during these years of construction.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not Solomon. It shows the beginning of his reign: a strong kingdom that seeks political alliances. The verses that follow say that Solomon loved the LORD, but that he still offered sacrifices at the high places. Some see in this marriage a warning sign, because the law required faithfulness to God; others see it only as a political fact. The text does not make this entirely clear.

We can do good things and still have areas to watch over. Let us ask God for wisdom so that our decisions, even practical ones, do not draw us away from Him.
exp.10:28:
This verse tells how Jeroboam left Jerusalem and on the road met the prophet Ahijah, from the town of Shiloh. Ahijah was wearing a new cloak, that is, a coat or outer garment that had never been worn. The two of them were alone in the open field, with no one else nearby. The phrase "met" simply means that Ahijah came upon him on the road.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Solomon had put Jeroboam, a strong and hardworking man, in charge of some of the labor of his kingdom. But Solomon had turned away from God, and for that reason God was going to divide the kingdom. This private meeting prepares the prophetic message that comes right after, with the cloak as the sign.

For today: God can speak to us in quiet moments when we are alone. If we set aside time to listen to him, he can guide us, and we should receive his word with humility and obedience, not with pride.
exp.15:12:
This verse explains why the house of Baasha fell. It happened because of all the sins Baasha and his son Elah had committed, and because they had caused Israel to sin as well. Their worthless idols provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger.

The narrator of the book of Kings explains what happened when Zimri killed the whole family of Baasha. This fulfilled what God had said earlier through the prophet Jehu. The text presents that end as the consequence of their sin and of having led the people astray with them.

For today: our example matters, because it influences others. We can ask God to help us live in a way that draws people closer to Him, and not one that pushes them away.
exp.4:6:
Hiram, king of Tyre, receives Solomon's message and rejoices greatly. Then he blesses the Lord, because God has given David a wise son to rule such a great people.

Solomon had asked Hiram for cedar wood from Lebanon to build the temple, as God had promised David. Hiram had been a friend of David. His reaction shows respect toward Solomon. We do not know for certain how much Hiram knew of the God of Israel, but his words acknowledge the work of the Lord.

For today: we can rejoice and give thanks to God for what he does in the lives of others, without envy. Recognizing the blessings of others strengthens friendship and helps us work together in good things.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that the LORD grew angry with Solomon. The reason is that Solomon's heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel. This was serious because the LORD had appeared to him twice. The verse of the word "angry" is that it means "grew angry," and "turned away" means "moved away from" or "turned off the path."

The narrator of the book explains why Solomon's kingdom would be divided. Solomon married many foreign women and built places of worship for their gods. God had already commanded him not to follow other gods, but he did not obey. The two appearances are mentioned earlier in the book (1 Kings 3 and 9).

A heart can drift away little by little, even after someone has come to know God well. Today it is worth asking ourselves what things are taking the place of God in our hearts, and returning to Him with humility before the drift grows.
exp.16:8:
God tells Elijah to get up and go to Zarephath, a town of Sidon, and stay there. He will live there, because God has already commanded a widow there to provide for him. The word "provide" means to supply him with food and care for his needs. "Stay" means to remain and live in that place.

God speaks to Elijah through his word. The brook where Elijah had been drinking had dried up because there was no rain. God did not leave him without help, but pointed him to another place. Zarephath was outside Israel, and his provision would come through a widow, someone who seemed to have very little.

For today: when something you were relying on dries up, do not keep staring at the empty brook. Ask God for direction and take the next step of obedience, even if the path seems strange. He can provide in ways you do not expect.
exp.6:44:
This verse continues the list of objects that Huram made for the temple. It names pots (large pots for collecting the ashes from the altar), shovels (tools for removing them), and sprinkling bowls (bowls used to hold the blood of the sacrifices). The Berean text describes all these articles as made of burnished bronze, meaning bronze that was polished until it shone. The verse does not give further detail about their size or design.

The text is narrated by the author of Kings, who describes the work of Huram, a craftsman from Tyre, for King Solomon. He wants to show the care and abundance with which the temple was prepared for the worship of God. These everyday objects were part of the sacred service.

For today: God values simple tasks done with care. What you do in everyday life, such as cleaning, serving, or preparing, can be an offering to God when you do it with excellence and a sincere heart.
exp.0:21:
It says that while Bathsheba was still speaking with King David, the prophet Nathan arrived. The phrase "just then" draws attention: something important was about to happen. "While Bathsheba was still speaking" shows that everything happened at just the right moment.

Bathsheba was asking David, who was already old and weak, to make clear who would be the next king. Adonijah, another son of David, had already proclaimed himself king on his own. Nathan had advised Bathsheba what to say, and he arrives to strengthen her request. Some see here a well-planned human strategy; others also see the hand of God guiding the transfer of the throne. The Bible presents both things together.

For today: when there is injustice or confusion, act with wisdom and courage, and trust that God can place the right people and the right moments in your path. Do not wait alone; seek wise counsel.
exp.0:6:
What it says: Adonijah, son of King David, conferred with Joab, son of Zeruiah, the commander of the army, and with Abiathar the priest. These two men supported him in his plan to become king. "Conferred" means that he talked matters over with them and joined forces with them. "Who supported him" shows that they actively backed his cause.

Context: The narrator of the book tells us that David was already old, and Adonijah wanted to take the throne on his own. Joab and Abiathar were very important men who had long served alongside David, so their backing gave strength to the attempt. The text does not explain their reasons; it only shows that other leaders, such as Zadok and Nathan, did not follow him.

For today: The people we associate with influence our decisions. Before following a plan, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it seeks God's will or only our ambition, and to surround ourselves with wise counselors who speak the truth to us.
exp.20:11:
This verse says that the city's leaders proclaimed a fast and gave Naboth a seat of honor at the front of the people. The verse's wording "a seat of honor among the people" is explained here as meaning a seat placed before the crowd. In this verse, the name is spelled "Naboth."

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not God. Jezebel, the queen, had written letters to the elders to take Naboth's vineyard from him, because he refused to sell it to King Ahab. The fast gave the appearance of a religious matter, and the seat of honor prepared the false trial. The exact details of that seat are not explained, but the plan was clear.

For today: religion can be used as a mask for injustice. Let us be honest, not lend ourselves to deception, and defend the innocent, even when those with power pressure us to stay silent.
exp.7:0:
Solomon calls together the elders of Israel, the tribal heads, and the family leaders, and gathers them before him in Jerusalem. The purpose is to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD up from Zion, the City of David, and into the temple. The verse says "assembled," and "the LORD" is the name used for God in this translation. The ark of the covenant was the sacred chest that represented God's presence with his people.

This is a third-person account from the book of Kings. The temple was already finished, and Solomon summons the whole people, through their representatives, to bring the ark to its place. Here "Zion" refers to the oldest part of Jerusalem, not to the temple mount.

For today: when something important relates to God, it is good to do it in community. Think of a decision or a project of faith that you are facing alone, and invite your family or your church to walk with you.
exp.0:33:
Here David gives orders for Solomon to be anointed as king over Israel. The priest Zadok and the prophet Nathan are to carry out the anointing, that is, they will pour oil on him as a sign that God has chosen him. Then they are to blow the ram's horn and declare, "Long live King Solomon!" to announce the new reign to the people. The word "anoint" means setting someone apart for a task.

David speaks as an old man who is now weak. His son Adonijah had proclaimed himself king on his own, without David's approval. That is why David acts at once and has Solomon brought up riding on his own mule, a sign of his backing. Benaiah answers "Amen," accepting the order and asking that God confirm it.

For today: before making important decisions, let us seek wise counsel and pray that God will confirm them, rather than acting only out of our own ambition.
exp.1:12:
Adonijah, son of Haggith, went to see Bathsheba, the mother of King Solomon. She asked him whether he came in peace, that is, without bad intentions, and he answered that he did.

Adonijah was the older brother of Solomon, and earlier he had tried to make himself king (1 Kings 1). Solomon had forgiven him on conditions. Bathsheba is suspicious, and that is why she asks. What follows shows that Adonijah was indeed seeking something: he wanted to ask her to request Abishag on his behalf, and that could be understood as a new attempt at the throne. The Bible does not say what his thoughts were, but his actions reveal them.

For today: saying "I come in peace" is easy, but God looks at the heart. Let us be sincere in our words and seek to have clean intentions before Him.
exp.3:0:
It says that Solomon ruled over Israel, that is, over the twelve tribes united. The word "ruled" is the plain verb here. The phrase is simple, but it shows that his rule was firm and recognized by all the people.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who cannot be identified with certainty. After the conflicts at the end of David's reign, the author shows how Solomon's kingdom was established. For this reason he follows with a list of his main officials: priests, scribes, and others in charge. This presents an orderly government, where the king did not rule alone.

For today: if God places you in a position of responsibility, at home, at work, or in the church, do not carry it alone. Seek capable and trustworthy people, and work with order, humility, and service.
exp.7:36:
When famine or plague comes upon the land, or blight or mildew or locusts or grasshoppers, or when their enemy besieges them in their cities, this verse lists the kinds of trouble that could strike Israel: hunger, disease, crop-destroying blight and mildew, swarms of locusts and grasshoppers, and an enemy army surrounding their towns. It ends with "whatever plague or sickness may come," which means the list leaves nothing out.

King Solomon is speaking in his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks that when the people suffer and turn back to God, God will hear the prayers they offer toward that place. The verses that follow say that God knows the heart of each person. The passage does not claim that every suffering is a punishment; it speaks of situations where there was sin.

For today: when a difficulty comes, whatever it is, you can come to God with a sincere heart. He listens, forgives, and knows your heart.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that Solomon went after other gods. Ashtoreth was a goddess of the Sidonians, a people neighboring Israel, and Milcom was the god of the Ammonites. The word for "abomination" means something detestable to God. "Followed" means that Solomon gave these gods a place in his life, not that he merely knew about them.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, the one who tells the story of Israel. He explains how Solomon, now old, turned away from God. The verses before this one point out that his many foreign wives led his heart astray. His heart was no longer fully devoted to the LORD, as his father David's had been. God had earlier warned him not to mix with those nations.

For today: the heart drifts little by little, often through the influences we let in. Honestly examine which people or habits draw you closer to God and which pull you away, and ask him to keep you faithful to the end.
exp.8:4:
God promises Solomon that he will establish his royal throne over Israel forever, just as he promised David, Solomon's father. The words "You will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel" mean that there would always be one of his descendants ruling. "Establish" means "make firm and secure."

The Lord speaks, responding to Solomon after he dedicated the temple and prayed. God accepts the temple, but the promise depends on a condition: that Solomon walk before him with integrity of heart, as David did. The verses that follow warn that if they turn away to worship other gods, there will be serious consequences. Some understand that the final promise is fully fulfilled in Christ, a descendant of David.

For today: God is faithful to his promises, but he invites us to respond with a sincere heart. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience, however small, and live it out honestly before God, trusting that his faithfulness sustains you.
exp.3:4:
This verse names two of Solomon's officials. Azariah was in charge of the governors, that is, the men appointed over the regions of the kingdom. Zabud was a priest and adviser to the king, someone who held the king's full trust. Both were sons of Nathan. Some think this is the prophet Nathan, but the text does not say so, so it is not certain.

The writer of the book of Kings is not describing a battle or a prophecy here. He presents the list of the highest posts in the kingdom at the beginning of Solomon's reign. By it he shows that the kingdom was well organized, with people responsible for each task, and that God had given Solomon wisdom to govern.

For today: God works through order and well-divided responsibilities. Give thanks for those who serve faithfully beside you, and seek to be a trustworthy and loyal person in whatever has been entrusted to you, however small it may seem.
exp.0:5:
