David never once corrected his son Adonijah. He never asked him, "Why have you done this?" In other words, David never called him to account or confronted him about his behavior. The verse also tells us that Adonijah was a very handsome man and that he was born right after Absalom.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. David is now old and very weak. Adonijah, one of his older sons, declares himself the future king without permission, arranging chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run ahead of him. The text suggests that this attitude grew out of a childhood without correction. His resemblance to Absalom, who also rebelled against his father, is probably meant as a warning.

For today: love includes correcting others with kindness and at the right time. Anyone who is a parent or who guides others should not stay silent out of a desire for comfort. Timely discipline protects people from pride and from the harm that pride brings.
exp.7:63:
On that same day, the passage tells us, Solomon set apart for God the middle of the courtyard in front of the Lord's house. There he offered the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar before the Lord was too small to contain all these offerings. The word "consecrated" means that he set the space apart for holy use.

The one telling this story is the author of the book of Kings, describing the great festival of the temple's dedication in Jerusalem. Solomon, as king, leads the people in worship. There were so many offerings that the usual altar could not hold them, so the space was adapted.

For today: when we want to honor God, we should not let the limits of what is customary hold us back. We can look for creative and generous ways to serve him, always with reverence and in line with his Word.
exp.13:30:
It says that King Rehoboam died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, that is, Jerusalem. The phrase "rested with his fathers" is an old, gentle way of saying that he died. It also names his mother, Naamah, who was an Ammonite, from a neighboring people of Israel. His son Abijam (also called Abijah) succeeded him as king.

This verse closes the summary of Rehoboam's reign in the book of 1 Kings. The narrator, who is the author of the book (tradition does not name for certain who he was), briefly reviews his life. Earlier he says there was constant war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, because the kingdom had been divided. Mentioning the mother is a detail the writer repeats with each king of Judah.

For today: our lives also have an end, and what we leave to those who come after us matters. Let us live today so that our faith and our example are a good inheritance for others.
exp.17:14:
Elijah answers Obadiah with an oath: "As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand." This means that God is real and that Elijah lives in service to him. He promises that he will present himself to Ahab that very day. The phrase "I will present myself to Ahab" means that Elijah will go to Ahab and let himself be seen by him.

Obadiah was the manager of Ahab's palace, but he feared God. He had hidden one hundred prophets during Jezebel's persecution. Now he was afraid that Ahab would kill him if he announced that Elijah was coming and then Elijah disappeared. That is why Elijah swears that he will not fail.

For today: when someone doubts us, integrity helps build trust. Keeping what we promise, knowing that we live before God, gives others security and shows that our faith is real.
exp.19:18:
This verse tells how the young officers serving the district governors marched out of Samaria to face the Syrian army. Behind them came the army of Israel. "Young officers" here means young assistants or soldiers serving under the governors, and "the district governors" refers to regional leaders.

The account is narrated, not spoken by a character. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had Samaria under siege with a great army and was confident, even drinking. A prophet had told King Ahab that God would give him the victory, and that it would begin with the young officers. So Israel, small and weak, went out to fight.

For today: God sometimes begins his work with what is small and what seems insufficient. If he calls you to take a step of obedience, take that step trusting in his power and not in your own resources.
exp.9:28:
This verse says that chariots and horses were imported from Egypt and then sent on to the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram. Each chariot cost six hundred shekels of silver, and each horse a hundred and fifty. Solomon's traders handled these sales and resales, acting as middlemen between Egypt and these kingdoms.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings describes the wealth and trade of Solomon's reign. These details show his great power. But the Law said the king must not multiply horses or send people back to Egypt for them (Deuteronomy 17:16). The text does not comment on this here, although the account that follows shows Solomon's decline.

For today: prosperity and the security that money provides can be deceptive. It is worth asking ourselves whether we trust our resources more than God, and whether we obey him even when it seems less practical.
exp.15:3:
This verse says that the relatives and descendants of Baasha who died, whether in the city or in the countryside, would not be buried with honor. Anyone belonging to Baasha who died in the city would be eaten by dogs, and anyone who died in the field would be eaten by the birds of the air.

God speaks through the prophet Jehu, son of Hanani. He had raised Baasha up from nothing to be king of Israel, but Baasha followed the sins of Jeroboam and led the people into sin. Therefore God announces that his family will meet the same fate as the house of Jeroboam. It was a severe and dishonorable judgment.

For today: God gives responsibilities and expects faithfulness. If He has given us a place, a family, or an influence, let us not use it to set a bad example. Let us ask for humility and obey His word.
exp.7:12:
Solomon tells God that he has built the temple as an exalted house, a place where He may dwell. The word "dwell" in this verse means to live in a place. The phrase "forever" shows the desire that God's presence remain there in a lasting way.

Solomon speaks right after finishing the temple and placing the ark in its place. A cloud filled the house, a sign of God's glory, and the priests could not continue ministering. Solomon recognizes that God had said He would dwell in the dark cloud, and he responds with this declaration of dedication. Later in this same chapter, he admits that even the heavens cannot contain God.

For today: God desires to be near His people, yet He is not confined to a building. We can prepare our hearts and our homes to receive Him with reverence, prayer, and obedience, knowing that He goes with us wherever we go.
exp.17:35:
At the hour of the evening sacrifice, which was offered every day, Elijah the prophet steps forward and prays aloud. He addresses God as "O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel," and asks that on this day it be made known that God is God in Israel and that Elijah is his servant, having done all these things at God's command. A "servant" is someone who obeys his master.

Elijah speaks before the people, who were divided between the Lord and Baal. He had proposed a test on Mount Carmel: the God who answers with fire is the true one. His prayer does not seek his own fame, but that the people would return to God.

For today: when you do something out of obedience to God, pray with humility and ask him to be the one who is shown, not you. Let your goal be that others come to know him.
exp.14:32:
This verse tells us that Baasha, son of Ahijah, became king of all Israel in the third year of Asa's reign over Judah. He made Tirzah his capital, and he reigned there for twenty-four years.

The author of the book of Kings keeps comparing the kings of Israel, the northern kingdom, with the kings of Judah, the southern kingdom. Baasha came to power after Nadab, the son of Jeroboam. The verses that follow say that Baasha also did evil and followed the sin of Jeroboam. The author wants to show that, although the king changed, the people kept walking in the same mistaken path.

For today: changing leaders or circumstances does not change the heart. Let us ask God to teach us to leave behind the bad habits we inherited and to truly follow him.
exp.1:42:
Solomon asks Shimei a pointed question: why did you not keep your oath to the LORD and the command I gave you? The phrase "your oath to the LORD" refers to a promise made in God's name. The word "command" shows that Solomon had placed a clear condition on him.

King Solomon is speaking. Shimei had cursed David years earlier, and David spared his life. Solomon set a limit for him: he was to live in Jerusalem and not leave. Shimei agreed, but later went to Gath. By doing so he broke his word, and Solomon held him accountable for it.

For today: our promises matter, especially the ones we make before God. Before saying "yes," let us think carefully, and then keep our word honestly, even when no one is watching.
exp.0:16:
Bathsheba reminds King David of a solemn promise. She tells him that he swore to her, in the name of the LORD his God, that Solomon, her son, would reign after him and sit on his throne. Calling herself "your maidservant" here is her way of speaking with humility before the king.

Bathsheba speaks with David, who is now very old and weak. Meanwhile, Adonijah, another son of David, has declared himself king without David's knowledge. Bathsheba seeks for David to act. The Bible does not record the oath she mentions earlier in this passage, so we know of it only from her words.

For today: promises made before God matter, and we should keep them. We also learn to speak with respect and courage when what is right must be defended, trusting that God guides events even in times of confusion.
exp.8:23:
Pharaoh's daughter, Solomon's wife, moved from the City of David to the palace the king had built for her. After that, Solomon built the supporting terraces. The exact nature of these terraces is uncertain; they were probably built up with earth or stone to support structures and level ground in Jerusalem.

The narrator of the book of Kings is reviewing the works of Solomon. Earlier he speaks of the work on the temple, the palace, and the cities. This verse shows the order of his projects. Some understand that the move of his foreign wife was because the City of David kept the ark, a holy place, although the text does not explain this here.

God asks us to take good care of the spaces and places where we live and worship. It is worth asking ourselves whether in our home and in our decisions there is an order that honors God.
exp.5:24:
The second cherub also measured ten cubits, and both cherubim had the same size and shape. The phrase "same size and shape" describes how the two figures matched each other exactly. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, perhaps about 45 centimeters, although the exact figure varies.

Here the narrator is the author of the book of Kings, describing the building of the temple that Solomon made. The cherubim stood in the most holy place, the innermost room, where the ark of the covenant was kept. The account gives their measurements to show the order and solemnity of that place, where God made himself present to his people.

For today: God cares about details and works with order. We can serve him with care, doing well even the small things, because everything we do for him has value.
exp.10:34:
God says he will take ten tribes of the kingdom from the hand of Solomon's son and give them to Jeroboam. "I will take ten tribes of the kingdom from his son's hand" means removing from him the power to rule over those tribes. "I will give them to you" is the promise that Jeroboam will receive them. The ten tribes would be the territory Jeroboam would rule.

God speaks through the prophet Ahijah, who addresses Jeroboam, a servant of Solomon. Solomon had turned to false gods through his foreign wives, such as Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Molech. For this reason God divided the kingdom. Even so, he left one tribe to the family of David, because of the promise made to David.

For today: the decisions of those who lead others have consequences for many people. Guard your faithfulness to God, for your example can either bless or harm your family and those who follow you. And remember that God keeps his promises, even when he corrects.
exp.17:36:
Elijah asks God to answer him with a clear sign. He wants the people to know that the LORD is the true God. He also says that God has turned their hearts back again, that is, that God is calling them back to himself. The word "answer" is the one he uses when he asks God to respond to him. The people here are the Israelites.

The prophet Elijah is speaking on Mount Carmel. Israel had drifted away from God and was following Baal. Elijah had prepared the altar and had it soaked with water, so that no one could doubt that what happened would come from God. After his prayer, fire fell from heaven, and the people cried out, "The LORD, He is God!"

For today: when you feel that your heart has grown cold, ask God to turn it back to himself. Elijah did not pray for fame, but so that God would be honored and the people would return to him.
exp.0:28:
King David makes a solemn oath. He swears by "the living LORD," that is, by the God who lives, and he remembers that the LORD has rescued his life from every trouble he has faced. With this oath he prepares what he is about to promise in the next verse.

David speaks as an old man, weak in body. His son Adonijah has declared himself king without David's command. Bathsheba and the prophet Nathan ask him to state who will reign. David answers with this oath and confirms that Solomon will be his successor, as he had promised before.

For today: when you have to keep a difficult promise, remember how the LORD has sustained you through past troubles. That grateful memory gives you the steadiness to be faithful to your word.
exp.20:0:
This passage starts a new story. It says that some time after the events just described, a man named Naboth, from the town of Jezreel, owned a vineyard there, next to the palace of Ahab, king of Samaria. A vineyard is a piece of land planted with grapevines.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings, who sets the scene before describing the conflict. The verse itself does not say why this matters, but the verses that follow show that the king wanted that land and Naboth refused to sell it. The vineyard's location right beside the palace sets up the problem that comes next.

For today: let us guard our hearts when we desire something that belongs to someone else. What we see close at hand and think we could easily have can become a temptation. Let us give thanks for what God has given us and respect what belongs to others.
exp.6:7:
The text says that Solomon's own palace was set further back, behind the hall, and was built in a similar style. He also built a palace like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter, the woman he had married. In this verse, "the hall" refers to the entrance area with its columns, and "lived" describes where Solomon made his home.

It is part of the account in the book of Kings about Solomon's buildings. The narrator, who is not named, describes the palace works after the temple, which took thirteen years according to verse 1. He mentions Pharaoh's daughter because Solomon married her as a political alliance. Some see here a warning sign, since his later marriages to foreign women led him away from God (1 Kings 11).

We can build great and beautiful things, but what matters most is that our hearts remain faithful to God. Check today whether your achievements and relationships bring you closer to Him or distract you from Him.
exp.2:26:
Here the king Solomon gives his final decision: the living baby must be handed over to the woman who wanted to save him, and he must not be killed. The command "Give the living baby to the first woman" and "By no means should you kill him" in the verse above express this. Solomon declares that she is his mother.

Two women claimed to be the mother of the same baby. Solomon proposed cutting the child in two, to see their reaction. One woman, moved by love, preferred to lose the child rather than see him die. The other accepted the division. In this way Solomon discovered the truth. Afterward, all Israel saw that God had given him wisdom to judge.

Today, true love seeks the good of the other, even when it costs us to give up what we want. When we face a conflict, let us ask God for wisdom and ask ourselves: am I seeking to win, or am I seeking to protect the one I love?
exp.12:13:
He says that the old prophet went out to look for the man of God and found him sitting under an oak tree, which gives shade. He asked him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" and the man answered, "I am."

The one speaking is an old prophet from Bethel. His sons had told him that a man of God had prophesied against Jeroboam's altar and then left. This old man wants to catch up with him. The text does not yet say why, but what follows shows that he will invite him to eat, even though God had already commanded the man of God not to eat bread in that place.

For today: not everyone who speaks kindly or with religious authority says what God wants. When God has already spoken to us clearly, we should not change course just because another person asks us to.
exp.6:24:
This verse describes how the bronze "sea," a huge basin of water for the temple, was supported. It rested on twelve bronze oxen, set in groups of three facing the four directions. The "sea" rested on them, and the hindquarters of the oxen faced inward, toward the center beneath the basin.

Here the writer of the book of Kings tells how Solomon had the temple in Jerusalem built. This cast bronze sea was part of the temple furnishings. Other passages suggest it was used for the priests to wash, though this text does not say so. The number twelve is often connected with the twelve tribes of Israel, but the passage does not explain this.

For today: God cares about the details of his house and of his service. We can serve him with order and devotion, and remember that he sustains us even in what no one sees.
exp.8:17:
It says that Solomon also built or rebuilt the cities of Baalath and Tamar in the Wilderness of Judah. It is not known for certain where Tamar was, though some connect it with Palmyra.

The author of the book of Kings recounts Solomon's great projects. These cities served to defend the kingdom, store supplies, and support trade. They show the power and prosperity that God had given him, though the book will also later show his failures.

For today: planning and working with order is good, even in difficult places. But what we build must not take the place of God. Ask him for wisdom to care for what you have without losing sight of what matters most: obeying him.
exp.1:32:
It says that the guilt for the blood Joab shed will fall on him and on his descendants forever. But for David, his descendants, his house and his throne, there will be peace from the LORD forever. The word "seed" in the old text means descendants, and the phrase "return upon the head" means that the consequences will come down on someone.

It is King Solomon who speaks, as he orders the death of Joab, David's former general. Joab had murdered Abner and Amasa, two military leaders, treacherously and in a time of peace. Solomon sees this as an unpaid debt of justice that could affect his own house. Some believe it was justice; others also see political motives, since Joab had supported Adonijah.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, and no one escapes being held accountable. But we can also seek his peace by living with honesty, without vengeance or betrayal, and trusting that he brings justice in his own time.
exp.17:30:
Elijah takes twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob. This is the same Jacob to whom the Lord's word came and said, "Israel shall be your name." With those stones Elijah rebuilds the altar. The word "tribes" refers to the family groups that came from Jacob's twelve sons.

Elijah is on Mount Carmel, before the people and the prophets of Baal. The kingdom was divided in two, but Elijah uses twelve stones to remind everyone that, before God, Israel is still one people. The prophets of Baal had cried out all day without receiving an answer. Now Elijah calls the people to return to the Lord.

For today: God does not forget his promises or his identity in us. When you feel you have drifted away, return to the basics: rebuild your life of prayer and trust in God, without looking for shortcuts or other supports.
exp.1:19:
Bathsheba tells her son, King Solomon, that she has one small request and asks him not to deny her. "Do not deny me" is her way of asking that he not refuse what she is about to ask. Solomon answers her with respect: "Make your request, my mother," and promises that he will not deny her.

Here Bathsheba, the king's mother, comes to ask something on behalf of Adonijah, Solomon's brother. Solomon receives her with honor and seats her at his right hand. Yet the request she calls "small" turns out to be very delicate, since the text that follows shows that it had political implications. Interpreters differ on whether she perceived this or not.

For today: before promising something quickly, let us hear the whole request. And when we ask for something, let us be clear and honest, without calling "small" what may have great consequences.
exp.14:21:
Then King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, with no exceptions, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. With these materials King Asa built up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah. "Summoned" means that he called them to gather, and "with no exceptions" means that no one was excused from helping.

It is a historical account, not a speech. Baasha, king of Israel, was fortifying Ramah to cut off the way into Judah. Asa paid Ben-hadad, king of Syria, to attack Israel, and Baasha had to stop the work. Then Asa made use of the materials. Later, 2 Chronicles 16 questions Asa's decision to trust Syria rather than God.

For today: a good work is accomplished when everyone cooperates. But it is also worth asking ourselves whether, when faced with problems, we first seek God or only our own solutions.
exp.8:7:
This verse describes the temple, the house that had once been greatly honored and admired, being reduced to ruins so complete that passersby would be stunned. The words "will be appalled" and "will hiss" show how people would react to such a disaster, with shock and scorn. They would ask why the LORD had done such a thing to this land and to this temple.

God speaks to Solomon after he has finished building the temple and dedicated it. He warns that if Solomon and the people turn away from God and worship other gods, serious judgment will come. The verses that follow explain the answer: everything would happen because the people abandoned the LORD, who had brought them out of Egypt.

For today: the blessings and good things of faith do not replace a faithful relationship with God. It is worth asking ourselves whether we are following him from the heart, not just in appearance, and returning to him when we have been distracted.
exp.21:11:
It says that all of King Ahab's prophets said the same thing: that he should go up to Ramoth-gilead, that he would triumph, and that the LORD would hand the city over to the king. "Triumph" means that he will win. "The same" means that all of them were saying alike.

Here about four hundred prophets who served Ahab, king of Israel, speak. He and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were planning to attack the Syrians. Jehoshaphat wanted to ask God for guidance, and these prophets gave the king the message he wanted to hear. Then Micaiah appears, who would say only what God actually told him.

For today: that many voices say the same thing does not prove it is true. Before deciding, let us compare what we hear with the Word of God and seek the truth, even when it is not pleasant.
exp.1:26:
This verse says that Solomon banished Abiathar from the priesthood of the LORD. The word "banished" means that he sent him away and removed him from his position. In this way, the word the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against the house of Eli was fulfilled.

Abiathar had supported Adonijah, who wanted to make himself king instead of Solomon. Solomon did not put him to death, because Abiathar had served David faithfully, but he sent him away to Anathoth, his homeland. The text presents this as the fulfillment of the warning given to the house of Eli (1 Samuel 2:27-36), although the passage does not explain every part of the process.

For today: God is faithful to his word, even when a long time passes. We also see that our decisions bring consequences, and that God does not forget faithful service. It is wise to remain loyal to him.
exp.10:40:
As for the rest of the acts of Solomon, all that he did and his wisdom, these are recorded in the Book of the Acts of Solomon. The phrase "the rest" means everything that is left to tell.

The author of 1 Kings is the one speaking, and he closes his account of Solomon's reign. Earlier he recounted Solomon's failings and the division that would follow. This Book of the Acts of Solomon is not known to us today; we do not know whether it was a court record or some other writing. The author mentions it as a source and to say that his summary is complete.

For today: every life leaves a record, and in the end how we live matters more than what we achieve. Solomon was wise, but he turned away. Let us ask God for a faithful heart to the end, not just a good beginning.
exp.21:5:
The king of Israel, Ahab, gathers about four hundred prophets and asks them whether he should go to war against Ramoth-gilead or refrain. They reply, "Go up," and tell him that the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, had asked to consult the word of the Lord. Ahab answers with many prophets who tell him what he wants to hear. But Jehoshaphat senses that something does not fit and asks for a prophet of the Lord. Many believe these men were agreeable prophets, although the text does not say so right away.

Today we can learn not to seek only the voices that approve of our plans. Before deciding, it is wise to ask God for sincerity and to listen to counsel that speaks to us with truth, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.21:2:
The king of Israel asks his servants whether they realize that Ramoth-gilead belongs to them. He reproaches them for failing to take it back from the king of Aram, doing nothing when they should have acted. The word "to" here means simply "from."

After three years without war, Ahab receives a visit from Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Ahab speaks like a man who has already decided to go to battle and wants to win the others over. Later on, Jehoshaphat asks him to seek the counsel of the LORD, something Ahab had not done first.

For today: before rushing into an important decision, even one that seems fair or logical, it is wise to stop and pray and seek God's direction, rather than relying only on our own desire or reasoning.
exp.1:45:
This verse says that Solomon gave the order to Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, and that he went out and struck Shimei down, and Shimei died. At the end, the text concludes that the kingdom was firmly established in the hand of Solomon.

Shimei was a man from the family of Saul who had cursed David harshly when David was fleeing from Absalom. Later, Solomon had set him a condition: that he not leave Jerusalem. Shimei broke it, and the king judged him. The narrator presents this as the final step in securing the throne. Some see justice here; others see a harsh political decision. The text does not fully explain it.

For today: our words and promises have consequences. Let us be people of our word, and seek peace and forgiveness before pride or bitterness lead us into mistakes that cannot be undone.
exp.13:22:
This verse says that the people of Judah built high places, which were places of worship on the hilltops. They also set up sacred pillars, and Asherah poles, which were wooden poles dedicated to the goddess Asherah (scholars explain these in several ways). They did all this on every high hill and under every green tree, that is, everywhere.

The narrator of the book of Kings, whose author is not identified with certainty, tells the story of the reign of Rehoboam. He wants to show that Judah, despite having Jerusalem and the temple, imitated the customs of the neighboring peoples. For this reason, shortly afterward, the invasion of Shishak, king of Egypt, came.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we allow to take the place of God, even when they are common customs. It is good to return to Him with sincerity and to worship Him alone.
exp.2:20:
This verse records what one of the two women says before the king. She says that she got up in the morning to nurse her son and found him dead. But when she looked at him more closely in the morning light, she realized that this child was not the son she had given birth to. "To nurse" means to feed a baby at the breast.

It is spoken by one of two women who lived together and had each had a baby a few days apart. They come to Solomon so that he can decide who the real mother is. The woman accuses the other of having switched the children during the night. There were no witnesses, so the case was very hard to resolve.

For today: before judging a situation, it is wise to look at it calmly and seek the truth. And when we lack wisdom, we can ask God for it, as Solomon did.
exp.21:1:
This verse says that, after three years with no war between Syria and Israel, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, went down to visit the king of Israel. The text says he "went down" because Jerusalem sits on high ground, and in the Bible people go "up" to Jerusalem and come "down" from it. Jehoshaphat is the king of Judah, and the Syrians are the people of Syria.

The narrator describes this moment of calm between nations. The king of Israel is Ahab, though he is not named here. Jehoshaphat, who followed God, makes a friendly visit. But the verses that follow show that Ahab takes the occasion to ask him for military help. Jehoshaphat agrees right away, without first seeking God's counsel, and that will lead him into trouble.

For today: when someone makes us a proposal, even one that comes from friendship or from a peaceful moment, it is wise to pause and pray before saying "yes." Seeking God's guidance first spares us from mistakes and commitments we later regret.
exp.13:13:
It says that God himself will raise up a new king over Israel, and that king will wipe out the whole family of Jeroboam. "Cut off" means to cut down or chop away, as one cuts down a tree. The final phrase, "This is the day, yes, even today!", points to judgment that was already beginning, so the warning was not far off.

The prophet Ahijah of Shiloh speaks to Jeroboam's wife, who came in disguise to ask about her sick son. Jeroboam had led the people into idolatry with the golden calves. God announces the punishment, but he also sees something good in that young man.

For today: God sees and values what is good, even in the midst of a bad environment. We can keep doing what is right, even when others do not, because God does not overlook our faithfulness.
exp.13:12:
It says that Jeroboam's sick son will be the only one of his family to receive a proper burial. All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. The LORD found some good in him, something that pleased Him.

The prophet Ahijah of Shiloh speaks on God's behalf to Jeroboam's wife, who had come in disguise to ask whether their son would recover. Jeroboam had led the people into idolatry, and God announces judgment on his house. The text does not explain what that good was, so it is better not to invent it.

For today: God sees and values what is good in a person, even in the middle of a very crooked environment. We can trust that our sincerity toward Him does not go unnoticed, and be encouraged to seek Him even when those around us do not.
exp.18:14:
God tells Elijah to get up and go back the way he came, toward the Desert of Damascus. When he arrives, he is to anoint Hazael as king over Aram, that is, set him apart with oil for the task.

Aram was the kingdom neighboring Israel, and its capital was Damascus.

Elijah had fled from Queen Jezebel and hidden in a cave on Mount Horeb. He felt alone and tired, and he poured out his complaint before God. God does not scold him; He gives him new tasks. In this way He shows him that He still rules over Israel and over the nations, and that Elijah's work is not finished.

For today: when you feel exhausted or alone, do not stay shut in with your complaint. Tell God everything honestly, and then take the next step He shows you, trusting that He is still in control.
exp.1:41:
Here King Solomon summons Shimei and reminds him of his promise. Earlier he had warned him, in the name of the LORD, that he would die on the day he left Jerusalem and went elsewhere. The king had made him swear by the LORD and given him a serious warning. Shimei had accepted the condition, saying, "The sentence is fair; I will comply."

Solomon speaks as the new king, after the death of David. Shimei had cursed David when David was fleeing from Absalom (2 Samuel 16). Solomon gave him a quiet life, but with a clear limit. Shimei went to Gath to recover his servants and so broke his oath. That is why Solomon calls him to account.

For today: when we give our word, especially before God, we should keep it, even when the matter seems small. And if we have received mercy, let us live with gratitude and respect his limits.
exp.17:16:
When King Ahab saw Elijah, he greeted him with an accusing question: "Is that you, O troubler of Israel?" Here the word "troubler" refers to someone who causes trouble, disturbs the peace, or brings ruin on the people.

It is King Ahab who speaks. More than three years of drought had passed in Israel, and Ahab blamed Elijah, because the prophet had announced that drought. Elijah, on the other hand, will answer that the real problem was the idolatry of the king and his family, who had abandoned the LORD to follow the Baals. This meeting prepares the challenge on Mount Carmel.

For today: sometimes we blame the messenger instead of looking into our own hearts. When God's truth makes us uncomfortable, we can pause and ask ourselves humbly: could it be that I need to correct something in my life?
exp.14:8:
This verse tells us when Asa became king of Judah. It places that moment in "the twentieth year of Jeroboam's reign over Israel," Jeroboam being the king of the northern kingdom. The phrase "became king" means that he took the throne. Judah was the southern kingdom.

The book of Kings does not name its author in the text. It tells the story of the reigns of Judah and Israel and lines them up against one shared timeline. Asa succeeds his father Abijam, who had just died. The verses that follow present him as a king who did what was right before God, and this marks a change after the crooked paths of earlier kings.

God works in history, even through changes of government and of generation. A family or a church may have a troubled past, but each person can choose today to follow God. Ask yourself: what step of obedience can I take today, without waiting for others to take it first?
exp.6:4:
This verse describes the House of the Forest of Lebanon, one of Solomon's buildings. It says that all the doorways had rectangular frames. The openings faced one another in three tiers. "Tiers" here means levels, one above another, and the detail about the openings facing one another refers to windows set opposite each other, letting in light and air.

Here no character is speaking; this is the account of the writer of Kings. After describing the building of the temple, he describes Solomon's works for his own house and palace, which took thirteen years. The detail suggests a large, orderly, well-planned work. Scholars do not fully agree on exactly what the windows or the building looked like.

For today: what we do deserves order and care. Planning well, attending to details, and letting light into our home and work, with humility and gratitude to God, honors what He has entrusted to us.
exp.4:2:
Solomon reminds Hiram that his father David could not build the temple for God. The reason was that David was surrounded by wars, with enemies pressing in on every side. God had not yet given David rest from these enemies. Only after God had put them under David's feet, bringing him victory and firm control over them, was the time right for building.

Solomon speaks with Hiram, king of Tyre, who had been a friend of David and had congratulated him on becoming king. Solomon writes to him to ask for timber for the temple. Before making the request, he explains why David did not build it and why now is the right time: God has given Solomon's reign peace.

For today: God has his time for every task. If you cannot yet accomplish something good you desire, it does not mean that God has rejected you. Stay faithful in your present season and trust that He will open the door at the right moment.
exp.16:21:
This verse tells that God listened to Elijah's prayer and restored the life of the widow's son. The child's life returned to him, and he lived again.

Elijah, the prophet, was staying in the house of a widow from Zarephath, who had shared her little food with him. When her son became ill and died, she felt that God was punishing her. Elijah, not hiding his grief, cried out to God with sincerity and asked him to restore the child's life. This is the first account of a resurrection in the Bible. Afterward, the woman recognized that the word of God spoken by Elijah was true.

For today: we can come to God with honesty, even with questions and pain, and trust that He hears us. Praying with sincerity is not a lack of faith; it is truly seeking Him.
exp.6:6:
This verse tells that Solomon built a special hall where his throne was placed so he could judge. It is called the Hall of Justice. The hall was paneled with cedar wood from floor to ceiling.

The author of the book recounts, like a report, the works of Solomon in Jerusalem, after describing the temple. Here he speaks of the king's palace and his buildings. This hall was where the king heard the cases of the people. Scholars are not sure of all the details of the construction.

For today: justice deserves an important and careful place in our lives. In the home, at work, or in the church, let us strive to decide with honesty and without favoritism, asking God for the wisdom that Solomon also needed.
exp.12:24:
This verse tells how some men passing along the road saw the body of the man of God lying there, with the lion standing beside it. They went and reported what they had seen in the city where the old prophet lived.

It is part of the narrative of the book. The man of God came from Judah with a clear command from the LORD: not to eat or drink in Bethel. But the old prophet deceived him by saying that an angel had spoken to him, and the man believed him and ate. The men who passed by know nothing of this; they only report what they saw. What is strange is that the lion did not devour the body or the donkey, a sign of something beyond the ordinary.

For today: the clear word of God is worth more than any voice that sounds religious. Before following a spiritual piece of advice, compare it with what God has already said in his Word.
exp.3:24:
In the time of Solomon, this verse says, the people of Judah and Israel lived in peace and security. "Each one under his own vine and his own fig tree" was a way of saying that every family had its own land, its livelihood, and its rest. "From Dan to Beersheba" means from north to south, across the whole country. The word "securely" means without fear of threats.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings, who cannot be identified with certainty. He is describing Solomon's kingdom at its best: there was peace with neighboring countries and abundance at the king's table. The account presents this as a blessing from God. Later in the same book, it shows that Solomon turned aside and the kingdom suffered the consequences.

For today: true peace is not merely having possessions, but living with confidence in God and in harmony with others. Take care of what God has given you, and do not let comfort draw you away from Him.
exp.7:61:
This verse says that King Solomon and all the people of Israel offered sacrifices to God. "Sacrifices" are animals that were brought to the altar as offerings. Everyone took part, not just the king.

The temple in Jerusalem had just been finished. Solomon had prayed in public, blessed the people, and encouraged them to keep their hearts wholly devoted to God. Now, with these sacrifices, the people dedicate the house of the Lord. The verses that follow speak of an enormous number of animals, and the Bible does not explain in more detail how all of it was carried out.

For today: when God gives us something good, such as a home, a job, or a church, we can dedicate it to Him with gratitude. Offering God the best of our time, affection, and resources, together with other believers, reminds us that everything comes from Him.
exp.20:26:
When Ahab heard the message of judgment that Elijah delivered to him, he showed his grief and repentance in visible ways. He tore his clothes, put on rough mourning clothes, fasted, and lay down in that sackcloth. The phrase "walked around meekly" describes him moving with a downcast, humbled manner, without pride.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Ahab had taken Naboth's vineyard with the help of Jezebel, and God confronted him through Elijah, announcing disaster on his house. Then God notices this humility and postpones the punishment until the days of his son. We do not know how deep his change was; the Bible only says that God saw his humility.

For today: when God shows us a wrong, we should not defend ourselves or minimize it. Acknowledging it with sincerity and humility opens the door to God's mercy.
exp.21:7:
The king of Israel, Ahab, admits that there is still one man through whom they can inquire of the LORD, Micaiah son of Imlah. But he says he hates him, because Micaiah never prophesies anything good for him, only bad. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, answers him respectfully: "The king should not say that!" "Hates" means he has a deep dislike for him, and "prophesies good" means he announces favorable things.

Ahab and Jehoshaphat have joined forces to attack Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets have already told Ahab what he wanted to hear, but Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the LORD. Ahab mentions Micaiah reluctantly, and Jehoshaphat gently corrects his attitude.

For today: let us not reject the truth just because it makes us uncomfortable. A sincere word, even when it hurts, can help us more than many compliments. Let us ask God for humility to listen to what we need to hear, not only what we like.
exp.7:19:
He says that God has done what he promised. Solomon tells how he has succeeded his father David and now sits on the throne of Israel, just as the Lord said he would. He also explains that he has built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.

The verse says "has fulfilled the word that He spoke," which means God has kept his promise and made it happen. The phrase "I have succeeded my father David" means Solomon has taken over the kingship from David.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem, in front of all the people. David wanted to build that house for God, but God told him that his son would build it. Solomon wants everyone to see that what God promised has come true, and so he praises God before he prays.

For today: when God seems slow to do what he has said, we can keep trusting. Write down the times you have seen his faithfulness and thank him, as Solomon did.
exp.5:5:
Around the temple, Solomon built three levels of side rooms. The lowest floor was five cubits wide, the middle one six, and the top one seven. A cubit was about half a meter. The "offset ledges" are steps or set-backs on the outside of the temple wall, so the wall became thinner as it rose. The beams of the rooms rested on those ledges and were not set into the walls of the temple, so nothing was inserted into its walls.

This is the account from the book of Kings, which describes the building of the temple under Solomon. It explains the method used: the side rooms were built against the temple, but without piercing its walls. The exact technical details are debated, but the general idea is clear.

For today: we can stay close to God and receive support from others without that harming what is sacred. Good structures, such as family or church, sustain faith without piercing what is essential.
exp.7:7:
The priests pulled out the poles used to carry the ark, so that their ends could be seen from the Holy Place, in front of the inner sanctuary. But they could not be seen from outside the Holy Place. The writer adds that the poles are there "to this day," meaning up to the time when this account was written.

This happens when Solomon dedicates the temple. The ark was no longer going to move from place to place, as it did in the wilderness, but was set in its permanent home. Scholars explain the detail of the poles in different ways, but all agree that it shows the ark had already found its place.

Today we can rest in the fact that God is faithful and keeps his promises. After so many uncertain journeys, he gives his people a secure place, and he gives us one too.
exp.21:20:
It says that, in a vision, a spirit came forward, stood before God, and offered to entice King Ahab. "Entice" means to draw someone in, often by making something attractive, so that they go along with it. God asked by what means it would do this, and the answer comes in the next verse: it would be a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets.

The prophet Micaiah, son of Imlah, is speaking. Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, wanted to attack Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets were promising the king victory, but Micaiah told this vision to show that this pleasing message was false and that Ahab was going to fall. This scene is a symbolic vision, and scholars explain it in several ways.

Today we can learn not to trust someone who only tells us what we want to hear. It is wise to compare every message with the Word of God and to listen with humility, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
exp.4:3:
Solomon says that God has given him rest on every side of his kingdom. There is no longer any enemy attacking him, and no crisis threatening him. The "adversary" is the enemy, and the "crisis" is a dangerous or sudden turn of events.

Solomon writes to Hiram, king of Tyre, to ask for cedar wood. He wants to build the temple, something his father David could not do because he was busy with many wars. Solomon explains that the peace God gave him makes this project possible. He also sees in it the fulfillment of the promise made to David.

For today: times of calm are a gift from God, and not only for resting. We can use them to serve him, help others, and build things that are worthwhile. Ask yourself what you can do now, in this peaceful season, to honor God.
exp.21:39:
This verse says that King Ahab died. The phrase "rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died and was gathered to his ancestors. Then his son Ahaziah became king of Israel in his place.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings sums up the end of Ahab's reign. Just before this, it is told that the word of the LORD about his blood and the dogs was fulfilled. The text mentions his works and buildings, but the focus is on God doing what he says. The account then moves on to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.

For today: human achievements pass away, and we all end our lives one day. What matters most is living in obedience to God, because his word is fulfilled. Today you can ask yourself what you are building and whether you are doing it to please him.
exp.17:43:
It says that, on the seventh time, Elijah's servant saw a small cloud, about the size of a man's hand, rising from the sea. Then Elijah sent word to Ahab: "Prepare your chariot and go down", that is, get ready to leave and come down from the mountain, so that the rain does not stop him on the way.

Elijah speaks here after the great contest on Carmel, when God answered with fire. There had been a drought for years. Elijah prays with his face between his knees and sends his servant to look toward the sea. Many understand that his prayer is persistent and confident, since he acts as if the rain were already coming.

For today: keep praying steadily, even when the answer takes time. Notice the small signs of God's work and be ready to act on them.
exp.9:18:
It says that Solomon's throne was reached by six steps. The top of the back was rounded, and on each side of the seat there were armrests. Beside each armrest stood a lion. The word "steps" refers to the stairs leading up to the seat, and "armrests" refers to the supports on each side of the seat.

Here the narrator of the book describes with admiration the wealth and splendor of Solomon's reign. The throne, covered with gold, showed his power before other nations. Lions were often a symbol of strength and authority. The text does not explain the meaning of each detail, so it is better not to invent one.

All of Solomon's luxury reminds us that power and wealth impress, but they are not what matters most. We know that later his heart turned away. Today we can ask God to keep us faithful, and not let success or material things take first place in our lives.
exp.6:39:
This verse says that Huram, the bronze craftsman who worked for Solomon, also made pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. With this he finished all the work he had taken on for King Solomon in the house of the LORD. The phrase about finishing "all the work that he had undertaken for King Solomon" tells us that nothing he was given was left unfinished.

This passage comes from the narrator of the book of Kings, who describes the building of the temple in careful detail. This Huram was a skilled worker from Tyre, not the same person as King Hiram of Tyre. His works are listed, such as the pillars, the bronze sea, and the stands, to show that the temple was completed with care and order.

For today: God notices work done well, even in small things like a pot or a bowl. We can serve him with steadiness and excellence in tasks no one applauds, finishing them faithfully.
exp.7:25:
And now, O God of Israel, Solomon asks, please confirm what you promised to your servant, his father David. The word "confirm" means to make certain and to fulfill. Here, "servant" describes someone who serves God with humility.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple, in front of all the people. God had promised David that his descendants would reign, on the condition that his sons remained faithful to him. Solomon already sees part of the promise fulfilled, since the temple is finished, and now he asks that God remain faithful in what is still to come.

For today: when we pray, we can rely on what God has already promised in his Word. Praying with God's promises is not demanding anything from him, but trusting his faithful character. Look for a promise in the Bible and present it to God today with humility and gratitude.
exp.2:24:
Here King Solomon gives a shocking order: cut the living child in two and give half to one woman and half to the other. The command is stated plainly as "cut" and "give." The two women are the ones the order is addressed to.

Two women claim to be the mother of the same child, and there are no witnesses. Solomon, newly made king, had asked God for wisdom to judge. This order was not a real plan, but a test to reveal the heart of each woman. What follows shows that the true mother would rather lose the child than see him die.

For today: before judging a conflict, let us seek the truth with patience and ask God for wisdom. Often sincere love shows itself more clearly than words do.
exp.10:6:
Solomon built a "high place," meaning a place of worship on a hill, for Chemosh, the god of Moab, and for Molech, the god of the Ammonites. The Bible calls these gods an "abomination" because worshiping them was a serious offense against the true God. The hill is east of Jerusalem, though the text does not name it.

The one telling the story is the writer of Kings. He explains why Solomon's kingdom weakened. Solomon married foreign women, and he allowed them to worship their own gods. Some think Molech and Milcom are the same god, but this is not certain.

For today: the heart can drift away slowly, through small concessions. Be careful about what influences your faith, and do not place anything alongside God.
exp.13:27:
It says that every time King Rehoboam entered the temple, the guards would carry the shields. Afterward, they would return them to the guardroom. The "guards" were the soldiers who protected the king, and the guardroom was the place where the shields were kept.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. Shishak, the pharaoh of Egypt, had plundered Jerusalem and taken away Solomon's gold shields. Rehoboam replaced them with shields of bronze, probably, according to the parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 12. The account shows a loss: the appearance of glory remains, but the gold was gone.

For today: it is easy to keep a good appearance on the outside while losing what is valuable on the inside. Ask God to renew your true faith, not just its appearance.
exp.21:38:
This verse is the official closing note of Ahab's reign. It says that the rest of his acts, along with all his accomplishments, the ivory palace he built, and the cities he founded, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. The word "accomplishments" points to what he carried out and achieved. The ivory palace was a palace decorated with ivory. That book of chronicles is not preserved today.

The narrator of the book of Kings uses this formula for many kings. It comes right after the violent death of Ahab, which fulfilled the word of the Lord. It is striking that his wealth and his building projects are mentioned, but nothing is said about his faith. For the writer, what weighs most heavily about Ahab is his disobedience to God.

For today: works and achievements can impress, but what truly matters is how we live before God. Ask yourself today whether you are building only visible things or also a life that is faithful to Him.
exp.1:9:
It says that David died and was buried in the City of David. "Rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died, as his ancestors did. The "City of David" is the old part of Jerusalem, which he conquered and where he established his kingdom.

The narrator of the book here recounts the end of David's life. Just before, the dying king gave his son Solomon his final counsel, including instructions about Shimei, who had cursed him. This verse marks the close of a reign of forty years and the beginning of Solomon's reign. Some understand David's words about Shimei as justice; others see them as a vengeance that is hard to explain.

For today: our life also has an end, and what we leave behind matters. Let us live in such a way that our last words and decisions leave peace, faith, and a good example to those who come after us.
exp.19:34:
One of the sons of the prophets, speaking by the word of the LORD, asked his companion to strike him. But the man refused to strike him. "Man" means a male person, "companion" means a friend or fellow, and the request to strike him means asking to be hit.

We have just seen that King Ahab made a covenant with Ben-hadad, king of Syria, and let him go instead of carrying out what God had commanded. This prophet wanted to give Ahab a message through a symbolic scene, and that is why he asked to be wounded. His companion did not want to, and because he did not obey the word of God, he received the punishment described afterward: a lion killed him.

For today: obeying God may cost us or seem uncomfortable, but partial obedience is disobedience. Let us ask him to give us courage to do what he commands, even when we do not fully understand it.
exp.1:33:
The verse says that Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up to Joab, struck him down, and killed him. The phrase "struck him down" means that he hit him, and "killed him" describes the same act in plain terms. Afterward Joab was buried at his own home in the wilderness, meaning in open country away from the town.

The account, which records the orders of King Solomon, speaks here. Joab, the commander of the army, had treacherously killed Abner and Amasa. He had also supported Adonijah against Solomon. Joab took refuge by the altar, but Solomon ordered that he be executed in keeping with the justice of that time. The text presents this as the settling of a debt of blood and as a step toward securing Solomon's kingdom.

Today, this passage reminds us that unjust decisions have consequences, even if those consequences take time to arrive. It invites us to live with integrity and to leave justice in God's hands rather than taking it into our own.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that Solomon appointed five hundred and fifty chief officers to direct and oversee the people who worked on his major building projects. The word "projects" describes the large construction work he had underway, and "supervisors" refers to those who held authority over the workers. They were responsible for making sure the work got done.

This is from the book of Kings, which explains how Solomon organized his construction, such as the temple and other buildings. Earlier, the text says that the forced labor fell on the peoples who remained in the land, not on the Israelites. This number appears differently in 2 Chronicles 8:10, which gives two hundred and fifty, and scholars explain the difference in several ways, for example as separate groups of supervisors or different levels of command. It is not known with certainty.

For today: God values order and responsibility in work. If you lead others, do so with justice and respect for their dignity, remembering that one day you too will give an account to God.
exp.20:2:
Naboth tells King Ahab that he will not give him his vineyard. He answers, "The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers." This means that God would not allow him to hand over the land his family received from their ancestors and meant to pass on to their children.

Naboth, a man from Jezreel, speaks in reply to the king's offer: an exchange for another vineyard or a payment in money. In the law of Moses, family land was not to be sold for good (Leviticus 25:23). That is why Naboth does not see it as a simple business deal, but as a matter of obedience to God. Ahab goes home sad and angry, and this prepares the way for Jezebel's wickedness.

For today: there are things that are not for sale, even when a powerful person asks for them with fine words. Let us ask God for the courage to remain faithful to Him, with respect and firmness.
exp.17:9:
Obadiah, the manager of Ahab's palace, speaks to Elijah. He swears "as surely as the LORD your God lives" that the king has sent people to search for Elijah in every nation and kingdom nearby. When they reported "he is not here," Ahab made each kingdom or nation swear that they had not found him. Making them swear means making them take an oath. Sending someone to search for you means sending people to look for you.

Obadiah was a believer, but he worked for a king who hated Elijah. After three years of drought, Elijah asks him to tell Ahab that he wants to see him. Obadiah is afraid, because Ahab could kill him if Elijah disappeared again. With these words he explains how desperate the king's search was.

For today: obeying God in a difficult setting can be frightening. But God uses faithful people in complicated places. We can ask him for courage and trust in his care.
exp.15:7:
This verse says that Elah, son of Baasha, became king of Israel in the twenty-sixth year of Asa's reign over Judah. His capital was Tirzah, and he reigned only two years. The phrase "became king" means that he was crowned.

The account in the book of Kings is a historical narrative. Baasha had just died, and his son inherited the throne. But the writer recalls that God had already announced judgment against the house of Baasha through the prophet Jehu, because of its wickedness. So this very short reign prepares the reader for what follows: the conspiracy of Zimri.

For today: positions and inheritances do not secure the future; what sustains a life is obedience to God. Let us ask him to help us live with humility and to leave our children an example of faithfulness, rather than wealth or position.
exp.14:7:
It says that King Abijam rested with his fathers, died, and was buried in the City of David, that is, Jerusalem. The phrase "rested with his fathers" is an old and gentle way of saying that he died. After him, his son Asa took his place as king of Judah.

This passage is part of the account in the book of Kings, which has no narrator identified with certainty. It briefly recounts the end of Abijam's reign, which was short and marked by wars with Jeroboam. The text looks first of all at the succession of the kings of Judah, and shows that the throne of David continued from father to son. Asa, according to the context that follows, would reign for a long time.

For today: no human power lasts forever, but God keeps working from one generation to the next. We can ask ourselves what we will leave to those who come after us: an example of faith, honesty, and love for God.
exp.14:26:
This verse tells how Baasha, son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar, plotted against King Nadab and struck him down at Gibbethon, a Philistine city. At that time Nadab and all Israel were besieging the city with their army. "Struck down" here means that he killed him, and "conspired" means he secretly planned to overthrow someone.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings. Nadab had followed the sins of his father Jeroboam, and the text that follows says that the destruction of his family fulfilled what the LORD had announced through the prophet Ahijah. Even so, the account does not approve of Baasha's violence; it only shows how that word was fulfilled.

For today: our choices and our example leave a mark on those who come after us. It is worth asking ourselves what we are sowing in our family, and seeking to walk with God rather than repeating the mistakes we inherited without thinking.
exp.17:26:
Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal at noon. He tells them to shout louder, because their god may be deep in thought, may be occupied, may be on a journey, or may be sleeping and need to be awakened.

Elijah speaks on Mount Carmel, in the contest before the people of Israel. He wanted to show who the true God was: the one who would answer with fire. The prophets of Baal had been calling on their god for hours without any answer, and Elijah uses mockery to expose how empty that worship was.

Today we might ask what things are taking God's place in our lives: money, success, approval. If we ask everything of something that cannot answer, we will end up worn out. Let us return to the living God, who listens to those who seek him sincerely.
exp.3:15:
This verse names Baana, son of Hushai, as one of the twelve governors whom Solomon set over Israel. His district was Asher and Aloth. Some understand Aloth to be a place or a neighboring area; others think it could be the name that appears as "Bealoth" in other versions. It is not known for certain.

Here there is no voice speaking in the first person. The narrator of the book presents the organization of Solomon's kingdom. Each governor was to supply provisions for the king and his household for one month of the year. The list shows an orderly government, with responsibilities spread across the whole territory.

For today: God uses people who carry out simple tasks, even though few remember their names. Let us faithfully do what is ours to do in the family, at work, or in the church, knowing that God sees and values our service.
exp.15:24:
This verse says that Omri, king of Israel, did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and that he acted more wickedly than all the kings who came before him. The phrase "did evil in the sight of the LORD" means acting in a way that God sees as sin.

The speaker here is the writer of the book of Kings, who summarizes each reign according to the king's faithfulness to God. Just before this, the writer mentions that Omri founded Samaria, an important political achievement. However, the writer does not measure him by his power or his works, but by his obedience. The next verse explains that he followed the sin of Jeroboam, who led the people into idolatry.

For today: success or fame is not what matters most to God. We can build a great deal and still fail in what is essential. Today you might ask yourself: does my life please God, and not only other people?
exp.11:19:
When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him, summoned him to the assembly, and made him king over all Israel. Only the tribe of Judah followed the house of David.

The verse says "sent for him" and "summoned him to the assembly." The assembly is the gathering of the people.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Rehoboam, son of Solomon, had refused to lighten the burdens of the people. The northern tribes rebelled, stoned his tax officer, and broke away. The kingdom was divided. Some understand that Benjamin also stayed with Judah, as the next verse shows.

For today: leaders who ignore the cry of those they lead can lose their trust. If you have authority at home, at work, or in church, listen with humility and serve with kindness, not harshness.
exp.16:5:
Elijah received his food in a miraculous way. The ravens brought him bread and meat each day, in the morning and in the evening, and he drank from the brook.

Elijah, a prophet of God, had announced a drought to King Ahab. God commanded him to hide by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan. God himself gives the order and promises the food. Elijah obeyed. The text does not explain how the ravens did it; it only states that God sent them.

For today: God often cares for us day by day, not all at once. Trust his provision for today and obey him even when you do not understand the whole plan. Notice also that the brook later dried up: sometimes God changes the way he sustains us, but he continues to care for us.
exp.21:50:
Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem, the city of David. "He slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died. His son Jehoram took the throne.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, closing the summary of Jehoshaphat's reign. Just before this, he tells how his ships were wrecked and how he refused an alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel. Then the account turns to Ahaziah, who followed the wicked ways of his family. The contrast shows two ways of ruling. The exact reasons Jehoshaphat refused are not explained here, and other biblical texts add details.

For today: our life is brief, and others will continue what we leave behind. It is worth thinking about what we are sowing in our family, and asking God for wisdom to choose well those with whom we join ourselves.
exp.7:57:
Here Solomon asks that God himself would turn his people's hearts toward him. The desire is that they would live according to his ways and keep the commandments, statutes, and ordinances he gave their fathers. "Statutes" are the rules he set down, and "ordinances" are his fair decisions or rulings. "Walk" means to live, to conduct oneself day by day.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has just blessed the people and reminded them that God kept the promises he made through Moses. Now he prays that Israel would respond with faithfulness, and that God would not abandon them.

For today: it is not enough to resolve to obey; we also need to ask God to change our desires. We can pray each morning, "Lord, turn my heart toward yours," and then take one concrete step of obedience that day.
exp.6:5:
Solomon built a colonnade fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so the structure was about 25 by 15 meters. The verse calls it "his colonnade," so it is the one described, and it stood in front of another building with its own pillars and a canopy.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. He describes the buildings Solomon constructed after the temple, such as his palace. With so many details, the author shows the splendor of his kingdom. It is not known for certain what exactly this colonnade was used for, and scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: Solomon spent seven years on the temple and thirteen on his own house. We can ask ourselves whether we give God first place and our best effort, or whether we leave him for later, after our own goals.
exp.10:37:
God tells Jeroboam that if he listens closely to everything God commands him, walks in God's ways, does what is right in God's sight, and keeps God's statutes and commandments as David did, God will be with him. The "sure house" God promises means a lasting family of kings, a dynasty that will endure. God also says he will give Israel to Jeroboam.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ahijah. Solomon had turned away from the Lord, and for that reason God decided to divide the kingdom. He promises Jeroboam ten tribes, but on one condition: that he be faithful. When Solomon learned of this, he wanted to kill Jeroboam, and Jeroboam fled to Egypt. The text does not say here how Jeroboam's story would end, but the promise depended on his obedience.

For today: the gifts and opportunities God gives do not replace obedience. If you have responsibility, work, or influence today, ask God for a faithful heart to care for what has been entrusted to you, day after day.
exp.20:3:
This verse tells how Ahab went home upset and sulking. Naboth had told him, "I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers." Then Ahab lay down on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat.

The narrator describes King Ahab's reaction. He wanted Naboth's vineyard so he could make a garden. Naboth refused out of loyalty to God, since the law of Moses protected family land in Israel (Leviticus 25:23). Ahab, though he was king, did not respect that limit and let his displeasure take control of him.

For today: when someone tells us "no," we can choose between becoming bitter or accepting the limit with humility. Desires that seem small, if we feed them, can lead us to worse things. Let us ask God for a grateful and contented heart.
exp.17:25:
The prophets of Baal took the bull that was given to them and prepared it. From morning until noon they called on the name of Baal, shouting, "O Baal, answer us!" But there was no sound, and no one answered. Meanwhile, they leaped around the altar they had made.

The account shows us Elijah's challenge on Mount Carmel. Israel was divided between the LORD and Baal. Elijah proposed a test: the God who answered with fire would be the true one. The people agreed, and the prophets of Baal went first, since there were many of them.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts: money, success, approval. In the end, what cannot answer cannot save us either. God does hear those who seek him sincerely.
exp.16:4:
He says Elijah obeyed God without arguing. He went and stayed by the Brook of Cherith, east of the Jordan.

The context: God had told Elijah to hide himself, because he had announced to King Ahab that there would be a drought. Ahab and his kingdom had turned away from God, and Elijah was in danger. God promised him water from the brook and food brought by ravens. It is not known with certainty where Cherith was; several places have been proposed.

For today: sometimes God asks us to take a step without showing us the whole path. Obeying today, trusting that He provides what is needed for today, is an act of simple and steady faith.
exp.19:42:
This verse says that King Ahab returned to his palace in Samaria with his spirit crushed and irritated. The verse tells us he went home "sullen and angry," so the reader can see that mood for themselves. Ahab does not repent; he simply goes away in a bad temper.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Earlier, Ahab had let go Ben-hadad, king of Syria, whom God had handed into his hands and who was under the ban, that is, under a sentence of destruction. A prophet in disguise, with a bandage over his eyes, presented a case so that Ahab himself would pronounce judgment on himself. When he removed the cloth from his eyes, he announced God's judgment. This verse shows Ahab's reaction.

For today: when correction makes us uncomfortable, we can either harden ourselves or humble ourselves. Let us ask God for a heart willing to listen, to acknowledge the mistake, and to obey, instead of remaining only with anger.
exp.0:20:
If King David dies without making clear who will be the next king, Bathsheba and her son Solomon will be treated as criminals. The phrase "rests with his fathers" is a way of saying "dies." Being counted as criminals would mean they would be seen as traitors or enemies, and could be punished.

Bathsheba speaks before King David, who is now old. Adonijah, another son of David, had declared himself king on his own and had not invited Solomon. Bathsheba reminds David of his promise and asks him to decide. She fears for her life and for her son's. Soon the prophet Nathan arrives to support her request.

For today: when there is injustice or danger, do not stay silent out of fear. Speak with respect and clarity to the one who has authority to help, and trust that God can use your words to protect others.
exp.7:20:
Solomon says that in the temple he has provided a place for the ark. Inside the ark was the covenant of the LORD, that is, the tablets of the law that God gave to Israel when he brought them out of Egypt. The verse calls God "the LORD," and a covenant is a solemn agreement between God and his people.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple, before all Israel. He has just recalled that God kept his promise to David: David's son would build the house. Now Solomon points out that the temple is not only a building, but the place where the symbol of God's faithfulness was kept. Soon he will pray, praising God because he keeps his covenant.

For today: God does what he promises, even when it takes years. You can write down the promises of God that you have already seen fulfilled and thank him for them, so that you trust him when you are still waiting for something.
exp.19:26:
The Israelites also got ready for battle. They gathered their fighting men, collected supplies, and marched out to meet the enemy. They set up camp facing the Syrians. The verse says Israel camped "like two small flocks of goats," which means Israel looked like a very small force beside them. The Arameans, by contrast, covered the countryside, spreading across all the land around.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings. A year earlier, Israel had defeated Ben-hadad, king of Aram, and his advisers suggested he raise another army and fight on open ground. Now they return with a huge force, and Israel seems to be at a clear disadvantage. Then a prophet announces that God will give the victory.

For today: when you feel small in front of a huge problem, remember that the outcome does not depend only on your own strength. Do what is yours to do, and trust God.
exp.3:9:
This verse mentions one of the twelve governors whom King Solomon appointed over Israel. Ben-Hesed was in charge of the region of Arubboth, and also of Socoh and all the land of Hepher. The verse says these places "belonged to him," meaning that this territory was his to govern.

The writer of the book describes how Solomon organized his kingdom. Each governor had to provide supplies for the king and his household for one month of the year. This list of names and places shows an orderly government. It is not known for certain where each place was, and about this governor we are told only that he was the son of Hesed.

God uses ordinary people, sometimes almost unknown ones, to sustain important things. Today, your faithful and steady work, even when no one notices it, also has value. Do well what you have been entrusted with, as for the Lord.
exp.15:28:
This verse says that Ahab, son of Omri, became king of Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa's reign over Judah. The phrase "became king" means that he took the throne. In this way the writer places Ahab in time by comparing his reign with that of the neighboring kingdom to the south.

The author of the book of Kings (no one knows for certain who he was) tells the story of the kings of Israel and of Judah. Here he has just reported the death of Omri and now introduces his son. This detail seems simple, but it brings in one of the worst kings of Israel, as the following verses show.

God sees beyond titles and dates. Leaders leave a mark through their decisions, for good or for evil. Today we can pray for those who govern us and take care of our own influence in the family and at work, choosing to walk with God.
exp.19:27:
A prophet, called "man of God," comes to the king of Israel with a message from the LORD. The Arameans had said that the LORD was a god of the hills and not of the valleys. So God promises to hand that enormous army over to the king, so that you will know that I am the LORD. Arameans refers to the people of Aram, and the great army refers to their huge force.

The king of Aram, Ben-hadad, had already attacked Israel the year before and lost. His advisers believed that Israel's God was a god of the mountains, so now he wanted to fight on the plain. The prophet is not named here. He speaks in God's name to the king of Israel, who is Ahab, according to the context of the chapter. God acts to defend his own name, not only for Israel's sake.

God is not small or limited to a place or situation. If today you feel you are in a difficult "valley," remember that God is also there and can act.
exp.19:10:
This verse says the king of Israel sends an answer to Ben-hadad: "The one putting on his armor should not boast like one taking it off." The image in the verse is of a soldier putting on armor before the battle, compared with a soldier taking it off after the battle is over. Putting on the armor means preparing to fight. Taking it off means the fight has already been won.

It is King Ahab who speaks. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, threatened him with a great army and boasted that Samaria would be destroyed.
