Ahab had already given in to other demands, but he did not accept the last one. With this saying he replies that the other should not celebrate victory before the fight. Shortly afterward, a prophet announces that God would grant the victory.

For today: do not boast of a triumph that has not yet arrived, and do not let yourself be frightened by the threats of others. Trust in God, do your part with humility, and wait for his outcome.
exp.14:33:
This verse says that Baasha, king of Israel, did evil in the sight of the LORD. He walked in the path of Jeroboam and continued in the sin that Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit.

Context: there is no character speaking here; this is the writer of Kings, who judges each king by how faithfully he followed God. Jeroboam had led Israel to worship golden calves (1 Kings 12:28-30), and Baasha did not turn away from that. Although he reigned 24 years, the writer sums up his life with this judgment.

For today: what we do influences others. We can ask ourselves what habits or examples we are repeating, and whether they lead others toward God or away from Him. Today we can choose a different path with his help.
exp.5:26:
This verse describes how Solomon placed two huge cherubim in the innermost room of the temple. Their outspread wings reached from wall to wall: the wing of the first cherub touched one wall, the wing of the second touched the other, and their wingtips met in the middle of the room. In this way the space was covered from one end to the other.

Here no character is speaking; this is the author's account of building the temple in Jerusalem. The cherubim stood beside the ark of the covenant, where God was understood to be present. We do not know for certain what they looked like, but the Bible presents them as beings who serve and guard the holiness of God.

For today: God deserves a place of reverence in our lives. We can set aside a quiet moment each day to pray with respect and gratitude, remembering that God is holy, yet near to those who seek him.
exp.21:15:
Here King Ahab presses the prophet Micaiah: "How many times must I make you swear to tell me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?" Ahab is demanding that Micaiah speak solemnly and honestly.

Ahab and King Jehoshaphat of Judah wanted to know whether they should attack Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets had already promised victory. Micaiah told them the same thing, but probably with a mocking or sarcastic tone, and Ahab noticed it. That is why he demands the truth. Many think Micaiah's tone showed that he did not speak in earnest, although the text does not say so in so many words.

For today: sometimes we ask for advice, but deep down we only want to hear what pleases us. Let us ask God and sincere people for the truth, and be willing to receive it, even when it hurts.
exp.5:4:
Solomon built rooms against the walls of the temple, arranged all the way around it, surrounding both the main hall and the inner sanctuary. The word "chambers" here means side rooms or spaces built against the outer walls, and the phrase "all around" means they ran along every side. The inner sanctuary is the most holy place, the innermost part of the temple, where the ark of the covenant was kept.

The verse is part of the historical account of building the temple in Jerusalem. It is the narrator who describes this, not God or a prophet speaking directly. The verses that follow explain that these rooms were arranged in three levels. Scholars are not certain what the rooms were used for; many think they stored objects and offerings belonging to the temple, but the text does not say.

For today: God cares about order and about the details of what is done for him. We can serve him with care and patience, even in tasks no one sees, such as storing, arranging, or preparing, trusting that all of this supports what is seen.
exp.7:8:
Inside the ark of the covenant there was nothing except the two stone tablets, the ten commandments. Moses had placed them there at Horeb, which is Mount Sinai, where the LORD made a covenant with Israel after they had come out of Egypt.

The narrator of the book describes the dedication of the temple that Solomon built. The priests had just brought the ark into the most holy place. Noting that only the tablets were inside recalls that the temple was built around God's covenant. Hebrews 9:4 mentions other objects that were once kept near the ark, but here the account focuses on the essentials.

For today: the most important part of our faith is not a building, but our relationship with God and his word. Ask yourself what place you give his word at the center of your daily life.
exp.20:17:
God tells the prophet Elijah to get up and go meet Ahab, king of Israel, who is in Samaria. He warns him that Ahab is in Naboth's vineyard, where he has gone to take possession of it.

The Lord speaks to Elijah. Ahab had allowed his wife Jezebel to have Naboth put to death through false accusations, because Naboth would not sell him his vineyard. Now Ahab is going to take it for himself. God does not stay silent in the face of this injustice, and he sends his prophet to confront the king.

For today: God sees what is done in secret, even when someone powerful manages to hide it. We should not take advantage of others or stay silent in the face of injustice. Let us ask God for an honest heart and the courage to speak the truth.
exp.15:31:
It says that King Ahab built a temple for Baal in Samaria, the capital of Israel, and set up an altar inside it for offering sacrifices to him. The verse says that Ahab set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria. Baal was the god of the Canaanites, to whom rain and harvests were attributed.

The one speaking here is not a character but the author of the book of Kings, who is recounting the history of the kings of Israel. He wants to show that Ahab went further than the kings before him in his sin. His wife Jezebel, daughter of a king of Sidon, had great influence in this. Ahab not only tolerated idolatry but made it official in the kingdom.

For today: what we build with our time, money and energy reveals whom we serve. Ask yourself honestly what things are taking the place of God in your life, and ask him for help to put him first again.
exp.19:29:
The rest of the Syrian soldiers who survived fled into the city of Aphek. There the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of the remaining men. King Ben-hadad also fled into the city and hid in an inner room, looking for a place to take cover.

This is the account of the narrator of Kings. The Syrians had said that the LORD was a god of the hills and not of the valleys. A prophet had told the king of Israel that God would give them the victory so that they would know that he is the LORD. That word was fulfilled. The text does not explain how the wall fell; it is presented as part of the defeat that God allowed.

For today: God is not limited to any place or circumstance. When you feel that your situation is too hard for him, remember that his power reaches every place. Trust him with humility.
exp.7:14:
Solomon begins with praise: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel." He is giving thanks to God. He notes that God spoke with his own mouth to his father David, and that God has now fulfilled that promise with his own hand, by his own power. The verse ends with "saying," and Solomon goes on to repeat the promise God made.

Solomon is speaking at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has turned to face the assembled people of Israel and is blessing them. Earlier, he prayed toward the finished temple. Now he recognizes that this work is not something he earned, but the fulfillment of what God had promised to David.

For today: when God fulfills something in your life, take a moment to thank him in a concrete way. You can also remember the promises God makes in the Bible and trust that he is faithful, even when fulfillment takes a long time.
exp.19:22:
The king of Aram's advisers explain to him why they lost to Israel: they believe the God of Israel is a god of the hills and has power only there. So they propose fighting on the plains, where they think they will win.

The Arameans had just been defeated near Samaria, an area of hills. Instead of recognizing the power of God, they look for an explanation based on their own way of thinking, which saw gods as tied to particular places. Later, a prophet will say that God would act again so that they would know that he is the Lord (v. 28).

For today: let us not confine God to our small ideas. He is not only with us in the high moments of life, but also in the valleys and difficulties. Trust that his power reaches every place where you are.
exp.2:23:
Here King Solomon asks for a sword, and his servants bring him one right away. The verse is simply a command and its fulfillment, with nothing more to add.

Two women are arguing before the king. Each one says the living child is hers, and that the dead child belongs to the other. Solomon, to whom God had just given wisdom, asks for the sword to bring out what is in the heart of each woman. Scholars agree that it was a test, although the text does not say what Solomon really intended to do.

For today: wisdom does not rush to judge by words alone. Before deciding in a conflict, let us ask God for discernment to see the motives of the heart, and let us listen patiently to everyone.
exp.9:22:
This verse says that King Solomon was greater than all the other kings of the known world, both in his wealth and possessions and in his wisdom. The word "surpassed" means that he went beyond them or stood above them.

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of Israel and here sums up the splendor of Solomon's reign. Just before this, he speaks of Solomon's gold, of his ships that brought riches from Tarshish (a distant place whose exact location is debated), and of his luxuries. Afterward he explains that people came to hear him because God had given him that wisdom. In this way the text presents his greatness as a gift from God.

For today: everything good we have, such as talent, work, or money, comes from God. We can receive it with gratitude and use it to serve others, without boasting or trusting in it more than in Him.
exp.1:2:
Here David tells his son Solomon to faithfully carry out what God asks. Keeping the charge means obeying what God has commanded. The statutes, commandments, ordinances and decrees are different ways of naming the laws and teachings of God. The phrase "so that you may prosper" means that things will go well for you, and "wherever you turn" means wherever you direct your steps.

David is about to die and gives his final advice to Solomon, who will be the new king. He asks him to be strong and to obey the law of Moses. According to the next verse, this is connected to God's promise that his family would continue to reign if they walked faithfully with God.

Today we can learn that a well-directed life begins when we take God's Word seriously. You could read a passage each day and ask God for help to put one specific teaching into practice in your decisions, your work and your family.
exp.21:3:
What it says: Ahab, king of Israel, asks Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, whether he will go with him to fight against Ramoth-gilead, a city Ahab wanted to take back. Jehoshaphat answers yes, and firmly: "I am as you are, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses." He puts his people and his horses at Ahab's disposal, that is, his army.

Context: Two allied kings are speaking. Ahab wanted to recover a city that was in the hands of Syria. Jehoshaphat was a king who sought God, but here he commits himself before asking the LORD for guidance. That is why, in the next verse, he asks Ahab to first seek the word of the LORD.

For today: It is good to be loyal and generous with others, but it is wise to ask God for direction before we commit ourselves. Before saying "yes" to an alliance, a business deal or a project, let us pray and seek his guidance in the Bible.
exp.5:12:
God promises that he will live among the Israelites and that he will not abandon his people. The wording is clear: "live" describes his presence, and "abandon" describes what he refuses to do. It is a promise of closeness and faithfulness.

God himself speaks here, addressing Solomon while he builds the temple. Just before this verse, God tells him that his promise to David will be fulfilled if Solomon obeys his commands. So the promise of his presence is tied to a call to live faithfully. Some understand that the building alone was not enough; what mattered was obedience of the heart.

For today: God wants to be near you, not only in special places. Today you can respond to him with simple obedience, such as praying, forgiving, or acting honestly, trusting that he will not abandon you.
exp.0:23:
Nathan comes before King David and asks him a direct question: did David say that Adonijah would reign after him and sit on his throne? "My lord the king" is a respectful way of addressing the king. "Adonijah will reign after me" means that he would be the one to succeed David.

David is now very old and weak. Nathan, a prophet of God, speaks together with Bathsheba. Adonijah has proclaimed himself king on his own, without David's permission. Nathan does not accuse suddenly, but asks so that David will react and act. The Bible does not say that Nathan doubted David; the question serves to show him what is happening.

For today: when you see an injustice or a deception, do not stay silent. Speak with respect, with clarity and at the right time, especially if it depends on you that someone with authority knows the truth.
exp.7:38:
It says that God hears from heaven, the place where he dwells. Solomon asks him to forgive, to act, and to repay each person according to all their ways. God can do this with justice because he knows each person's heart, and only he knows the hearts of all people completely. The word "since" in this verse presents God's knowledge of the heart as the reason he is able to judge fairly, and "repay" means God will respond to each person as their ways deserve.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple. He is praying for the people in times of famine, plague, or war, when someone feels the pain or guilt of their own heart. He asks that God hear the prayers directed toward that house.

Today, you can pray honestly, without pretending or hiding anything. God already knows your heart, so you can come to him with confidence, acknowledge your need, and ask for his forgiveness and help.
exp.8:11:
This verse tells that Hiram, the king of Tyre, went out from his city to inspect the twenty towns that Solomon had given him in Galilee. When he saw them, he was not pleased. He was not happy with them and thought they were of little value.

Here the narrator tells what happened after twenty years of building. Hiram had helped Solomon with cedar wood, cypress and gold for the temple and the palace. Solomon gave him those towns as payment or as a gift. The text does not explain in detail why Hiram was disappointed. Some think the land was not very fertile; others think the deal was not equal to what he had contributed. This is an interpretation, not a certain fact.

For today: when someone helps us, it is good to give thanks generously and fairly, not offering the bare minimum. And if we feel disappointed, it is better to speak frankly and respectfully, as Hiram did when he addressed Solomon as "brother."
exp.13:8:
God tells Jeroboam that he has done more evil than all the kings who came before him. He made for himself other gods and idols of metal, and so provoked God to anger. The phrase "flung Me behind your back" means that Jeroboam ignored God and turned away from him on purpose.

The prophet Ahijah, sent by God, speaks to Jeroboam's wife, who came in disguise to ask about their sick son. God had made Jeroboam king, but he set up golden calves so that the people would not go up to worship in Jerusalem. That is why judgment comes upon his house.

For today: God deserves first place, not last. We can ask ourselves what things, such as money, fear, or pride, have taken his place, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.21:19:
In a vision, God asks the heavenly beings who will entice Ahab to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead, where he will die. The word "entice" here means to draw someone on, to lead them to do something by persuasion. The beings of heaven offered different ideas: one suggested one plan, and another suggested something else.

The prophet Micaiah speaks, telling what he saw before Ahab and Jehoshaphat. Ahab wanted Micaiah to give him good news, but Micaiah announces judgment. The scene is a picture of God's throne and shows that God governs even the decisions of the king. Scholars explain in different ways how to understand the lying spirit, and it is wise to read it carefully.

For today: do not seek only voices that tell you what you want to hear. Ask God for humility to listen to the truth, even when it hurts, and always compare it with his Word.
exp.6:27:
This verse begins to describe how the ten bronze stands were made. They were like small carts or bases used to hold large basins. The verse says they had side panels attached to uprights, meaning flat boards fixed to upright supports that framed them.

This is not a character speaking; it is the account of the writer of Kings about the building of Solomon's temple. So much detail is given because the temple was the place where Israel drew near to God, and for the narrator every piece mattered. Some technical details of these pieces are not entirely clear, and scholars interpret them in various ways.

For today: God cares about what is done with care and dedication. We can serve him with excellence in small, unseen tasks, doing our daily work as something offered to him.
exp.18:13:
Elijah answers God that he has felt a very great zeal for Him. The phrase "I have been very zealous" in the verse means: "I have been very passionate for the LORD." He says that the Israelites have forsaken God's covenant, torn down his altars, and killed his prophets with the sword. He feels alone, and believes they now want to kill him too.

Elijah, a prophet of the kingdom of Israel, speaks here. He fled from Queen Jezebel and came to Mount Horeb, tired and afraid. God had just spoken to him in a still, small voice, and asks him: "What are you doing here?" Elijah repeats his complaint. God does not scold him; He sends him back to his mission and gives him Elisha as a companion and successor.

When you feel alone and worn out, honestly tell God what you feel. He listens to you with tenderness, and often reminds you that you are not alone and gives you new steps and people to walk with you.
exp.17:15:
Obadiah did what Elijah had asked him to do: he went to tell King Ahab that Elijah was there. Then Ahab went out to meet the prophet. The wording is easy to follow: "went to inform" means he went to tell the king the news, and Ahab's going to meet Elijah follows right after.

The narrator tells this moment after three years of drought. Obadiah, an official of Ahab who feared God, was afraid the king would kill him if Elijah disappeared again. Elijah had sworn, in the name of the God he serves, that he would appear that very day. So Obadiah took courage to bring the message, and the meeting between the king and the prophet was set in motion.

For today: faithfulness sometimes calls for a step that feels frightening. Obadiah trusted Elijah's promise and obeyed. When God asks us to do something hard, we can move forward with confidence, knowing that He keeps His word.
exp.15:17:
Zimri saw that the city of Tirzah had been captured. Then he entered the citadel of the royal palace, burned it down upon himself, and so he died. The text says he burned the palace down, meaning he set the fire himself. Some understand the palace to refer to a tower or fortress within the king's house.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Zimri had killed King Elah and seized the throne, but the army proclaimed Omri king. Zimri reigned only seven days. The text that follows says his end came because of his sins, since he followed the evil way of Jeroboam.

For today: power taken by violence and without God does not last. Instead of seeking success at any cost, let us strive to live with honesty and trust that God guides our path.
exp.7:34:
This verse is part of a prayer asking God to hear his people when they go through a drought. It says that if the skies are shut and there is no rain because the people have sinned, and they pray toward the temple, confess God's name, and turn from their sins, then God will hear them. The phrase "because You have afflicted them" shows that the drought is understood as God's correction.

King Solomon speaks this during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. Before all Israel, he asks that God answer the prayers offered in that place. The law of Moses already warned that the lack of rain could be the result of disobedience. Here Solomon does not speak of punishment without a way out, but of an open door to repentance.

Today, when we face a crisis, we can pause to examine our hearts. If there is something to put right, let us come to God with sincerity, for He receives whoever turns back to Him.
exp.16:10:
Here Elijah, the prophet, asks something more of a widow. She was already going to get him a little water, and he calls to her again: "Please bring me a piece of bread." The meaning is simply that he asked for a small piece of bread.

Elijah speaks by God's command, who sent him to Zarephath, where a widow would sustain him. It was a time of famine and drought. What follows shows that she had almost no food left. His request is a test of faith, and God promises to care for her (v. 14). Some scholars stress how difficult this request was; the text only shows that she was poor and desperate.

For today: sometimes God invites us to trust and to give even when we have little. We can take a small step of obedience, believing that He is faithful to care for us.
exp.7:3:
Here it is told that the ark of the Lord, the Tent of Meeting, and all its sacred furnishings were moved into the new temple. It was the priests and the Levites who carried them.

The narrator of the book of Kings recounts the dedication of the temple that Solomon built. All Israel was gathered, and the ark, a symbol of God's presence, was to take its place. It is not known with certainty which tent is meant: some think of the one David set up in Jerusalem, others of the older one from Moses' time.

God deserves to be treated with respect and order. Today we can serve him with seriousness and care: pray with reverence, value his Word, and faithfully carry out what is entrusted to us in the church.
exp.4:7:
Hiram, king of Tyre, sends back his reply to Solomon. He tells Solomon that he has received his message and that he will do everything Solomon asks regarding the timber.

The reply in your verse speaks of cedar and cypress timber. Some scholars think the word translated cypress may refer to pine or another fine wood, and there is no complete certainty about it.

The one speaking is Hiram, a Phoenician king who had enjoyed a good relationship with David. Solomon was preparing to build the temple and needed cedars from Lebanon. Hiram rejoices and blesses the LORD for David's wise son. His answer opens an agreement: he provides the timber, and Solomon provides food for his household.

For today: a kind and willing response helps great works get done. We can cooperate with others, even with people unlike ourselves, and recognize God in the good we see, as Hiram did.
exp.7:46:
If Israel's people are carried off as captives to another land because of their sins, and there they come to their senses, that is, they recognize their wrong, turn back to God, and plead with Him, God will hear them. The prayer names three confessions: "we have sinned," "we have done wrong," and "we have acted wickedly." "Wickedness" means living without reverence for God. "Repent" means to turn back to God.

King Solomon speaks in the prayer he offers when he dedicates the temple in Jerusalem. He asks God that, if the people should sin and be taken away into exile, God would not abandon them but would hear their plea. This is said before the exile happens, as a request for mercy. Later, the history of Israel shows that the exile did come.

For today: when you realize you have failed, do not hide from God. Honestly acknowledge what you did, without excuses, and return to Him. Even when you feel far away, God remains ready to hear you.
exp.3:20:
This verse says that Solomon ruled over many kingdoms, from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt. The text says he ruled over all the kingdoms in that whole region. The word for "ruled" means that he held authority and commanded them, and the word for what they gave him means tribute, the payments those peoples made to him. They paid him and served him for as long as he lived.

Here the narrator describes the splendor of Solomon's reign. It comes right after saying that Judah and Israel were very numerous and lived in contentment. The text shows how God's promises to Abraham about a wide land and a great people were being fulfilled. The details about his fame and power prepare what follows.

For today: when God gives us peace, success, or influence, it is a blessing that we should guard with humility and gratitude. Let us remember that later Solomon became spiritually careless, so what matters is staying faithful to God, not only enjoying what we have.
exp.8:26:
He says that Hiram, king of Tyre, sent his servants to serve in the fleet with Solomon's servants. They were sailors who knew the sea, men with a great deal of experience sailing. They worked alongside Solomon's servants.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, recounting Solomon's reign. After finishing the temple, Solomon pursued other projects, such as a fleet at Ezion-geber, beside the Red Sea. Israel did not have a long seafaring tradition, so Hiram, its ally, supplied crew members with experience. The text that follows says they went to Ophir, a place whose exact location is not known for certain.

For today: no project is done alone. Recognizing what we do not know and accepting the help of capable people is wisdom. God often blesses teamwork and the humility to learn from others.
exp.21:14:
Micaiah comes before King Ahab, who asks him whether they should go up to fight against Ramoth-gilead or hold back. Micaiah replies: "Go up and triumph, for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king." The word "triumph" here means that things will go well for them.

The one who speaks first is Ahab, king of Israel, who is looking for an opinion. Earlier, four hundred prophets had promised him victory, and a messenger pressed Micaiah to say the same thing. Micaiah had sworn to say only what God gave him. So the king immediately demands the truth from him. Many understand that Micaiah spoke with irony, mockingly repeating what everyone was saying, but the text does not clearly indicate the tone.

Today: do not seek out only voices that tell you what you want to hear. Ask God for the courage to listen to the truth, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.1:15:
Adonijah tells Bathsheba that he has one request to make of her. He asks her not to refuse him. She answers, "State your request," meaning that she is ready to listen.

Adonijah was the older brother of Solomon, and he had wanted to be king. Now he speaks with the mother of the new king. He acknowledges that God gave the kingdom to Solomon, but his request, to marry Abishag, hides a dangerous motive. Many believe he was seeking to get closer to the throne, and for that reason Solomon took it as a threat. The text does not reveal with certainty all his intentions.

For today: before asking someone for a favor, examine your motives. Asking with kind words is not enough; God looks at the heart. Let us always seek with sincerity and without hidden agendas.
exp.14:16:
Baasha, king of the northern kingdom of Israel, went to war against Judah, the southern kingdom, and fortified the town of Ramah. His goal was to block the roads: no one could leave or enter the territory of King Asa.

This is the narrator's account of the book, describing the ongoing conflict between these two divided kingdoms. Ramah was very close to Jerusalem, so Baasha wanted to cut off Judah's trade and put pressure on it. This sets up Asa's response, which was not to seek God but to pay a foreign king to help him.

When we feel cornered, it is easy to look for quick, human solutions. This passage invites us to stop first, pray, and ask God for direction before making desperate decisions, trusting that He can open paths where others close them.
exp.10:29:
This verse tells that the prophet Ahijah took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces. The word "took hold" means grabbed, and the word "tore" means ripped apart.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Solomon had turned away from God, and God had announced that he would divide the kingdom. Ahijah meets alone with Jeroboam, a young worker whom Solomon had placed in charge of building projects and workers. The torn cloak is a symbolic act: the twelve pieces stand for the twelve tribes of Israel, and God uses it to show what is going to happen.

For today: God sees our decisions and speaks with clarity. When we receive responsibility or success, it is good to remain faithful and humble, because God's promises do not replace obedience.
exp.0:51:
Solomon answers Adonijah's plea with a condition. "Character" means a man who is good, honest, and loyal. If Adonijah shows himself to be this kind of man, not a single hair of his head will fall to the ground; in other words, no one will harm him. But if evil is found in him, he will die.

King Solomon speaks. Adonijah had tried to make himself king, although God and David had chosen Solomon. Now he was afraid and clung to the altar, seeking refuge. Solomon does not condemn him at once, but he also does not grant him freedom without conditions: he offers mercy on probation. Afterward, he sends him home.

For today: mercy is not naivety. We can forgive and give a new opportunity, but we also expect real change. And when we have failed, God invites us to return in humility and to live with integrity.
exp.13:5:
Ahijah, although he was blind, knew who was coming as soon as he heard her footsteps at the door. He greeted her as the wife of Jeroboam and asked her why she was disguised. The "bad news" is a hard message of judgment that God had sent him to deliver.

Jeroboam was the king of Israel, and his son was sick. He sent his wife in disguise to Shiloh to consult the prophet, perhaps so that no one would recognize her. But God had already told Ahijah beforehand, and so the disguise was of no use.

For today: we cannot hide anything from God, whether behind disguises or religious appearances. It is better to come to Him honestly, just as we are, and to be willing to hear even what is hard to hear, trusting that He corrects in order to heal.
exp.7:65:
On the fifteenth day, when the feast was over, Solomon sent the people away. They blessed the king and went home glad and joyful in heart. They were thankful for all the good things the LORD had done for His servant David and for His people Israel. The verse says "home," so no note is needed about older words for dwellings or tents. "Sent away" means that Solomon sent them back to their own homes.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings, who describes how the dedication of the temple came to an end. There were two weeks of celebration, with sacrifices and offerings made before God. The exact date is explained in different ways by scholars, since the parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 7:10 gives the twenty-third day of the month. The central point is that the people went home thankful.

For today: after worshiping, we can return home remembering what God has done. A grateful life turns everyday moments into praise. Today, write down three blessings and thank God for them.
exp.19:2:
Ben-hadad, king of Syria, sends word to Ahab that everything of value in his city belongs to him: his silver and gold, his best wives, and his best children. The words "Your silver and gold are mine" and "your best wives and children are mine" show that he demands total surrender.

Ben-hadad speaks through messengers while he has Samaria under siege with a great army and thirty-two allied kings. Ahab, afraid, answers that he submits. This demand is a pressure meant to humiliate him and break his will before any fighting. Later the passage shows that God intervened on Israel's behalf, although Ahab was a very questionable king.

For today: there are voices that demand everything from us with threats and fear. Before giving in, it is wise to stop, pray, and remember that our life belongs to God, not to the one who tries to dominate us.
exp.21:51:
This verse says that Ahaziah, son of King Ahab, began to rule over Israel from Samaria, his capital. This happened in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat's reign in Judah, and Ahaziah reigned only two years. The phrase "began to reign" means that he became king.

The narrator of the book of Kings presents here the start of a new reign, placing it in relation to the king of Judah. In this way he situates the reader within the history of the two kingdoms. What follows shows that Ahaziah followed in the ways of his father and mother, Ahab and Jezebel, serving Baal and provoking the Lord to anger, and also walked in the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin. The account emphasizes that his short life as king was marked by that evil path.

For today: children often repeat what they see at home, for good or for ill. We can ask ourselves what example we are setting and which inherited habits we need to surrender to God so that we may walk in a different direction.
exp.13:7:
God tells Jeroboam that he was the one who tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to him. But Jeroboam was not like David, who kept God's commandments, followed him with all his heart, and did only what was right in God's eyes. David was the standard of faithful devotion that Jeroboam failed to meet.

God speaks through the prophet Ahijah, who was already old and could no longer see. Jeroboam's wife came in disguise to ask about their sick son. God makes it clear that he knows who she is and delivers a harsh message: Jeroboam received a great privilege, but he answered it with idolatry. God measures Jeroboam's faithfulness against that of David, although David also failed and repented.

For today: what God entrusts to us is a responsibility, not an excuse to drift away from him. We can ask ourselves whether the blessings we have draw us closer to God or make us forget him. And when we fail, let us return to him with sincerity.
exp.14:31:
This verse says there was war between Asa, king of Judah, and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout the whole time that both of them reigned. In other words, it was not a single battle but a conflict that lasted for years. The phrase "throughout their days" refers to the length of their reigns.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing the history of the two kingdoms. After the death of Solomon, the people were divided into two kingdoms: Judah in the south and Israel in the north. The nearby verses show that Baasha followed the evil path of Jeroboam, and the text presents that division as a constant wound between brothers.

For today: when there is division, resentment can last for years and wear everyone down. We can ask God for help in seeking peace, take the first step toward reconciliation, and not feed old conflicts in the family or in the church.
exp.9:14:
This verse continues to speak of Solomon's riches. It says that, in addition to the 666 talents of gold he received each year, he also received revenue from the merchants, the traders, all the kings of Arabia, and the governors of the land.

Here the narrator of the book presents the greatness of Solomon's reign. It comes after the visit of the queen of Sheba and before the list of gold objects. Some understand that the "kings of Arabia" were allied chiefs or rulers who paid tribute or traded with him, although the text gives no further details.

For today: wealth can be a blessing, but it can also be a test. Let us ask God for wisdom to receive and use what we have with humility, generosity and gratitude, without placing our security in it.
exp.16:13:
Here Elijah tells the widow what God has promised. The large jar that holds the flour and the small jug that holds the oil are the containers in view. "Will not be exhausted" and "will not run dry" mean the supply will not run out. The face of the earth is the surface of the ground. The promise lasts until the LORD sends rain again.

Elijah, a prophet of God, speaks with a widow in Zarephath during a very severe drought. She has only a little flour and oil, and she plans to prepare one last meal for herself and her son before they die. Elijah asks her to first make him a small cake, but he gives her God's promise so that she does not have to be afraid.

For today: when you feel that what you have is not enough, take the next step of obedience with the little you have, trusting that God keeps his word and cares for you day by day.
exp.6:2:
It says that the roof of the House of the Forest of Lebanon was roofed with cedar, laid above the beams. Those beams rested on the pillars, forty-five beams in all, fifteen to each row. The phrase "above the beams" means on the upper part, above the structure that held up the roof.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing in detail the works of Solomon. After the temple, Solomon built his palace and other buildings. There are doubts about exactly what this building was like, since the text mentions four orders of columns and then three rows of fifteen. Scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: the text invites us to review our priorities. Solomon took seven years on the temple and thirteen on his house. Ask yourself whether you give God first place and your best effort, not just what is left over.
exp.7:22:
Solomon praises the Lord by saying that there is no God like him, either in heaven above or on earth below. He says that the Lord keeps his covenant, that is, his promises, and shows loving devotion to his servants, those who walk before him with all their hearts. The phrase "walk before" means living in a way that pleases God.

The king, Solomon, is speaking during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He stands before the altar, with his hands stretched out toward heaven, in front of all the people. Before he asks for anything, he remembers that God has been faithful to his people and to his father David. This is how his prayer begins.

For today: before you ask God for things, take a moment to remember how he has been faithful to you. That strengthens trust. Then seek to love him sincerely, not only in words, but with a whole heart lived out in everyday life.
exp.9:10:
This verse says that Hiram's fleet, the ships that brought gold from Ophir, also brought back a great cargo of almug wood and precious stones. The word "almug" is a Hebrew term, and it is not known for certain which tree it refers to. Some suggest sandalwood, but that is only a guess.

The narrator of Kings describes Solomon's wealth right after the visit of the queen of Sheba. She recognized that God had set Solomon as king to bring about justice. The text shows the abundance of his kingdom and how that wood was used in the temple, in the palace, and in musical instruments.

For today: the best we have, whether little or much, can serve to honor God and bless others. Ask yourself what resource, talent, or time you can put at the service of your church or your community.
exp.8:2:
God tells Solomon that he has heard his prayer and his petition. He says that he has consecrated the temple Solomon built by placing his Name there forever. He also promises that his eyes and his heart will be there at all times, meaning that he will watch over it with care and affection. The word "petition" means a humble request or plea, and "consecrated" means set apart for God.

The LORD speaks, appearing to Solomon a second time, after the temple and the palace were finished. He had earlier appeared to him at Gibeon. This answer follows Solomon's prayer of dedication for the temple. The verses that follow make clear that the promise of an enduring throne depended on Solomon walking faithfully, as David did.

For today: God hears our prayers and cares about us. We can pray with confidence, but we should also answer him with a sincere and obedient heart, because his closeness is a gift that invites us to live faithfully.
exp.5:17:
This verse describes the inside of the temple that Solomon built. The walls were covered with cedar paneling, and that wood was carved with gourds and open flowers. The cedar covered everything inside, so that not a stone could be seen.

This is the account in the book of Kings, which tells in detail how Solomon built the house of God in Jerusalem. The text does not name its author, and we do not know for certain who wrote it. These details highlight the care and beauty with which a place was prepared where Israel would worship God and where the ark of the covenant would stand.

For today: if such care was given in that time to what was offered to God, we too can give Him the best of our time, talents and heart, not just what we have left over.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that Solomon finished building the temple of the Lord, his own palace, and everything else he had set out to do. It is the beginning of a sentence that is completed in the following verse. The reader will see the word "finished" here, so the verse is simply read as "finished" and "the royal palace," with no comment needed on the wording.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings, who is not named; Jewish tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though this is not certain. He tells that after about twenty years of building (according to 1 Kings 9:10), God answers Solomon after his prayer of dedication of the temple. This is the second time God appears to him, the first being at Gibeon.

For today: when we finish an important project, it is a good time to pause and seek God. He listens to us, and He cares not only about what we accomplish, but about keeping our hearts close to Him.

sum.16: Elijah tells King Ahab that there will be no rain, and God takes care of him beside the Brook Cherith, where ravens bring him bread and meat. When the brook dries up, God sends him to a widow in Zarephath, whose flour and oil never run out. Later, God restores the life of her son, showing that his word is true.
sum.20: King Ahab wanted Naboth's vineyard, but Naboth refused to sell the inheritance of his fathers. Then Jezebel had Naboth put to death through false accusations, and Ahab took the vineyard. God sent Elijah to announce punishment to him, but when Ahab humbled himself, God postponed the judgment until the days of his son.
sum.11: Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders and answered the people harshly when they asked him for fairer treatment. Then the kingdom split: Israel followed Jeroboam, and Judah remained with Rehoboam. Jeroboam made golden calves so that the people would not go up to Jerusalem, and in this way he led them into sin.
sum.9: The Queen of Sheba traveled to Jerusalem with gifts to test Solomon with hard questions, and she was amazed at his wisdom and his wealth. She praised Yahweh for having placed him on the throne as king. The chapter shows how Solomon surpassed all the kings in wisdom and riches, and how he accumulated gold, chariots, and horses.
sum.3: Solomon ruled over all of Israel with officials and twelve governors who supplied his household, and the people lived numerous, at peace and secure, each under his own vine and fig tree. God gave him enormous wisdom, greater than that of the wise men of other peoples, and people from many nations came to listen to him.
sum.19: Ben-hadad, king of Syria, lays siege to Samaria and demands everything Ahab has. God gives Israel victory twice, so that they will know that He is the LORD, and that He is also the God of the valleys. Afterward Ahab spares Ben-hadad and makes a treaty with him. A prophet then tells Ahab that, because he let go the man God had condemned, he will pay with his own life and with the lives of his people.
sum.8: When Solomon finishes the temple and his palace, God appears to him again and promises to establish his kingdom if he walks with integrity, as David did. God also warns him that if Israel turns away to other gods, they will lose the land and the temple. The chapter then describes the cities given to Hiram, Solomon's building projects, his forced labor, and his ships.
sum.5: Solomon began building the temple of the LORD in the fourth year of his reign, and he finished it in seven years. He built it with cedar, gold, and beautiful decorations, and inside he placed the Most Holy Place with two large cherubim. God promised him that He would dwell among His people if Solomon obeyed His commands.
sum.6: Solomon took thirteen years to finish his own palace and other buildings made of cedar and carved stone. Then he brought in Hiram, an expert in bronze, who made the two pillars, the great bronze basin set on twelve oxen, ten stands with their basins, and many utensils. Golden articles for the temple were also made, and Solomon stored away what David had dedicated.
sum.0: When King David was very old, his son Adonijah declared himself king on his own. But the prophet Nathan and Bathsheba reminded David of his promise. David had Solomon anointed as king. Adonijah, frightened, took refuge at the altar, and Solomon spared his life on one condition: that he behave himself.
sum.21: Ahab, king of Israel, convinces Jehoshaphat of Judah to attack Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets promise them victory, but Micaiah, the only one who says what God shows him, announces defeat and is thrown into prison. Ahab disguises himself, but an arrow shot at random wounds him, and he dies, just as God had said.
sum.13: Jeroboam sends his wife, disguised, to ask the prophet Ahijah about their sick son, but God reveals the deception and announces judgment because of the king's idolatry. The child dies, and Judah also turns away from God under Rehoboam. God sees the heart and cannot be fooled.
sum.4: Hiram, king of Tyre, congratulates Solomon, and Solomon asks him for cedar wood from Lebanon to build the temple, because God had promised David that his son would build it. Hiram agrees, and Solomon pays him with wheat and olive oil. God gives Solomon wisdom, there is peace between the two kings, and thousands of workers labor on the project.
sum.17: After three years of drought, Elijah challenges the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and asks the people to decide whom they will follow. Only Jehovah answers with fire from heaven, and the people acknowledge that he is God. Then Elijah prays, and the rain returns.
sum.1: As David neared death, he told Solomon to be strong and to keep the commands of God, and he left him instructions concerning Joab, Barzilai, and Shimei. Once he was king, Solomon ordered the execution of Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei, and removed Abiathar from the priesthood. In this way his kingdom was firmly established.
sum.10: Solomon filled his life with foreign wives, and they turned his heart toward other gods, even though God had warned him. Because of this, God decided to take most of the kingdom away from his family and raised up adversaries against him. He promised ten tribes to Jeroboam, but left one tribe to the house of David.
sum.2: At Gibeon, God told Solomon to ask for whatever he wanted. Solomon asked for a wise heart so that he could govern the people, rather than asking for riches or a long life. God granted his request and also gave him wealth and honor. Then, through his judgment in the case of the two mothers, Solomon showed the wisdom of God.
sum.15: God announced through the prophet Jehu that the house of King Baasa would be destroyed because he followed the sin of Jeroboam, and this came to pass when Zimri killed Elah and all his family. Then came a series of coups, Omri took the throne and built Samaria, and his son Ahab, together with Jezebel, promoted the worship of Baal. The chapter shows that God's word is fulfilled and that the sin of leaders drags the people along with them.
sum.18: Elijah flees from Jezebel, exhausted and wishing to die, but God cares for him with food and rest and leads him to Mount Horeb. There God does not reveal himself in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in a gentle whisper. He gives Elijah new tasks, tells him that seven thousand faithful remain, and calls Elisha to be his helper.
sum.7: Solomon gathered Israel together, and the priests carried the ark into the newly built temple, and the cloud of the glory of the LORD filled the house. Solomon blessed the people and prayed, acknowledging that God cannot be contained even by the heavens, and he asked God to listen and to forgive Israel, and also the foreigner who prays toward that place.
sum.12: A man of God from Judah announces judgment against Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, and God confirms his word with signs. But the man of God disobeys by believing the lie of an old prophet, and he dies. The lesson: one must obey God even when another voice sounds convincing, and Jeroboam did not repent.
sum.14: In Judah, King Abijam followed the sins of his father, but God kept the line of David going for David's sake. Then Asa did what was right: he removed idols, though he left the high places standing, and in a war he put his trust in Syria. In Israel, Nadab died and Baasha, who was also evil, took the throne.
